(Forty-six verses.)

His saying: (Makkan). The most accurate of the views on the Makkan and Madinan (classification of surahs) is that whatever was revealed after the Hijrah is Madinan, even if it was revealed in Makkah, and whatever was revealed before the Hijrah, meaning before the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah, is Makkan, even if it was revealed outside Makkah. This is the most accurate definition of Makkan and Madinan that has been stated.

Generally, Makkan verses are characterized by the strength and intensity of their expression and by their brevity, and their subject matter is mostly the foundations of religion and the affirmation of Tawhid (the oneness of God).

As for Madinan verses, the opposite is true: their expression is easier and longer, and their subject matter is mostly the branches of religion, because most people had by then established Tawhid. There are well-known rules and indicators for them in the principles of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis).

Here he says that it is Makkan.

Know that if a surah is Makkan but some of its verses are excepted, for example he says: "Makkan except such-and-such verse," this exception is not accepted from the one who says it without evidence. This is because the basic principle is that a surah is one unit. That is, when a verse was revealed, the Messenger ﷺ would say: "Place it in such-and-such position in such-and-such surah." [Narrated by Abu Dawud (786), al-Tirmidhi (3086), Ahmad in al-Musnad (399), and al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (7953), from the hadith of Uthman.]

So Makkan surahs are Makkan, and nothing is excepted from them, and a Madinan surah is Madinan, and nothing is excepted from it unless there is evidence. Evidence of this kind is not sufficient if a scholar merely says "except such-and-such." It must have a chain of transmission (isnad), because this is a report, and reports must have a chain of transmission until they reach their ultimate source.

As for the author's saying: "It has forty-five or forty-six verses," this does no harm. Differing in the count of verses is not a harmful matter. This is why, in Surah al-Fatihah, as you know, the scholars differed over whether the basmalah is one of its verses or a separate verse, while agreeing that al-Fatihah has seven verses.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾.

The basmalah is a separate verse of the Book of Allah. It is not a follow-on to what precedes it, nor an introduction to what follows it. That is, it is not part of the verse before it nor part of the verse after it. Yet it is recited at the beginning of surahs as a sign of their beginning, except in Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah), because Allah the Exalted did not send down the basmalah in it. Why?

Some scholars say: because it is part of Surah al-Anfal.

Others say: because it was revealed with the sword and with severity against the hypocrites and disbelievers, and beginning it with the basmalah, which is ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾, does not suit this, since the basmalah is blessing and mercy, which does not fit with harshness, sternness, killing and fighting.

But this is not correct. Rather, the closest view is that the Companions were uncertain whether it belonged to al-Anfal or was a separate surah, so they placed a separator but did not write the basmalah. They did not decide either way. We know that Allah did not send it down, because if it had been sent down (between al-Anfal and Bara'ah), its preservation would have been certain, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr 9]. On this basis, the ijtihad (independent reasoning) of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, corresponds exactly to the actual situation.

As for its i'rab (grammatical analysis): it has been mentioned many times before, and we have said that the best grammatical analysis of it is that the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is related to an implied, delayed verb that suits the context.

So if you want to perform wudu' (ablution) and say "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," the implied meaning is: "In the name of Allah I perform ablution."

﴿All praise is due to Allah, Creator of the heavens and the earth﴾ and so on to the end [Fatir: 1]. Know that praise (hamd) is describing the one praised with perfection, together with love and exaltation. This is praise. Allah has praised Himself, glorified be He and exalted, at the beginning and end of matters. At the beginning of cosmic matters He said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Creator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir: 1], and ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1].

At the beginning of legislative matters He said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who sent down to His Servant the Book and has not made therein any deviance﴾ [al-Kahf: 1].

He also praised Himself at the end of matters. Allah the Exalted said at the end of Surah al-Zumar: ﴿And it will be judged between them in truth, and it will be said: "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]. So Allah, glorified be He, praised Himself at the beginning and at the end of the matter, because the command belongs to Allah, glorified be He, at first and at last, and all His command is praiseworthy, because it is based on wisdom and mercy.

Here he says: ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ [Fatir: 1]. ﴿Al-hamd﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿lillah﴾ is its predicate (khabar). The lam here indicates entitlement (istihqaq) and exclusivity (ikhtisas), both together. As for it indicating entitlement: no one is more worthy of praise than Allah the Mighty and Majestic, for He is praiseworthy in every situation, because everything He does and everything He legislates, glorified be He, is praiseworthy for its perfection.

As for it indicating exclusivity: the alif-lam in "al-hamd" here is for totality (istighraq), meaning every praise belongs to Allah and is established for Him. It is well known that no one is exclusively described by this general, all-encompassing attribute except Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because whoever is praised other than Allah is praised only for particular things, and particularity is not comprehensive. But the One who is praised for everything is Allah. By this we know that the lam indicates entitlement and exclusivity together.

He says: ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ [Fatir: 1]. The author said: (He praised Himself with that, as He explained at the beginning of Saba'). At the beginning of Saba' He said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Him is the praise in the Hereafter﴾ [Saba': 1].

But there is praise of Himself for the generality of His dominion, that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and here He praises Himself for the beginning of His creation. He said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Creator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir: 1].

﴿Creator of the heavens and the earth﴾. The author said in his tafsir: (...). Rather, they (the angels) have intellects more distinguished than human intellects, because human intellects may be overcome by desire, so that a person loses his reason.

﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾ [Fatir: 1]: plural of (rasul, messenger). He says: (to the prophets). The correct view is: to the prophets and others. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not neglect﴾ [al-An'am: 61]. The messengers of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, go to this dying person to take his soul. So they are messengers to the prophets and to others. Restricting the verse to the prophets is considered a deficiency in the tafsir.

﴿Possessors of wings﴾ [Fatir: 1]. ﴿Ulي (possessors)﴾ means "owners of," meaning that the angels have wings, which is the plural of (janah, wing). They fly with these wings at a remarkable speed, faster than the jinn. The evidence is that the ifrit (powerful jinn) of the jinn said to Solomon, when he said: ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?﴾ [al-Naml 38]: ﴿An ifrit of the jinn said: "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place"﴾ [al-Naml 38-39].

He had a habit of rising at a specific time, so he said: ﴿before you rise from your place﴾ [al-Naml 39], meaning at the specified time, otherwise the matter would have been vague. ﴿One who had knowledge from the Book said: "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you"﴾ [al-Naml 40], meaning, for example, the glance is the furthest thing; he said it that way: before your glance returns to you, he would bring it to you, and indeed he did; for this reason it says: ﴿So when he saw it settled before him﴾ [al-Naml 40].

The scholars said: the one who had knowledge from the Book knew the Greatest Name of Allah, and he called upon Allah by His Greatest Name, so the angels carried the throne and placed it before Solomon. This shows that the angels are faster than the jinn. There is no doubt that they are faster and stronger. They have wings with which they fly at an extraordinary and tremendous speed.

Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, had six hundred wings, each with tremendous strength in carrying and flying. What then would his speed be? There is no doubt that it is exceedingly extraordinary, because when we see jet airplanes now, the "wings" that carry them, which are the propellers that push air to lift the plane, do not reach this degree, nor a tenth of it, yet they climb with this great speed and this great height. So Jibril, peace be upon him, has six hundred wings that filled the horizon, and this shows you that they have extraordinary and tremendous speed.

These wings: ﴿two, three, or four﴾ [Fatir: 1]. And more, or not? Yes, and more: ﴿He adds to creation what He wills﴾ [Fatir: 1].

His saying ﴿two﴾: its apparent meaning is that this refers to number, not type, because this is the basic meaning. It may also refer to type, because we see, for example, that a bird has two wings, but each feather of these wings has a specific function in adjusting flight. Among them, for example, is what it raises to ascend, lowers to descend, and spreads to settle. This is something observed. For this reason, sometimes certain things are plucked from a wing and then the bird cannot fly, even though what remains in its wing is far more than what was plucked.

So it is possible that His saying ﴿two﴾ means by type, ﴿three and four﴾ [Fatir: 1], and it is possible that it means by number, and that some angels have two wings, some three, and some four. This does not contradict the fact that Jibril, peace be upon him, has six hundred wings, because Allah says: ﴿He adds to creation what He wills﴾ [Fatir: 1], and among what He added is that He gave Jibril six hundred wings.

﴿Possessors of wings﴾ [Fatir: 1]. If you say: Do we know the nature of these wings?

The answer is: No. Do you know?

* Student: In a hadith (...).
* Shaykh: What color are they?
* Student: (...) that each wing has such-and-such of rubies and emeralds; it described the wing of Jibril. And Allah knows whether the hadith is authentic. Here it says such-and-such of rubies and emeralds.
* Shaykh: Yes, God willing, this is verified from the hadith.
* Student: (...) the flower seller.
* Shaykh: Yes, like the flower seller, and all of this (...) never. Withered, dry flowers that never received life at all.

The nature of these wings we do not know. Its counterpart is exactly what has come concerning the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We know the meaning of the attribute, but we do not know its modality (kayfiyyah). Allah has a Face. We know what the meaning of "face" is, but do we know its modality? No. For what is hidden from you is not addressed to you by Allah except with an explanation of its meaning only. As for its modality, you cannot grasp it, because it is unseen and has no equal. A thing is known only by seeing it, or seeing its like, or a true report about it.

He says: ﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾, ﴿two, three, and four﴾. How do we parse ﴿mathna (two)﴾?

* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Attached to the dual.
* Shaykh: Attached to the dual? No.
* Student: An adjective of ﴿wings﴾.
* Shaykh: Complete it. There is a substitute (badal) or an adjective; it is correct to be an adjective. But parse it, the important thing is the parsing... As for its position in i'rab, the matter is permissible in this and that.

﴿mathna﴾ [Fatir: 1] is a substitute (badal) or an adjective of ﴿wings﴾ [Fatir: 1].

* Student: A genitive substitute.
* Shaykh: And the substitute of the genitive is genitive. And the sign of its genitive case is an implied kasrah?
* Student: It is genitive by a fatha, because it is diptote (ghayr munsarif).
* Shaykh: An implied fatha on what? On the alif as a substitute?
* Student: As a substitute for the kasrah.
* Shaykh: And the preventer of declension?
* Student: The descriptive quality and the deviation (adl).
* Shaykh: The descriptiveness and the deviation. And we say the same of ﴿thula-th and rubaa'﴾ [Fatir: 1]; that is why it says ﴿thula-th﴾ and did not say thalathan, and ﴿rubaa'﴾ and did not say rubaa'an or rubaa'in with a kasrah. It did not say thalathan wa rubaa'in.

﴿He adds to creation what He wills﴾ (﴿He adds to creation﴾ among the angels and others).

﴿He adds to creation﴾, whether among the angels or others. ﴿He adds﴾, ﴿what He wills﴾, according to what His wisdom, glorified be He and exalted, requires. For this reason you find that created beings have hands and feet according to their need for them. The children of Adam have feet with which they walk, and hands with which they seize, and they do not walk with their hands, because these hands are the place of taking and giving. Man was honored by having his hands not used for walking. This differs from animals; the hands of animals are used for walking, because they take with their mouths, give with their mouths, and carry with their mouths. Even the cat, when she wants to carry her kittens, does so with her mouth. But the human being is honored, so Allah the Exalted made his hands not used for walking.

So He adds to creation what He wills, according to what wisdom and the need of that creature require. Everything Allah the Mighty and Majestic mentioned that is linked to His will has already been shown to us to be connected with wisdom.

﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ [Fatir: 1]. This is a justification (ta'lil) for His saying: ﴿He adds to creation what He wills﴾. It is as if a questioner asks: Is that difficult for Him? So the answer from this sentence is that it is easy, because Allah is over all things competent.

﴿Over all things competent﴾: every existing thing is capable of being annihilated, and every non-existent thing is capable of being brought into existence.

But if someone asks you: Is He capable of making a moving thing still in a single instant?

* Student: It is not permissible; no text has come with it.
* Shaykh: Is He capable of making a moving thing still in a single instant? It is not about making a moving thing still, meaning making the moving thing come to rest, or making the still thing move, which is clear. But in a single instant?
* Student: He is capable, but (...).
* Shaykh: He is capable?
* Student: ﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shadow?﴾ [al-Furqan 45].
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿and if He willed, He would have made it still﴾. It does not contradict. We say: the moving thing. He is capable of making the moving thing still, but it is not still in the state of its movement, because "a moving thing that is still" is impossible.
* Student: He is capable, but this is not what custom has carried.
* Shaykh: No. The Mighty and Majestic is capable of making the sun rise at twelve o'clock at night, but this is not what custom has carried. However, the word "moving" is the opposite, or contradiction, of "still." If you describe it as moving, it is certainly not still; if you describe it as still, it is certainly not moving. For this reason the scholars said: the impossible is not within the scope of power, because it is impossible, meaning its existence is not possible. It is not that it is not possible in terms of Allah's power, but if Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, wills to make this moving thing moving, it becomes moving and not still. As for it being a moving thing that is still, how can a moving thing be still? The moving is not still.

It is said that Satan used to rejoice at the death of a scholar. When it was said, "So-and-so the scholar has died," he rejoiced, held a celebration, and was pleased. But when it was said, "A worshipper has died," he said: "This is trivial, it doesn't matter, whether he dies or not, do you understand?"

His soldiers said to him: "O our master, why do you rejoice at the death of this scholar with such great joy, while the death of a worshipper does not concern you, even though the worshipper is detached from the world, ascetic in the world, and constant in remembrance and prayer and so on?"

He said: "Yes, because the scholar is more harmful to me than the worshipper." They said: "How?" He said: "I will show you now. Go to the worshipper and say to him: Is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, able to put the heavens and the earth inside an egg? Inside the shell of an egg or not?" They went to the worshipper and said to him: "Is Allah able to put the heavens and the earth inside the shell of an egg?" He said: "This is impossible. The heavens and the earth, despite their vastness, cannot become an egg. My head, if it became an egg, would crack; his head, which is nothing compared to you, this is not valid, this is not possible, and Allah is not capable of this." He said: "Good." Then say to him: "Is Allah able to create the like of Himself? To create the like of Allah?" They went to him and said: "What do you say, is Allah able to create the like of Allah?" He said: "Yes, this is simple. Indeed Allah is over all things competent. Allah is able to create a lord like Him."

So this worshipper disbelieved in both directions: his denial of power in the first was disbelief, and his affirmation of power in the second was disbelief. He said: "Come on, look, go to the scholar, ask him the two questions." They came to the scholar and said: "Is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, able to put the heavens and the earth inside the shell of an egg?"

Shaykh: Yes, he says: "Be, and it is." Either the heavens and the earth become smaller, or the egg becomes larger. The point is that when He wills something, He says, and it is.

He said: Can God create the like of Himself? He said: This is impossible. This is an impossible matter, and likeness cannot ever be exact. Even if there were no great difference except that this is created and that is the One who possesses existence in Himself, this would be impossible. He said: "Yalla, look."

The point is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is capable of all things, but an impossible thing that cannot be conceived is not conceived. What is meant here is not what is impossible by custom. What is impossible by custom, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, can overturn, because Allah is the Creator of custom and is able to change it. This fire that burns became cool and safe for Ibrahim (Abraham). This flowing water became solid like a mighty mountain. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, can change custom with complete ease. But the discussion concerns what is prevented and impossible.

The scholars say: power does not relate to it, because it is impossible. For this reason al-Safarini said in his creed:

*…and He has power, a power that relates to the possible…*

This is a matter agreed upon among the rational.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ [Fatir 1], there is no exception in it. ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾ Al-Jalal (Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti), may Allah have mercy on him, wrote on this verse in Surat al-Ma'idah: "[Reason] excluded His essence, so He is not competent over it." That means: He is competent over all things except His own essence, over which He is not competent. What do you say about this exception? Is it invalid? We say: this is without doubt invalid, because the verse says: ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾, ﴿all things﴾. Your saying that reason excluded His essence so He is not competent over it: we say that reason cannot specify this statement without evidence. If we went about specifying such general statements by reason, we would invalidate much of the indications of the Book and the Sunnah.

What do you mean by your saying: "[Reason] excluded His essence so He is not competent over it"? If you mean that He, glorified and exalted, is not capable of acting upon Himself, meaning that He cannot, for example, make Himself ill or annihilate Himself, glorified and exalted be He, then this is a principle over which power does not relate, because this is one of the impossible matters. If you mean that He is not able to act, and perhaps this is what he intends, that He is not competent to act, because the Ash'aris and those like them deny voluntary acts, then this is false. Rather, reason indicates that He, glorified and exalted, has not ceased and does not cease being truly active in what He wills.

There is an expression that is common among people: "Indeed, Allah is competent over whatever He wills." What do you say about this expression?

* Students: (...)
* Shaykh: (...) We will discuss it. This is not a trivial matter. Commit to a position or withdraw. Why?
* Student: If he said: "Indeed, Allah is competent over whatever He wills," this would give the impression that over what He does not will He is not competent, like the power (...).
* Shaykh: This gives the impression that what He does not will, He is not competent over. That is one point.
* Student: If a person means, "I want this," (...) willing does not necessarily entail affirmation (...) negation. That is, "competent over whatever He wills" does not negate that He is competent over other things.
* Shaykh: That He is incapable.
* Student: That He is incapable over what He does not will. Allah, glorified and exalted, affirmed this for Himself.
* Shaykh: Leave aside that He affirmed it. But is this expression found in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Messenger?
* Student: Yes, it is found.
* Shaykh: Where?
* Student: "Indeed, Allah over whatever He wills..."
* Another student: "Indeed, Allah is effective of what He wills."
* Shaykh: Leave aside ﴿Effective of what He wills﴾.
* Student: It is will and volition.
* Shaykh: Acting is other than power. Is it ﴿And Allah does what He wills﴾? This is in the Qur'an: ﴿And Allah does what He wills﴾ [Ibrahim 27]. But power?
* Student: There is no disagreement about this.
* Shaykh: No, because one who is competent may act or may not act.
* Student: Yes, but it cannot be that He is competent over what He does not will.
* Shaykh: No, in any case your response is not sound, because his saying "over whatever He wills" is also fronted, and fronting indicates restriction. It is fronted before its governing element, and fronting indicates restriction, meaning: over whatever He wills.
* Student: How do you refute this as well?
* Shaykh: By whose language do you refute it?
* Student: The Qur'an.
* Shaykh: Give us some of that, the small amount.
* Student: In this... in a surah...
* Shaykh: You have now, from now until two weeks, to read the Qur'an from beginning to end. If you find that "Allah is competent over whatever He wills," then...
* Student: No, it is not "Indeed, Allah is competent over whatever He wills," but in the same meaning and not in this wording.
* Shaykh: It contradicts nothing, even if in the same meaning. It is as if you want Allah to have said: ﴿And He, over their gathering when He wills, is competent﴾ [Ash-Shura 29]. But here the willing relates not to the power, but to the gathering. That is, when He wills to gather them, He is competent over them. This is in response to those who denied resurrection and said: "How can Allah gather people and resurrect them after they have died?" That is one point.

Second: if you say, "He is competent over whatever He wills," you have opposed the Qur'anic expression in which Allah made it absolute and general: ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ [Fatir 1].

Third: this is taken from the doctrine of the Qadariyyah, because the Qadariyyah say that Allah is not competent over the action of the servant, so it is not included in Allah's power, and if He is not competent over it, He does not will it.

Likewise they say: when the act of the servant is outside His will, He is not competent over it, because Allah is competent only over what He wills.

For this reason we say that this expression is not appropriate, even if its speaker intends a correct meaning. He may intend a correct meaning, as is apparent from the expression of many Muslims today who say this thing. We say that it is more perfect to say: "Indeed, Allah is over all things competent."

If you say: it has been reported in the story of the man whom Allah will be the last to admit into Paradise, and Allah says to him, when he says: "This is for you, and ten times its like," Allah says to him: "Indeed, I am competent over whatever I will"? [Reported by Muslim (187/310) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.] This is a sacred hadith (hadith qudsi).

The answer: this is in a specific case. That is, if something occurs which a person finds strange and considers unlikely, we may say that when Allah, Exalted, wills something, He is competent over it, meaning that He does it, as in His saying: ﴿And Allah does what He wills﴾ [Ibrahim 27]. This differs from bare power unconnected to action, for this is not restricted by will (...).

The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that all the angels are messengers. Is this apparent meaning intended?

You say: it is not intended, based on His saying: ﴿Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind﴾ [Al-Hajj 75].

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir 1].

* In this noble verse: a demonstration of the perfection of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in that He praised Himself with praise, saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ [Fatir 1].
* Also in it: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is merciful to His servants, teaching them how to praise Him, because His saying ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ is a report in form, but its meaning is guidance and instruction, as He said in another verse: ﴿And say: All praise is due to Allah, who has not taken a son, and has no partner in dominion﴾ [Al-Isra 111].

For this reason some scholars held that whenever "al-hamdu lillah" (all praise is due to Allah) occurs, it is with the implied "say" (qul). They even said in His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Al-Fatihah 2], the meaning is: say, "All praise is due to Allah."

But the correct view is otherwise: that this is a report from Allah, and we recite it and praise Allah by it, and there is no need for Allah to command us to do so.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of the name "Allah" for the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. This name is specific to Him and is not said of anyone else, and it is the root of the names. For this reason the names generally come after it as attributes of Him, and do not come before it except rarely, as in His saying: ﴿To the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy, Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ [Ibrahim 1, 2]. Otherwise, the general rule is that the names come following Him. He is the root of the names; for this reason no one else is ever named with it, neither as a proper name nor as an attribute, under any circumstances.

Is it derived or a fixed noun? The correct view, without doubt, is that it is derived, because all the names of Allah, Exalted, are derived, meaning that they indicate the meanings from which they are taken. From what is "Allah" derived?

* Students: From "al-Ilah" (the deity).
* Shaykh: From divinity (uluhiyyah). Derivations are formed from the verbal noun. What is the root of "al-Ilah"? Yes, its root is "al-Ilah," but from where is "al-Ilah" derived? From divinity.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, and no one shares Him in that, because of His saying: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir 1].
* And among them, that is, among the benefits of the noble verse: the perfection of His power and wisdom, in that He began creating these great heavens and this earth in this wondrous order without a prior model to imitate and follow. It is known that the origin of a craft testifies to its maker's expertise and power. That is, whoever brings something new into being, and this new thing becomes perfectly ordered and utterly well-made, is testified to be what? Perfect and expert.

In His being the Originator of the heavens and the earth is evidence of power and wisdom, because He created them without any prior model.

* Among its benefits: that the heavens are multiple. Allah has explained in another verse that they are seven, saying: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 86]. As for the earth, it is mentioned in the singular by way of genus. How many earths are there?
* Student: The number of the earth?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: One.
* Shaykh: Only one?
* Another student: Seven layers.
* Shaykh: How many earths?
* Student: Seven earths.
* Shaykh: Seven earths. What is your evidence from the Qur'an and Sunnah? From the Qur'an?
* Student: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them﴾ [At-Talaq 12].
* Shaykh: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them﴾ [At-Talaq 12]. And from the Sunnah?
* Student: The hadith: "Whoever seizes a span of land unjustly, it will be hung around his neck from seven earths." [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2452) and Muslim (1610/137), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]
* Shaykh: "Whoever seizes a span of land unjustly, it will be hung around his neck from seven earths." May Allah bless you.
* Student: In a third hadith: "The seven heavens and the seven earths."
* Shaykh: I say: there are hadiths in it, this is not a hadith...
* Student: But is there not something more explicit than this?
* Shaykh: No, this is more explicit.
* Student: (...) hang it around his neck.
* Shaykh: From seven earths.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of the angels, based on His saying: ﴿Who made the angels﴾ [Fatir 1].
* And among its benefits: that among the angels are those whom Allah has chosen as messengers to creation, bringing revelation and other than revelation, by revelation and other than it, based on His saying: ﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾ [Fatir 1].
* And among them: that these messengers have wings, wings of many kinds and many individual forms, meaning that they are multiple in quantity and in quality, based on His saying: ﴿Possessors of wings, two, three, or four﴾ [Fatir 1].
* And among them, that is, among the benefits of the verse: it indicates the swiftness of the angels' movement because of the strength of their wings, based on His saying: ﴿Possessors of wings﴾. I say this regarding the strength of their wings because, were it not that these wings have a great distinction that warrants their being specifically mentioned, other things such as heads would have been mentioned. But wings are mentioned because of the strength they have for carrying these angels, and because they are swifter when sent. We have given an example of this indicating that angels are swifter than others in flight, in the story of the throne of Bilqis.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, adds to two, three, and four whatever He wills, based on His saying: ﴿He increases in creation what He wills﴾ [Fatir 1].
* And also among them: that Allah, Exalted, has given preference to some creatures over others, based on His saying: ﴿He increases in creation﴾, and increase is contrasted with decrease.

So there is a distinction among creatures, some over others.

But is the intended meaning strength, or the largeness of the body, or intellect, or knowledge, or nobility of substance?

The answer: it is general, because He said: ﴿He increases in creation what He wills﴾ [Fatir 1]. This one He increases in strength of body, this one He increases in strength of intellect, this one He increases in strength of (...), and this one He increases in knowledge, and so on.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: if you find in yourself a deficiency in your make-up, from whom should you seek it?
* Student: From Allah, glorified and exalted.
* Shaykh: We seek it from whom? From Allah. Because His saying ﴿He increases in creation what He wills﴾ means: do not ask for an increase in form or in character except from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for He is the Giver of what He increases, glorified and exalted.
* Among its benefits: affirmation of will, based on His saying: ﴿what He wills﴾. It has already passed with us that will, in every place where it occurs, is conditioned by what? By wisdom, and we cited as evidence His saying: ﴿And you do not will unless Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan 30].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of general power: ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ [Fatir 1]. He is competent to increase in creation what He wills, and competent to bring into existence and to annihilate.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: a refutation of the Qadariyyah, who claim that the acts of the servant are not created by Allah and are not within His power. From where is this derived? What is the basis for deriving it?
* Student: (...) all this thing is indefinite, "all thing" (...).
* Shaykh: Whenever we need to say it: indefinite, because "all" (kull) is one of the forms of generality, whether indefinite or definite.
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: Correct, based on the generality of His saying: ﴿over all things competent﴾, and the acts of the servant are among things.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 35, verse 2–4 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whatever mercy Allah grants to mankind, none can withhold it, and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him. And He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ He says: ﴿Whatever He grants﴾. ﴿Mā﴾ is a conditional particle that jazms (apocopates) the verb following it, as evidence of this ﴿مَا يَفْتَحِ﴾ (ma yaftaḥi). But the verb after it is before us with a kasra: ﴿مَا يَفْتَحِ اللَّهُ﴾. So we say: this kasra is a passing vowel, for the sake of avoiding the meeting of two sukun (sākinayn). Otherwise the verb is jazm (apocopated). Its original form is (ma yaftaḥ), with the final letter elided and given a kasra because of the meeting of two sukun, like the Exalted's saying ﴿لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ [al-Bayyinah 1], whose original form is lam yakun.

And His saying ﴿مَا يَفْتَحِ اللَّهُ لِلنَّاسِ مِنْ رَحْمَةٍ﴾ [Fatir 2]. Al-fatḥ (opening) of a thing is the removal of the barriers in front of it. For example, "I opened the house," meaning I removed the barrier preventing entry into it, which is the door.

When mercy is opened, a person enters into it and (...) within it.

And His saying ﴿مِنْ رَحْمَةٍ﴾: ﴿مِنْ﴾ explains ﴿مَا﴾, and ﴿مَا﴾ as a conditional particle conveys generality. On this basis, there is generality in the verse: whatever mercy Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, opens for people, no one can withhold it.

And His saying ﴿مِنْ رَحْمَةٍ﴾: the author said: (like provision and rain). This is by way of example, not limitation, because Allah's mercy is more than that. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 53], and ﴿And if you should count the favours of Allah, you could not enumerate them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl 18]. So the mercy of Allah the Mighty and Majestic cannot be counted in its kinds, let alone its individual instances.

And His saying ﴿فَلَا مُمْسِكَ لَهَا﴾ [Fatir 2]: that is, none can withhold it; rather it will reach the one for whom Allah has opened it, and no one can turn it back. As in the authentic hadith that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say after rising from bowing: "O Allah, there is none who can withhold what You give, and none who can give what You withhold, and the might of the mighty will not benefit him against You"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (844) and Muslim (593 / 137), from the hadith of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah.]]. And he would say it also after the prayer. And the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: "Know that if the whole nation gathered to harm you with something, they would not harm you except with something Allah had already written for you"[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2516) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]].

No one can withhold Allah's mercy, whatever he does. Even if envy and slander try, and withholding provision, they cannot. When Allah opens mercy for a servant, no one can come between him and it.

For this reason ﴿لَا مُمْسِكَ لَهَا﴾ came with ﴿لَا﴾ as the negation of the genus, which is the most explicit thing in terms of generality. Therefore the generality of ﴿لَا﴾ of genus negation admits no specification at all.

He said: ﴿فَلَا مُمْسِكَ لَهَا﴾, and here: ﴿مَا يَفْتَحِ اللَّهُ لِلنَّاسِ مِنْ رَحْمَةٍ فَلَا مُمْسِكَ لَهَا﴾ [Fatir 2]. The pronoun in ﴿لَهَا﴾ refers to mercy.

﴿وَمَا يُمْسِكْ فَلَا مُرْسِلَ لَهُ﴾ [Fatir 2]. You may expect the verse to read: "and whatever He withholds, none can send it for her," since the discussion is about mercy, and the first clause said ﴿فَلَا مُمْسِكَ لَهَا﴾, which would imply the second clause should mirror it: "and whatever He withholds, none can release it for her." You would expect this, but the matter is not so, because His saying ﴿وَمَا يُمْسِكْ﴾ is not restricted to mercy, so that we would say the expected form is "none can release it for her." Rather He said ﴿وَمَا يُمْسِكْ﴾ and deleted the complement to convey generality: whatever He withholds of mercy, and whatever He withholds of harm, none can send it to him or convey it to you. Even the harm that Allah withholds, no one can send it to you. Even the mercy that Allah has withheld from you, no one can send it to you. Therefore sometimes a person pursues what he sees as mercy from Allah, such as provision and other things, and then fate comes between him and it. Sometimes a person is exposed to dangers but is spared from them. A car may overturn or crash, and people taller than you and stronger than you die, while you remain.

So: has Allah withheld harm from you or not? Had this withholding not occurred, you would have perished along with those who perished.

So we say: ﴿مَا يُمْسِكْ فَلَا مُرْسِلَ لَهُ﴾, that is, for whatever He withholds. The pronoun in (لا مرسل له) therefore refers to the wording of ﴿مَا﴾.

Is the word ﴿مَا﴾ masculine or feminine? The word ﴿مَا﴾ is masculine, unlike the first clause, which referred to mercy because mercy is feminine.

Now it has become clear to us that the context is at its utmost eloquence, and that we had expected it to say "none can release it for her," but it is not as we expected, why? Because His saying ﴿وَمَا يُمْسِكْ﴾ does not refer only to mercy; rather it is general. Therefore we say that the author's statement (and whatever He withholds of that) is deficient, because his saying (of that) refers to mercy. Rather we say: "and whatever He withholds of that and other than that, ﴿فَلَا مُرْسِلَ لَهُ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ (none can send it after Him)."

As for His saying ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾, the author said: (that is, after its withholding). There is no doubt this is one possibility, and it is possible that the pronoun refers to "withholding" (imsāk), inferred from His saying ﴿يُمْسِكْ﴾.

If it is asked: is there a parallel in which a pronoun refers to a verbal noun understood from the preceding verb? It is known that the referent of a pronoun must be a noun, mentioned before, after, or implied.

The essential point is that the referent of a pronoun is a noun. The noun is either mentioned explicitly, either before or after, or implied, or it is taken from the verbal noun of a preceding verb.

Here, regarding the author's statement ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾, he says: (that is, after its withholding).

We say: where is the word "withholding" (imsāk)? Has it been mentioned? Yes, it has been mentioned, because "yumsik" is a verb derived from what? From "imsāk."

So the verb has included that referent, which is withholding. A parallel is His saying: ﴿اعْدِلُوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَى﴾ [al-Ma'idah 8]: ﴿هُوَ﴾ refers to justice, understood from ﴿اعْدِلُوا﴾ ("be just"), "it is nearer to righteousness."

The second [scholar] says: the basic rule for the referent of a pronoun is that it be an explicitly mentioned noun, earlier, agreeing in gender and number, though it may be delayed, may be implied, or may be understood from a verbal noun of a preceding verb, as in His saying ﴿اعْدِلُوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَى﴾ and as in this verse according to the author's interpretation.

Can the pronoun refer to something other than withholding? Look at the verse: it is Allah, the Exalted, because He said: ﴿مَا يَفْتَحِ اللَّهُ لِلنَّاسِ مِنْ رَحْمَةٍ فَلَا مُمْسِكَ لَهَا وَمَا يُمْسِكْ فَلَا مُرْسِلَ لَهُ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ [Fatir 2], that is: after Allah. This is like His saying: ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god, and Allah has sent him astray knowingly, sealed his hearing and his heart, and placed over his sight a veil? Who then will guide him after Allah?﴾ [al-Jathiyah 23]. The pronoun in ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ refers to Allah, the Exalted, and this is closer, because it is more indicative of the complete disposal in the right of Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

Then He said: ﴿وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ﴾ [Fatir 2]. He [the author] said: (the Mighty, who prevails over His command, the Wise in His action). I think each of you can say that this explanation is deficient, that the author's explanation now is deficient, because his saying (the Mighty who prevails over His command) is one meaning of "al-'Aziz." "Al-'Aziz" has three meanings: honour of rank, dominance, and inaccessibility. Dominance is the meaning of his saying (who prevails over His command).

We say that it includes the one who prevails over His command and cannot be overcome, and this is the Subduer, the one of lofty and high rank. This is the meaning of what we call "honour of rank." "Honour of inaccessibility" means that He is protected from anything harmful, deficient, or defective reaching Him. So "al-'Aziz" has three meanings, not one meaning.

As for ﴿الْحَكِيمُ﴾, the author said: (in His action). This too is deficient, for Allah is wise in His action and His speech, in His decree and His legislation, in everything. Indeed "al-Hakim" has another meaning, because it derives from judgment (hukm) and perfection (ihkam). So He is possessor of judgment and possessor of perfection. Judgment is cosmic (kawni) and legislative (shar'i), and perfection is in the end or in the form in which a thing is. Altogether, these are four types.

But Allah always pairs might with wisdom, because of the completeness of His might (...).

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [Fatir 3]. We say: beginning address with a vocative indicates concern and attention to it, because the vocative includes alerting. Hence when you say to a student, "O boy!", he pays attention. So opening a ruling with a vocative shows care for it, because the vocative conveys alertness.

And His saying ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ﴾: the author said: (the people of Makkah). This is undoubtedly deficient, because "al-nās" (people) is general, and it is obligatory for us, in the Qur'an and Sunnah, to keep the general on its generality until evidence establishes that the specific is intended. Otherwise it must be kept general, because we have no right to alter the meanings of words contrary to their apparent sense, except with evidence from the speaker, or from one who speaks explaining his speech, such as the Messenger ﷺ. So the vocative is general to all people.

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ﴾. ﴿اذْكُرُوا﴾: remembrance here means remembering the blessing in the heart, mentioning it with the tongue, and acting upon it with the limbs. Remembering it in the heart: that a person reflects on where this blessing came from. Who created you? Who supplied you with provision while you were in your mother's womb, not yet having come out? Who prepared you to accept what passes through you, to perceive it, understand it, and carry it out?

The answer: Allah. So if you remember in your heart these matters (and we ask Allah to protect us and you from heedlessness), you will know that whatever blessing you have is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Remembering the blessing in the heart means that a person reflects and says: Who brought me into existence? Who? Answer! Allah. Who supplied me with blessings while I was in my mother's womb, when no one could bring me a morsel of food or a sip of water? It is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Then who prepared me and made me fit to benefit from what is good for me in this world and the Hereafter? Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So blessings are creation, provision, and preparation.

The third part is preparation (i'dād). Creation, provision, and preparation are all from Allah, glorified and exalted be He. This is remembrance with the heart. Remembrance with the tongue is to praise Allah for them: ﴿وَأَمَّا بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ فَحَدِّثْ﴾ [al-Duha 11], so one speaks of blessings not for the sake of boasting, but for the sake of praise.

Remembrance with the limbs is that the effect of this blessing be seen upon him. If the blessing is knowledge, the effect of that knowledge is seen on him through good conduct, dignity, tranquility, good manners, spreading knowledge, and calling to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is an example. If it is wealth, the effect of the blessing is seen on him through spending on what Allah loves: obligatory zakat and obligatory expenditures, recommended charity, fine clothing, and the like. Allah loves that when He bestows a blessing on His servant, the effect of His blessing be seen on him. This remembrance is by what? By the limbs.

So remembrance comprises three things: remembrance with the heart, and then the tongue, and the limbs.

Among remembering the blessing with the limbs is also that one stands in gratitude for it. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has commanded us to remember His blessing for the purpose of: He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you, and be grateful to Me and do not deny Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 152]. The intent is not merely to remember the blessing, but remembrance must be coupled with gratitude: ﴿اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [Fatir 3].

His saying ﴿نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾: ﴿نِعْمَتَ﴾ here is in construct (muḍāf), an indefinite construct, so it includes all blessings, and they are (...). ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُدُّوا نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ لَا تُحْصُوهَا﴾ [Ibrahim 34].

﴿اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ﴾: the author said: (by your settling in the sanctuary and the prevention of raids against you). This explanation is based on the addressees being the people of Makkah. But we say: ﴿اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ refers to the countless blessings, which are very many, as we have already given examples. The blessing is by creation, provision, and preparation, all of which are from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾.

﴿هَلْ مِنْ خَالِقٍ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ [Fatir 3]: that is, once it is established that you remember Allah's blessing upon you, we address you with this question which implies negation: ﴿هَلْ مِنْ خَالِقٍ﴾ (﴿مِنْ﴾ is extra. ﴿خَالِقٍ﴾ is a subject. ﴿غَيْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ in the nominative and genitive is an adjective of ﴿خَالِقٍ﴾ in form and position. The predicate of the subject is ﴿يَرْزُقُكُمْ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ﴾).

First: ﴿هَلْ مِنْ خَالِقٍ﴾: ﴿هَلْ﴾ is an interrogative particle, and ﴿مِنْ﴾ is extra, extra.

How is it "extra, extra"? We have said this: it is extra in wording, extra in meaning, because it conveys emphasis of negation and explicit generality.

﴿هَلْ مِنْ خَالِقٍ﴾: ﴿خَالِقٍ﴾ is therefore a subject, nominative with an understood dammah, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the place by the kasra of the extra preposition.

﴿غَيْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ has two readings, ﴿غَيْرُ﴾ and ﴿غَيْرِ﴾, and both are correct.

On the reading with the genitive, ﴿غَيْرِ اللَّهِ﴾, it is an adjective following the wording of ﴿خَالِقٍ﴾, which is genitive.

On the reading with the nominative, it is an adjective following the position of ﴿خَالِقٍ﴾, since its position is nominative as a subject.

Therefore the author said: (in the nominative and genitive an adjective of "khāliq" in form and position). In the author's statement there is a disordered laff wa-nashr (chiasmus). This will be made clear in the author's statement, a disordered laff wa-nashr.

* A student: (...) it is in every case, the laff wa-nashr (...) is that it precedes.
* The Shaykh: I do not want you to define it for me, I know it.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Who knows (...)?
* The student: Because he said: in the genitive.
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: He said: an adjective of ﴿خَالِقٍ﴾.
* The Shaykh: After ﴿غَيْرُ اللَّهِ﴾, what does he say?
* Student: (nominative and genitive) (...)
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: Since he mentioned the nominative and genitive after it, he put the genitive first, he said (...).
* The Shaykh: And this genitive? Its position is for the nominative. No, this is a disordered laff wa-nashr.
* Student: Not in order.
* The Shaykh: We say "not in order" when it is in the Qur'an or the hadith; but in human speech we say "disordered." Let it be disordered.

(In the nominative and genitive an adjective of ﴿خَالِقٍ﴾). Had it been in order, he would have said: an adjective of ﴿خَالِقٍ﴾ in position and in form, because in the nominative it is an adjective of position, and in the genitive an adjective of form.

In any case, ﴿غَيْرُ اللَّهِ﴾ has two readings, and each has its basis in Arabic.

As for His saying ﴿يَرْزُقُكُمْ﴾, the author says: (the predicate of the subject). Is the verb itself the predicate of the subject, or the clause?

* The students: The clause.
* The Shaykh: The clause. But in parsing they are lenient.

For example, if you say, "So-and-so is in the mosque," you say "in the mosque" is a prepositional phrase as the predicate of the subject.

﴿هَلْ مِنْ خَالِقٍ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ يَرْزُقُكُمْ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾ [Fatir 3]: he says ﴿يَرْزُقُكُمْ﴾ is the predicate of the subject, even though it is a clause.

The Exalted said: ﴿هَلْ مِنْ خَالِقٍ﴾ is an interrogative with the meaning of negation. We have mentioned earlier that when an interrogative carries the meaning of negation, it is infused with the meaning of challenge. If he had said, "No creator other than Allah provides for you," the sentence would be correct, but when he said ﴿هَلْ مِنْ خَالِقٍ﴾ it became more eloquent, because it includes negation and challenge, as if he were saying: show me a creator other than Allah who provides for you from heaven and earth, as He said in another verse: ﴿Show Me what they have created from the earth﴾ [Fatir 40].

He says: ﴿هَلْ مِنْ خَالِقٍ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ﴾. ﴿خَالِقٍ﴾: creation (khalq) in the language means measuring, and from it is the poet's saying:

"And you measure what you have made, while some people create and do not measure."

(تفري ما خلقت) means "what you measured"; but it is also applied to creation preceded by measurement. So here ﴿خَالِقٍ﴾ means what?

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it means "one who brings into existence with prior measurement."

﴿هَلْ مِنْ خَالِقٍ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ يَرْزُقُكُمْ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 35, verses 2–4 (part 2 of 3):

The answer is no. There is no creator other than Allah who provides for us from the heaven and the earth. We have already raised an objection to the denial of creation from anything other than Allah. We said that texts indicate that other than Allah does create, and how did we answer that? We said that the creation of other than Allah is not bringing into existence (*ijad*), but rather transforming something from one form into another, and also that it is not general.

The third point: the creation of other than Allah is in reality part of Allah's creation, as in ﴿Allah created you and what you do﴾ [al-Saffat 96]. Until (...) when you create this thing, meaning you bring it into being in the sense of changing it from one state into another, then your action is itself created by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Therefore we say: the true Creator is Allah.

His saying ﴿yarzuqukum﴾ ("provides for you") means "gives you," because *rizq* means giving, as in His saying: ﴿so provide for them from it﴾ [al-Nisa 8].

His saying ﴿min al-sama'﴾ ("from the heaven"): the author (al-Mu'allif) explained the provision from the heaven as rain. There is no doubt that this is included, since rain is provision that descends from the heaven. Is there any other provision that descends from the heaven?

*Student:* Revelation.

*Shaykh:* Yes, revelation, though it is not what we are discussing here, and that is a different matter.

*Student:* Manna and quail (*al-Mann wa al-Salwa*).

*Shaykh:* Manna and quail. What are manna and quail?

*Student:* (...) They were sent down to the Children of Israel.

*Shaykh:* To the Children of Israel. Why don't we say birds in general, for example? ﴿Have they not seen the birds subjected in the atmosphere of the sky?﴾ [al-Nahl 79]. They descend from the sky and are also provision for the servants.

*Student:* And from the earth.

*Shaykh:* And from the earth. They come from the earth and from the sky.

Can we say that dew is part of the provision? (...) Moisture comes from the sky too, and it is provision, because it benefits trees.

As for His saying ﴿min al-sama'﴾ and ﴿wa﴾ "(from) ﴿al-ard﴾": the author estimated the particle *min* (from) before "the earth," to indicate that "the earth" is conjoined to "the heaven." Plants are correct, right?

*Student:* (...).

*Shaykh:* Correct, but it is incomplete, because provision from the earth is more than plants. There are plants, minerals, waters, and other things. Much comes from the earth.

His saying: (And the interrogative is for affirmation, meaning there is no creator who provides other than Him.)

His saying "(for affirmation)" and then "(meaning there is no creator)" is something like a contradiction, because his saying "there is no creator" requires that its meaning be negation, and it is so. It is a negation carrying a challenge, and that there is no creator except Allah. If there is no creator except Allah, glory be to Him and exalted is He, then what is obligatory? That we worship Allah alone, or not?

Listen. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿There is no god but He﴾, meaning there is no true object of worship except Him. How can you know that there is no provider who provides for us from the heaven and the earth except Allah, and then go and worship other than Him? Is this not only a deficiency in conception, and a deficiency in intellect and conduct as well? A deficiency in conception, intellect, and conduct. Is that not so? If there is no provider except Allah, how do you worship al-Lat, al-'Uzza, Manat, Hubal, trees, stones, the sun, the moon, and cattle too? There are people who worship cattle. It is said that there are people in India who worship cows, and that if a cow crosses the railway track, the train must stop even if everyone in it is crushed. Of course, the train moves quickly, and if it stops, the carriages collide, and those in them die and are crushed. They say: it must be so, because this is a god, and a god cannot be run over.

*Student:* (...) She enters the shop and eats.

*Shaykh:* And eats whatever she wants and leaves whatever she wants. The point is: are these minds? They are not minds. In the pre-Islamic period they made a god from dates, and when they were hungry they ate it. They ate their god.

If Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is the sole provider by your acknowledgment and confession, then He must be the sole object of worship, because of His saying: ﴿There is no god but He﴾. The grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of this great sentence, by which a person enters Islam or leaves it, is this: a person enters if he affirms it, and leaves if he denies it.

Its grammatical analysis: scholars of grammar have six opinions regarding it, and some scholars wrote a treatise on it. But the best thing said about its analysis is that ﴿la﴾ (no) is a negation of the genus, and ﴿ilaha﴾ (god) is its noun, and its predicate is omitted, its estimated form being *haqq* (true), so: "no god [is] true." ﴿Illa﴾ (except) is a particle of exception, and ﴿Allah﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for the omitted predicate.

Does the negation here apply to existence, or to existence in truth? It applies to existence in truth, because there are gods other than Allah that are worshipped, but not in truth. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ [al-Qasas 88], and He said: ﴿So their gods, whom they invoked besides Allah, did not avail them anything﴾ [Hud 101]. So the gods exist, but they do not deserve to be gods, because they have no lordship.

﴿Fa-anna tu'fakun﴾ [Fatir 3] ("then how are you turned away?") (From where are you turned away from His monotheism, while acknowledging that He is the Creator?) If the author had said: "from His worship," it would have been better, because "There is no god but He" is monotheism of lordship or monotheism of worship? 

*Students:* Worship.

*Shaykh:* Worship. The word "monotheism" (*tawhid*) includes lordship too. If he had said: "Then how are you turned away from worshipping Him alone, while acknowledging that He alone is the Creator," it would have been better.

As for His saying ﴿tu'fakun﴾ [Fatir 3], he said: "(meaning you are turned away)." *Ifk* means turning away. Its past tense is *afaka*, and its present is *ya'fiku ifkan*, not *ifkan* (with a kasra). *Ifk* with a kasra means lying. In reality, lying agrees with *afk* in meaning, because lying is reporting contrary to reality, so it is turning a thing away from its reality. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾ [al-Dhariyat 9], meaning: turned away from it is whoever has been turned away.

So: ﴿tu'fakun﴾ means you are turned away from worshipping Him alone, while acknowledging that He alone is the Creator.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿fa-anna tu'fakun﴾ is for rebuke and reproach. That is, how do you acknowledge that He alone is the Creator, and then worship others along with Him?

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if they deny you﴾ [Fatir 4] (O Muhammad, in your bringing monotheism, resurrection, reckoning, and punishment) ﴿then messengers before you were denied﴾.

He said: ﴿wa in yukadhdhibukum﴾. ﴿In﴾ here is conditional. What is the condition verb? ﴿yukadhdhibuka﴾. And its answer? ﴿faqad kudhdhibat﴾, and it is connected with *fa* because it begins with *qad*.

﴿In yukadhdhibuka﴾ means: they attribute lying to you, saying: you are a liar, you are not a messenger of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, rather you are a magician, a madman, a soothsayer, a poet, and similar things. Some of them say: there is no resurrection, no recompense, no reckoning, and no punishment.

If they deny you, this is not something new among the children of Adam, and it is not strange from the conduct of the children of Adam. ﴿Then messengers before you were denied﴾ [Fatir 4]. Who denied them? Their peoples denied them, until the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I saw a prophet with a group, a prophet with a man or two men, and a prophet with no one with him."[1]

Noah, peace be upon him, remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty years, calling them secretly and openly, with rebuke, warning, and promise, and yet only a few believed with him.

His saying ﴿rusul﴾ ("messengers"): the indefiniteness here is for multiplicity and magnification, meaning many messengers and also great messengers. ﴿Kudhdhibat﴾: Noah was denied, Abraham was denied, Moses was denied, Aaron was denied, Jesus was denied. These are the messengers of firm resolve (*ulu al-'azm*), and the best of messengers were denied. So your being denied is not new.

This is meant for two things. The first is consoling the Prophet ﷺ. When a person knows that others were afflicted with a similar calamity, he is consoled by it. If someone is hit by an accident, and then we see accidents, one whose arm is broken, one whose finger is broken, one whose thigh is broken, and one whose spine is broken, and the one whose finger is broken starts crying out and complaining, we say to him: so-and-so's spine is broken, what then? The pain becomes lighter for him and he forgets it, because the soul's consolation by others has a great effect. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged, that you will be sharing in the punishment﴾ [al-Zukhruf 39]. So your sharing in the punishment will not lessen it for you, as is the case with people in this world. And al-Khansa' lamented her brother Sakhr. What did she say?

She said:
"Were it not for the abundance of those weeping around me
over their brothers, I would have killed myself.
They do not weep like my brother, but
I console my soul about him through consolation."

Notice how she says: "I console my soul about him through consolation." I say: this one's brother died, and that one's brother died, and that one's brother died, so you and others are equal.

﴿Then messengers before you were denied, and to Allah are returned all matters﴾ [Fatir 4]. In His saying ﴿ila Allah turja'u al-umur﴾, the prepositional phrase is connected to ﴿turja'u﴾ and is placed first to indicate restriction, because matters are returned to Allah and to no other.

It may also be said that it is placed first for a verbal benefit, which is observing the rhyme (*fawasil*).

The author said: ﴿turja'u al-umur﴾ (in the Hereafter, so He will recompense the deniers and grant victory to the messengers). This is also a deficiency, because ﴿turja'u al-umur﴾ applies in the Hereafter and in this world too. Allah grants victory to the messengers in this world and punishes the deniers: ﴿Indeed, We will support Our messengers and those who believed in the life of this world and on the day when the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghafir 51].

So: ﴿turja'u al-umur﴾ [Fatir 4] is general: matters of this world and the Hereafter, matters of the Sharia, and matters of destiny. All matters are returned to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He is the First and the Last; from Him is the beginning, and to Him is the end. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command﴾ [al-A'raf 54]. Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Whoever has something, let him bring it," because Allah says: ﴿Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command.﴾ What remains? If creation, which is bringing into being, belongs to Allah, and command, which is in disposal, and disposal belongs to Allah, what remains for us? Nothing remains. For this reason nothing belongs to anyone from anyone else, ever. All matters belong to Allah.

Here "matters" (*al-umur*) is the plural of *amr*. What is the meaning of *amr* here? Is it a request for an action in the manner of superiority?

*Student:* Affairs.

*Shaykh:* "Matters" in the sense of affairs. The *amr* that means a request for an action in the manner of superiority has the plural *awamir*, not *umur*. So "matters" here is the plural of *amr* in the sense of *sha'n* (affair). That is, the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, and the affairs of destiny and the Sharia, all return to Allah, glory be to Him and exalted is He.

Since they return to Allah, and the messengers were denied, what is the fate of the messengers and of the deniers? The fate of the messengers is victory in this world and the Hereafter. The fate of the deniers is abandonment, disgrace, and shame in this world and in the Hereafter. And Allah knows best (...).

﴿O mankind, remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾ [Fatir 3].

* From this noble verse benefits are derived, among them: the obligation to remember Allah's favor in the three places we pointed out earlier: the heart, the tongue, and the limbs.

* Also derived from it: the importance of remembering the favor, because it begins with what? With ﴿O mankind﴾ [Fatir 3]. This indicates importance, because what begins with a call means alerting the addressee to listen.

* Also derived from this verse: the disbelievers are addressed by the laws. From where is this taken? "Mankind" (﴿ya ayyuha al-nas﴾). Just as it is obligatory for a Muslim to remember Allah's favor, it is obligatory for a disbeliever too to remember Allah's favor. Accordingly, he will be punished in the Hereafter for not remembering the favor, and perhaps he will be punished for it in this world too.

* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: showing Allah's grace upon His servants with favors. ﴿Remember the favor of Allah﴾ [Fatir 3]: not one favor only, but it is a genus, so it includes all that Allah has bestowed upon us of the favors of religion and worldly life, whether in the body, the intellect, honor, or wealth.

* Also among its benefits: there is no creator except Allah, based on what?

*Student:* There is no creator except Allah.

*Shaykh:* Yes. Based on what?

*Student:* Because He created us.

*Shaykh:* From the verse here? We are now discussing the benefits of the verse, so we want to derive the benefit from every word or every sentence.

*Student:* His saying, glory be to Him and exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, remember the favor of Allah upon you. Is there any creator other than Allah﴾ [Fatir 3].

*Shaykh:* In which word? Specify the place of the benefit for me.

*Student:* ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah﴾.

*Shaykh:* ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah﴾, yes. What is the indication that there is no creator other than Allah?

*Student:* It is that He is the one who provides for us.

*Shaykh:* No. The indication is from the form of the wording ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah﴾.

*Student:* They acknowledged it.

*Another student:* Here the interrogative means negation.

*Shaykh:* Correct. The interrogative with the meaning of negation, as if He said: there is no creator except Allah.

* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: provision comes to a person from above and from below. From where is this taken?

*Student:* ﴿From the heaven and the earth﴾ [Fatir 3].

*Shaykh:* ﴿From the heaven and the earth﴾, like that? As Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿They would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-Ma'idah 66].

* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: showing that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has the bringing into being (*ijad*), the preparation (*i'dad*), and the provision (*imdad*). From where is this taken?

*Student:* ﴿He provides for you from the heaven﴾ [Fatir 3].

*Shaykh:* Yes, this contains provision (*imdad*), because provision is a supply to a person.

*Student:* ﴿There is no creator other than Allah﴾ [Fatir 3].

*Shaykh:* That is bringing into being (*ijad*). The third?

*Student:* (...).

*Shaykh:* How is that? That Allah prepared for us the acceptance of truth, or not? If Allah prepared you for this acceptance, and for inferring from the evidences their indications, then how are you turned away from them?

* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: that acknowledging the monotheism of lordship necessitates acknowledging the monotheism of worship. From where is this taken?

*Student:* ﴿Is there any creator other than Allah﴾ (...).

*Shaykh:* How is that?

*Student:* (...) There is no creator other than Allah (...) His worship.

*Shaykh:* (...) That is, that He alone is the Creator, so He alone must be the one worshipped. For this reason we say: the monotheism of worship (*tawhid al-uluhiyya*) includes the monotheism of lordship (*tawhid al-rububiyya*) and of names and attributes. It includes them; that is, none is worshipped except one who is known to be the Lord, the Creator, perfect in His attributes. And the monotheism of lordship necessitates the monotheism of worship and the monotheism of names and attributes.

* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: the falsity of the divinity of anything other than Allah. ﴿There is no god but He﴾. How do you reconcile this negation with the affirmation of gods for other than Allah in His saying: ﴿So their gods did not avail them﴾ [Hud 101]?

*Student:* (...).

*Shaykh:* That true divinity belongs only to Allah. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾ [al-Hajj 62].

* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: the foolishness of those people who worship other than Allah along with Him while acknowledging that He is the Creator and Provider. From where is this taken?

*Student:* ﴿Then how are you turned away﴾ [Fatir 3].

*Shaykh:* From His saying ﴿Then how are you turned away﴾, because the interrogative here means denunciation and rebuke.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if they deny you, then messengers before you were denied﴾, to the end [Fatir 4].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the denial of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is not something new. The messengers were denied before him, and this is clear from the wording.

* Among its benefits: Allah's, the Mighty and Majestic, care for His Messenger ﷺ. From where is this taken?

*Student:* (...).

*Shaykh:* Is it taken from the fact that Allah, glory be to Him and exalted is He, consoled [him]?

*Student:* His messenger (...).

*Shaykh:* By mentioning those who denied before.

We said: * Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the laws of Allah the Exalted regarding His creation are manifest. How?

*Student:* ﴿And if they deny you, then [messengers] were denied﴾ [Fatir 4]. If you were denied, then the messengers were denied. They denied the messengers just as the Prophet ﷺ was denied. This is, I mean, the sunnah.

*Shaykh:* Because denial is an act of the unseen? Is it not an act of Allah?
