He mentioned the righteous and lengthened the mention of the bliss they have, because He mentioned a number of their deeds: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor, a spring from which the servants of Allah will drink﴾ [Al-Insan 5–6]. Look: the righteous are the servants of Allah. ﴿They fulfil vows and fear a Day whose evil is widespread, and they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive, (saying): "We feed you only for the countenance of Allah"﴾ [Al-Insan 7–9]: complete sincerity. ﴿We wish from you no reward or gratitude. Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day austere and distressing﴾ [Al-Insan 9–10]. Yes, the repetition of these qualities among their qualities, and since He lengthened the mention of their deeds, He lengthened the mention of their recompense, unlike the disbelievers. This is without doubt from the eloquence of the Qur'an.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: rewards differ, from His saying: ﴿and a great reward﴾. They differ according to what? They differ according to the deed, they differ according to the doer, and if the deed is transitive, they differ according to the one who benefits from it. For example, they differ according to the deed: "The best of deeds is the prayer at its appointed time" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (527), Muslim (85/139), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud]. Obligatory acts are better than recommended ones. According to the doer: there has passed with us: "The best charity is that which is given from surplus wealth" [Narrated by al-Bukhari (1426), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not insult my companions. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if any of you were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, it would not reach a mudd of one of them nor half of it" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3673), Muslim (2541/222), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id]. This is according to what?

* Student: The doer.

* Shaykh: According to the doer. They also differ according to the place, if the deed is transitive: charity to a relative is both charity and maintaining kinship, and charity to one who is in greater need is better than charity to one who is less in need, and so on. The difference in deeds necessitates a difference in rewards as well. They also differ (...) according to sincerity.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: According to sincerity: meaning that the more sincere a person is in his deed, the better his deed is. Or not? We can also say: they differ according to conformity to the Sunna, and the more a person's conformity is to Allah (...), the more complete it is. In any case, these differences, in their existence, make rewards differ.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him and he sees it as good...﴾ [Fatir 8].

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: (...) ﴿Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾. You will find that this verse, ﴿He sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾, that this will is according to wisdom. Whoever Allah's wisdom requires that He send astray, He sends astray, and this is the one who does not want good, by His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [As-Saff 5]. And His saying: ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾ [Fatir 8] refers to the guidance of success (tawfiq). Perhaps we could say: the guidance of success and guidance by indication, but the more important is the guidance of success, and perhaps this is what is meant here, because those whom Allah has sent astray, Allah has guided them with the guidance of indication. Then the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah invites to the Abode of Peace﴾ [Yunus 25], and this is general, but as for guidance, He said: ﴿and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus 25]. So not every one invited is guided.

His saying: ﴿So do not let yourself go in pursuit of them, [wasting yourself] in regret﴾ [Fatir 8]. Is this a prohibition concerning what has occurred or concerning what has not occurred? The apparent meaning is that it is a prohibition concerning what has occurred: the Messenger (ﷺ) used to grieve over these deniers who were denying him. A prohibition against a thing may be a prohibition against what has occurred and may be a prohibition against what has not occurred. His saying to the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿So do not invoke with Allah another deity, lest you be among those punished. And warn your closest kindred﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 213–214]. This is a prohibition concerning what?

* Student: What has not occurred.

* Shaykh: Concerning what has not occurred? Or what has occurred?

* Students: (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿So do not invoke with Allah another deity, lest you be among those punished. And warn your closest kindred﴾.

* Students: Concerning what has not occurred.

* Shaykh: Concerning what has not occurred, correct, because the Messenger did not do it. Right? ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [An-Nisa' 29]?

* Student: Concerning what has not occurred.

* Shaykh: Or concerning what has occurred?

* Student: Concerning what has occurred.

* Another student: Concerning what has not occurred.

* Shaykh: Does (...) in himself (...)?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Meaning (...).

* Student: In relation to (...).

* Shaykh: (...) "Do not kill yourselves." Is the meaning: that none of you kills another? This is correct. It is a prohibition concerning what has not occurred and what has occurred. But if it is a prohibition that a person kill himself, this certainly has not occurred, since it is not possible for him to kill himself except while he exists.

* Student: If he commits suicide, does he not kill himself, O Shaykh?

* Shaykh: Yes, but you do not say "do not kill yourself" [in that case]...

* Student: While he is alive?

* Shaykh: Yes, before he dies. As for after (...), it is not possible. So then, do we say this is a prohibition concerning what has not...?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Subhan Allah, (...) has occurred.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: The Messenger (ﷺ) used to grieve over the loss of (...), and the evidence (...): ﴿Perhaps you would leave out some of what is revealed to you and your breast is constrained by it because they say, "Why has a treasure not been sent down to him or an angel not come with him?"﴾ [Hud 12]. And the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 3]; that is, destroy yourself.

So the Messenger (ﷺ) grieved over these people because of their not believing. Here He says: ﴿So do not let yourself go in pursuit of them [wasting yourself] in regret﴾, meaning: do not let yourself perish on their account. Yes, as one says: "I wept for you through the ages," meaning: on your account. So the meaning is: do not let yourself perish on their account in regret.

His saying: ﴿ḥasarāt﴾ (regrets). It has been said that it is a state (ḥāl), being a verbal noun used in the sense of the active participle, i.e., "regretful." Regret (ḥasra) is intense distress and grief over what has been lost. Whoever loses something he loves and seeks grieves and is distressed over it, so it is said: "he regretted (taḥassara)." It has also been said that ḥasarāt is a verbal noun (...) and is an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlih). The meaning: "Do not let yourself go," i.e., do not perish for the sake of regrets over them.

The author said: (﴿So do not let yourself go in pursuit of them﴾, i.e., of those who adorned their evil for them, ﴿[wasting yourself] in regret﴾ by your grief that they do not believe. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾ [Fatir 8], so He will recompense them for it).

In this sentence there is both a threat and consolation: a threat to these opponents, and consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: do not (...), for their reckoning is with Allah and He will recompense them.

The Exalted said: ﴿So do not let yourself go in pursuit of them [wasting yourself] in regret﴾, or from its beginning, I think, meaning from the beginning of the verse.

The Exalted said: ﴿So is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him and he sees it as good...﴾ to the end.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: some people's hearts become so blind that they see an evil deed as good, and conversely see good as evil, by His saying: ﴿So is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him and he sees it as good?﴾

* Among its benefits: the vagueness of the agent, so as to include everything that may proceed from him this act, by His saying: ﴿whose evil deed has been made attractive to him﴾. It has already passed with us that the one who makes it attractive is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in origin, and the devils in direct action.

* Among its benefits: the division of deeds into evil and righteous, by His saying: ﴿his evil deed﴾.

* Among its benefits: a refutation of the Jabriyya (determinists), by His saying: ﴿his evil deed﴾, where He attributed the deed to him. They say that deeds are not attributed to the human being, because he is compelled to them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that whoever is in this state is not equal to one who is not, in that he sees evil as evil and good as good. We derive this from the fact that the omitted element is the counterpart of what is mentioned, because the interrogative particle here is for equalizing: "Are these two equal?" The answer: they are not equal.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that guidance and misguidance are in the hand of Allah, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾.

* Among its benefits, and it branches from this benefit: when we know this, we ask Allah for guidance, and we seek refuge in Allah from misguidance. We seek refuge in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from misguidance, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿whom He wills﴾. But it has passed with us that every act that Allah ties to His will is connected with wisdom. The proof of this is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan 30].

* Among its benefits: a refutation of the Qadariyya, by His saying: ﴿He sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾. The Qadariyya say that the acts of the servant, whether misguidance or guidance, are not connected to the will of Allah, because their doctrine (the Qadariyya's) is that the human being is independent in his deeds, with no connection of Allah to them at all. Even their extremists claim that Allah does not know the servant's deed until it occurs, and they say: the matter is "unprecedented" (unuf), i.e., newly begun: Allah's knowledge comes into being after it was not.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Mighty One who sent him, grieved a great grief, such that his soul nearly perished from its intensity, by His saying: ﴿So do not let yourself go in pursuit of them [wasting yourself] in regret﴾. The reason is that the basic meaning of a prohibition is that it concerns what has occurred, though it may concern what has not occurred, and this is also common. The fact that this is something that has occurred is shown by the Exalted's saying: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 3].

* Among its benefits: the compassion of the Prophet (ﷺ) for his community.

* Among its benefits as well: the Messenger (ﷺ) does not grieve over their not believing or obeying for his own benefit, but for their benefit, by His saying: ﴿So do not let yourself go in pursuit of them [wasting yourself] in regret﴾.

* Among them: the Prophet (ﷺ) is a human being, who is affected by what affects human beings of causes of joy and causes of sorrow. This is an actual matter. "The Prophet (ﷺ) once entered upon 'A'isha, radiant, with the lines of his face shining. She asked him about that, and he said: 'Have you not seen that Mujazziz al-Mudlaji entered upon Usama ibn Zayd and Zayd ibn Haritha while they were covered with a cloak, their feet showing, and he said: "Indeed, these feet are part of one another"?'" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3731), Muslim (1459/39), from the hadith of 'A'isha]. The Prophet (ﷺ) rejoiced until it showed on his face. So human attributes befall the Prophet (ﷺ) as they befall other human beings: joy, sorrow, grief, delight, forgetfulness, lack of knowledge, and other things, because he is distinguished from human beings by only one thing, which is revelation. The Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Say, "I am only a human being like you"﴾ [Al-Kahf 110]. Look: ﴿a human being﴾ is sufficient without ﴿like you﴾, but this is for emphasis, lest someone think that he is a human being who has been singled out in something, so He said: ﴿a human being like you﴾. Then He mentioned the distinction: ﴿It is revealed to me that your God is but one God﴾ [Al-Kahf 110]. In this there is a clear refutation of those people who claim that the Prophet (ﷺ) has an influence on creation like the lordship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For if that were so, his soul would not have perished in grief over them, for he would have guided them, and would have been spared these regrets that befall his soul.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, of everything we do, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾ [Fatir 8].

Among its benefits: God's care for His Messenger ﷺ in this sentence, which conveys consoling him and making the matter easier for him, and that the reckoning of these people is in no way upon him, just as his reckoning is in no way upon them.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 35, verses 5–8 (part 1 of 4):**

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true﴾ [Fatir 35:5]. The address is directed to all of mankind, every person, believer and disbeliever alike. He said: ﴿indeed the promise of Allah﴾. The author said: (with the resurrection and other things). He spoke truly. Everything that Allah has promised is true, whether it is the resurrection, the punishment, the reward, the victory, the abandonment, or anything else that Allah has promised.

﴿true (ḥaqq)﴾: both words mean truthful and established. Thus, considered as a report, it is truthful and it will occur; and considered in terms of its occurrence, it is established.

* Student: It is non-existent.
* The Shaykh: No, what is non-existent? It is established. Considered in terms of its occurrence, it is established without doubt. So "ḥaqq" here means truthful in terms of the report about it, and realized in terms of its being established, and that it is a matter that will certainly come to pass. The promise of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is not like the promise of anyone else; it has...

The prohibition here is emphasized with the nun: ﴿so let not the worldly life deceive you﴾ [Fatir 35:5]. This is an emphasis (...). ﴿So let it not deceive you﴾, that is, let it not delude you. This follows from what precedes it, because a person whom worldly life deceives will have weak faith in the promise of Allah the Exalted, since the world distracts him and deceives him until he is swept away after it.

As for His saying ﴿the worldly life﴾: there is no doubt that what is in it now is life, and its opposite is death. And "dunyā" (worldly) is an elative (ism al-tafḍīl, comparative/superlative form). What is its masculine form?

* Student: Dunī.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Students: Adnā.
* The Shaykh: Adnā, like ʿulyā and aʿlā. It is called "dunyā" for two reasons. The first: it comes before the Hereafter, so it is nearer to people than the Hereafter. For this reason it is called the first life. It is also called "dunyā" from the nearness of its rank, for it is "dāniyah," meaning near, because it is the first; and it is near in the sense of nearness of rank. For whatever blessings it contains, if they are granted, they are subject to a future disturbance or a present disturbance. Present disturbance? Present disturbance, because the very blessing you enjoy in this world must be mixed with turbidity, as the poet said:

*One day for us and one day against us,*
*one day we are grieved and one day we are made joyful.*

If you reflect on this, you will find it so. Every day of the week, look at yourself. One day you are content, at ease and happy; one day you are sorrowful; and one day external things come to you that make you happy, and another day the reverse. Then, even if it is supposed that its pure part is free of this, meaning it is not mixed with harm, the future will still spoil that purity for you, as the poet said:

*There is no pleasure in life while it is spoiled,*
*its delights reminded of death and old age.*

So one of two things is inevitable: either a swift death or a decrepit old age. When a person grows old, if Allah has extended his life, he returns to his former state: ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most decrepit age﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:70]. He returns to his former state, his discernment falls away, and he becomes worse than a child. That is, his being a burden on others is worse than a child's being a burden on others, because a child has no reason and discernment, and at most he cries. Yes, you soothe him with something to play with and he becomes quiet. But this old man still has some discernment; you find him shouting at his family, for example, shouting at them, raising his voice, and saying: "How do you forget my need? (...) I was young, and I commanded you, and I brought you food and drink, and today you forget (...) more." Yes.

Then he is also heavy. You can carry a child on your arm and walk with him left and right until he is quiet, but this is a problem. Therefore, if a person remembers that he will either die or reach this state, then whatever his life is, it will be...

* The Students: Spoiled.
* The Shaykh: Spoiled. For this reason we say: this life is "dunyā." From where is it derived? From the nearness of time, and nearness...?

* The Students: Of rank.
* The Shaykh: Of rank and of degree.

﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you﴾ [Fatir 35:5] from faith in that; that is, from the promise of Allah. How many people have been heedless of the promise of Allah! And how many people rely on apparent means and forget the causes that lie behind them!

Many people say: ﴿Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾ [al-Ḥajj 22:40]. How can Allah help the Muslims when they are few, against their disbelieving enemies who are so numerous and so powerful? How can this be? So they rely on the worldly life and on material means, without what lies behind them. It is our duty to believe in the promise of Allah. Allah made His promise to help those who help Him: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth, as He made successors those before them﴾ [al-Nūr 24:55]. Someone will say: How will Allah make me a successor upon the earth when there are the Russians, the Americans, the English, and other powerful and numerous nations? What does this mean? And what is the answer to this?

The answer: ﴿Indeed the promise of Allah is true; so let not the worldly life deceive you.﴾ Let the world not deceive you even regarding victory. The causes of victory are not only material; there is something behind them, which is the strength of the Mighty, the Majestic: ﴿Indeed Allah is Strong, Mighty﴾ [al-Ḥajj 22:40].

(﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you, nor let the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾ — in His forbearance and His respite — ﴿the Deceiver﴾: Satan.) That is: let not one whose attribute is deception deceive you either. For this reason He described him with the word "al-Ghurūr" (the Deceiver). "Ghurūr" (with a fatḥah on the ghayn) is an intensive adjective form (ṣifah mushabbahah, a quality adjective). Since his deceiving was a constant characteristic of him, the way that is necessary for him. And "al-Ghurūr" (with a ḍammah on the ghayn) is different: "al-Ghurūr" with a ḍammah is a verbal noun, while "al-Ghurar" (with a fatḥah) is an adjective indicating the meaning, and (...) the meaning. So "al-Ghurūr" here is Satan, that is, the satans of mankind or of jinn?

* Student: All of them.
* The Shaykh: Yes, all of them. Among the satans of the jinn is one who deceives, and he is well known: he is the devil who casts into your heart what you contrive. And among the satans of mankind also there is one who deceives, and they are the bad companions who come to a person and enter into him, as water enters clay or fire enters charcoal. He does not realize they have entered, so that he is like a sleeper or like a corpse before the one who washes it. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has warned us against these: ﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah.﴾

The author said: (in His forbearance and His respite). It is true that a person may be deceived concerning Allah in His forbearance and His respite. He says to himself: "If I were in error, Allah would punish me. And since Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, provides for me and grants me well-being, this is evidence that I am upon the truth." But this is one of the false wishful thinkings against which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ warned, when he said: "The intelligent person is one who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death, and the incapable one is one who follows his desires and wishes vain wishes from Allah."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhī (2459) and Ibn Māja (4260) from the hadith of Shaddād ibn Aws, without the addition "al-amānī" (the vain wishes).]] This hadith, although it has what it has regarding authenticity, its meaning is undoubtedly sound, for the intelligent, prudent person is the one who works for what comes after death. He said: ﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾, that is: let not He deceive you concerning Allah in His forbearance and His respite, and in other matters relating to His acts and His rulings. ﴿Let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾, that is, the Deceiver, who is Satan.

As for his saying: (Satan). This is a name for Satan, who is Iblīs. It is derived from "shāṭa yashīṭu" (to be enraged) or from "shaṭana yashṭinu" (to be far away). Both attributes apply to Satan: he has recklessness and bad conduct like the angry one, like one who rages with anger; and he is also "shāṭin," that is, far from the mercy of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, for Allah cursed him. He said: ﴿Indeed upon you is My curse until the Day of Recompense﴾ [Ṣād 38:78]. And His saying: ﴿Indeed Satan is an enemy to you﴾ [Fāṭir 35:6]. ﴿An enemy (ʿaduwwun)﴾ here, as you see, is emphasized with ﴿indeed (inna)﴾ and the lām?

* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: And the lām, or not?
* Students: (...) a prepositional phrase...
* The Shaykh: This is a prepositional phrase (...). ﴿To you is an enemy﴾, and He did not say "Indeed Satan is your enemy," because this enmity is established. ﴿To you is an enemy﴾. For this reason He used the nominal sentence consisting of a subject and predicate. So ﴿enemy (ʿaduwwun)﴾ is a postponed subject, and ﴿to you (lakum)﴾ is a preposed predicate. Placing the predicate first here conveys restriction (ḥaṣr): it is as if he is an enemy only to you. It is as if He said: he is not an enemy except to you. It is known that whoever's enmity is confined to a particular person must be guarded against more and more. His saying ﴿enemy (ʿaduww)﴾ is on the pattern "faʿūl," so it is a quality adjective (ṣifah mushabbahah). "ʿAduww" is the opposite of "walī" (ally). If the ally is the helper who takes charge of your affairs and cares for them, the enemy is the traitor who does not concern himself with your affairs. So Satan is an enemy.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿So take him as an enemy﴾ [Fāṭir 35:6]. When He affirmed that he is an enemy to us, He emphasized this further and said: ﴿So take him as an enemy.﴾ The "fa" here is what they call the "fa" of consequence (fāʾ al-tafrīʿ), that is: because it is established that he is an enemy, therefore take him as an enemy. That is, make him an enemy to you, such that you recoil from him as you recoil from enemies. If someone asks: What shows us his enmity, or how do we take him as an enemy? The answer: we take him as an enemy by hating him and detesting him, and by not submitting to his command and his whispering. For he, as Allah said of him: ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to immorality﴾ [al-Baqara 2:268]. He commands only immorality, evil, and disobedience to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. So if you sense in yourself that you desire sin, know that this is an inspiration from Iblīs, an inspiration from Satan, and you must recoil from it, because it comes from an enemy of yours who wants nothing but to harm you and to forsake you. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [Fāṭir 35:6].

The author said: (﴿So take him as an enemy﴾ by obeying Allah, and do not obey him). That is: obey Allah and do not obey Satan. And if you obey Allah, this is the greatest weapon that enrages this Satan who is your enemy. When you obey Allah the Mighty and Majestic, you thereby enrage Satan, repel him, and humble him, just as you humble his allies and enrage them. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾ [al-Fatḥ 48:29], up to His saying: ﴿that He may enrage the disbelievers by them﴾ [al-Fatḥ 48:29]. So these people, with their described qualities, enrage the disbelievers, and the disbelievers are the allies of Satan. And if they enrage the disbelievers, they also enrage Satan. So the greatest thing for enraging Satan is that you perform obedience to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. It is related that "Satan says about the children of Adam: I destroyed them with sins, and they destroyed me with 'lā ilāha illā Allāh' and with seeking forgiveness."[[Narrated by Abū Yaʿlā (no. 136) from the hadith of Abū Bakr, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Hold fast to 'lā ilāha illā Allāh' and seeking forgiveness, and increase in them, for Iblīs said: I destroyed people with sins, and they destroyed me with 'lā ilāha illā Allāh' and seeking forgiveness. When I saw that, I destroyed them with desires, and they think they are guided."]] So monotheism and asking for forgiveness undoubtedly enrage Satan.

(He, the Exalted, says: ﴿He only invites his party﴾ [Fāṭir 35:6], that is, his followers in disbelief, ﴿that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [Fāṭir 35:6], the intense fire.)

﴿He only invites﴾: "innamā" (only) is a particle of restriction, which establishes the ruling for what is mentioned and negates it for anything else. That is: he invites his party only to this action, that they become among the companions of the Blaze. The "lām" in His saying ﴿that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ is a lām of purpose: he invites his party to evil and immorality in order that they become among the companions of the Blaze. And the author's saying: (﴿his party﴾: his followers in disbelief).

It may be said that there is a deficiency in this, because the absolute party of Satan are without doubt disbelievers. But whoever disobeys Allah the Mighty and Majestic in some sin, even if he is not a disbeliever, has a share of the partisanship of Satan in proportion to what he disobeyed Allah in. However, the absolute party are the disbelievers. He said: ﴿that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾, that is, among the companions of the Fire. And "saʿīr" is the intense fire. He invites them to this because, when he went astray, may Allah protect us, and was arrogant toward obeying Allah: ﴿He said: Because You have caused me to go astray, I will surely sit in wait for them upon Your straight path﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:16], and ﴿He said: My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them upon the earth and mislead them all﴾ [al-Ḥijr 15:39].

When he was forsaken, may Allah protect us, and cast out, and became one who goes astray, he was eager to have followers in his error. This is an observed matter: the people of truth wish to have followers in truth, and the people of falsehood wish to have followers in falsehood. So Satan, may Allah protect us, since he was among the companions of the Fire, wished that people, that is, the children of Adam, all of them be among the companions of the Fire. These offspring, the offspring of Adam, are they not? And Iblīs's wretchedness was only due to his refusal to prostrate to Adam. So it is inevitable that he should lead his offspring astray and try by every means he can to mislead them until they become among the companions of the Fire.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment﴾ [Fāṭir 35:7]. ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ is the subject, and its predicate is the clause ﴿for them is a severe punishment﴾. "ʿAdhāb" means punishment. He used the nominal sentence to establish or confirm the permanence of this punishment, because disbelievers abide forever in the Fire of Hell. And "shadīd" (severe) means strong.

As for others, He said: ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [Fāṭir 35:7]. ﴿Those who believe﴾: faith has its seat in the heart, that is, they affirm what must be believed, with acceptance and submission. Pay attention: faith is not mere assent; it is assent accompanied by acceptance and submission, acceptance of what one believes in and submission that this faith requires. As for mere assent, it is not faith. And if you wish, we can give an example with Abū Ṭālib, for Abū Ṭālib affirmed the Prophet ﷺ but he did not accept and did not submit, so this assent did not benefit him.

So ﴿those who believe﴾ means: they affirm what must be believed, with an affirmation that entails acceptance and submission. As for His saying ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾, righteous action is necessary for faith to be completed, confirmed, and made manifest.

Righteous action: the scholars said it is that which is sincere and correct, sincere for Allah and correct in conformity with the Sharīʿah of Allah. This definition covers this expression and others. Whatever is sincere for Allah and conforms to His Sharīʿah is righteous, and whatever is not so is corrupt. If sincerity is absent from an action, it is not righteous; and if sincerity is present but it is not in accordance with the Sharīʿah, it is not righteous either.

On this basis, innovated actions are not righteous even if their doer is sincere in them, and legislated actions are not righteous if showing off and displaying to people is mixed with them.

His saying ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ is repeated frequently in the Quran. According to what the grammarians say, it is of the type where the modified noun is omitted and the adjective remains to indicate it, because the original is: "and do the righteous deeds" (al-aʿmāl al-ṣāliḥāt).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 35, verses 5–8 (part 2 of 4):**

﴿They will have forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ In ﴿those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ there is mention of two deeds for them, and mention of two rewards for them. For those who disbelieved, He mentioned one deed and one reward: ﴿Those who disbelieved will have a severe punishment﴾ [Fatir 7]. The deed is disbelief, and the reward is severe punishment. As for ﴿those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾, these are two deeds, and the reward is ﴿forgiveness and a great reward﴾: forgiveness for their sins, and ﴿a great reward﴾ for their righteous deeds. Forgiveness (maghfirah) is the removal of sin and overlooking it, because it is derived from al-maghfar (ghafr), which is what one covers the head with for protection against arrows. This is only so when it is strong and prevents. Forgiveness is not merely concealment, because mere concealment and punishment are not forgiveness. Rather, two things are required: concealment and non-punishment. As for His words ﴿and a reward﴾, al-ajr (reward) is the recompense with which the worker is repaid. Even the wage, for example, if you hire a man to do a task for you and you give him a wage, this is ajr. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, named the reward ajr because the worker must receive it, so it is like the wage of the one who hires or the wage of the hired worker. The worker must receive it. This is like His saying: ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah 245]. Thus the deed done for Allah is called a loan, because a loan must be repaid. Verses like these show that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has obligated Himself to reward the worker. As for His words ﴿a great reward﴾: is "great" in its size, or great in its meaning?
* The students: Both.
* The Shaykh: Both. Because the lowest-ranked person in Paradise is one who looks at his kingdom from a distance of two thousand years, seeing its farthest part as he sees its nearest. This is undoubtedly great and vast. Likewise in meaning, because it is lasting and permanent. He said: (This is an explanation of what is for the allies of Satan and what is for his opponents). (The allies of Satan): who are they?
* Students: Those who disbelieved.
* The Shaykh: Those who disbelieved. And his opponents? Those who believed and did righteous deeds. So it is incumbent upon us to take Satan as an enemy through faith and righteous deeds.

The author said: (It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and others: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him so that he sees it as good...﴾ [Fatir 8]), and so on to the end. Abu Jahl was called Abu al-Hakam in the Jahiliyyah, meaning that he possessed wisdom, intellect and deliberation. But he was called Abu Jahl in Islam, because his greatest ignorance was remaining upon his disbelief and not believing in Allah. The verse was revealed: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him so that he sees it as good...﴾ [Fatir 8]. The hamzah in ﴿Afa-man﴾ is an interrogative particle, and the fa' is a conjunction (harf 'atf). The element it conjoins with is disputed. Some said that it is an implied element between the hamzah and the conjunction, determined by context. Others said that what it conjoins with is what precedes.

According to the first view, we supply the omitted element to suit the context. For example, His saying ﴿Have they not travelled in the land?﴾ [Yusuf 109]; the implied meaning is: "Have they been negligent and so not travelled in the land?" Here He says ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him...﴾, and we supply what suits it. We say in the implied meaning: "Do you perceive this matter? Then is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him...?" Or we say: "Are the believer and the disbeliever equal? Then is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him...?"

But the second view on the matter, that it is conjoined with what precedes, is better. Why? Because the original state is not to supply anything, and because at times it is difficult for a person to supply the omitted element. According to this view, they say that the fa' is considered to precede the hamzah (...). The conjunction is considered to precede the hamzah, so there is transposition, and the meaning according to this is: "Then is one to whom his evil deed has been made attractive...?"

His words ﴿was made attractive to him the evil of his deed﴾: who is the one who makes it attractive? Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned that the one who makes it attractive is Satan, and He mentioned that the one who makes it attractive is Allah: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have made their deeds attractive to them, so they wander blindly﴾ [al-Naml 4]. And He said: ﴿And Satan made their deeds attractive to them and debarred them from the way﴾ [al-Naml 24]. In some verses the one who makes attractive is unspecified, as in this verse, and as in His saying: ﴿Attractive to people is love of desires, of women and children﴾ [Al 'Imran 14], and so on. So the one who makes attractive is Allah, and the one who makes attractive is Satan.

If you ask: How do you reconcile this with that? The answer: The direct one who makes attractive is Satan, but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, makes attractive by decree. That is, He is the one who decreed that Satan should make attractive to them. It is known that Allah, the Exalted, created Satan, and whatever results from his actions is attributed to Allah, just as we say about a human being: he is created by Allah, and whatever results from his actions is created by Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So Allah's making attractive is according to decree; that is, He is the one who decreed that Satan should make their deeds attractive to them.

His words ﴿was made attractive to him the evil of his deed﴾: "deed" (ʿamal) is a singular noun in construct, and it includes all deeds, whether it is shirk, aggression against others, bad conduct, corruption of morals, or other things. The important point is that it includes all deeds.

The author said: (by deception). What is the meaning of "by deception"? It means that he deceives people into thinking that the deed he performs is a good deed. ﴿and he sees it as good﴾, meaning he sees the evil of his deed as good. This is the most severe condition: that a person is in error and yet sees himself as correct, because such a person hardly ever gives up his error, since he regards it as right.

From examples of this: the cunning deceivers who use all kinds of tricks. The hypocrite, for example, has had his evil deed made attractive to him, because he sees himself as clever: ﴿When they meet those who believed, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed we are with you"﴾ [al-Baqarah 14]. This is among evil deeds. Those who devise tricks to get around usury by various means: these too have had the evil of their deeds made attractive to them. For this reason you hardly find them giving up what they are upon, because it has been made attractive in their souls, so they do not give it up. The important point is that this has many examples.

It remains for us to say: "man" (من) is a subject (mubtada'); where is its predicate (khabar)? The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "man" is a subject whose predicate is "like one whom Allah has guided". After it?
* A student: (No, it is indicated by something else).
* The Shaykh: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him...﴾ means: "like one to whom his evil deed has not been made attractive, and who sees his evil deed as evil", because the one whose evil deed has been made attractive will continue upon it, while the one who sees it as evil will avoid it. This is the meaning of the author's words: "like one whom Allah has guided". Such an expression occurs often in the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord? Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ [al-Zumar 9]. So the predicate is omitted, meaning "like one who is not so". He says: (No). What is the meaning of "No"?
* A student: It means "not".
* The Shaykh: It means that this is not like that, because there is a difference between them. The one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him will remain in his misguidance, while the one to whom his evil deed has not been made attractive, and who sees it as evil, will avoid it and not fall into it.

The author said: (Indicated by ﴿Indeed, Allah misguides whom He wills﴾). Indicated by (...).
﴿Indeed, Allah misguides whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [Fatir 8]. On this basis, the fa' here is not placed in the predicate of the subject; rather the predicate is omitted, but the fa' is a conjunction to that predicate. That is: "Indeed Allah misguides whom He wills from the truth, so he does not get guided to it, and guides whom He wills to the truth, so he adheres to it."

Here He says ﴿misguides whom He wills﴾. We often encounter the attaching of things to will (mashi'ah). We have said, and we say, that this will is joined with wisdom. Whoever the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, requires to be misguided, He misguides; and whoever His wisdom requires to be guided, He guides. Who is it whom the wisdom of Allah requires to be misguided? It is the one who wanted misguidance, as He said: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff 5]. So Allah's misguidance of the servant is in its proper place, when this man does not want good but wants evil.

Know that guidance and misguidance are either justice or grace. Misguidance is justice, because he is recompensed according to what he wanted. When he wanted misguidance, may Allah protect us, and his heart deviated, it was made to deviate. As for guidance, it is grace from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which He bestows upon whom He wills of His servants. For this reason we say: If someone says: How does Allah make this one guided and this one misguided? Is this not injustice? The answer: No. Because withholding guidance from this misguided person is only according to His justice, while guiding the one who is guided is by His grace. So we say: If He withholds from you what is yours, He has wronged you; and if He withholds His grace, then grace is given to whom He wills. Had you not been unworthy of guidance, Allah would not have withheld guidance from you.
* A student: Shaykh, what about (...)?
* The Shaykh: In this verse there are many benefits:
* First: The importance of affirming the promise of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is shown by His opening with the address: ﴿O mankind﴾ [Fatir 5].
* Second: That the disbelievers are addressed with the branches and roots of the religion, because the address here is general: ﴿O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true﴾.
* Third among its benefits: that the promise of Allah must come to pass, because it is the report of One who is truthful and able. His words ﴿indeed the promise of Allah is true﴾ mean: it is true at the time of its being reported, and it occurs at the time of its being fulfilled. So among the benefits of this verse is that whatever Allah has promised is true and must come to pass.
* Among its benefits: a person must not be deceived by this world, however much of its splendour and bliss he attains. His saying: ﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you﴾ [Fatir 5].
* Among its benefits also: whoever (...) by this world is deceived. His saying: ﴿So let them not deceive you﴾ means "let them not deceive you", because the intelligent person is not deceived by it.
* Among them is an indication of the obligation to attend to the Hereafter. His saying: ﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you﴾. When we are forbidden from the worldly life, its meaning is that we are required or commanded to attend to the Hereafter, because it is, in reality, the destination.

As for this world, a person passes through it only as a traveller. Even the graves in which a person remains for years known only to Allah are a place of passing. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Rivalry in worldly increase diverts you, until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur 1–2]. A Bedouin heard a man recite this verse and said: "By Allah, the visitor is not a resident", or: "Indeed the visitor is one who departs", because He said ﴿until you visit﴾, and it is known that the visitor remains for a period and then departs.
* Among its benefits also: the lowliness of this world in rank and its baseness. His saying: ﴿the worldly (dunya)﴾: though it is a life, it is "worldly" (dunya). This implies praise of the Hereafter, because describing a co-wife with a defect indicates describing her co-wife with perfection. Indeed, Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿But you prefer the worldly life, while the Hereafter is better and more lasting﴾ [al-A'la 16–17].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of a person enjoying the world in a manner that does not deceive him. His saying: ﴿So let them not deceive you﴾, and He did not say: "Do not enjoy anything of the world", but He said: ﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you﴾.
* Among them: the greatness of the danger of abundant wealth and easy living, because this may preoccupy a person. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "By Allah, I do not fear poverty for you; rather I fear that the world will be opened to you, and you will compete for it as they competed for it, and it will destroy you as it destroyed them."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4015) and Muslim (2961/6), from the hadith of 'Amr ibn 'Awf.]]
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation to beware of Satan and his whisperings. His saying: ﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you about Allah﴾ [Fatir 5]. Whether Satan is human or jinn, because the human satan deceives a person just as the satan of the jinn deceives him.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: intense caution against this deceiver who deceives us, whether among the satans of mankind or jinn, because He described him with the words: ﴿the Deceiver (al-ghurur)﴾. As we have said, al-ghurur is either a resembling attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah) or an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah); we did not say that it is a verbal noun (masdar).

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾ [Fatir 6], and so on to the end.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Satan, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed Satan is an enemy to you﴾.
* Among them: the affirmation of his emphatic enmity toward the human being, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed Satan is an enemy to you﴾.
* Among them: the importance of our believing in this. What is its basis?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: ﴿Satan is an enemy to you﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but what is the basis for the importance of our knowing that he is an enemy?
* Students: Restriction (al-hasr).
* The Shaykh: Or it is for emphasis. What is the basis for that?
* A student: He emphasized it (...) with the lam.
* The Shaykh: No, the lam is not for emphasis. But the basis is that because it was emphasized, our knowledge of this became important.
* A student: (...) if it is emphasized that Satan is an enemy to us, then we should beware of him more than (...).
* Another student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) We have studied in rhetoric (balaghah) that the informative address (al-khitab al-khabari) is the address delivered to the addressee without emphasis. Have we studied this? In rhetoric, the informative address is that which is delivered to the addressee without emphasis, and that emphasis is not used in the context of informative address except for a reason. If an informative address is delivered to a person whose mind is blank, it is not emphasized, because there is no need for emphasis. Emphasis adds nothing but words without benefit. But if the matter is of importance, it is emphasized even if the person's mind is blank. If he already knows the matter, emphasis becomes even further justified. We do not need emphasis in every case.

So now we say: Allah emphasized this statement, and the addressee is either blank-minded or already aware of it. This indicates the importance of believing in this matter, that Satan is an enemy.

The scholars of rhetoric have said: When a statement is delivered to someone who already knows it, with emphasis, that is because this addressee has been treated as one who denies it, since he has not done what this address requires. They illustrated this with His saying: ﴿Then indeed you, after that, will surely die﴾ [al-Mu'minun 15].

We all know that we will die, yet why was death emphasized for us while we know it and are certain of it? Because our conduct is that of one who denies death, since we do not believe in it and do not act for what comes after death. So from this verse we take the importance of our believing that Satan is an enemy to us. From where do we know this? Because He emphasized the report, though it is delivered to a person whose mind is blank and does not know that Satan is an enemy, or to a person who knows it but has been treated as one who denies it, since he has not taken Satan as an enemy.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation to keep away from what Satan commands. His saying: ﴿So take him as an enemy﴾ [Fatir 6].
* Among its benefits also: mentioning blameworthy qualities when the purpose is to advise the addressee. His saying: ﴿Indeed Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾ [Fatir 6]. If you see a person deceived by another whom he takes as a friend, while this person is an enemy to him and we know that he wants to bring every evil upon him, then it is incumbent upon us to advise him against that person and mention the faults of this person, so that he is not deceived by him. We say: "You are keeping company with so-and-so, and he is your enemy." Yes, even if his enmity is because he guides him to the path of Hellfire. Yes indeed.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's mercy toward His servants, because knowledge of Satan's enmity is not something they could perceive. But He, the Exalted, is the One who informed us of it, then urged us, indeed commanded us, to oppose him, because of His saying: ﴿So take him as an enemy﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 35, verses 5–8 (part 3 of 4):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Satan has evil aims toward the children of Adam (...). But the verse contains no proof that some people enter the Fire without abiding in it and so are not among its companions. We say: it is possible. Satan wants people to reach the peak of disobedience, and when they reach the peak of disobedience and disbelieve, then they are among the companions of the Fire who abide in it. As for the sins below that, their doers will not (...) the Fire, as the texts indicate, so they are not among its companions.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment﴾ [Fatir 7], to the end.

* Student: (...) even the believers who have sins?

* Shaykh: No. Here it says "the party." The party of Satan may be a party that has (...), and this may be... we do not say "it does not happen." But Satan wants, from this, everyone who answers his call to be among the companions of the Fire.

He said: ﴿Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment﴾. In this verse is the affirmation of reward and punishment, by His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment, and those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [Fatir 7].

* Among its benefits: the eloquence of the Qur'an, in that it combines a thing with its opposite. This is the fulfilment of the Exalted's saying: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of statements, a Book consistent and repeating (mathani)﴾ [Az-Zumar 23]. (...) said regarding His saying "mathani" that its meanings are repeated within it. Here, when He mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers, He mentioned the reward of the believers.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the eloquence of the Qur'an from another aspect, in that it began by mentioning the punishment of the disbelievers after having mentioned: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [Fatir 6]. So it began with what contains warning after what contains good tidings, from the verses of connection (munasaba).

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the disbeliever's punishment is severe, meaning it is not an easy punishment (...). The severity of the punishment of the disbelievers (...). From where is this (...)?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: I am asking you: from where?

* Student: From the aspect of their following Satan.

* Shaykh: What type of cause is that? What is the aspect of its severity?

* Student: Its aspect of severity?

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: That they are in the Fire, a severe punishment.

* Shaykh: (...) its severity. Is it in its quality or its quantity?

* Student: In quantity and quality.

* Shaykh: In quantity and quality, because it is everlasting, and because it is a punishment without equal. Yes.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: reward is established only (...) in two qualities. One of them is faith, and the second is righteous deeds.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the division of deeds into righteous and corrupt, which is derived from His saying: ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾. What is the criterion? We said earlier that the criterion is that whatever is sincere and correct is righteous, and whatever contains shirk or innovation (bid'a) is not righteous.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that those who believe and do righteous deeds (...), their reward is doubled: the removal of what is disliked, established in His saying: ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾, and the attainment of what is desired, established in His saying: ﴿and a great reward﴾.

* Among its benefits as well: the eloquence of the Qur'an, because when He mentioned one deed for the disbelievers, He mentioned one recompense, and when He mentioned two qualities for the believers, He mentioned two qualities in their reward. This is also clear in a surah like Surat al-Insan: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worthy of mention?﴾ [Al-Insan 1]. If you reflect on it, you will find that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned concerning the disbelievers and their punishment only a little compared to the righteous (abrar). The cause: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blazing fire﴾ [Al-Insan 4]. He said "for the disbelievers" only, and did not mention any of their deeds, but rather the recompense was brief: ﴿chains and shackles and a blazing fire﴾.

He mentioned the righteous and lengthened the mention of the bliss they have, because He mentioned a number of their deeds: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor, a spring from which the servants of Allah will drink﴾ [Al-Insan 5–6]. Look: the righteous are the servants of Allah. ﴿They fulfil vows and fear a Day whose evil is widespread, and they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive, (saying): "We feed you only for the countenance of Allah"﴾ [Al-Insan 7–9]: complete sincerity. ﴿We wish from you no reward or gratitude. Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day austere and distressing﴾ [Al-Insan 9–10]. Yes, the repetition of these qualities among their qualities, and since He lengthened the mention of their deeds, He lengthened the mention of their recompense, unlike the disbelievers. This is without doubt from the eloquence of the Qur'an.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: rewards differ, from His saying: ﴿and a great reward﴾. They differ according to what? They differ according to the deed, they differ according to the doer, and if the deed is transitive, they differ according to the one who benefits from it. For example, they differ according to the deed: "The best of deeds is the prayer at its appointed time" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (527), Muslim (85/139), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud]. Obligatory acts are better than recommended ones. According to the doer: there has passed with us: "The best charity is that which is given from surplus wealth" [Narrated by al-Bukhari (1426), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not insult my companions. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if any of you were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, it would not reach a mudd of one of them nor half of it" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3673), Muslim (2541/222), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id]. This is according to what?

* Student: The doer.

* Shaykh: According to the doer. They also differ according to the place, if the deed is transitive: charity to a relative is both charity and maintaining kinship, and charity to one who is in greater need is better than charity to one who is less in need, and so on. The difference in deeds necessitates a difference in rewards as well. They also differ (...) according to sincerity.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: According to sincerity: meaning that the more sincere a person is in his deed, the better his deed is. Or not? We can also say: they differ according to conformity to the Sunna, and the more a person's conformity is to Allah (...), the more complete it is. In any case, these differences, in their existence, make rewards differ.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him and he sees it as good...﴾ [Fatir 8].

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: (...) ﴿Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾. You will find that this verse, ﴿He sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾, that this will is according to wisdom. Whoever Allah's wisdom requires that He send astray, He sends astray, and this is the one who does not want good, by His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [As-Saff 5]. And His saying: ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾ [Fatir 8] refers to the guidance of success (tawfiq). Perhaps we could say: the guidance of success and guidance by indication, but the more important is the guidance of success, and perhaps this is what is meant here, because those whom Allah has sent astray, Allah has guided them with the guidance of indication. Then the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah invites to the Abode of Peace﴾ [Yunus 25], and this is general, but as for guidance, He said: ﴿and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus 25]. So not every one invited is guided.

His saying: ﴿So do not let yourself go in pursuit of them, [wasting yourself] in regret﴾ [Fatir 8]. Is this a prohibition concerning what has occurred or concerning what has not occurred? The apparent meaning is that it is a prohibition concerning what has occurred: the Messenger (ﷺ) used to grieve over these deniers who were denying him. A prohibition against a thing may be a prohibition against what has occurred and may be a prohibition against what has not occurred. His saying to the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿So do not invoke with Allah another deity, lest you be among those punished. And warn your closest kindred﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 213–214]. This is a prohibition concerning what?

* Student: What has not occurred.

* Shaykh: Concerning what has not occurred? Or what has occurred?

* Students: (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿So do not invoke with Allah another deity, lest you be among those punished. And warn your closest kindred﴾.

* Students: Concerning what has not occurred.

* Shaykh: Concerning what has not occurred, correct, because the Messenger did not do it. Right? ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [An-Nisa' 29]?

* Student: Concerning what has not occurred.

* Shaykh: Or concerning what has occurred?

* Student: Concerning what has occurred.

* Another student: Concerning what has not occurred.

* Shaykh: Does (...) in himself (...)?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Meaning (...).

* Student: In relation to (...).

* Shaykh: (...) "Do not kill yourselves." Is the meaning: that none of you kills another? This is correct. It is a prohibition concerning what has not occurred and what has occurred. But if it is a prohibition that a person kill himself, this certainly has not occurred, since it is not possible for him to kill himself except while he exists.

* Student: If he commits suicide, does he not kill himself, O Shaykh?

* Shaykh: Yes, but you do not say "do not kill yourself" [in that case]...

* Student: While he is alive?

* Shaykh: Yes, before he dies. As for after (...), it is not possible. So then, do we say this is a prohibition concerning what has not...?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Subhan Allah, (...) has occurred.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: The Messenger (ﷺ) used to grieve over the loss of (...), and the evidence (...): ﴿Perhaps you would leave out some of what is revealed to you and your breast is constrained by it because they say, "Why has a treasure not been sent down to him or an angel not come with him?"﴾ [Hud 12]. And the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 3]; that is, destroy yourself.

So the Messenger (ﷺ) grieved over these people because of their not believing. Here He says: ﴿So do not let yourself go in pursuit of them [wasting yourself] in regret﴾, meaning: do not let yourself perish on their account. Yes, as one says: "I wept for you through the ages," meaning: on your account. So the meaning is: do not let yourself perish on their account in regret.

His saying: ﴿ḥasarāt﴾ (regrets). It has been said that it is a state (ḥāl), being a verbal noun used in the sense of the active participle, i.e., "regretful." Regret (ḥasra) is intense distress and grief over what has been lost. Whoever loses something he loves and seeks grieves and is distressed over it, so it is said: "he regretted (taḥassara)." It has also been said that ḥasarāt is a verbal noun (...) and is an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlih). The meaning: "Do not let yourself go," i.e., do not perish for the sake of regrets over them.

The author said: (﴿So do not let yourself go in pursuit of them﴾, i.e., of those who adorned their evil for them, ﴿[wasting yourself] in regret﴾ by your grief that they do not believe. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾ [Fatir 8], so He will recompense them for it).

In this sentence there is both a threat and consolation: a threat to these opponents, and consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: do not (...), for their reckoning is with Allah and He will recompense them.

The Exalted said: ﴿So do not let yourself go in pursuit of them [wasting yourself] in regret﴾, or from its beginning, I think, meaning from the beginning of the verse.

The Exalted said: ﴿So is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him and he sees it as good...﴾ to the end.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: some people's hearts become so blind that they see an evil deed as good, and conversely see good as evil, by His saying: ﴿So is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him and he sees it as good?﴾

* Among its benefits: the vagueness of the agent, so as to include everything that may proceed from him this act, by His saying: ﴿whose evil deed has been made attractive to him﴾. It has already passed with us that the one who makes it attractive is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in origin, and the devils in direct action.

* Among its benefits: the division of deeds into evil and righteous, by His saying: ﴿his evil deed﴾.

* Among its benefits: a refutation of the Jabriyya (determinists), by His saying: ﴿his evil deed﴾, where He attributed the deed to him. They say that deeds are not attributed to the human being, because he is compelled to them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that whoever is in this state is not equal to one who is not, in that he sees evil as evil and good as good. We derive this from the fact that the omitted element is the counterpart of what is mentioned, because the interrogative particle here is for equalizing: "Are these two equal?" The answer: they are not equal.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that guidance and misguidance are in the hand of Allah, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾.

* Among its benefits, and it branches from this benefit: when we know this, we ask Allah for guidance, and we seek refuge in Allah from misguidance. We seek refuge in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from misguidance, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿whom He wills﴾. But it has passed with us that every act that Allah ties to His will is connected with wisdom. The proof of this is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan 30].

* Among its benefits: a refutation of the Qadariyya, by His saying: ﴿He sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾. The Qadariyya say that the acts of the servant, whether misguidance or guidance, are not connected to the will of Allah, because their doctrine (the Qadariyya's) is that the human being is independent in his deeds, with no connection of Allah to them at all. Even their extremists claim that Allah does not know the servant's deed until it occurs, and they say: the matter is "unprecedented" (unuf), i.e., newly begun: Allah's knowledge comes into being after it was not.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Mighty One who sent him, grieved a great grief, such that his soul nearly perished from its intensity, by His saying: ﴿So do not let yourself go in pursuit of them [wasting yourself] in regret﴾. The reason is that the basic meaning of a prohibition is that it concerns what has occurred, though it may concern what has not occurred, and this is also common. The fact that this is something that has occurred is shown by the Exalted's saying: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 3].

* Among its benefits: the compassion of the Prophet (ﷺ) for his community.

* Among its benefits as well: the Messenger (ﷺ) does not grieve over their not believing or obeying for his own benefit, but for their benefit, by His saying: ﴿So do not let yourself go in pursuit of them [wasting yourself] in regret﴾.

* Among them: the Prophet (ﷺ) is a human being, who is affected by what affects human beings of causes of joy and causes of sorrow. This is an actual matter. "The Prophet (ﷺ) once entered upon 'A'isha, radiant, with the lines of his face shining. She asked him about that, and he said: 'Have you not seen that Mujazziz al-Mudlaji entered upon Usama ibn Zayd and Zayd ibn Haritha while they were covered with a cloak, their feet showing, and he said: "Indeed, these feet are part of one another"?'" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3731), Muslim (1459/39), from the hadith of 'A'isha]. The Prophet (ﷺ) rejoiced until it showed on his face. So human attributes befall the Prophet (ﷺ) as they befall other human beings: joy, sorrow, grief, delight, forgetfulness, lack of knowledge, and other things, because he is distinguished from human beings by only one thing, which is revelation. The Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Say, "I am only a human being like you"﴾ [Al-Kahf 110]. Look: ﴿a human being﴾ is sufficient without ﴿like you﴾, but this is for emphasis, lest someone think that he is a human being who has been singled out in something, so He said: ﴿a human being like you﴾. Then He mentioned the distinction: ﴿It is revealed to me that your God is but one God﴾ [Al-Kahf 110]. In this there is a clear refutation of those people who claim that the Prophet (ﷺ) has an influence on creation like the lordship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For if that were so, his soul would not have perished in grief over them, for he would have guided them, and would have been spared these regrets that befall his soul.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, of everything we do, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾ [Fatir 8].

Among its benefits: God's care for His Messenger ﷺ in this sentence, which conveys consoling him and making the matter easier for him, and that the reckoning of these people is in no way upon him, just as his reckoning is in no way upon them.

Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾ [Fatir 9]. In one reading it is ﴿الرِّيحَ﴾ (ar-rīḥa, singular). ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾: Allah alone sends these winds, not anyone else. No one can send any of these winds. Even if all of creation gathered together to send the wind, they could not do it. If they gathered together to soften its violence, they could not do that either. That is in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Allah alone sends the winds.

Consider His words ﴿أَرْسَلَ﴾ (arsala, "sent"). He made the wind a messenger, as if it conveys or carries out what it has been commanded, just as a messenger conveys what he was sent with. Thus it is "sent." For this reason, it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he forbade cursing the wind, because cursing the wind ultimately returns to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since it is He who sent it. It is directed and subjected by Him.

His words ﴿الرِّيَاحَ﴾ (ar-riyāḥ, plural), and in one reading ﴿الرِّيحَ﴾ (ar-rīḥ, singular). The reading here is one of the seven canonical readings (qirāʾa sabʿiyya). The difference between them is that ar-riyāḥ is plural and ar-rīḥ is singular, but this singular carries the sense of the plural because it has the definite article (al-), which here is for comprehensiveness (istighrāq, "encompassing all members of a class"). So it includes all winds, whether they come from the north, the south, the east, or the west. Allah, the Exalted, is the One who sends them. Know that, generally, when winds are plural they are associated with goodness, and when the wind is singular it tends to be the opposite. This is the general rule.

For this reason, it is related from the Prophet ﷺ in his supplication concerning the wind: "O Allah, make it winds (riyāḥan) and do not make it a wind (rīḥan)." [Narrated by ash-Shāfiʿī in his Musnad (537), and Abū Yaʿlā (2456).] However, in spite of this, one may be used in place of the other, and there is an indication (qarīna) that determines the meaning. In His words, the Exalted: ﴿And in ʿĀd, when We sent upon them the barren wind﴾ [adh-Dhāriyāt 41]: this is in the context of evil. ﴿Until, when you are in the ships and they sail with them by a good wind﴾ [Yūnus 22]: this is for good, because it is described (as "good"). ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good news before His mercy﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 57]: this is for good. And here too it is for good: ﴿He sends the winds, and they stir up clouds﴾ [ar-Rūm 48]. (tuthīru, "they stir up") is the present tense conjoined to the past tense. The expected pattern would be to conjoin a past tense to a past tense, saying "and Allah who sent the winds, and they stirred up," but why did He shift from the past to the present?

The author explained it, may Allah have mercy on him, saying: "The present tense is used for narrating a past situation." That is, He expressed the past with the present tense to depict the situation at the time of their sending, because it is more vivid in the imagination, as if they were now before you stirring up these clouds. This is more effective in conveying the image to a person, because it brings the past situation to mind as though it were happening now. As we all know, the present tense (al-muḍāriʿ) can refer to the present and the future. It may be made specifically past by an accompanying indicator, and it may be made specifically present or future by other indicators. Its basic use is for the present and future, and it refers to the past only with an indicator. Therefore we say: He shifted from the past tense here in order to narrate a past situation, so that it is as if you are witnessing it now, stirring up these clouds.

The author said regarding (tuthīru, "they stir up"): that is, they agitate (tuzʿiju). This meaning may be debated, because agitation (al-izʿāj) is more specific than stirring up (al-ithāra). Stirring up (ithāra) means causing something to rise, as one says: "I stirred up the camel," meaning I made it stand up after it had been kneeling.

His words ﴿فَتُثِيرُ سَحَابًا﴾ (fa-tuthīru saḥāban, "so they stir up clouds"): it is as though this cloud was originally on the earth, and then these winds stirred it up. It is known that clouds come from the vapor of the sea, and sometimes from the air saturated with moisture, according to what the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, requires. This is a matter that is known through the natural sciences.

His words ﴿فَتُثِيرُ سَحَابًا﴾: the sahāb (cloud) is this well-known cloud (...). It moves (yanḥasib) through the air, as you observe, and that is why it is called saḥāb, from its gliding (insiḥāb) through the air. ﴿So they stir up clouds﴾.

(﴿فَسُقْنَاهُ﴾, "so We drove it," involves a shift from the third person to the first person [iltifāt, "a shift in grammatical person"]). There is also a shift from the present to the past tense. Note this carefully. ﴿He sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, so We drove it﴾ [Fatir 9]. He shifted from the present to the past because the subjects of the two verbs differ. In (tuthīru), the subject is (the winds), and in (saqnāhu, "We drove it"), the subject is (Allah). So it is appropriate for it to be in the past tense, conjoined to His words ﴿أَرْسَلَ﴾ ("sent"), because the one who sent is Allah. Since the subject of both verbs ﴿أَرْسَلَ﴾ and (saqnā, "We drove") is the same, it would be more eloquent for both to be in the past tense. But there is a shift from the third person in His words ﴿And it is Allah who sent﴾ [Fatir 9] to the first person in His words ﴿so We drove it﴾. Why? It has been pointed out to us that iltifāt has a constant benefit, which is what?

* Student: Alerting the listener.
* Shaykh: Alerting? How? Because a uniform style keeps the mind flowing along without stopping. But when the style changes, the mind pauses to see what has happened, and changing it is therefore an alert to the addressee. Yes, that is one benefit.

But here there is also a second benefit, which is showing the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿So We drove it﴾, meaning: We. He attributed it to Himself because that shows His power more clearly. So when ﴿Allah, who sent﴾ is combined with the fact that He, glorified and exalted is He, drove the cloud that the wind had stirred up, that is a clearer indication of power than if it had come in one uniform style: ﴿So We drove it to a dead land﴾ [Fatir 9], with both the doubled and single consonant readings (bi-t-tashdīd wa-t-takhfīf).

The second benefit is the demonstration of complete power, because when it begins in the third person and then comes in the first person, it is a stronger and greater indication of power.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, this is from the perspective of iltifāt, from the basic structure.

He says: ﴿إِلَى بَلَدٍ مَيِّتٍ﴾ (ilā baladin mayyit, "to a dead land") has two readings: mayyit and mayt. It has been said that al-mayt (with the lighter form) refers to one who has already died, and al-mayyit (with the doubled form) refers to one who is going to die. They cite as evidence His words: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ [az-Zumar 30], meaning "you will die." And His words: ﴿Is one who was dead (maytan) and We gave him life﴾ [al-Anʿām 122], where maytan here refers to one who has already died. Some scholars made this distinction. The apparent view, however, is that the Arabic language uses both forms for both meanings. This verse is an example: mayyit, "one who will die" or "one who has died"? 

* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿إِلَى بَلَدٍ مَيِّتٍ﴾? 
* Students: It has died.
* Shaykh: It has died, and yet it came with the doubled form.

(﴿إِلَى بَلَدٍ مَيِّتٍ﴾, with both the doubled and single forms, meaning there is no vegetation in it.) This is the death of the land. By "land" (al-balad) here is not meant only the inhabited part of the earth, but something more general, including both the inhabited and uninhabited. Restricting "balad" to the inhabited is a customary restriction; otherwise, the whole earth is a balad, because it is flat and spread out (inbilād wa-tasṭīḥ). For this reason He says: ﴿to a dead land, and We revived by it the earth﴾ [Fatir 9]. ﴿فَأَحْيَيْنَا بِهِ﴾ ("We revived by it"): We drove, and ﴿fa-aḥyaynā﴾ ("We revived"). Here the verbs and pronouns are in one consistent style. And His words ﴿فَأَحْيَيْنَا بِهِ الْأَرْضَ﴾ ("We revived by it the earth"). He says: (from the land). What is the meaning of "from the land"? It means the earth of that land, which was dead, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revived it. With what did He revive it? He revived it with vegetation.

For this reason the author said: (﴿بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا﴾ "after its death", meaning its drying out; that is, We made grain and pasture grow from it). This is something observed: the earth comes dry and lifeless, its stalks crumbling, then Allah sends down rain upon it, and it stirs and turns green, with every lovely pair in it. Who revived it? Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Creation cannot revive it at all, no matter what. Even the pasture that grows from rain does not grow from flowing water, as is observed. That is, if you water this land with flowing water as much as you like, the pasture that grows from rain will not grow from this water. So it is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who revived this land after its death, meaning after it had been dry and lifeless with no vegetation, Allah, glorified and exalted, revived it by His power.

He said: (﴿كَذَلِكَ النُّشُورُ﴾ "Thus is the resurrection", meaning the raising and the reviving). ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ (the kāf here is a noun meaning "like"), and it is the predicate placed first, and ﴿النُّشُورُ﴾ (an-nushūr, "the resurrection") is the delayed subject. That is: the resurrection is like that. It is also permissible to say that ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ (the kāf) is a preposition, not meaning "like"; that is, it is not on the pattern of (...). You make it a prepositional phrase functioning as a predicate placed first, and an-nushūr is the delayed subject. The meaning is: the resurrection exists in that manner. The nushūr is the spreading of the dead over the surface of the earth and their revival after they had been dead.

Here the comparison: is it a comparison of cause and effect, or of effect only? That is, does the meaning mean that the resurrection of the dead occurs by means of water that Allah sends down, causing these bodies to grow and then come to life? Or is the comparison only with the outcome, that is, the revival of the dead is like the revival of the earth regardless of the first cause? For the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah, the Exalted, will send upon the earth a rain from beneath the Throne, a heavy rain, until it reaches the bodies, and they grow in the graves as a seed grows in the earth. Then when the bodies are complete, the Trumpet is blown, and the spirits go out to their bodies." Based on this, the comparison here also refers to both cause and effect. This is the well-known view among the people of knowledge. He says: ﴿Thus is the resurrection﴾.

﴿مَنْ كَانَ يُرِيدُ الْعِزَّةَ﴾ ("Whoever desires honor") [Fatir 10]. Is ﴿مَنْ﴾ (man, "whoever") an interrogative or a conditional?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is not after (...). What comes after ﴿مَنْ﴾ is an interrogative, but the answer and the condition are clear in it. That is, we say: Whoever desires honor, then to Allah belongs all honor. ﴿مَنْ كَانَ﴾ is general, because interrogative particles, conditional particles, and relative nouns all convey generality.
