That is: anyone who desires honor or seeks it and is eager for it. Honor (al-ʿizza) is dominance, protection, and subduing enemies. ﴿فَلِلَّهِ الْعِزَّةُ جَمِيعًا﴾ ("then to Allah belongs all honor") [Fatir 10]: that is, let him seek it from Him, since honor belongs to Him as possession and sovereign disposal. It is not sought from anyone else. It is like saying: "Whoever wants money, the money is with Zayd." The meaning: let him get the money from Zayd. Here, ﴿مَنْ كَانَ يُرِيدُ الْعِزَّةَ﴾: let him seek honor from Allah, not from anyone else. This is meant as a refutation (...). They worshipped idols in order to take honor from them. In this verse there is an indication that these idols have no honor: ﴿And they took besides Allah gods so that they might be for them a source of honor﴾ [Maryam 81].

The answer: ﴿No!﴾ They will not be a source of honor for them. On the contrary, they will humiliate them at the very time they need honor most: ﴿They will deny their worship of them and will be opposed to them﴾ [Maryam 82]. So where is the honor in these idols or these deities they took besides Allah?!

Regarding honor, it is mentioned in many verses of the Qur'an. In another verse: ﴿And honor belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 8]. There is no contradiction between it and this verse. Honor belongs to Allah in origin; to His Messenger from Allah; and to the believers from Allah. So all honor belongs to Allah, as Allah, the Exalted, said in Surat Āl ʿImrān: ﴿Say: O Allah, Possessor of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You remove sovereignty from whom You will, You honor whom You will and You humiliate whom You will; in Your hand is all good. Indeed You are over all things competent﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 26]. So whoever has honor, it is not an inherent honor of his own essence, but it is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. How is the honor that a person acquires, which comes from Allah, obtained? It is obtained through what Allah has tied honor to, which is faith: ﴿And honor belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾. So whenever a person desires honor, let him be a believer, and the more faith he has in Allah and the stronger his faith in Allah, the more honor he will have and the stronger his honor. For this reason ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We are a people whom Allah has honored through Islam, so whenever we seek honor through other than it, Allah will humiliate us." [Narrated by al-Ḥākim (208).]

He spoke the truth, may Allah be pleased with him. When the Arabs were Arabs without Islam, what were they? They were humble and poor. They would go to Yemen in winter to bring goods from there, and to Syria in summer to bring goods from there. They were poor, eating from others. But when they believed, they became the wealthy ones, and the treasures of Khosrow and Caesar came to Madinah to be spent upon them from Madinah.

So, however much we desire honor, we will only be honored through Islam. The enemies of Allah will never be a cause of our honor. On the contrary, if we take them as allies and befriend them, that is a cause of humiliation: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates those other than yourselves; they will not spare you corruption. They love what causes you distress. Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, but what their breasts conceal is greater. We have made the signs clear to you, if you use reason﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 118].

If you examine reality, you will find it a witness to this saying of Allah, and that the enemies of the Muslims can never strive to raise up the Muslims. Rather, they strive with all their effort to humiliate the believers and abandon them, but they scheme, deceive, mock, and ridicule so that they may attain their aims and set people against one another. The upshot is: if honor belongs to Allah, from where do we seek it? From Allah, not from anyone else: ﴿Then to Allah belongs all honor﴾ [Fatir 10]. ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ (jamīʿan, "all") is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the honor, which is the delayed subject. In His words ﴿فَلِلَّهِ الْعِزَّةُ﴾ ("then to Allah belongs honor"), is there a restriction (ḥaṣr) of honor to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic? What is its aspect?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. If you say: placing the prepositional phrase first is an error, placing the object first is an error, placing the lām first is an error, placing the predicate first is correct.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the prepositional phrase may be other than a predicate. What is the intended meaning? I only know your wording, and I judge by what I hear. If you had said: placing the predicate first, the problem would be solved, whether it is a prepositional phrase or not. So placing the predicate first conveys restriction, because we have a principle we studied: placing what should be delayed first. And His words ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ refer to the types: that is, the generality of types, the generality of times, and the generality of places.

Generality of types: the honor of power, dominance, and invincibility. Times: this world and the Hereafter. Places: in the east and west of the earth: ﴿So to Allah belongs all honor﴾.

The author said: (that is, in this world and the Hereafter). He said: (so it is not attained from Him) — that is, honor is not attained from Allah (except through obeying Him, so let him obey Him). Here in your text is it (fa-yuṭiʿhu, "let him obey Him") or (fa-nuṭiʿhu, "let us obey Him") with the nūn?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, (fa-yuṭiʿhu), that is, whoever desires honor, because He said: ﴿whoever desires honor﴾ [Fatir 10]. The author informed us that the response to the condition is omitted, which is His words (fa-yuṭiʿhu). But the correct view is that the implied meaning is: let him seek it from Him, ﴿whoever desires honor, then to Allah belongs all honor﴾ [Fatir 10], so let him seek it from Him. This includes seeking by the state of one's conduct and seeking by the speech of one's tongue.

As for the opinion of the author, he restricts seeking to the state of conduct only. So the correct view is that the response to the condition is omitted, and its implied meaning is: let him seek it from Him, so that this includes seeking by speech and seeking by conduct. Seeking by speech is for you to say: "O Allah, honor me; O Allah, grant me victory over so-and-so," for example, over my enemy. Seeking by conduct is for you to act in obedience to Allah, indeed in obedience to Allah together with the realization of faith, because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And honor belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 8].

Now, honor has been mentioned. How many places in the Qur'an do you know that mention it besides what we have mentioned? ﴿They say: If we return to Madinah, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 8].

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: At the end of the verse; we have mentioned it.
* Student: (...).

Shaykh: This is "So Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty toward the disbelievers" [al-Ma'idah 54]. Good, and Allah knows best.

﴿To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fatir 10]. ﴿To Him﴾ is a prepositional phrase placed before its governing verb, which is ﴿ascends﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿To Him﴾ refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. When He mentioned that all might belongs to Allah, the Most High then explained the causes of might, saying: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾. The word ﴿ascends﴾ means rises and ascends. As for ﴿the good word﴾, the author says: "(He knows it)", explaining the ascent of the good word as Allah's knowledge of it. This is a distortion of the words from their places. Rather, the verse is meant in its apparent sense: the good word ascends to Allah, that is, it climbs up to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But the author, may Allah forgive us and him, wanted to avoid affirming the essential highness of Allah, so he said "(He knows it)". Had the meaning been knowledge, He would not have said ﴿To Him ascends﴾, because knowledge does not necessarily entail ascent; indeed, the one who knows a thing may be lower than it, is that not so? As when you are at the bottom of a well and you know what is above. In any case, this is a slip by the author, and we ask Allah to pardon him.

We say: to Allah ascends the good word, that is, the good word rises, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is above. The evidences for His highness have been explained in the books of creed, and they are five types: the Book, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma'), reason, and innate nature (fitrah). All of them agree on the highness of Allah, the Most High, in His essence. We have already read in the book al-Iqna' that Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: whoever claims that Allah is with us in His essence, in place, is a disbeliever.

He says here: ﴿the good word﴾. "Kalim" is a collective noun of "kalimah" (word), so it indicates plurality. What is meant by "the good word"? The good word is every word that brings one closer to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Every word that brings one closer to Allah is a good word. So "There is no god but Allah" is among the good words, and "Glory be to Allah," "Praise be to Allah," and "Allah is greatest" are all among the good words. The Qur'an is among the good words, enjoining good and forbidding evil is among the good words, and studying knowledge is among the good words. Every speech that brings one closer to Allah is a good word.

The good word is opposed by two kinds of speech: a bad, wicked word, and a word that is neither this nor that, which cannot be described as good nor as wicked. As for the wicked word, it is like the word of disbelief, cursing, insulting, and cursing those whom it is not permitted to curse, insult, or revile. As for the word that is neither this nor that, it is most of people's speech. Both kinds do not ascend to Allah. The first, because it is wicked, and Allah is Good and accepts only what is good. The second, because it was not intended for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so as to be raised to Him. This second kind, namely that which is neither this nor that, may be good not in itself but because of something else, for the purposes it leads to that are good. A person may speak to someone words that are not good in themselves, but he intends by them to win this man over and bring him comfort and joy, so this speech, which is idle in itself, becomes praiseworthy because of what it was intended for. Likewise, this speech, which is idle in itself, if it is intended to harm someone whom it is not permitted to harm, becomes wicked speech because of something else. Is it wicked in itself or because of something else? Because of something else; that is, because of what it was intended for.

In any case, the good word, whether good in itself or because of something else, ascends to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If you say: how does the good word ascend, since the word is not a body? The word is not a body, but sounds heard through specific movements of the mouth, tongue and lips?

The answer: Allah, the Most High, is able to make the intelligible into something perceptible, as is established in the authentic hadith: "Death will be brought in the form of a white ram, and it will be slaughtered between Paradise and the Fire, and it will be said to the people of Paradise: eternity without death, and to the people of the Fire: eternity without death."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4730), and Muslim (2849/40), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]

He said: His saying "the good word" is in the collective form only because of the multiplicity of its kinds, and the multiplicity of kinds indicates the multiplicity of individual instances all the more. The kinds are many, and the individuals within each kind are likewise many; therefore it is in the plural.

("To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it" [Fatir 10]: "He accepts it".) The author, by his words "He accepts it", informs us that the subject of ﴿raises it﴾ refers to Allah, that is, Allah raises it, and that the pronoun "it" in ﴿raises it﴾ refers to the righteous deed; that is, the righteous deed is accepted by Allah. That the pronoun referring to the subject is Allah, and the object pronoun refers to the deed, this we do not dispute with the author, because it is possible. But we dispute with him his explanation of "raising" as "acceptance", and all of this is an escape from affirming the essential highness, may Allah forgive him.

Rather, we say: the meaning of ﴿raises it﴾ is that it raises this deed, from raising, which is the opposite of descending, raises it to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, because He is above. This explanation of the referents of the pronouns, mentioned by the author, is one of the interpretations mentioned for this verse.

The second interpretation: the righteous deed is raised by the good word. This makes the pronoun in the subject position refer to ﴿the good word﴾, and the pronoun "it" refer to the righteous deed, so the righteous deed is raised by the good word. Those who hold this argue that the righteous deed is not accepted except with Islam, which is the good word "There is no god but Allah"; for if a person does a great many righteous deeds but is not a Muslim, that deed is not raised. So only the good word raises the righteous deed.

The third view is the reverse: the righteous deed raises the good word, so the subject of "raises" is the righteous deed, and the object is "the good word", the reverse of the previous view. What is the reasoning for this? It is said: the righteous deed raises the good word, because the good word without deed does not benefit its speaker; so the good word necessarily requires a righteous deed that raises that good word.

The closer view, and Allah knows best, is that what the author adopted is correct; that is, Allah raises the righteous deed, just as the good word ascends to Allah. When the good word ascends to Allah, Allah bestows favor on the speaker by raising the righteous deed he does. However, we do not agree with the author in explaining "raising" as "acceptance"; we agree with him on the referents of the pronouns, but not on explaining "raising" as "acceptance". Then we say: who raises the righteous deed? Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, raises the righteous deed. So in this verse Allah mentioned speech and deed: He mentioned that the word ascends and that the deed is raised, because raising the deed is like a reward for the good word. When a person speaks a good word and it ascends to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, He accepts it, then raises the righteous deed: "and the righteous deed raises it."

He says: (﴿And those who plot evil deeds﴾ the plottings ﴿evil﴾ against the Prophet) and so on to the end. The waw is for resumption. ﴿Those who﴾ is the subject, and the clause ﴿for them is a severe punishment﴾ is the predicate. His saying ﴿those who plot evil deeds﴾ contains some difficulty, because deeds are not plotted; rather, plotting is done by means of them, that is, one plots through evil deeds. So why is the verb transitive to them? The author informs us that ﴿evil﴾ is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; the estimate is: the evil plottings. So the adjective here modifies the act itself, not what the plotting was done by, because their act itself is an evil plotting, as Allah the Most High said: ﴿And the evil plotting does not encompass anyone but its own people﴾ [Fatir 43]. So ﴿evil﴾ is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, estimated as "the plottings". Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, called the evil deeds "plotting" because a person in reality deceives himself by them and deceives others by them; he holds out to himself hopes of repentance, saying he will repent, or he holds out to himself the vastness of Allah's forbearance and forgiveness, that Allah is abundant in forbearance, forgiveness and mercy, and so He will not punish him for this. So a person's wishful thinking in this matter is of two aspects:

The first aspect: he holds out to himself the hope of repentance, though he does not know whether he will be able to repent. Perhaps his evil deeds will surround him and he will not be able to repent, or perhaps death will come upon him suddenly and he will not be able to repent.

The second kind of deceiving oneself in committing evil deeds: he entertains false hopes from Allah, saying: Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, Allah's mercy is vast, He will pardon me. As many people do when you forbid them from a sin, what do they say to you? They say: Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. Some argue with the verse: ﴿Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa 48], and say: I have not associated partners with Allah, and what is less than shirk Allah forgives. Our answer to this is very simple: we say to him, prove that you are among those whom Allah wills to forgive, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did not say "and He forgives what is less than that" and stop there; rather He restricted it with "for whom He wills." So you must establish that you are among those whom Allah wills to forgive, and then you would have a proof. But to commit the sin which is the cause of punishment, and then to hope from Allah for something He did not promise you, indeed He said "for whom He wills," this is without doubt misguidance on your part.

His saying ﴿the evil deeds﴾: the evil deeds are those whose doing harms the person. Such as what? Drinking wine, theft, adultery, usury, and the like. If you say: this does not harm the person who does it.

Our answer to this: if you mean that its doing never harms the person, this is not correct, because on the Day of Resurrection he will regret, and the doing will harm him on that day. In this world too, it harms him, and how is that? Because sins have effects on the hearts: sins become a black spot in the heart. If the person repents, the heart is polished and returns to its whiteness; otherwise the black spot spreads and the heart becomes dark, and we seek refuge in Allah, until it is sealed so that good cannot reach it, as Allah the Most High said: ﴿Nay, rather, what they used to earn has rusted upon their hearts﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 14]. Indeed sins have great effects on the heart, requiring it to be constricted, and if a person takes some pleasure in this sin, there follows great grief and tightness in the heart. And read, if you wish, the saying of Allah the Most High: ﴿So is one whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam and who is upon light from his Lord? Woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾ [az-Zumar 22]. It becomes clear to you that sin harms its doer, even if he may not feel it, because what he was doing has rusted upon his heart.

Thus the ﴿evil deeds﴾ are evil in every case: they harm their doer in this world, though it may not appear, and may not be clear to him; but in the Hereafter it appears to him and becomes clear, and he wishes he could return to the world to do righteousness.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (﴿And those who plot﴾ the plottings ﴿evil﴾ against the Prophet in the Dar an-Nadwah: by confining him, killing him, or expelling him, as mentioned in al-Anfal.) In truth, if the author means that this is the only thing meant by the verse, to the exclusion of anything else, then it is deficient; but if he means it as an example, then it is correct, for there is no doubt that those people plotted against the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, as Allah the Most High said: ﴿And [recall] when those who disbelieved plotted against you to confine you, kill you, or expel you. They plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of planners﴾ [al-Anfal 30]. The meaning of ﴿to confine you﴾ is to imprison you and detain you; ﴿or kill you﴾ is clear; ﴿or expel you﴾ from Makkah. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of planners.﴾ Thus they, praise be to Allah, did not achieve any of these: they did not confine him, nor kill him, nor expel him. All of these were negated, despite their intense eagerness to carry them out; nothing of them came to pass.

He says: ﴿For them is a severe punishment﴾. This clause is a declarative sentence, and it is in the place of raising as the predicate of what?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) the first?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The predicate of ﴿those who plot﴾.

﴿For them is a severe punishment﴾: punishment means penalty, and "severe" means strong: strong in its pain and affliction, and in its various kinds of heat, cold, thirst, hunger, and other intensities. For them, we seek refuge in Allah, are garments of tar; whenever their skins are burned, Allah the Most High said: ﴿We will replace them with other skins that they may taste the punishment. Indeed Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise﴾ [an-Nisa 56]; ﴿Whenever it subsides, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra 97]. Look at ﴿whenever it subsides, We increase them,﴾ and it becomes clear to you that the increase comes immediately. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is able to keep the blaze at its increase, but it subsides so that in their hearts there remains some hope for lightening of the punishment or for escape; then it returns, and this is more severe, because striking a person with a punishment after hope of its removal is more grievous to him than if the matter were continuous.

His saying ﴿for them is a severe punishment﴾ is detailed in the Book and the Sunnah; whoever traces it in the Qur'an will do well.

He says: ﴿For them is a severe punishment, and the plotting of those will perish﴾. ﴿The plotting﴾ is the subject; where is its predicate? The clause ﴿it will perish﴾ (huwa yabur). The pronoun ﴿huwa﴾ cannot here be a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), because the rule is that a separating pronoun falls between two nouns, not between a noun and a verb; rather it is a subject whose predicate is the clause ﴿yabur﴾, and the nominal clause of subject and predicate is the predicate of ﴿plotting﴾. This structure is used to magnify and emphasize the matter. And his saying ﴿the plotting of those﴾, rather than "the plotting of these", is either to make them remote, because they are not worthy of being brought near, or because they placed themselves in the position of the exalted, who are pointed to from afar. So it makes clear that those who exalted themselves through their plotting, even though they were at the top according to their own claim, this plotting perishes. Perishing means destruction, as Allah the Most High said: ﴿And caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin, Hell, which they will burn in﴾ [Ibrahim 28-29]. So their plotting perishes: it dissolves and vanishes, and benefits them nothing.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the demonstration of Allah's power in sending these gentle winds which carry or stir up this heavy cloud; Allah the Most High said: ﴿And He produces the heavy clouds﴾ [ar-Ra'd 12].

* And among its benefits: the affirmation of causes, and that effects are tied to their causes; by His saying ﴿He sends the winds, and they stir up﴾, for the fa' here indicates causation.

* And among its benefits: in important matters it is appropriate to phrase the past in the form of the present, bringing it vividly to mind; by His saying ﴿and stirs it into clouds﴾ [Fatir 9]. Phrasing the past in the present tense undoubtedly fixes the matter in a person's mind more than mere past tense does.

* And among its benefits: this cloud moves by Allah's command; by His saying ﴿then We drive it to a dead land﴾.

* And among them: (...) that this cloud has awareness, meaning it knows and perceives. Can this be derived from His saying?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, (...), from His saying: ﴿So We drive it﴾, like a camel is driven. On this is based the authentic hadith about the man who heard a voice from the clouds saying: "Water the garden of so-and-so"[[Recorded by Muslim (2984 / 45) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Directing the command to it indicates that it has awareness, and there is no doubt that all creatures, with regard to the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are beings of awareness. Allah the Exalted said concerning the earth and the heaven: ﴿Then He said to them and to the earth, "Come both of you, willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We come willingly."﴾ [Fussilat 11].
* Among its benefits: the demonstration of the power of Allah, glorified and exalted, to bring the earth back to life after its death; by His saying: ﴿So We drive it to a dead land, and bring to life thereby the earth after its death﴾.
* Among them: the validity of describing the earth with life and death, although it is not among the animals; by His saying: ﴿a dead land, and We bring to life thereby﴾.
* Among them: a refutation of the people of kalam (scholastic theology) who say that nothing inanimate can be described as living or dead; for here He affirmed life and death to the earth, and it is inanimate. And Allah the Exalted said about the idols: ﴿They are dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾ [An-Nahl 21].
* And among its benefits: the demonstration of the power of Allah, glorified and exalted, in bringing the earth back to life after its death; for this earth, which was dry and barren, returns to quivering with greenery and flourishing; by His saying: ﴿and We bring to life thereby﴾, where He attributed the giving of life to Himself.
* Also among them: the affirmation of causes; by His saying: ﴿and We bring to life thereby﴾, for the "bi" here denotes causation.
* Among them: the permissibility of attributing a thing to its known cause; by His saying: ﴿and bring to life thereby the earth﴾. Attributing a thing to its known cause is a matter found in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, meaning that it is not required that you associate Allah with it. So if you attribute a thing to its known cause, even without mentioning Allah along with it, there is no harm. But what is forbidden is attributing it to an unknown cause, neither legislated nor sensed, or attributing it to a known cause while associating Allah with it by a particle that implies equality. For example, attributing healing to amulets, loops, threads, and the like is not permissible, because this cause is unknown and so it is not valid. Attributing the softening of the stomach to the medicine you took, so that it softened your stomach, is valid, or not? It is valid, because it is a cause known by the senses. Is attributing healing to the recitation of al-Fatihah permissible?
* Student: Permissible.
* Shaykh: Because it is a cause known by the senses and by the Law: "And how do you know that it is a ruqyah?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2276) and Muslim (2201 / 65) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]. The prohibited thing, then, is attributing a thing to a cause that is neither legislated nor sensed, or attributing it to a legislated or sensed cause while associating Allah with it by a particle that implies equality, such as: "Were it not for Allah and so-and-so." This is not permissible, because it is shirk, in that Allah is associated with another by the "wa" that implies what? Equality. Rather, say: "Were it not for Allah, then so-and-so."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the validity of qiyas (analogy); by His saying: ﴿Thus is the resurrection﴾. The affirmation of qiyas is abundant in the Qur'an; every parable Allah has coined is evidence for qiyas, whether it concerns this world, or humans, or idols, or anything else, for it is evidence for the establishment and validity of qiyas. Yes, because the purpose of a parable is the comparison of the parabled matter with that to which it is compared, and this is qiyas.
* Among its benefits: an indication that the resurrection of the dead is like the revival of the earth after its death, i.e., that rain descends, as has come in the reports: rain descends upon the earth like the semen of men, and it remains for forty days, and bodies grow from it. Then after that He will blow into the Trumpet, and the spirits return to their bodies.

Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Whoever desires honor—then to Allah belongs all honor﴾, to the end.

* In this: an exhortation to seek honor from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; for the meaning is not that whoever desires honor should seek it from Allah, meaning (...) only. You find that everyone desires honor, but if you desire honor, from whom do you seek it? From Allah. So in it is the affirmation that honor is sought from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among its benefits: that there is no honor without Allah, and this is achieved by performing obedience to Allah, seeking His help, and relying on Him. If a person takes pride in his numbers, he will be defeated, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When your great number pleased you, but it availed you nothing, and the earth was confining for you despite its vastness﴾ [At-Tawbah 25]. Even if a person takes pride in his material strength, such as the strength of weapons for example, he will be defeated; and if he seeks help from Allah, he will not be defeated—except for a wisdom that accompanies that specific matter, in which case it may happen.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of honor to Allah, glorified and exalted; by His saying: ﴿then to Allah belongs all honor﴾.
* Among its benefits: that honor has a whole and parts. From where is this taken?
* Student: ﴿jamee'an﴾ (all).
* Shaykh: ﴿Jamee'an﴾, meaning: it indicates that there is a whole and parts. This is because the scholars divided the honor that Allah is described with into three categories: the honor of unassailability, the honor of standing, and the honor of dominance.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's exaltedness (ʿUluw). From where is it taken?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: ﴿To Him ascends﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿To Him ascends﴾, for ascent is elevation.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the good word does not ascend to Allah... rather, the impure word does not ascend to Allah; by His saying: ﴿the good word﴾. This is confirmed by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed Allah is Good and accepts only what is good"[[Recorded by Muslim (1015 / 65) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication of the division of speech; by His saying: ﴿the good﴾, for this description singles out what is other than it. We have mentioned that what is opposed to the good word is of two kinds of speech: the evil, and that which is neither good nor evil. As for the evil, it is rejected in every case, because it is evil in its essence. As for that which is neither good nor evil, we said that this category of speech may be good by virtue of something else, evil by virtue of something else, and free of both qualities.
If it is good by virtue of something else, does it ascend to Allah or not? It ascends, by the generality of His saying: ﴿the good word﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, does not raise any deeds except those that are righteous; by His saying: ﴿and righteous deed raises it﴾. Righteous deed is that which comprises two qualities. What are they?
* Student: Sincerity and following (the Sunnah).
* Shaykh: Sincerity to whom?
* Student: To Allah, glorified and exalted, and following His Law.
* Shaykh: And following His Law. Sincerity to Allah, and following His Law. If sincerity is absent, it is not a righteous deed, because it is shirk; and if following is absent, it is not a righteous deed, because it is an innovation.
﴿And those who plot evil deeds—for them is a severe punishment, and their plotting will perish﴾, to the end [Fatir: 10].
* Among its benefits:
* Firstly: that evil deeds are a plot; by His saying: ﴿And those who plot evil deeds﴾. This applies if we take it in its general sense. But if we say that "evil deeds" is a general term intended in a specific sense, like the plot that the Quraysh carried out against the Messenger ﷺ, then it is specific. However, the principle in general speech is that it is intended in its generality, and that it remains upon its generality until there is evidence that it is intended in a particular sense, or that it is restricted.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the severe warning against those who plot evil deeds; by His saying: ﴿for them is a severe punishment﴾ [Fatir 10].
* Among its benefits also: that the plot of these people is perishing and vanishing, with no benefit in it; by His saying: ﴿and their plotting will perish﴾ [Fatir 10], and even their deeds will not benefit them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will advance to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [Al-Furqan 23].
These are the apparent benefits of these noble verses, and perhaps upon reflection a person will find more, for the words of Allah, glorified and exalted, cannot be encompassed, but people differ in understanding.

Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾ [Fatir 9]. In one reading it is ﴿الرِّيحَ﴾ (ar-rīḥa, singular). ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾: Allah alone sends these winds, not anyone else. No one can send any of these winds. Even if all of creation gathered together to send the wind, they could not do it. If they gathered together to soften its violence, they could not do that either. That is in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Allah alone sends the winds.

Consider His words ﴿أَرْسَلَ﴾ (arsala, "sent"). He made the wind a messenger, as if it conveys or carries out what it has been commanded, just as a messenger conveys what he was sent with. Thus it is "sent." For this reason, it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he forbade cursing the wind, because cursing the wind ultimately returns to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since it is He who sent it. It is directed and subjected by Him.

His words ﴿الرِّيَاحَ﴾ (ar-riyāḥ, plural), and in one reading ﴿الرِّيحَ﴾ (ar-rīḥ, singular). The reading here is one of the seven canonical readings (qirāʾa sabʿiyya). The difference between them is that ar-riyāḥ is plural and ar-rīḥ is singular, but this singular carries the sense of the plural because it has the definite article (al-), which here is for comprehensiveness (istighrāq, "encompassing all members of a class"). So it includes all winds, whether they come from the north, the south, the east, or the west. Allah, the Exalted, is the One who sends them. Know that, generally, when winds are plural they are associated with goodness, and when the wind is singular it tends to be the opposite. This is the general rule.

For this reason, it is related from the Prophet ﷺ in his supplication concerning the wind: "O Allah, make it winds (riyāḥan) and do not make it a wind (rīḥan)." [Narrated by ash-Shāfiʿī in his Musnad (537), and Abū Yaʿlā (2456).] However, in spite of this, one may be used in place of the other, and there is an indication (qarīna) that determines the meaning. In His words, the Exalted: ﴿And in ʿĀd, when We sent upon them the barren wind﴾ [adh-Dhāriyāt 41]: this is in the context of evil. ﴿Until, when you are in the ships and they sail with them by a good wind﴾ [Yūnus 22]: this is for good, because it is described (as "good"). ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good news before His mercy﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 57]: this is for good. And here too it is for good: ﴿He sends the winds, and they stir up clouds﴾ [ar-Rūm 48]. (tuthīru, "they stir up") is the present tense conjoined to the past tense. The expected pattern would be to conjoin a past tense to a past tense, saying "and Allah who sent the winds, and they stirred up," but why did He shift from the past to the present?

The author explained it, may Allah have mercy on him, saying: "The present tense is used for narrating a past situation." That is, He expressed the past with the present tense to depict the situation at the time of their sending, because it is more vivid in the imagination, as if they were now before you stirring up these clouds. This is more effective in conveying the image to a person, because it brings the past situation to mind as though it were happening now. As we all know, the present tense (al-muḍāriʿ) can refer to the present and the future. It may be made specifically past by an accompanying indicator, and it may be made specifically present or future by other indicators. Its basic use is for the present and future, and it refers to the past only with an indicator. Therefore we say: He shifted from the past tense here in order to narrate a past situation, so that it is as if you are witnessing it now, stirring up these clouds.

The author said regarding (tuthīru, "they stir up"): that is, they agitate (tuzʿiju). This meaning may be debated, because agitation (al-izʿāj) is more specific than stirring up (al-ithāra). Stirring up (ithāra) means causing something to rise, as one says: "I stirred up the camel," meaning I made it stand up after it had been kneeling.

His words ﴿فَتُثِيرُ سَحَابًا﴾ (fa-tuthīru saḥāban, "so they stir up clouds"): it is as though this cloud was originally on the earth, and then these winds stirred it up. It is known that clouds come from the vapor of the sea, and sometimes from the air saturated with moisture, according to what the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, requires. This is a matter that is known through the natural sciences.

His words ﴿فَتُثِيرُ سَحَابًا﴾: the sahāb (cloud) is this well-known cloud (...). It moves (yanḥasib) through the air, as you observe, and that is why it is called saḥāb, from its gliding (insiḥāb) through the air. ﴿So they stir up clouds﴾.

(﴿فَسُقْنَاهُ﴾, "so We drove it," involves a shift from the third person to the first person [iltifāt, "a shift in grammatical person"]). There is also a shift from the present to the past tense. Note this carefully. ﴿He sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, so We drove it﴾ [Fatir 9]. He shifted from the present to the past because the subjects of the two verbs differ. In (tuthīru), the subject is (the winds), and in (saqnāhu, "We drove it"), the subject is (Allah). So it is appropriate for it to be in the past tense, conjoined to His words ﴿أَرْسَلَ﴾ ("sent"), because the one who sent is Allah. Since the subject of both verbs ﴿أَرْسَلَ﴾ and (saqnā, "We drove") is the same, it would be more eloquent for both to be in the past tense. But there is a shift from the third person in His words ﴿And it is Allah who sent﴾ [Fatir 9] to the first person in His words ﴿so We drove it﴾. Why? It has been pointed out to us that iltifāt has a constant benefit, which is what?

* Student: Alerting the listener.
* Shaykh: Alerting? How? Because a uniform style keeps the mind flowing along without stopping. But when the style changes, the mind pauses to see what has happened, and changing it is therefore an alert to the addressee. Yes, that is one benefit.

But here there is also a second benefit, which is showing the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿So We drove it﴾, meaning: We. He attributed it to Himself because that shows His power more clearly. So when ﴿Allah, who sent﴾ is combined with the fact that He, glorified and exalted is He, drove the cloud that the wind had stirred up, that is a clearer indication of power than if it had come in one uniform style: ﴿So We drove it to a dead land﴾ [Fatir 9], with both the doubled and single consonant readings (bi-t-tashdīd wa-t-takhfīf).

The second benefit is the demonstration of complete power, because when it begins in the third person and then comes in the first person, it is a stronger and greater indication of power.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, this is from the perspective of iltifāt, from the basic structure.

He says: ﴿إِلَى بَلَدٍ مَيِّتٍ﴾ (ilā baladin mayyit, "to a dead land") has two readings: mayyit and mayt. It has been said that al-mayt (with the lighter form) refers to one who has already died, and al-mayyit (with the doubled form) refers to one who is going to die. They cite as evidence His words: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ [az-Zumar 30], meaning "you will die." And His words: ﴿Is one who was dead (maytan) and We gave him life﴾ [al-Anʿām 122], where maytan here refers to one who has already died. Some scholars made this distinction. The apparent view, however, is that the Arabic language uses both forms for both meanings. This verse is an example: mayyit, "one who will die" or "one who has died"? 

* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿إِلَى بَلَدٍ مَيِّتٍ﴾? 
* Students: It has died.
* Shaykh: It has died, and yet it came with the doubled form.

(﴿إِلَى بَلَدٍ مَيِّتٍ﴾, with both the doubled and single forms, meaning there is no vegetation in it.) This is the death of the land. By "land" (al-balad) here is not meant only the inhabited part of the earth, but something more general, including both the inhabited and uninhabited. Restricting "balad" to the inhabited is a customary restriction; otherwise, the whole earth is a balad, because it is flat and spread out (inbilād wa-tasṭīḥ). For this reason He says: ﴿to a dead land, and We revived by it the earth﴾ [Fatir 9]. ﴿فَأَحْيَيْنَا بِهِ﴾ ("We revived by it"): We drove, and ﴿fa-aḥyaynā﴾ ("We revived"). Here the verbs and pronouns are in one consistent style. And His words ﴿فَأَحْيَيْنَا بِهِ الْأَرْضَ﴾ ("We revived by it the earth"). He says: (from the land). What is the meaning of "from the land"? It means the earth of that land, which was dead, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revived it. With what did He revive it? He revived it with vegetation.

For this reason the author said: (﴿بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا﴾ "after its death", meaning its drying out; that is, We made grain and pasture grow from it). This is something observed: the earth comes dry and lifeless, its stalks crumbling, then Allah sends down rain upon it, and it stirs and turns green, with every lovely pair in it. Who revived it? Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Creation cannot revive it at all, no matter what. Even the pasture that grows from rain does not grow from flowing water, as is observed. That is, if you water this land with flowing water as much as you like, the pasture that grows from rain will not grow from this water. So it is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who revived this land after its death, meaning after it had been dry and lifeless with no vegetation, Allah, glorified and exalted, revived it by His power.

He said: (﴿كَذَلِكَ النُّشُورُ﴾ "Thus is the resurrection", meaning the raising and the reviving). ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ (the kāf here is a noun meaning "like"), and it is the predicate placed first, and ﴿النُّشُورُ﴾ (an-nushūr, "the resurrection") is the delayed subject. That is: the resurrection is like that. It is also permissible to say that ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ (the kāf) is a preposition, not meaning "like"; that is, it is not on the pattern of (...). You make it a prepositional phrase functioning as a predicate placed first, and an-nushūr is the delayed subject. The meaning is: the resurrection exists in that manner. The nushūr is the spreading of the dead over the surface of the earth and their revival after they had been dead.

Here the comparison: is it a comparison of cause and effect, or of effect only? That is, does the meaning mean that the resurrection of the dead occurs by means of water that Allah sends down, causing these bodies to grow and then come to life? Or is the comparison only with the outcome, that is, the revival of the dead is like the revival of the earth regardless of the first cause? For the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah, the Exalted, will send upon the earth a rain from beneath the Throne, a heavy rain, until it reaches the bodies, and they grow in the graves as a seed grows in the earth. Then when the bodies are complete, the Trumpet is blown, and the spirits go out to their bodies." Based on this, the comparison here also refers to both cause and effect. This is the well-known view among the people of knowledge. He says: ﴿Thus is the resurrection﴾.

﴿مَنْ كَانَ يُرِيدُ الْعِزَّةَ﴾ ("Whoever desires honor") [Fatir 10]. Is ﴿مَنْ﴾ (man, "whoever") an interrogative or a conditional?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is not after (...). What comes after ﴿مَنْ﴾ is an interrogative, but the answer and the condition are clear in it. That is, we say: Whoever desires honor, then to Allah belongs all honor. ﴿مَنْ كَانَ﴾ is general, because interrogative particles, conditional particles, and relative nouns all convey generality. That is: anyone who desires honor or seeks it and is eager for it. Honor (al-ʿizza) is dominance, protection, and subduing enemies. ﴿فَلِلَّهِ الْعِزَّةُ جَمِيعًا﴾ ("then to Allah belongs all honor") [Fatir 10]: that is, let him seek it from Him, since honor belongs to Him as possession and sovereign disposal. It is not sought from anyone else. It is like saying: "Whoever wants money, the money is with Zayd." The meaning: let him get the money from Zayd. Here, ﴿مَنْ كَانَ يُرِيدُ الْعِزَّةَ﴾: let him seek honor from Allah, not from anyone else. This is meant as a refutation (...). They worshipped idols in order to take honor from them. In this verse there is an indication that these idols have no honor: ﴿And they took besides Allah gods so that they might be for them a source of honor﴾ [Maryam 81].

The answer: ﴿No!﴾ They will not be a source of honor for them. On the contrary, they will humiliate them at the very time they need honor most: ﴿They will deny their worship of them and will be opposed to them﴾ [Maryam 82]. So where is the honor in these idols or these deities they took besides Allah?!

Regarding honor, it is mentioned in many verses of the Qur'an. In another verse: ﴿And honor belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 8]. There is no contradiction between it and this verse. Honor belongs to Allah in origin; to His Messenger from Allah; and to the believers from Allah. So all honor belongs to Allah, as Allah, the Exalted, said in Surat Āl ʿImrān: ﴿Say: O Allah, Possessor of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You remove sovereignty from whom You will, You honor whom You will and You humiliate whom You will; in Your hand is all good. Indeed You are over all things competent﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 26]. So whoever has honor, it is not an inherent honor of his own essence, but it is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. How is the honor that a person acquires, which comes from Allah, obtained? It is obtained through what Allah has tied honor to, which is faith: ﴿And honor belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾. So whenever a person desires honor, let him be a believer, and the more faith he has in Allah and the stronger his faith in Allah, the more honor he will have and the stronger his honor. For this reason ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We are a people whom Allah has honored through Islam, so whenever we seek honor through other than it, Allah will humiliate us." [Narrated by al-Ḥākim (208).]

He spoke the truth, may Allah be pleased with him. When the Arabs were Arabs without Islam, what were they? They were humble and poor. They would go to Yemen in winter to bring goods from there, and to Syria in summer to bring goods from there. They were poor, eating from others. But when they believed, they became the wealthy ones, and the treasures of Khosrow and Caesar came to Madinah to be spent upon them from Madinah.

So, however much we desire honor, we will only be honored through Islam. The enemies of Allah will never be a cause of our honor. On the contrary, if we take them as allies and befriend them, that is a cause of humiliation: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates those other than yourselves; they will not spare you corruption. They love what causes you distress. Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, but what their breasts conceal is greater. We have made the signs clear to you, if you use reason﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 118].

If you examine reality, you will find it a witness to this saying of Allah, and that the enemies of the Muslims can never strive to raise up the Muslims. Rather, they strive with all their effort to humiliate the believers and abandon them, but they scheme, deceive, mock, and ridicule so that they may attain their aims and set people against one another. The upshot is: if honor belongs to Allah, from where do we seek it? From Allah, not from anyone else: ﴿Then to Allah belongs all honor﴾ [Fatir 10]. ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ (jamīʿan, "all") is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the honor, which is the delayed subject. In His words ﴿فَلِلَّهِ الْعِزَّةُ﴾ ("then to Allah belongs honor"), is there a restriction (ḥaṣr) of honor to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic? What is its aspect?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. If you say: placing the prepositional phrase first is an error, placing the object first is an error, placing the lām first is an error, placing the predicate first is correct.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the prepositional phrase may be other than a predicate. What is the intended meaning? I only know your wording, and I judge by what I hear. If you had said: placing the predicate first, the problem would be solved, whether it is a prepositional phrase or not. So placing the predicate first conveys restriction, because we have a principle we studied: placing what should be delayed first. And His words ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ refer to the types: that is, the generality of types, the generality of times, and the generality of places.

Generality of types: the honor of power, dominance, and invincibility. Times: this world and the Hereafter. Places: in the east and west of the earth: ﴿So to Allah belongs all honor﴾.

The author said: (that is, in this world and the Hereafter). He said: (so it is not attained from Him) — that is, honor is not attained from Allah (except through obeying Him, so let him obey Him). Here in your text is it (fa-yuṭiʿhu, "let him obey Him") or (fa-nuṭiʿhu, "let us obey Him") with the nūn?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, (fa-yuṭiʿhu), that is, whoever desires honor, because He said: ﴿whoever desires honor﴾ [Fatir 10]. The author informed us that the response to the condition is omitted, which is His words (fa-yuṭiʿhu). But the correct view is that the implied meaning is: let him seek it from Him, ﴿whoever desires honor, then to Allah belongs all honor﴾ [Fatir 10], so let him seek it from Him. This includes seeking by the state of one's conduct and seeking by the speech of one's tongue.

As for the opinion of the author, he restricts seeking to the state of conduct only. So the correct view is that the response to the condition is omitted, and its implied meaning is: let him seek it from Him, so that this includes seeking by speech and seeking by conduct. Seeking by speech is for you to say: "O Allah, honor me; O Allah, grant me victory over so-and-so," for example, over my enemy. Seeking by conduct is for you to act in obedience to Allah, indeed in obedience to Allah together with the realization of faith, because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And honor belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 8].

Now, honor has been mentioned. How many places in the Qur'an do you know that mention it besides what we have mentioned? ﴿They say: If we return to Madinah, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 8].

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: At the end of the verse; we have mentioned it.
* Student: (...).

Shaykh: This is "So Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty toward the disbelievers" [al-Ma'idah 54]. Good, and Allah knows best.

﴿To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fatir 10]. ﴿To Him﴾ is a prepositional phrase placed before its governing verb, which is ﴿ascends﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿To Him﴾ refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. When He mentioned that all might belongs to Allah, the Most High then explained the causes of might, saying: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾. The word ﴿ascends﴾ means rises and ascends. As for ﴿the good word﴾, the author says: "(He knows it)", explaining the ascent of the good word as Allah's knowledge of it. This is a distortion of the words from their places. Rather, the verse is meant in its apparent sense: the good word ascends to Allah, that is, it climbs up to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But the author, may Allah forgive us and him, wanted to avoid affirming the essential highness of Allah, so he said "(He knows it)". Had the meaning been knowledge, He would not have said ﴿To Him ascends﴾, because knowledge does not necessarily entail ascent; indeed, the one who knows a thing may be lower than it, is that not so? As when you are at the bottom of a well and you know what is above. In any case, this is a slip by the author, and we ask Allah to pardon him.

We say: to Allah ascends the good word, that is, the good word rises, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is above. The evidences for His highness have been explained in the books of creed, and they are five types: the Book, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma'), reason, and innate nature (fitrah). All of them agree on the highness of Allah, the Most High, in His essence. We have already read in the book al-Iqna' that Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: whoever claims that Allah is with us in His essence, in place, is a disbeliever.

He says here: ﴿the good word﴾. "Kalim" is a collective noun of "kalimah" (word), so it indicates plurality. What is meant by "the good word"? The good word is every word that brings one closer to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Every word that brings one closer to Allah is a good word. So "There is no god but Allah" is among the good words, and "Glory be to Allah," "Praise be to Allah," and "Allah is greatest" are all among the good words. The Qur'an is among the good words, enjoining good and forbidding evil is among the good words, and studying knowledge is among the good words. Every speech that brings one closer to Allah is a good word.

The good word is opposed by two kinds of speech: a bad, wicked word, and a word that is neither this nor that, which cannot be described as good nor as wicked. As for the wicked word, it is like the word of disbelief, cursing, insulting, and cursing those whom it is not permitted to curse, insult, or revile. As for the word that is neither this nor that, it is most of people's speech. Both kinds do not ascend to Allah. The first, because it is wicked, and Allah is Good and accepts only what is good. The second, because it was not intended for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so as to be raised to Him. This second kind, namely that which is neither this nor that, may be good not in itself but because of something else, for the purposes it leads to that are good. A person may speak to someone words that are not good in themselves, but he intends by them to win this man over and bring him comfort and joy, so this speech, which is idle in itself, becomes praiseworthy because of what it was intended for. Likewise, this speech, which is idle in itself, if it is intended to harm someone whom it is not permitted to harm, becomes wicked speech because of something else. Is it wicked in itself or because of something else? Because of something else; that is, because of what it was intended for.

In any case, the good word, whether good in itself or because of something else, ascends to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If you say: how does the good word ascend, since the word is not a body? The word is not a body, but sounds heard through specific movements of the mouth, tongue and lips?

The answer: Allah, the Most High, is able to make the intelligible into something perceptible, as is established in the authentic hadith: "Death will be brought in the form of a white ram, and it will be slaughtered between Paradise and the Fire, and it will be said to the people of Paradise: eternity without death, and to the people of the Fire: eternity without death."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4730), and Muslim (2849/40), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]

He said: His saying "the good word" is in the collective form only because of the multiplicity of its kinds, and the multiplicity of kinds indicates the multiplicity of individual instances all the more. The kinds are many, and the individuals within each kind are likewise many; therefore it is in the plural.

("To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it" [Fatir 10]: "He accepts it".) The author, by his words "He accepts it", informs us that the subject of ﴿raises it﴾ refers to Allah, that is, Allah raises it, and that the pronoun "it" in ﴿raises it﴾ refers to the righteous deed; that is, the righteous deed is accepted by Allah. That the pronoun referring to the subject is Allah, and the object pronoun refers to the deed, this we do not dispute with the author, because it is possible. But we dispute with him his explanation of "raising" as "acceptance", and all of this is an escape from affirming the essential highness, may Allah forgive him.

Rather, we say: the meaning of ﴿raises it﴾ is that it raises this deed, from raising, which is the opposite of descending, raises it to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, because He is above. This explanation of the referents of the pronouns, mentioned by the author, is one of the interpretations mentioned for this verse.

The second interpretation: the righteous deed is raised by the good word. This makes the pronoun in the subject position refer to ﴿the good word﴾, and the pronoun "it" refer to the righteous deed, so the righteous deed is raised by the good word. Those who hold this argue that the righteous deed is not accepted except with Islam, which is the good word "There is no god but Allah"; for if a person does a great many righteous deeds but is not a Muslim, that deed is not raised. So only the good word raises the righteous deed.

The third view is the reverse: the righteous deed raises the good word, so the subject of "raises" is the righteous deed, and the object is "the good word", the reverse of the previous view. What is the reasoning for this? It is said: the righteous deed raises the good word, because the good word without deed does not benefit its speaker; so the good word necessarily requires a righteous deed that raises that good word.

The closer view, and Allah knows best, is that what the author adopted is correct; that is, Allah raises the righteous deed, just as the good word ascends to Allah. When the good word ascends to Allah, Allah bestows favor on the speaker by raising the righteous deed he does. However, we do not agree with the author in explaining "raising" as "acceptance"; we agree with him on the referents of the pronouns, but not on explaining "raising" as "acceptance". Then we say: who raises the righteous deed? Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, raises the righteous deed. So in this verse Allah mentioned speech and deed: He mentioned that the word ascends and that the deed is raised, because raising the deed is like a reward for the good word. When a person speaks a good word and it ascends to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, He accepts it, then raises the righteous deed: "and the righteous deed raises it."

He says: (﴿And those who plot evil deeds﴾ the plottings ﴿evil﴾ against the Prophet) and so on to the end. The waw is for resumption. ﴿Those who﴾ is the subject, and the clause ﴿for them is a severe punishment﴾ is the predicate. His saying ﴿those who plot evil deeds﴾ contains some difficulty, because deeds are not plotted; rather, plotting is done by means of them, that is, one plots through evil deeds. So why is the verb transitive to them? The author informs us that ﴿evil﴾ is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; the estimate is: the evil plottings. So the adjective here modifies the act itself, not what the plotting was done by, because their act itself is an evil plotting, as Allah the Most High said: ﴿And the evil plotting does not encompass anyone but its own people﴾ [Fatir 43]. So ﴿evil﴾ is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, estimated as "the plottings". Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, called the evil deeds "plotting" because a person in reality deceives himself by them and deceives others by them; he holds out to himself hopes of repentance, saying he will repent, or he holds out to himself the vastness of Allah's forbearance and forgiveness, that Allah is abundant in forbearance, forgiveness and mercy, and so He will not punish him for this. So a person's wishful thinking in this matter is of two aspects:

The first aspect: he holds out to himself the hope of repentance, though he does not know whether he will be able to repent. Perhaps his evil deeds will surround him and he will not be able to repent, or perhaps death will come upon him suddenly and he will not be able to repent.

The second kind of deceiving oneself in committing evil deeds: he entertains false hopes from Allah, saying: Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, Allah's mercy is vast, He will pardon me. As many people do when you forbid them from a sin, what do they say to you? They say: Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. Some argue with the verse: ﴿Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa 48], and say: I have not associated partners with Allah, and what is less than shirk Allah forgives. Our answer to this is very simple: we say to him, prove that you are among those whom Allah wills to forgive, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did not say "and He forgives what is less than that" and stop there; rather He restricted it with "for whom He wills." So you must establish that you are among those whom Allah wills to forgive, and then you would have a proof. But to commit the sin which is the cause of punishment, and then to hope from Allah for something He did not promise you, indeed He said "for whom He wills," this is without doubt misguidance on your part.

His saying ﴿the evil deeds﴾: the evil deeds are those whose doing harms the person. Such as what? Drinking wine, theft, adultery, usury, and the like. If you say: this does not harm the person who does it.

Our answer to this: if you mean that its doing never harms the person, this is not correct, because on the Day of Resurrection he will regret, and the doing will harm him on that day. In this world too, it harms him, and how is that? Because sins have effects on the hearts: sins become a black spot in the heart. If the person repents, the heart is polished and returns to its whiteness; otherwise the black spot spreads and the heart becomes dark, and we seek refuge in Allah, until it is sealed so that good cannot reach it, as Allah the Most High said: ﴿Nay, rather, what they used to earn has rusted upon their hearts﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 14]. Indeed sins have great effects on the heart, requiring it to be constricted, and if a person takes some pleasure in this sin, there follows great grief and tightness in the heart. And read, if you wish, the saying of Allah the Most High: ﴿So is one whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam and who is upon light from his Lord? Woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾ [az-Zumar 22]. It becomes clear to you that sin harms its doer, even if he may not feel it, because what he was doing has rusted upon his heart.

Thus the ﴿evil deeds﴾ are evil in every case: they harm their doer in this world, though it may not appear, and may not be clear to him; but in the Hereafter it appears to him and becomes clear, and he wishes he could return to the world to do righteousness.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (﴿And those who plot﴾ the plottings ﴿evil﴾ against the Prophet in the Dar an-Nadwah: by confining him, killing him, or expelling him, as mentioned in al-Anfal.) In truth, if the author means that this is the only thing meant by the verse, to the exclusion of anything else, then it is deficient; but if he means it as an example, then it is correct, for there is no doubt that those people plotted against the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, as Allah the Most High said: ﴿And [recall] when those who disbelieved plotted against you to confine you, kill you, or expel you. They plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of planners﴾ [al-Anfal 30]. The meaning of ﴿to confine you﴾ is to imprison you and detain you; ﴿or kill you﴾ is clear; ﴿or expel you﴾ from Makkah. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of planners.﴾ Thus they, praise be to Allah, did not achieve any of these: they did not confine him, nor kill him, nor expel him. All of these were negated, despite their intense eagerness to carry them out; nothing of them came to pass.

He says: ﴿For them is a severe punishment﴾. This clause is a declarative sentence, and it is in the place of raising as the predicate of what?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) the first?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The predicate of ﴿those who plot﴾.

﴿For them is a severe punishment﴾: punishment means penalty, and "severe" means strong: strong in its pain and affliction, and in its various kinds of heat, cold, thirst, hunger, and other intensities. For them, we seek refuge in Allah, are garments of tar; whenever their skins are burned, Allah the Most High said: ﴿We will replace them with other skins that they may taste the punishment. Indeed Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise﴾ [an-Nisa 56]; ﴿Whenever it subsides, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra 97]. Look at ﴿whenever it subsides, We increase them,﴾ and it becomes clear to you that the increase comes immediately. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is able to keep the blaze at its increase, but it subsides so that in their hearts there remains some hope for lightening of the punishment or for escape; then it returns, and this is more severe, because striking a person with a punishment after hope of its removal is more grievous to him than if the matter were continuous.

His saying ﴿for them is a severe punishment﴾ is detailed in the Book and the Sunnah; whoever traces it in the Qur'an will do well.

He says: ﴿For them is a severe punishment, and the plotting of those will perish﴾. ﴿The plotting﴾ is the subject; where is its predicate? The clause ﴿it will perish﴾ (huwa yabur). The pronoun ﴿huwa﴾ cannot here be a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), because the rule is that a separating pronoun falls between two nouns, not between a noun and a verb; rather it is a subject whose predicate is the clause ﴿yabur﴾, and the nominal clause of subject and predicate is the predicate of ﴿plotting﴾. This structure is used to magnify and emphasize the matter. And his saying ﴿the plotting of those﴾, rather than "the plotting of these", is either to make them remote, because they are not worthy of being brought near, or because they placed themselves in the position of the exalted, who are pointed to from afar. So it makes clear that those who exalted themselves through their plotting, even though they were at the top according to their own claim, this plotting perishes. Perishing means destruction, as Allah the Most High said: ﴿And caused their people to alight in the abode of ruin, Hell, which they will burn in﴾ [Ibrahim 28-29]. So their plotting perishes: it dissolves and vanishes, and benefits them nothing.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the demonstration of Allah's power in sending these gentle winds which carry or stir up this heavy cloud; Allah the Most High said: ﴿And He produces the heavy clouds﴾ [ar-Ra'd 12].

* And among its benefits: the affirmation of causes, and that effects are tied to their causes; by His saying ﴿He sends the winds, and they stir up﴾, for the fa' here indicates causation.

* And among its benefits: in important matters it is appropriate to phrase the past in the form of the present, bringing it vividly to mind; by His saying ﴿and stirs it into clouds﴾ [Fatir 9]. Phrasing the past in the present tense undoubtedly fixes the matter in a person's mind more than mere past tense does.

* And among its benefits: this cloud moves by Allah's command; by His saying ﴿then We drive it to a dead land﴾.

* And among them: (...) that this cloud has awareness, meaning it knows and perceives. Can this be derived from His saying?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, (...), from His saying: ﴿So We drive it﴾, like a camel is driven. On this is based the authentic hadith about the man who heard a voice from the clouds saying: "Water the garden of so-and-so"[[Recorded by Muslim (2984 / 45) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Directing the command to it indicates that it has awareness, and there is no doubt that all creatures, with regard to the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are beings of awareness. Allah the Exalted said concerning the earth and the heaven: ﴿Then He said to them and to the earth, "Come both of you, willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We come willingly."﴾ [Fussilat 11].
* Among its benefits: the demonstration of the power of Allah, glorified and exalted, to bring the earth back to life after its death; by His saying: ﴿So We drive it to a dead land, and bring to life thereby the earth after its death﴾.
* Among them: the validity of describing the earth with life and death, although it is not among the animals; by His saying: ﴿a dead land, and We bring to life thereby﴾.
* Among them: a refutation of the people of kalam (scholastic theology) who say that nothing inanimate can be described as living or dead; for here He affirmed life and death to the earth, and it is inanimate. And Allah the Exalted said about the idols: ﴿They are dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾ [An-Nahl 21].
* And among its benefits: the demonstration of the power of Allah, glorified and exalted, in bringing the earth back to life after its death; for this earth, which was dry and barren, returns to quivering with greenery and flourishing; by His saying: ﴿and We bring to life thereby﴾, where He attributed the giving of life to Himself.
* Also among them: the affirmation of causes; by His saying: ﴿and We bring to life thereby﴾, for the "bi" here denotes causation.
* Among them: the permissibility of attributing a thing to its known cause; by His saying: ﴿and bring to life thereby the earth﴾. Attributing a thing to its known cause is a matter found in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, meaning that it is not required that you associate Allah with it. So if you attribute a thing to its known cause, even without mentioning Allah along with it, there is no harm. But what is forbidden is attributing it to an unknown cause, neither legislated nor sensed, or attributing it to a known cause while associating Allah with it by a particle that implies equality. For example, attributing healing to amulets, loops, threads, and the like is not permissible, because this cause is unknown and so it is not valid. Attributing the softening of the stomach to the medicine you took, so that it softened your stomach, is valid, or not? It is valid, because it is a cause known by the senses. Is attributing healing to the recitation of al-Fatihah permissible?
* Student: Permissible.
* Shaykh: Because it is a cause known by the senses and by the Law: "And how do you know that it is a ruqyah?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2276) and Muslim (2201 / 65) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]. The prohibited thing, then, is attributing a thing to a cause that is neither legislated nor sensed, or attributing it to a legislated or sensed cause while associating Allah with it by a particle that implies equality, such as: "Were it not for Allah and so-and-so." This is not permissible, because it is shirk, in that Allah is associated with another by the "wa" that implies what? Equality. Rather, say: "Were it not for Allah, then so-and-so."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the validity of qiyas (analogy); by His saying: ﴿Thus is the resurrection﴾. The affirmation of qiyas is abundant in the Qur'an; every parable Allah has coined is evidence for qiyas, whether it concerns this world, or humans, or idols, or anything else, for it is evidence for the establishment and validity of qiyas. Yes, because the purpose of a parable is the comparison of the parabled matter with that to which it is compared, and this is qiyas.
* Among its benefits: an indication that the resurrection of the dead is like the revival of the earth after its death, i.e., that rain descends, as has come in the reports: rain descends upon the earth like the semen of men, and it remains for forty days, and bodies grow from it. Then after that He will blow into the Trumpet, and the spirits return to their bodies.

Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Whoever desires honor—then to Allah belongs all honor﴾, to the end.

* In this: an exhortation to seek honor from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; for the meaning is not that whoever desires honor should seek it from Allah, meaning (...) only. You find that everyone desires honor, but if you desire honor, from whom do you seek it? From Allah. So in it is the affirmation that honor is sought from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among its benefits: that there is no honor without Allah, and this is achieved by performing obedience to Allah, seeking His help, and relying on Him. If a person takes pride in his numbers, he will be defeated, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When your great number pleased you, but it availed you nothing, and the earth was confining for you despite its vastness﴾ [At-Tawbah 25]. Even if a person takes pride in his material strength, such as the strength of weapons for example, he will be defeated; and if he seeks help from Allah, he will not be defeated—except for a wisdom that accompanies that specific matter, in which case it may happen.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of honor to Allah, glorified and exalted; by His saying: ﴿then to Allah belongs all honor﴾.
* Among its benefits: that honor has a whole and parts. From where is this taken?
* Student: ﴿jamee'an﴾ (all).
* Shaykh: ﴿Jamee'an﴾, meaning: it indicates that there is a whole and parts. This is because the scholars divided the honor that Allah is described with into three categories: the honor of unassailability, the honor of standing, and the honor of dominance.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's exaltedness (ʿUluw). From where is it taken?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: ﴿To Him ascends﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿To Him ascends﴾, for ascent is elevation.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the good word does not ascend to Allah... rather, the impure word does not ascend to Allah; by His saying: ﴿the good word﴾. This is confirmed by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed Allah is Good and accepts only what is good"[[Recorded by Muslim (1015 / 65) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication of the division of speech; by His saying: ﴿the good﴾, for this description singles out what is other than it. We have mentioned that what is opposed to the good word is of two kinds of speech: the evil, and that which is neither good nor evil. As for the evil, it is rejected in every case, because it is evil in its essence. As for that which is neither good nor evil, we said that this category of speech may be good by virtue of something else, evil by virtue of something else, and free of both qualities.
If it is good by virtue of something else, does it ascend to Allah or not? It ascends, by the generality of His saying: ﴿the good word﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, does not raise any deeds except those that are righteous; by His saying: ﴿and righteous deed raises it﴾. Righteous deed is that which comprises two qualities. What are they?
* Student: Sincerity and following (the Sunnah).
* Shaykh: Sincerity to whom?
* Student: To Allah, glorified and exalted, and following His Law.
* Shaykh: And following His Law. Sincerity to Allah, and following His Law. If sincerity is absent, it is not a righteous deed, because it is shirk; and if following is absent, it is not a righteous deed, because it is an innovation.
﴿And those who plot evil deeds—for them is a severe punishment, and their plotting will perish﴾, to the end [Fatir: 10].
* Among its benefits:
* Firstly: that evil deeds are a plot; by His saying: ﴿And those who plot evil deeds﴾. This applies if we take it in its general sense. But if we say that "evil deeds" is a general term intended in a specific sense, like the plot that the Quraysh carried out against the Messenger ﷺ, then it is specific. However, the principle in general speech is that it is intended in its generality, and that it remains upon its generality until there is evidence that it is intended in a particular sense, or that it is restricted.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the severe warning against those who plot evil deeds; by His saying: ﴿for them is a severe punishment﴾ [Fatir 10].
* Among its benefits also: that the plot of these people is perishing and vanishing, with no benefit in it; by His saying: ﴿and their plotting will perish﴾ [Fatir 10], and even their deeds will not benefit them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will advance to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [Al-Furqan 23].
These are the apparent benefits of these noble verses, and perhaps upon reflection a person will find more, for the words of Allah, glorified and exalted, cannot be encompassed, but people differ in understanding.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾ [Fatir 11]. When He, glorified and exalted, had made clear the preceding signs that point to His power—the sending of the winds, the stirring up of the clouds, their driving to a dead land, the giving of life to the earth after its death—and that deeds are raised up to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and likewise words (deeds, whether words or actions, are raised up to Allah), He said here: ﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾. This is with regard to the origin, which is Adam. Hence He said: (by the creation of your father Adam from it), for Allah, exalted is He, created him from dust. This verse, as you see, states that Allah created him from dust, and in another verse that He created him from clay (ṭīn), and in a third verse that He created him from ṣalṣāl like pottery, and in a fourth verse from ḥama’ masnūn (black mud molded into shape). So what is the answer concerning this variation?

The answer is that this is a variation of attributes, not a variation of essences, and therefore there is no contradiction, since it is permissible for several attributes to apply to one described thing. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High (1), who created and proportioned (2), and who determined and guided (3), and who brought forth the pasture﴾ [al-A'la 1–4], although He is one. The conclusion is that here one should say that this variation is a variation of attributes, not a variation of essences and entities.
