The substance is one, but its first state was dust; when water is added to it, it becomes clay (ṭīn); when it is left and takes a period of time, it becomes ḥama’ masnūn, changed—that is, clay, when water is poured into it, you find it turns black and has an odour. The fourth stage, ṣalṣāl like pottery, is after it was ḥama’ masnūn and dried out and became ṣalṣāl like pottery; then Allah breathed into it the spirit. So this variation is a variation of attributes, and its origin is dust.

He said: ﴿And Allah created you from dust, then from a drop (nuṭfah)﴾ [Fatir 11]. ﴿Then﴾ He used (thumma), which indicates delay and sequence, because thumma indicates delay and sequence, whereas the fā’ indicates sequence without delay. Here He said: ﴿then from a drop﴾, because when Allah created Adam, and created his offspring, these offspring were propagated through this water which is the nuṭfah, and the nuṭfah is a small quantity of water.

He said: ﴿then from a drop﴾, meaning semen (maniyy) that gushes forth. Do you have (bi-khalq)? (by creating His offspring from it), that is, from this drop. And it is remarkable that scholars of medicine mention that this small drop contains millions of sperm cells, and these [...] claim they are millions—and they know better than us about that. That is, usually only one, or two, or three, or four of them are suitable. This [...] I have not heard that four thousand enter the woman and one remains. And Allah is capable of all things; He may increase, ﴿He increases in creation what He wills﴾ [Fatir 1].

He says: (﴿Then He made you pairs﴾, males and females). Regarding His words ﴿pairs﴾, the author here explained "pairs" as males and females, by the indication of His words: ﴿and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾ [Fatir 11]. Pay attention: the pairs here are with regard to the two sexes, male and female, and His words ﴿and no female conceives﴾ confirm the restriction of "pairs" here to maleness and femaleness.

As for when we look at the word "pairs" (azwāj), its meaning is kinds, and kinds are more general than maleness and femaleness, for it includes the wretched and the happy, the black and the white, the tall and the short, and other things. But what led the author to restrict the speech to maleness and femaleness only is His words ﴿and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His power and wisdom, made this offspring that came out of this one man into males and females, for the survival of the progeny, since the survival of the progeny is not possible except by this. Although Allah, glorified and exalted, is able to preserve the progeny without that, it is said: mankind includes those created without a mother or father, those created from a father without a mother, those created from a mother without a father, and those created between two parents. So who was created without mother or father?

* Students: Adam.
* The Shaykh: And from a father without a mother?
* Students: Ḥawwā’ (Eve).
* The Shaykh: Ḥawwā’. And from a mother without a father?
* Students: ʿĪsā.
* The Shaykh: And the rest of people?
* Students: Between two parents.
* The Shaykh: Between two parents, male and female.

He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾. (mā) here [...] and the second?
* Student: Transitive.
* The Shaykh: [...] or the transitive?
* Student: [...].
* The Shaykh: [...] intransitive or transitive?
* Student: The first is from the intransitive.
* The Shaykh: From the intransitive.
* Student: And the second is from the transitive.
* The Shaykh: And the second is from the transitive, correct?
* Student: Correct.
* The Shaykh: [...] a superfluous preposition; ﴿unthā﴾ is the subject of ﴿taḥmilu﴾, nominative with an assumed ḍamma on its final letter, prevented from appearing by the difficulty (ta‘adhdhur)—is that so? ﴿unthā﴾ is a subject, nominative with an assumed ḍamma on its last letter, prevented from appearing by the difficulty?
* Student: Preoccupation of the position (ishtighāl al-maḥall).
* The Shaykh: There is no preoccupation here, [...].
* Student: The difficulty (ta‘adhdhur).
* The Shaykh: Fine, the difficulty; but it occurs in terms of the wording, genitive in wording.
﴿unthā and lā taḍa‘﴾ meaning the female; (﴿except with His knowledge﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: known to Him). Look: ﴿what she carries of a female﴾, meaning, what female carries? Of the children of Adam, or of them and others? Of them and others. [...] ﴿and does not give birth except with His knowledge﴾. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾ [al-An‘am 59]. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, knows what every female carries, at the beginning of the pregnancy, its development, its outcome, and everything related to it. ﴿And she does not give birth except with His knowledge﴾: the first thing from which the pregnancy begins in the womb is known to Allah, and when she gives birth, it is known to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

As for the author's words (ḥāl), what is the meaning of ḥāl? It means that the preposition-phrase is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause [...]. ﴿Except with His knowledge﴾: he said, except (known to Him). It is possible to say that there is no need for this interpretation; rather we say that the bāʼ here is for accompaniment and concomitance, meaning: neither conception nor birth occurs except [...] with the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and [...] also to that, that it is with His knowledge and His will. [...] in the benefits, that there is evidence in it that whoever affirms knowledge must affirm will. Hence the People of the Sunnah, regarding the Qadariyyah, said: debate them with knowledge. Al-Shāfi‘ī and others said: debate them with knowledge; if they deny it, they disbelieve, and if they affirm it, they are refuted. If they say that Allah does not know [...], and if they say He knows, they are refuted, because if He knows that, then either the thing occurs contrary to what He knows or in agreement with it; if it is in agreement with it, then by His will, and if it is contrary to it [...].
* Student: [...].
* The Shaykh: It is [...] the deceit.
* Student: [...] and not a noun or...?
* The Shaykh: Rather it is a noun, like "he is standing" [...] "he is standing", [...], and the sentence is its predicate, but [...] emphasis; meaning, when He said: ﴿and the plotting of those—it will perish﴾ [Fatir 10], it is as if He said: the plotting of those, the plotting of those will perish [...].

﴿And no one is granted long life, nor is anything reduced from his life, except that it is in a Book﴾ [Fatir 11]. ﴿And no one is granted long life﴾: (mā) here is also negative, as evidenced by His words ﴿except that it is in a Book﴾, and another proof: the verb is in the nominative [...].

(﴿And no one is granted long life﴾ means no addition is made to the life of one who is long-lived.) ﴿Nor is anything reduced from his life﴾, meaning: that long-lived person, or another long-lived person, ﴿except that it is in a Book﴾.

His words ﴿is granted long life﴾: the meaning of ta‘mīr is increase in life. The meaning: no one's life is increased, nor is anything reduced from his life, except in a Book.

[...] And His words ﴿min mu‘ammar﴾: ﴿min﴾ here is a superfluous preposition entering upon the deputy of the subject, so we say of ﴿mu‘ammar﴾: deputy of the subject, nominative with an assumed ḍamma on its final letter, [...] the vowel of the superfluous preposition.

And His words ﴿nor is anything reduced from his life except that it is in a Book﴾: here He says ﴿from his life﴾. The author said: (meaning: that long-lived person, or another long-lived person). As for the pronoun in His words ﴿from his life﴾ referring to another long-lived person, there is no difficulty in this, because that one is long-lived, so the second is reduced. But the difficulty arises if we say the pronoun refers to the same long-lived person: how can he be long-lived while at the same time reduced in his life? ﴿And no one is granted long life, nor is anything reduced from his life, except that it is in a Book﴾ — this appears to be a point of difficulty, or not? [...]
* Student: Yes indeed.
* The Shaykh: Fine. ﴿And no one is granted long life [...] nor is anything reduced from his life﴾: if we say the pronoun refers to that long-lived person, then it refers to [...], so he is long-lived and reduced in his life.

If we say it refers to another long-lived person, ﴿And no one is granted long life nor is anything reduced from his life﴾, meaning: from the life of another long-lived person, [...] the first; the reduction then refers to another person. So we have Zayd who is long-lived and ʿAmr whose life is reduced, and there is no difficulty in this. But regarding the first difficulty, the exegetes differed in its interpretation. Some of them said: ﴿And no one is granted long life nor is anything reduced from his life﴾ [Fatir 11]: the reduction here is in contrast to the increase, because a person, each time he advances a day in this world, his life is reduced with respect to the end of his life. For example, one who is ten years old, when he becomes eleven, if it is decreed that he will die at twenty, is his life reduced or not? Whenever it increases in one respect, it decreases in another respect. So the meaning is that its reduction is recorded just as its increase is recorded, so it is said, for example: so-and-so has reached ten years of age, and his life has been reduced—that is, from the end of his life—by ten years; he reached eleven, and his life was reduced by eleven, so nine remain, and so on. This is the view of some of the Successors (tābiʿūn).

But others among the scholars of the exegetes said: this refers to what the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed in his saying: "Whoever wishes that his provision be expanded and his lifespan (athar) be extended, let him maintain the ties of kinship." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (2067), Muslim (2557/20), from the hadith of Anas ibn Mālik.] [...] that a person's life is reduced and increased according to maintaining ties of kinship; then his life is reduced if he does not maintain his kinship ties, and not increased if he maintains them. The meaning according to this distinction is that the increase or decrease of life is written with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is written: whoever is decreed that his life will be lengthened through maintaining kinship will be decreed to maintain his kinship; and whoever is decreed that his life be shortened through severing kinship will be severing his kinship, because causes are linked to their causes, known to Allah. Have you understood? This removes the difficulty raised by some scholars concerning this hadith. They tried to interpret the increase of life as blessing in a person's life, because when Allah sends blessing into a life, even if short, it becomes better, or better than a long life without blessing. But it has already been stated that this does not remove the difficulty, because blessing too is written or not written?
* Student: Written.
* The Shaykh: Written, and likewise its removal is written, so that does not remove us from the difficulty. Only saying this removes us from the difficulty: that the lengthened life of a person through maintaining kinship has been written, and it has been written that he will maintain his kinship. Then what is the benefit of the Messenger's saying: "Whoever wishes that his provision be expanded and his lifespan be extended"?
The answer: the benefit of it is the encouragement to maintain kinship, just as we say: whoever wishes to enter Paradise, let him do righteous deeds. No one should say: if Paradise is written, how [...] does he act? And how, if he acts, is Paradise written for him? We say: it is written beforehand [...], but Paradise has been written for him, and it has been written that he will do its deeds. On this basis, all of us, according to Allah's decrees, are such that this does not reduce life; the difficulty applies to everyone, but the answer to it is easy: it is said that this is written as a result of this cause, and it is known to Allah, whereas with us it is not known.

Alright, then the best of the possibilities for the verse is that what is meant by ﴿from his life﴾ is: from the long-lived person; a person may be increased in life for some reason, and may be reduced in life for another reason.

He said: ﴿except that it is in a Book﴾. ﴿Book﴾ is a faʿāl in the sense of maf‘ūl, like firāsh meaning mafrūsh (spread), ghirās meaning maghrūs (planted), binā’ meaning mabnī (built), so kitāb means maktūb (written). What is this Book? The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (it is the Preserved Tablet, al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ). The Preserved Tablet [...]; it is preserved in several respects: it is preserved from anyone attaining it, because it is specific to Allah's decree; preserved from being changed or altered; and therefore whatever is written in the Preserved Tablet will be as Allah the Exalted said to the pen: "Write what is to occur until the Day of Resurrection" [al-Tirmidhī (2155), Abū Dāwūd (4700), from the hadith of ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit]. Likewise it is preserved from error, so that nothing is written in it [...] and what is written in it does not fail to occur; that is, error does not enter it, so it is [...] in every respect.

(﴿Indeed that is easy for Allah﴾, i.e., easy.) ﴿Indeed that﴾: the referent is everything previously mentioned: the increase in life, the decrease, the Book, all of it is easy for Allah, meaning easy for Him, even if it is difficult and hard for created beings; but it is easy and simple with Allah, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, when He wills something, says to it: "Be," and it is.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the two seas are not alike﴾ [Fatir 12]. ﴿Are not alike﴾: ﴿mā﴾ is negative, and ﴿yastawī﴾ means "equal" and "similar". ﴿The two seas﴾: this is general, and "sea" is abundant water, so every large body of water is called a sea. "The two seas" here is general, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, explained it by His words: ﴿this one is sweet, fresh, pleasant to drink, and this one is salty, bitter﴾. ﴿This one is sweet, fresh﴾: "sweet" means pleasant and agreeable to drink; "fresh" (furāt), the author says in his explanation: (very sweet). ﴿Pleasant to drink﴾ means easy and smooth; because it is sweet and pure, and nothing in it spoils it with filth, excessive heat, or excessive cold. In short, it is sweet, fresh, and pleasant to drink.

The second: (﴿and this one is salty, bitter﴾, very salty). ﴿Salty﴾: very salty. Are the two equal?
* Students: They are not equal.
* The Shaykh: No. Is this meant literally, or is it a parable Allah struck for the believer and the disbeliever? It has been said: it is meant literally, by the evidence of His words: ﴿and from both you eat tender flesh﴾. And it has been said: it is meant as a parable which Allah struck for the believer and the disbeliever: the believer is in the position of the sweet fresh water, and the disbeliever is in the position of the salty bitter water. But we have a principle in speech that when a matter is between being literal or not literal, it must be taken as literal. So it is literal, and His words ﴿and from both you eat tender flesh﴾ also support this, for such a qualification indicates that it is literal and not figurative. Moreover, we say there is no figurative usage in the Qur'an or elsewhere, as has often passed before us. Yet, nevertheless, there is no harm in [...] the negation of connection between these two seas, and the negation of connection between any two different things; that is, there is no objection to the mind moving from the negation of equality between these two sensible things to the negation of equality between intelligible matters [...].

He said: ﴿and from both you eat tender flesh﴾. ﴿From both﴾ is connected to His words ﴿you eat﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 35, verses 11–12 (part 2 of 3):**

(﴿Fresh flesh﴾ is fish.) *Tari'* (fresh) means that which has not changed by putrefaction. This is one of the characteristics of fish: even when it dies, it remains fresh, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The game of the sea and its food are made lawful to you, as a provision for you and for the travelers﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 96]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Its game is what is eaten alive, and its food is what is eaten dead."[[Recorded by al-Daraqutni in his Sunan (4728), and Ibn Mansur in his Tafsir (833), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]]

* Second: Among the benefits of these two descriptions: (﴿and you extract﴾ from the salt; and it is said: from both of them) ﴿an ornament you wear﴾, which is pearls and coral, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿From both of them come out pearls and coral﴾ [Ar-Rahman 22]. People have differed: does this come out only from the salt water, or does it come out from both salt and sweet water? Most of the commentators hold that it comes out only from the salt water, and they interpreted His saying ﴿From both of them come out pearls and coral﴾ [Ar-Rahman 22] to mean from their combined waters, not from each of them individually. So here, if we say: we have two seas, one sweet and one salt, from which come out pearls and coral, "from both of them" means from the combination, not from each one separately. But the correct view is that it comes out from both, because this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and Allah, the Glorified, knows best what He has created. Pearls and coral are now known to come out from this and from that. For this reason the author said: (and it is said: from both of them).

﴿an ornament you wear﴾. He mentioned wearing because that is the furthest benefit obtained from this ornament. Otherwise, it is known that whoever extracts this ornament makes it a trade, and the trade in pearls and coral, both in the past and up to now, has remained a strong trade. But these merchants who trade in it, what is the purpose? Wearing. Because the one who buys it from them wants it for wearing. If he wants it for profit, then to whom will he sell it?

* Students: He wears it.

* The Shaykh: He wears it. So Allah mentioned two benefits in these two seas: an apparent benefit and a hidden benefit. Clothing for the body on the inside, and clothing for the body on the outside. Clothing for the body on the inside: what is it? Eating the flesh. Eating the flesh is clothing for the body on the inside. For this reason He said to Adam: ﴿Indeed, it is [granted] to you that you will not be hungry therein or be naked﴾ [Ta-Ha 118]. He did not say "nor be thirsty," but said ﴿nor be naked﴾, because hunger is nakedness of the inside, and nakedness is nakedness of the outside.

Then we say: Allah mentioned two garments: the inner garment, by eating the flesh, and the outer garment, by this ornament.

﴿And from each you eat﴾ ﴿and you extract﴾. (﴿And you see﴾ means: see; ﴿the ships﴾ means the vessels; ﴿in it﴾ means in each of them; ﴿plowing﴾ means cutting through.)

He said: ﴿And you see﴾, i.e., (you see). Addressed to whom? To everyone to whom the address is directed. The seeing here is visual sight. Whoever observes the ships in the seas sees them cutting through the water, i.e., splitting it.

As for His saying ﴿in it, plowing﴾, the author said: (in each of them). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, indicated that the difficulty (...) is that here He says ﴿And the two seas are not alike﴾, and then says ﴿and you see the ships in it﴾. The context would require the expression to be: "and you see the ships in them (the two)." But the pronoun here does not refer to the two seas; it refers to ﴿each﴾, and "each" is a word whose form is singular. So the pronoun in this verse refers to ﴿each﴾ according to what? According to the wording, since it is singular. For this reason the author said: (in each of them), and the difficulty is resolved.

As for His saying ﴿plowing﴾, he said: (cutting through the water, i.e., splitting it by their running in it, going forward and backward with one wind). This is one of the blessings of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He subjected the ships for us to run on this water, cutting through the surging waves of the water, carrying all kinds of provisions and carrying many people. For this reason you see that ships are now considered a complete town: when you enter them, they are like a town. This is one of the blessings of Allah, the Glorified. So He mentioned here three blessings: the first is eating the flesh, the second is the ornament, and the third is the ships that cross or split the water from one side to another, to carry provisions and human beings.

Reflect on His saying here: ﴿and you extract an ornament﴾ and ﴿you eat﴾ and ﴿you see the ships in it, plowing﴾. For fish, eating it is easy and requires no effort, so He mentioned eating directly. Pearls and coral require effort and labor, because they need diving, equipment, long breath, or carrying things that help one breathe. For this reason, what did He say? ﴿you extract﴾, i.e., you seek an ornament. As for the ships, He said: ﴿and you see the ships in it, plowing﴾, because seeing them with the eye while they cut through the water is one of the greatest signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾ (﴿that you may seek﴾ means: that you may pursue; ﴿of His bounty﴾ means: of His bounty, the Exalted, through trade; ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾ to Allah for that). The meaning: He subjected the ships and made them plow through this sea for two reasons. First, ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾, i.e., that you may seek provision when these ships carry it. (...) for example, provisions from America and from Japan, (...) the other distant places, cannot reach us except through these ships that carry many things. This is from the bounty of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic (...) ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾.

As for His saying ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾, the word (perhaps, la'alla) here: we do not know its meaning until we survey the meanings that la'alla can carry. La'alla comes to express hope, comes to express expectation, comes to express apprehension, and comes to express causation. So which of these meanings is it in this verse?

* Students: Causation.

* The Shaykh: Causation. That is, so that you may be grateful to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. When you see these ships cutting through the water and bringing provisions from one place to another, this requires that you thank Allah, the Exalted, for this blessing. The scholars said, in defining gratitude (shukr): it is acting in obedience to the Benefactor, acknowledging (the blessing) in the heart, speaking of it with the tongue, and obeying with the limbs. So its locations are three: the heart, the tongue, and the limbs. For this reason the poet said:

* A student: 

*"The blessings from me have benefited you in three ways:*
*my hand, my tongue, and the hidden heart."*

* The Shaykh: 

*"The blessings from me have benefited you in three ways:*
*my hand, my tongue, and the hidden heart."*

So gratitude occurs in these three locations, while praise (hamd) occurs with the tongue. The object of gratitude is more general and its cause more specific, while the object of praise is more specific and its cause more general. Praise occurs in return for a blessing, and it also occurs in return for the perfection of the one praised. So praise is more general in terms of its object, unlike gratitude, which is more specific. Gratitude is more general in its object and more specific in its cause, and praise is the reverse.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾ [Fatir 11], and so on to the end.

* In this noble verse: a demonstration of the power of Allah, the Exalted, in the beginning of the creation of the children of Adam, by creating them from dust, then from a drop (of semen), and so on to the end.

* Among its benefits also: Allah, by His wisdom and mercy, made the children of Adam into pairs, male and female, for the preservation of offspring and the attainment of enjoyment.

* Among its benefits: the comprehensive knowledge of Allah of everything, based on His saying: ﴿and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾ [Fatir 11].

* Among its benefits: affirming the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying: ﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾, because creation does not occur except after knowledge and power.

* Among its benefits also: that the lifespans, long and short, are all written with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in a Book.

* Among its benefits: affirming two levels of the levels of *qadar* (divine decree): knowledge and writing.

* Among its benefits also: the ease of this matter for Allah, the Exalted, namely creation and writing, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is easy for Allah﴾. Here is the third level of the levels of *qadar*, which is creation. So there are three levels: knowledge, writing, and creation. What comes after them? Will (*mashi'ah*). (...) Will. Can we derive it from the verse?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: How?

* A student: He creates what He wills.

* The Shaykh: (...) ﴿from dust, then from﴾ [Fatir 11]. And this does not occur except by His will, because Allah did not (...) this. So the verse affirms the four levels of *qadar*: knowledge, then writing, then will, then creation. These four levels have been gathered in a verse (of poetry) (...).

* A student:

*"Knowledge, writing, the will of our Lord,*
*and His creation, which is bringing into existence and forming."*

* The Shaykh:

*"Knowledge, writing, the will of our Lord,*
*and His creation, which is bringing into existence and forming."*

These are the four levels of *qadar*.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the two seas are not alike﴾, and so on to the end [Fatir 12].

* In this verse, among the benefits:

* First: that mixed things cannot be equal, based on His saying: ﴿And the two seas are not alike﴾, and so on to the end. From this benefit it follows that equality cannot be established between man and woman in rights or in anything else, yes. Why? Because the creation of the woman differs from the creation of the man. For this reason Allah (...) made for her works that suit her, and for the man works that suit him. 'A'ishah asked the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, "Is there jihad for women?" He said: "For them is a jihad without fighting: the Hajj and the 'Umrah."[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (1520), and Ibn Majah (2901), the wording being his, from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]] The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "A people will never prosper who entrust their affairs to a woman."[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (4425), from the hadith of Abu Bakrah Nufay' ibn al-Harith.]] The Prophet ﷺ prohibited a woman from marrying herself off.[[Recorded by Abu Dawud (2083), al-Tirmidhi (1102), and Ibn Majah (1879), from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]] And so on, with the differences between men and women that you know. In inheritance, He gave the woman half of the man's share when they are of the same category, such as brothers, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles.

* Students: No (...).

* The Shaykh: Like brothers. Alright, and paternal uncles?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Brothers (...) and paternal uncles?

* A student: They do not inherit.

* Another student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Because the paternal aunt does not inherit. The paternal aunt does not inherit. That is, if a person dies leaving a paternal uncle and a paternal aunt, the paternal aunt does not inherit, (...). Yes indeed. Alright, let us complete the benefits, (...).

* A student: How can they be from one sea, ﴿and from each you eat﴾ [Fatir 12] (...)?

* The Shaykh: (...). The apparent meaning of the Qur'an: from this and from that. As for the matter of fish, both of them have no difficulty and no one says it comes from one (sea). But what is difficult is the matter of pearls and coral: does it come from one or not? This will come to us, Allah willing, among the benefits. Likewise, the intended meaning is not only pearls and coral; people may adorn themselves with things that come out of the sea other than these two types.

(...) The brothers of Joseph were too wise to address their father in a way that would have him go to the walls to ask. But ﴿Indeed, we will destroy the people of this town﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 31]: the intended meaning of "town" is its dwellings, is it not? The dwellings of the people. The evidence is His saying: ﴿the people of this town﴾. So you now see that this word has, in this place, a meaning that it cannot bear in another place. Context plays a great role in knowing the intended meaning of speech.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a demonstration of the power of Allah, the Exalted, in that from this water He made these two distant kinds: two seas of water, one of which is ﴿sweet, palatable, pleasant to drink﴾ [Fatir 12], and the second ﴿salty and bitter﴾ [Fatir 12]. They are one thing, yet they differ in this way.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: that sweet water is pleasant to drink, and the opposite is salty water. It follows from this that a person should not drink what he does not find palatable, because that affects him and harms him. Likewise, there is no harm in his taking what his soul desires, even if in some cases it is harmful to him. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in *Zad al-Ma'ad* that the soul's desire for a thing has a great effect in removing its harm. He gave an example of this, I think, in the case of carrion, which is foul and harmful. When a person is compelled to eat it and his need becomes intense (...), the soul accepts it and finds it palatable, then digests it, so it does not harm him. Because if it harmed (carrion would harm) the compelled person just as it harms the one not compelled, then its being lawful for him would entail his killing himself. For this reason, if he is compelled to eat and has nothing but poison, it is not lawful for him to eat the poison. Clear? He also gave an example of this with the story of Suhayb al-Rumi: "He had an eye ailment," meaning his eye hurt him from an inflammation he had. "Dates were brought to the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, ate some of them. Suhayb went to eat, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to him: 'You have an eye ailment.' (It is known that the one with an inflamed eye does not eat dates.) He said: 'O Messenger of Allah! I will chew it on the other side.'" How? For example, if the right eye has the inflammation, he chews it on the left side. "The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, laughed and said to him: 'Eat.'"[[Recorded by al-Hakim in his Mustadrak (8468), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Suhayb.]] He said: because his soul was now strongly craving it, and this craving removes the harm. So the main point is that a thing that is not palatable should not be taken by a person, and he should not force himself to it. For this reason it is said: "Eat what your stomach craves, and do not eat what your mouth craves." I do not know whether this is correct or not. Yes, it is correct, because some people enjoy a type of food, but their insides do not accept it. You find that when they eat it, their stomach begins to rumble, and perhaps they get diarrhea. We say: do not eat that, even if your mouth craves it, because it is harmful to you.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's blessing upon His servants through what they extract from these seas of flesh, based on His saying: ﴿and from each you eat fresh flesh﴾, without hardship and without fatigue (...). Yet the flesh of fish is among the best of meats. Likewise, the blessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in what we extract from these seas: from what? From the ornaments we wear.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the difference between the perfection of the flesh from these seas and the perfection of the ornaments. For regarding flesh He said: ﴿you eat﴾, and He did not mention the effort by which we reach this eating, because it is easy and light and is not worth mentioning. But regarding the ornament He said: "you extract," because it requires hardship and toil.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's power in carrying this heavy ship laden with goods upon the surface of the water, yet it is able to push the water and cut through it, based on His saying: ﴿and you see the ships in it, plowing﴾ [Fatir 12]. Otherwise, water is heavy and not easy. For this reason, when a person swims in water he needs strength to push the water. But these ships cut through the water, and the effect of this blessing does not appear fully unless a person remembers the old ships that moved by the winds.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah the Exalted's blessing upon us in attaining what we seek of His bounty through these ships, based on His saying: ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾.

Among its benefits: a person should take the means that lead to the desired goal, based on His saying: ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [Fatir 12]. As for a person who says, "I will sit at home, and my provision will come to me," and claims he is reliant upon Allah, do we agree with his statement? No. We say: if you are reliant upon Allah (tawakkul), do not be one who depends on others without effort (tawakkul vs. tawākul). There is a difference between tawakkul and tawākul. Take the means! This Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was the master of those who rely upon Allah, and yet he would take the means that bring benefit and repel harm, would he not? Very well, then seek of Allah's bounty and take the means, for the sky does not rain down gold or silver, and provision comes only through a person's seeking. The matter is too clear to need examples, but otherwise we would illustrate it with something very close to hand: if someone says, "If Allah has decreed a child for me, it will come to me," and he has not married, do we say this is the speech of a madman? Yes, a madman. How could a child come to you when you have not married? We know of no child that sprouts from (...) at all; rather, children come about through taking their causes, such as marriage. Very well, this likewise implies that provision needs to be sought (...).

Among its benefits: the obligation to be grateful for Allah's blessings, glorified and exalted is He, based on His saying: ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾. Indeed, Allah made these blessings and subjected them for you (...) so that we may give thanks to Him, glorified and exalted is He. We have previously mentioned many times that gratitude has its place in the tongue, the heart, and the limbs.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾ [Fatir 11]. When He, glorified and exalted, had made clear the preceding signs that point to His power—the sending of the winds, the stirring up of the clouds, their driving to a dead land, the giving of life to the earth after its death—and that deeds are raised up to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and likewise words (deeds, whether words or actions, are raised up to Allah), He said here: ﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾. This is with regard to the origin, which is Adam. Hence He said: (by the creation of your father Adam from it), for Allah, exalted is He, created him from dust. This verse, as you see, states that Allah created him from dust, and in another verse that He created him from clay (ṭīn), and in a third verse that He created him from ṣalṣāl like pottery, and in a fourth verse from ḥama’ masnūn (black mud molded into shape). So what is the answer concerning this variation?

The answer is that this is a variation of attributes, not a variation of essences, and therefore there is no contradiction, since it is permissible for several attributes to apply to one described thing. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High (1), who created and proportioned (2), and who determined and guided (3), and who brought forth the pasture﴾ [al-A'la 1–4], although He is one. The conclusion is that here one should say that this variation is a variation of attributes, not a variation of essences and entities. The substance is one, but its first state was dust; when water is added to it, it becomes clay (ṭīn); when it is left and takes a period of time, it becomes ḥama’ masnūn, changed—that is, clay, when water is poured into it, you find it turns black and has an odour. The fourth stage, ṣalṣāl like pottery, is after it was ḥama’ masnūn and dried out and became ṣalṣāl like pottery; then Allah breathed into it the spirit. So this variation is a variation of attributes, and its origin is dust.

He said: ﴿And Allah created you from dust, then from a drop (nuṭfah)﴾ [Fatir 11]. ﴿Then﴾ He used (thumma), which indicates delay and sequence, because thumma indicates delay and sequence, whereas the fā’ indicates sequence without delay. Here He said: ﴿then from a drop﴾, because when Allah created Adam, and created his offspring, these offspring were propagated through this water which is the nuṭfah, and the nuṭfah is a small quantity of water.

He said: ﴿then from a drop﴾, meaning semen (maniyy) that gushes forth. Do you have (bi-khalq)? (by creating His offspring from it), that is, from this drop. And it is remarkable that scholars of medicine mention that this small drop contains millions of sperm cells, and these [...] claim they are millions—and they know better than us about that. That is, usually only one, or two, or three, or four of them are suitable. This [...] I have not heard that four thousand enter the woman and one remains. And Allah is capable of all things; He may increase, ﴿He increases in creation what He wills﴾ [Fatir 1].

He says: (﴿Then He made you pairs﴾, males and females). Regarding His words ﴿pairs﴾, the author here explained "pairs" as males and females, by the indication of His words: ﴿and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾ [Fatir 11]. Pay attention: the pairs here are with regard to the two sexes, male and female, and His words ﴿and no female conceives﴾ confirm the restriction of "pairs" here to maleness and femaleness.

As for when we look at the word "pairs" (azwāj), its meaning is kinds, and kinds are more general than maleness and femaleness, for it includes the wretched and the happy, the black and the white, the tall and the short, and other things. But what led the author to restrict the speech to maleness and femaleness only is His words ﴿and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His power and wisdom, made this offspring that came out of this one man into males and females, for the survival of the progeny, since the survival of the progeny is not possible except by this. Although Allah, glorified and exalted, is able to preserve the progeny without that, it is said: mankind includes those created without a mother or father, those created from a father without a mother, those created from a mother without a father, and those created between two parents. So who was created without mother or father?

* Students: Adam.
* The Shaykh: And from a father without a mother?
* Students: Ḥawwā’ (Eve).
* The Shaykh: Ḥawwā’. And from a mother without a father?
* Students: ʿĪsā.
* The Shaykh: And the rest of people?
* Students: Between two parents.
* The Shaykh: Between two parents, male and female.

He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾. (mā) here [...] and the second?
* Student: Transitive.
* The Shaykh: [...] or the transitive?
* Student: [...].
* The Shaykh: [...] intransitive or transitive?
* Student: The first is from the intransitive.
* The Shaykh: From the intransitive.
* Student: And the second is from the transitive.
* The Shaykh: And the second is from the transitive, correct?
* Student: Correct.
* The Shaykh: [...] a superfluous preposition; ﴿unthā﴾ is the subject of ﴿taḥmilu﴾, nominative with an assumed ḍamma on its final letter, prevented from appearing by the difficulty (ta‘adhdhur)—is that so? ﴿unthā﴾ is a subject, nominative with an assumed ḍamma on its last letter, prevented from appearing by the difficulty?
* Student: Preoccupation of the position (ishtighāl al-maḥall).
* The Shaykh: There is no preoccupation here, [...].
* Student: The difficulty (ta‘adhdhur).
* The Shaykh: Fine, the difficulty; but it occurs in terms of the wording, genitive in wording.
﴿unthā and lā taḍa‘﴾ meaning the female; (﴿except with His knowledge﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: known to Him). Look: ﴿what she carries of a female﴾, meaning, what female carries? Of the children of Adam, or of them and others? Of them and others. [...] ﴿and does not give birth except with His knowledge﴾. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾ [al-An‘am 59]. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, knows what every female carries, at the beginning of the pregnancy, its development, its outcome, and everything related to it. ﴿And she does not give birth except with His knowledge﴾: the first thing from which the pregnancy begins in the womb is known to Allah, and when she gives birth, it is known to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

As for the author's words (ḥāl), what is the meaning of ḥāl? It means that the preposition-phrase is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause [...]. ﴿Except with His knowledge﴾: he said, except (known to Him). It is possible to say that there is no need for this interpretation; rather we say that the bāʼ here is for accompaniment and concomitance, meaning: neither conception nor birth occurs except [...] with the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and [...] also to that, that it is with His knowledge and His will. [...] in the benefits, that there is evidence in it that whoever affirms knowledge must affirm will. Hence the People of the Sunnah, regarding the Qadariyyah, said: debate them with knowledge. Al-Shāfi‘ī and others said: debate them with knowledge; if they deny it, they disbelieve, and if they affirm it, they are refuted. If they say that Allah does not know [...], and if they say He knows, they are refuted, because if He knows that, then either the thing occurs contrary to what He knows or in agreement with it; if it is in agreement with it, then by His will, and if it is contrary to it [...].
* Student: [...].
* The Shaykh: It is [...] the deceit.
* Student: [...] and not a noun or...?
* The Shaykh: Rather it is a noun, like "he is standing" [...] "he is standing", [...], and the sentence is its predicate, but [...] emphasis; meaning, when He said: ﴿and the plotting of those—it will perish﴾ [Fatir 10], it is as if He said: the plotting of those, the plotting of those will perish [...].

﴿And no one is granted long life, nor is anything reduced from his life, except that it is in a Book﴾ [Fatir 11]. ﴿And no one is granted long life﴾: (mā) here is also negative, as evidenced by His words ﴿except that it is in a Book﴾, and another proof: the verb is in the nominative [...].

(﴿And no one is granted long life﴾ means no addition is made to the life of one who is long-lived.) ﴿Nor is anything reduced from his life﴾, meaning: that long-lived person, or another long-lived person, ﴿except that it is in a Book﴾.

His words ﴿is granted long life﴾: the meaning of ta‘mīr is increase in life. The meaning: no one's life is increased, nor is anything reduced from his life, except in a Book.

[...] And His words ﴿min mu‘ammar﴾: ﴿min﴾ here is a superfluous preposition entering upon the deputy of the subject, so we say of ﴿mu‘ammar﴾: deputy of the subject, nominative with an assumed ḍamma on its final letter, [...] the vowel of the superfluous preposition.

And His words ﴿nor is anything reduced from his life except that it is in a Book﴾: here He says ﴿from his life﴾. The author said: (meaning: that long-lived person, or another long-lived person). As for the pronoun in His words ﴿from his life﴾ referring to another long-lived person, there is no difficulty in this, because that one is long-lived, so the second is reduced. But the difficulty arises if we say the pronoun refers to the same long-lived person: how can he be long-lived while at the same time reduced in his life? ﴿And no one is granted long life, nor is anything reduced from his life, except that it is in a Book﴾ — this appears to be a point of difficulty, or not? [...]
* Student: Yes indeed.
* The Shaykh: Fine. ﴿And no one is granted long life [...] nor is anything reduced from his life﴾: if we say the pronoun refers to that long-lived person, then it refers to [...], so he is long-lived and reduced in his life.

If we say it refers to another long-lived person, ﴿And no one is granted long life nor is anything reduced from his life﴾, meaning: from the life of another long-lived person, [...] the first; the reduction then refers to another person. So we have Zayd who is long-lived and ʿAmr whose life is reduced, and there is no difficulty in this. But regarding the first difficulty, the exegetes differed in its interpretation. Some of them said: ﴿And no one is granted long life nor is anything reduced from his life﴾ [Fatir 11]: the reduction here is in contrast to the increase, because a person, each time he advances a day in this world, his life is reduced with respect to the end of his life. For example, one who is ten years old, when he becomes eleven, if it is decreed that he will die at twenty, is his life reduced or not? Whenever it increases in one respect, it decreases in another respect. So the meaning is that its reduction is recorded just as its increase is recorded, so it is said, for example: so-and-so has reached ten years of age, and his life has been reduced—that is, from the end of his life—by ten years; he reached eleven, and his life was reduced by eleven, so nine remain, and so on. This is the view of some of the Successors (tābiʿūn).

But others among the scholars of the exegetes said: this refers to what the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed in his saying: "Whoever wishes that his provision be expanded and his lifespan (athar) be extended, let him maintain the ties of kinship." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (2067), Muslim (2557/20), from the hadith of Anas ibn Mālik.] [...] that a person's life is reduced and increased according to maintaining ties of kinship; then his life is reduced if he does not maintain his kinship ties, and not increased if he maintains them. The meaning according to this distinction is that the increase or decrease of life is written with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is written: whoever is decreed that his life will be lengthened through maintaining kinship will be decreed to maintain his kinship; and whoever is decreed that his life be shortened through severing kinship will be severing his kinship, because causes are linked to their causes, known to Allah. Have you understood? This removes the difficulty raised by some scholars concerning this hadith. They tried to interpret the increase of life as blessing in a person's life, because when Allah sends blessing into a life, even if short, it becomes better, or better than a long life without blessing. But it has already been stated that this does not remove the difficulty, because blessing too is written or not written?
* Student: Written.
* The Shaykh: Written, and likewise its removal is written, so that does not remove us from the difficulty. Only saying this removes us from the difficulty: that the lengthened life of a person through maintaining kinship has been written, and it has been written that he will maintain his kinship. Then what is the benefit of the Messenger's saying: "Whoever wishes that his provision be expanded and his lifespan be extended"?
The answer: the benefit of it is the encouragement to maintain kinship, just as we say: whoever wishes to enter Paradise, let him do righteous deeds. No one should say: if Paradise is written, how [...] does he act? And how, if he acts, is Paradise written for him? We say: it is written beforehand [...], but Paradise has been written for him, and it has been written that he will do its deeds. On this basis, all of us, according to Allah's decrees, are such that this does not reduce life; the difficulty applies to everyone, but the answer to it is easy: it is said that this is written as a result of this cause, and it is known to Allah, whereas with us it is not known.

Alright, then the best of the possibilities for the verse is that what is meant by ﴿from his life﴾ is: from the long-lived person; a person may be increased in life for some reason, and may be reduced in life for another reason.

He said: ﴿except that it is in a Book﴾. ﴿Book﴾ is a faʿāl in the sense of maf‘ūl, like firāsh meaning mafrūsh (spread), ghirās meaning maghrūs (planted), binā’ meaning mabnī (built), so kitāb means maktūb (written). What is this Book? The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (it is the Preserved Tablet, al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ). The Preserved Tablet [...]; it is preserved in several respects: it is preserved from anyone attaining it, because it is specific to Allah's decree; preserved from being changed or altered; and therefore whatever is written in the Preserved Tablet will be as Allah the Exalted said to the pen: "Write what is to occur until the Day of Resurrection" [al-Tirmidhī (2155), Abū Dāwūd (4700), from the hadith of ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit]. Likewise it is preserved from error, so that nothing is written in it [...] and what is written in it does not fail to occur; that is, error does not enter it, so it is [...] in every respect.

(﴿Indeed that is easy for Allah﴾, i.e., easy.) ﴿Indeed that﴾: the referent is everything previously mentioned: the increase in life, the decrease, the Book, all of it is easy for Allah, meaning easy for Him, even if it is difficult and hard for created beings; but it is easy and simple with Allah, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, when He wills something, says to it: "Be," and it is.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the two seas are not alike﴾ [Fatir 12]. ﴿Are not alike﴾: ﴿mā﴾ is negative, and ﴿yastawī﴾ means "equal" and "similar". ﴿The two seas﴾: this is general, and "sea" is abundant water, so every large body of water is called a sea. "The two seas" here is general, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, explained it by His words: ﴿this one is sweet, fresh, pleasant to drink, and this one is salty, bitter﴾. ﴿This one is sweet, fresh﴾: "sweet" means pleasant and agreeable to drink; "fresh" (furāt), the author says in his explanation: (very sweet). ﴿Pleasant to drink﴾ means easy and smooth; because it is sweet and pure, and nothing in it spoils it with filth, excessive heat, or excessive cold. In short, it is sweet, fresh, and pleasant to drink.

The second: (﴿and this one is salty, bitter﴾, very salty). ﴿Salty﴾: very salty. Are the two equal?
* Students: They are not equal.
* The Shaykh: No. Is this meant literally, or is it a parable Allah struck for the believer and the disbeliever? It has been said: it is meant literally, by the evidence of His words: ﴿and from both you eat tender flesh﴾. And it has been said: it is meant as a parable which Allah struck for the believer and the disbeliever: the believer is in the position of the sweet fresh water, and the disbeliever is in the position of the salty bitter water. But we have a principle in speech that when a matter is between being literal or not literal, it must be taken as literal. So it is literal, and His words ﴿and from both you eat tender flesh﴾ also support this, for such a qualification indicates that it is literal and not figurative. Moreover, we say there is no figurative usage in the Qur'an or elsewhere, as has often passed before us. Yet, nevertheless, there is no harm in [...] the negation of connection between these two seas, and the negation of connection between any two different things; that is, there is no objection to the mind moving from the negation of equality between these two sensible things to the negation of equality between intelligible matters [...].

He said: ﴿and from both you eat tender flesh﴾. ﴿From both﴾ is connected to His words ﴿you eat﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 35, verses 11–12 (part 2 of 3):**

(﴿Fresh flesh﴾ is fish.) *Tari'* (fresh) means that which has not changed by putrefaction. This is one of the characteristics of fish: even when it dies, it remains fresh, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The game of the sea and its food are made lawful to you, as a provision for you and for the travelers﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 96]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Its game is what is eaten alive, and its food is what is eaten dead."[[Recorded by al-Daraqutni in his Sunan (4728), and Ibn Mansur in his Tafsir (833), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]]

* Second: Among the benefits of these two descriptions: (﴿and you extract﴾ from the salt; and it is said: from both of them) ﴿an ornament you wear﴾, which is pearls and coral, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿From both of them come out pearls and coral﴾ [Ar-Rahman 22]. People have differed: does this come out only from the salt water, or does it come out from both salt and sweet water? Most of the commentators hold that it comes out only from the salt water, and they interpreted His saying ﴿From both of them come out pearls and coral﴾ [Ar-Rahman 22] to mean from their combined waters, not from each of them individually. So here, if we say: we have two seas, one sweet and one salt, from which come out pearls and coral, "from both of them" means from the combination, not from each one separately. But the correct view is that it comes out from both, because this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and Allah, the Glorified, knows best what He has created. Pearls and coral are now known to come out from this and from that. For this reason the author said: (and it is said: from both of them).

﴿an ornament you wear﴾. He mentioned wearing because that is the furthest benefit obtained from this ornament. Otherwise, it is known that whoever extracts this ornament makes it a trade, and the trade in pearls and coral, both in the past and up to now, has remained a strong trade. But these merchants who trade in it, what is the purpose? Wearing. Because the one who buys it from them wants it for wearing. If he wants it for profit, then to whom will he sell it?

* Students: He wears it.

* The Shaykh: He wears it. So Allah mentioned two benefits in these two seas: an apparent benefit and a hidden benefit. Clothing for the body on the inside, and clothing for the body on the outside. Clothing for the body on the inside: what is it? Eating the flesh. Eating the flesh is clothing for the body on the inside. For this reason He said to Adam: ﴿Indeed, it is [granted] to you that you will not be hungry therein or be naked﴾ [Ta-Ha 118]. He did not say "nor be thirsty," but said ﴿nor be naked﴾, because hunger is nakedness of the inside, and nakedness is nakedness of the outside.

Then we say: Allah mentioned two garments: the inner garment, by eating the flesh, and the outer garment, by this ornament.

﴿And from each you eat﴾ ﴿and you extract﴾. (﴿And you see﴾ means: see; ﴿the ships﴾ means the vessels; ﴿in it﴾ means in each of them; ﴿plowing﴾ means cutting through.)

He said: ﴿And you see﴾, i.e., (you see). Addressed to whom? To everyone to whom the address is directed. The seeing here is visual sight. Whoever observes the ships in the seas sees them cutting through the water, i.e., splitting it.

As for His saying ﴿in it, plowing﴾, the author said: (in each of them). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, indicated that the difficulty (...) is that here He says ﴿And the two seas are not alike﴾, and then says ﴿and you see the ships in it﴾. The context would require the expression to be: "and you see the ships in them (the two)." But the pronoun here does not refer to the two seas; it refers to ﴿each﴾, and "each" is a word whose form is singular. So the pronoun in this verse refers to ﴿each﴾ according to what? According to the wording, since it is singular. For this reason the author said: (in each of them), and the difficulty is resolved.

As for His saying ﴿plowing﴾, he said: (cutting through the water, i.e., splitting it by their running in it, going forward and backward with one wind). This is one of the blessings of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He subjected the ships for us to run on this water, cutting through the surging waves of the water, carrying all kinds of provisions and carrying many people. For this reason you see that ships are now considered a complete town: when you enter them, they are like a town. This is one of the blessings of Allah, the Glorified. So He mentioned here three blessings: the first is eating the flesh, the second is the ornament, and the third is the ships that cross or split the water from one side to another, to carry provisions and human beings.

Reflect on His saying here: ﴿and you extract an ornament﴾ and ﴿you eat﴾ and ﴿you see the ships in it, plowing﴾. For fish, eating it is easy and requires no effort, so He mentioned eating directly. Pearls and coral require effort and labor, because they need diving, equipment, long breath, or carrying things that help one breathe. For this reason, what did He say? ﴿you extract﴾, i.e., you seek an ornament. As for the ships, He said: ﴿and you see the ships in it, plowing﴾, because seeing them with the eye while they cut through the water is one of the greatest signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾ (﴿that you may seek﴾ means: that you may pursue; ﴿of His bounty﴾ means: of His bounty, the Exalted, through trade; ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾ to Allah for that). The meaning: He subjected the ships and made them plow through this sea for two reasons. First, ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾, i.e., that you may seek provision when these ships carry it. (...) for example, provisions from America and from Japan, (...) the other distant places, cannot reach us except through these ships that carry many things. This is from the bounty of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic (...) ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾.

As for His saying ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾, the word (perhaps, la'alla) here: we do not know its meaning until we survey the meanings that la'alla can carry. La'alla comes to express hope, comes to express expectation, comes to express apprehension, and comes to express causation. So which of these meanings is it in this verse?

* Students: Causation.

* The Shaykh: Causation. That is, so that you may be grateful to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. When you see these ships cutting through the water and bringing provisions from one place to another, this requires that you thank Allah, the Exalted, for this blessing. The scholars said, in defining gratitude (shukr): it is acting in obedience to the Benefactor, acknowledging (the blessing) in the heart, speaking of it with the tongue, and obeying with the limbs. So its locations are three: the heart, the tongue, and the limbs. For this reason the poet said:

* A student: 

*"The blessings from me have benefited you in three ways:*
*my hand, my tongue, and the hidden heart."*

* The Shaykh: 

*"The blessings from me have benefited you in three ways:*
*my hand, my tongue, and the hidden heart."*

So gratitude occurs in these three locations, while praise (hamd) occurs with the tongue. The object of gratitude is more general and its cause more specific, while the object of praise is more specific and its cause more general. Praise occurs in return for a blessing, and it also occurs in return for the perfection of the one praised. So praise is more general in terms of its object, unlike gratitude, which is more specific. Gratitude is more general in its object and more specific in its cause, and praise is the reverse.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾ [Fatir 11], and so on to the end.

* In this noble verse: a demonstration of the power of Allah, the Exalted, in the beginning of the creation of the children of Adam, by creating them from dust, then from a drop (of semen), and so on to the end.

* Among its benefits also: Allah, by His wisdom and mercy, made the children of Adam into pairs, male and female, for the preservation of offspring and the attainment of enjoyment.

* Among its benefits: the comprehensive knowledge of Allah of everything, based on His saying: ﴿and no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾ [Fatir 11].

* Among its benefits: affirming the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying: ﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾, because creation does not occur except after knowledge and power.

* Among its benefits also: that the lifespans, long and short, are all written with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in a Book.

* Among its benefits: affirming two levels of the levels of *qadar* (divine decree): knowledge and writing.

* Among its benefits also: the ease of this matter for Allah, the Exalted, namely creation and writing, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is easy for Allah﴾. Here is the third level of the levels of *qadar*, which is creation. So there are three levels: knowledge, writing, and creation. What comes after them? Will (*mashi'ah*). (...) Will. Can we derive it from the verse?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: How?

* A student: He creates what He wills.

* The Shaykh: (...) ﴿from dust, then from﴾ [Fatir 11]. And this does not occur except by His will, because Allah did not (...) this. So the verse affirms the four levels of *qadar*: knowledge, then writing, then will, then creation. These four levels have been gathered in a verse (of poetry) (...).

* A student:

*"Knowledge, writing, the will of our Lord,*
*and His creation, which is bringing into existence and forming."*

* The Shaykh:

*"Knowledge, writing, the will of our Lord,*
*and His creation, which is bringing into existence and forming."*

These are the four levels of *qadar*.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the two seas are not alike﴾, and so on to the end [Fatir 12].

* In this verse, among the benefits:

* First: that mixed things cannot be equal, based on His saying: ﴿And the two seas are not alike﴾, and so on to the end. From this benefit it follows that equality cannot be established between man and woman in rights or in anything else, yes. Why? Because the creation of the woman differs from the creation of the man. For this reason Allah (...) made for her works that suit her, and for the man works that suit him. 'A'ishah asked the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, "Is there jihad for women?" He said: "For them is a jihad without fighting: the Hajj and the 'Umrah."[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (1520), and Ibn Majah (2901), the wording being his, from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]] The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "A people will never prosper who entrust their affairs to a woman."[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (4425), from the hadith of Abu Bakrah Nufay' ibn al-Harith.]] The Prophet ﷺ prohibited a woman from marrying herself off.[[Recorded by Abu Dawud (2083), al-Tirmidhi (1102), and Ibn Majah (1879), from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]] And so on, with the differences between men and women that you know. In inheritance, He gave the woman half of the man's share when they are of the same category, such as brothers, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles.

* Students: No (...).

* The Shaykh: Like brothers. Alright, and paternal uncles?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Brothers (...) and paternal uncles?

* A student: They do not inherit.

* Another student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Because the paternal aunt does not inherit. The paternal aunt does not inherit. That is, if a person dies leaving a paternal uncle and a paternal aunt, the paternal aunt does not inherit, (...). Yes indeed. Alright, let us complete the benefits, (...).

* A student: How can they be from one sea, ﴿and from each you eat﴾ [Fatir 12] (...)?

* The Shaykh: (...). The apparent meaning of the Qur'an: from this and from that. As for the matter of fish, both of them have no difficulty and no one says it comes from one (sea). But what is difficult is the matter of pearls and coral: does it come from one or not? This will come to us, Allah willing, among the benefits. Likewise, the intended meaning is not only pearls and coral; people may adorn themselves with things that come out of the sea other than these two types.

(...) The brothers of Joseph were too wise to address their father in a way that would have him go to the walls to ask. But ﴿Indeed, we will destroy the people of this town﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 31]: the intended meaning of "town" is its dwellings, is it not? The dwellings of the people. The evidence is His saying: ﴿the people of this town﴾. So you now see that this word has, in this place, a meaning that it cannot bear in another place. Context plays a great role in knowing the intended meaning of speech.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a demonstration of the power of Allah, the Exalted, in that from this water He made these two distant kinds: two seas of water, one of which is ﴿sweet, palatable, pleasant to drink﴾ [Fatir 12], and the second ﴿salty and bitter﴾ [Fatir 12]. They are one thing, yet they differ in this way.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: that sweet water is pleasant to drink, and the opposite is salty water. It follows from this that a person should not drink what he does not find palatable, because that affects him and harms him. Likewise, there is no harm in his taking what his soul desires, even if in some cases it is harmful to him. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in *Zad al-Ma'ad* that the soul's desire for a thing has a great effect in removing its harm. He gave an example of this, I think, in the case of carrion, which is foul and harmful. When a person is compelled to eat it and his need becomes intense (...), the soul accepts it and finds it palatable, then digests it, so it does not harm him. Because if it harmed (carrion would harm) the compelled person just as it harms the one not compelled, then its being lawful for him would entail his killing himself. For this reason, if he is compelled to eat and has nothing but poison, it is not lawful for him to eat the poison. Clear? He also gave an example of this with the story of Suhayb al-Rumi: "He had an eye ailment," meaning his eye hurt him from an inflammation he had. "Dates were brought to the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, ate some of them. Suhayb went to eat, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to him: 'You have an eye ailment.' (It is known that the one with an inflamed eye does not eat dates.) He said: 'O Messenger of Allah! I will chew it on the other side.'" How? For example, if the right eye has the inflammation, he chews it on the left side. "The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, laughed and said to him: 'Eat.'"[[Recorded by al-Hakim in his Mustadrak (8468), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Suhayb.]] He said: because his soul was now strongly craving it, and this craving removes the harm. So the main point is that a thing that is not palatable should not be taken by a person, and he should not force himself to it. For this reason it is said: "Eat what your stomach craves, and do not eat what your mouth craves." I do not know whether this is correct or not. Yes, it is correct, because some people enjoy a type of food, but their insides do not accept it. You find that when they eat it, their stomach begins to rumble, and perhaps they get diarrhea. We say: do not eat that, even if your mouth craves it, because it is harmful to you.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's blessing upon His servants through what they extract from these seas of flesh, based on His saying: ﴿and from each you eat fresh flesh﴾, without hardship and without fatigue (...). Yet the flesh of fish is among the best of meats. Likewise, the blessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in what we extract from these seas: from what? From the ornaments we wear.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the difference between the perfection of the flesh from these seas and the perfection of the ornaments. For regarding flesh He said: ﴿you eat﴾, and He did not mention the effort by which we reach this eating, because it is easy and light and is not worth mentioning. But regarding the ornament He said: "you extract," because it requires hardship and toil.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's power in carrying this heavy ship laden with goods upon the surface of the water, yet it is able to push the water and cut through it, based on His saying: ﴿and you see the ships in it, plowing﴾ [Fatir 12]. Otherwise, water is heavy and not easy. For this reason, when a person swims in water he needs strength to push the water. But these ships cut through the water, and the effect of this blessing does not appear fully unless a person remembers the old ships that moved by the winds.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah the Exalted's blessing upon us in attaining what we seek of His bounty through these ships, based on His saying: ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾.

Among its benefits: a person should take the means that lead to the desired goal, based on His saying: ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [Fatir 12]. As for a person who says, "I will sit at home, and my provision will come to me," and claims he is reliant upon Allah, do we agree with his statement? No. We say: if you are reliant upon Allah (tawakkul), do not be one who depends on others without effort (tawakkul vs. tawākul). There is a difference between tawakkul and tawākul. Take the means! This Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was the master of those who rely upon Allah, and yet he would take the means that bring benefit and repel harm, would he not? Very well, then seek of Allah's bounty and take the means, for the sky does not rain down gold or silver, and provision comes only through a person's seeking. The matter is too clear to need examples, but otherwise we would illustrate it with something very close to hand: if someone says, "If Allah has decreed a child for me, it will come to me," and he has not married, do we say this is the speech of a madman? Yes, a madman. How could a child come to you when you have not married? We know of no child that sprouts from (...) at all; rather, children come about through taking their causes, such as marriage. Very well, this likewise implies that provision needs to be sought (...).

Among its benefits: the obligation to be grateful for Allah's blessings, glorified and exalted is He, based on His saying: ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾. Indeed, Allah made these blessings and subjected them for you (...) so that we may give thanks to Him, glorified and exalted is He. We have previously mentioned many times that gratitude has its place in the tongue, the heart, and the limbs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 35, verses 13–14 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, said, showing the perfection of His power and His blessings as well. He said: (﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾, meaning He makes it enter, so it increases, ﴿and He causes the day to enter into the night﴾, meaning He makes it enter, so it increases). Pay attention to the author's words. Does this agree with the apparent meaning or not? (﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾, so it increases.) What is it that increases?

* Students: The day.
* Other students: The night.
* Sheikh: Alright, let us see. The day rose and the night increased, although the pronoun refers to the nearest mentioned noun, which is the day, so it increases. This requires examination. But its explanation of ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾ [Fatir 13] is that some of the night becomes part of the day. This is one explanation: that some of the night becomes part of the day. When some of the night becomes part of the day, it means the day has increased. It is as if he is saying: the night entered into the day and so it became day. Then what increases? The day. And the reverse is the reverse. But the apparent meaning of the noble verse is that He makes the night enter into the day, so that a portion of the day becomes night.

Now, if you say: "I have added this to the irrigation channel in this land." Do you know what the irrigation channel (sāqiyah) is or not? (...) in the land. The part that entered the channel made the land an irrigation channel.

So, I have made the night enter into the day: I made a part of the day into night. In that case, it is the night that lengthens.

The causing of the night to enter the day and the day to enter the night is undoubtedly a sign of the perfection of Allah's power, glorified and exalted, because if all of creation gathered together to cause even a small part of the night to enter the day, or the reverse, they would never be able to do it.

Then this entering is also an entering in an orderly manner. What is meant by "in an orderly manner"? It means that it comes gradually, little by little, so that human nature adapts to this entering. What do you think would happen if the night came in its full length all at once? For example, today the night lasted eight hours and thirty-five minutes, and the next night it lasted twelve hours and five minutes. What would the state of people be? They would be thrown into turmoil. But Allah, glorified and exalted, causes it to enter little by little. This is with regard to the disturbance.

On another point: if it entered like that all at once, you know that the reason for the length of the day is the sun's nearness to being directly overhead. When the sun comes close to being directly overhead, it must be extremely hot. That means this day would be in the depth of winter, and the day after it in the depth of summer, and this would be a great harm. But Allah, glorified and exalted, causes it to enter little by little, and this is part of the completeness of His power, wisdom and mercy.

Also, the entering of the night into the day, and the reverse, has a great effect on the climate, because the weather changes from severe cold over a long period to severe heat, also over a long period. Do you not know that this intense heat kills harmful germs in a way that none but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, knows?

To give a simple example that we all see: when the heat becomes intense, mosquitoes die and no trace of them remains. This is why they are most numerous in the period between summer and winter. Likewise, the intense cold kills germs, and none but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, knows the extent of this.

For this reason the scholars said: the people of the earth most afflicted by diseases are those on the equator and near it. Why? Because they have no winter that kills, nor a hot summer that kills either. This is an observed matter.

So, the entering of the night into the day contains several wisdoms. This is why He mentioned it: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and He causes the day to enter into the night﴾ [Fatir 13].

﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾ [Fatir 13], meaning: He made them subservient to His servants.

﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾. The sun is known, and the moon is known. He subjected them, meaning He made them submissive. Submissive to whom? To the benefits of the servants. For in the sun and the moon there are great benefits for the servants, which those with knowledge in this field understand: great benefits.

Allah has not explained to us the weight or the size of these sun and moon, because that is not beneficial knowledge for us (...). Ignorance of it does no harm, and knowledge of it is superfluous knowledge (fudūl al-'ilm). If it does not distract you from what is more important, then occupy yourself with it. Rather, He has explained the benefits that follow from the subjection of the sun and the moon. He said: ﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾ [Fatir 13]. By the sun there is day and night, is that not so? And also the ripening of fruits, and great lights. What do you think is made available to the world in energy after the sun rises? Much that cannot be counted, because it provides electricity, and it also provides softening of things, as things need softening and heat. Moreover, in recent times they have begun to extract great and enormous energy from the heat of the sun.

As for the moon, it has been subjected for us as well through the light it gives at night, and through the knowledge of reckoning it provides, the counting of years, and so on.

And if you want more on this, refer to the book Miftah Dar al-Sa'adah by Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him. He mentioned many great benefits of the sun and the moon, and others have also mentioned this. But a person will notice a difference between the research of Ibn al-Qayyim, for example, and the research of the scientists of nature, because the scientists of nature look at these things from a dark, pitch-black, purely material perspective, in which a person is not nurtured with a religious upbringing and does not recognise through them Allah's power and blessing. But when someone like Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, speaks about this, he always derives from it the mercy, power and wisdom of Allah, so a person, along with his knowledge of this vast body of sciences, finds within himself the fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, His exaltation, and love for Him.

He said: (﴿Each﴾ of them ﴿runs﴾ in its orbit ﴿until a specified term﴾ [Fatir 13], which is the Day of Resurrection). Each of which? Of the sun and the moon. ﴿Runs﴾ means it moves in its orbit. ﴿Until a specified term.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, likened the falak (orbit) to the whorl of a spindle (falakat al-mighzal). The whorl of a spindle is a disc with a rod at its top and at its base a stick around which the thread being spun is wound. Perhaps some of you have seen it. Yes, this turns, because the woman spinning turns it this way until it spins and tightens the thread. The falak here is the orbit for the sun, in which it turns, and for the moon, in which it turns.

In attributing running to each of them there is evidence that they move by their own essence and revolve around the earth. This is an observed matter: the sun revolves around the earth, and likewise the moon.

As for what the astronomers (ʿulamāʾ al-hay'ah) claim, that the earth is what turns and the sun does not turn around the earth, we deny them until there is a sensory proof for us, which would be a proof before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for departing from the apparent meaning of His words. Otherwise, our duty regarding these matters is not to depart from the apparent meaning of Allah's words, because Allah, exalted is He, is the Creator, and the Creator knows best what He has created, more than others. Is this accepted or not?
