The Messenger said: "Whoever kills an enemy, he has his spoils."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3051) and Muslim (1754/45), from Salamah ibn al-Akwa'.]] This is in jihad in the way of Allah, and his spoils are what he wears of clothing and the like, and this is a reward.

The scholars said: it is permissible to give a reward (ju'l) to whoever points them to a fortress or something similar, from matters that are of benefit to the mujahideen. It is permissible to give him a reward. And you have already learned that the Imam may inform the detachment (of the army), or not, when it returns and when it sets out. All of these are from the category of reward for doing good, and this is established.

But my intention is: do we derive it from the verse?

We say: we can derive it from the verse by way of reverse analogy.

If you say: "Establish for us reverse analogy, since we doubt the establishment of analogy in the first place"?

We say: we have the establishment of reverse analogy. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "And in the intercourse of one of you there is charity." That is, when a man comes to his wife, it is charity. The Companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, will one of us fulfil his desire and yet have a reward for it?" He said: "Tell me, if he had placed it in the unlawful, would he have incurred a sin?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Likewise, if he places it in the lawful, he has a reward."[[Narrated by Muslim (1006/53), from Abu Dharr.]] Do you understand?

* Also in the verse: evidence of the completeness of (Allah's) power, by His saying: "And that is not difficult for Allah" [Fatir 17].
* And in it: the correctness of the division by Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah) of Allah's attributes into affirmative (thubutiyyah) and negative (salbiyyah). I have mentioned to you that some people doubted the term "negative" and said: we should say (...).

Then He, exalted, said: "And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another" [Fatir 18], to the end.

* It is derived from the noble verse that a person does not bear the sins of others, by His saying: "And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another" [Fatir 18].
This benefit entails the establishment of the perfect justice of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, since He does not burden anyone with the burden of another.

* And among its benefits also: that imposing burdens is accepted only from one who is fit for it, by His saying: "bearer" (wazirah); because one who is not a bearer does not bear the sin of himself, let alone the sin of others. But the bearer bears the sin of himself and does not bear the sin of another.

* Among its benefits also: the prohibition of reliance on others. A person may act and say: "Allah will prepare for me someone who will supplicate for me, or ask forgiveness for me, or the like." We say: do not rely on this.

If someone says: what is the answer to His saying: "And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens" [al-'Ankabut 13]?

* A student: "And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens" [al-'Ankabut 13]; because they are the examples in that, in misguiding others, and by the following of others after them, they bear their burdens.

* The Shaykh: Because the burdens of others are in reality arising from their burdens, so it is as if they were the ones who did them. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection."[[Narrated by Muslim (1017/69), from Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah.]]

* From the benefits of the noble verse: we look at the reverse analogy. If the soul does not bear the sin of another, is it obligated to perform the duty of another, or does it stand in (...) for another?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: No. That is, just as a person does not bear the sin of another for committing sin, he does not bear the sin of another for abandoning an obligation. So if your father, or your son, or your maternal uncle, or your paternal uncle abandons an obligation, you do not bear its sin. The sin is upon that very man (...).

Because he says: "in" (inna), which is for emphasis, but "ma" (the restrictive particle) has been attached to it. His saying: "And to Allah" (...).

Read to us: that one other than oneself does not bear the burden of another even if he calls him to it; because of His saying: "And if one heavily laden calls [another] to [carry] its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he should be a close relative" [Fatir 18]. This is unlike the worldly life, where if someone calls you to help him with what he carries, or to carry it for him, you respond. But in the Hereafter, no. "And if one heavily laden calls [another] to [carry] its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he should be a close relative" [Fatir 18]. Therefore He said: "even if he should be a close relative" [Fatir 18].

* And among its benefits also: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is a warner; by His saying: "You are only a warner" [Fatir 18].

* And (this is a new benefit): only those who fear their Lord will benefit from his warning; by His saying: "You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen" to the end [Fatir 18].

* And among its benefits also: the fear that is praiseworthy is that which is in the unseen; by His saying: "Who fear their Lord unseen" [Fatir 18]. Because fear in public may be prompted by concern for the servants of Allah, but when it is in private, this is clear evidence that its possessor is sincere in his fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* And among its benefits also: the virtue of prayer, and that it (prayer) is a cause for benefiting from the warning of the Prophet ﷺ, like fear; by His saying: "And they establish prayer" [Fatir 18].

* And among its benefits also: that a man, or if you wish, say: that a person, when he purifies himself, the benefit of his purification is for himself, and Allah, glorified and exalted, gains nothing from it; by His saying: "And whoever purifies himself only purifies himself for [the benefit of] his own soul" [Fatir 18].

* A branch of this benefit: the commands of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are not for a benefit He gains by our obedience, but for our own mercy and benefit. Allah, exalted, said: "If you disbelieve, indeed Allah is free of need from you; and He does not approve for His servants disbelief. And if you are grateful, He approves it for you. And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another" [al-Zumar 7].

* And among them: the encouragement to purify the soul; by His saying: "And whoever purifies himself only purifies himself for [the benefit of] his own soul" [Fatir 18]. Every sensible person, when he knows that the benefit of an act returns to him, he will be concerned with it and perform it. So when you know that your purification of yourself is for your own benefit, you will be extremely eager for it.

Purification, as we have indicated, includes purifying the heart from all shirk, doubt, rancor, hatred, enmity and the like; and purifying speech from every objectionable utterance, meaning that a person says only what is good. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good or remain silent."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6475) and Muslim (47/74), from Abu Hurayrah.]]

Purifying actions also includes abstaining from indecencies, bad morals, and whatever else a person must purify himself from.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse also: the perfection of this Islamic religion, since it urges the purification of the self outwardly and inwardly: outwardly by words and deeds, and inwardly by the hearts.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that the return of all creatures is to Allah in His cosmic, legislative, and retributive rulings.
As for the cosmic rulings: it is evident that the return is to Allah, because no one can reverse Allah's cosmic decree, right?
As for the legislative: likewise, since the servants are created, nurtured, and worshipping Allah, Mighty and Majestic, it is required that they conform to His legislative rulings.
As for the retributive: the matter is clear, since none recompenses those who act for their deeds except Allah, glorified and exalted.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the prohibition of referring to other than Allah in matters that are specific to Allah; by His saying: "And to Allah is the destination" [Fatir 18]. So it is not permissible for us to refer to man-made systems of human invention, while we have the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ.

The Almighty said: (﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah﴾ at all times, ﴿while Allah is the Free of need﴾ from His creation, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾ in His dealings with them).

﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah﴾ [Fatir 15]. This address is general, to believer and disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked, the young and the old, male and female: all of mankind. Allah introduced this ruling with this form of address, which is a call (nida'), in order to alert the listener and to show the importance of the matter.

It may be said: everyone knows that he is in need of Allah, but have we acted according to the requirements of this knowledge? No. ﴿Nay, indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-'Alaq 6-7]. So Allah established this constant state, from which no human being is free, namely need of Allah, so that he would act in accordance with it, return to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and ask none but Allah.

﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need﴾ [Fatir 15]: this is a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya) which implies exclusivity (hasr), because both of its parts are definite. ﴿You are﴾ (antum) is a pronoun of definiteness, and ﴿the ones in need﴾ (al-fuqara') is marked with the definite article (al-), so it is definite.

﴿You are the ones in need﴾. And what of others than mankind: are they free of need of Allah or not? No, but since it is man who may see himself as independent of Allah, the need is restricted to him, as if He were saying: if no one is in need of Allah, then you are in need without doubt. If the rational human being who manages his own affairs is in need of Allah, then what of the beast? Is it not greater in need? Indeed it is greater in need of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, than man. But He addressed man with this because it is man who sees himself as having become independent of Allah and self-sufficient before Him.

Rather, some of the children of Adam have reversed the matter, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich﴾ [Ali 'Imran 181], and we seek refuge in Allah. So they reversed the matter, contrary to the reality to which the natural disposition (fitra) bears witness.

He said: ﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah﴾ [Fatir 15]. The word ﴿to﴾ (ila) here expresses the end point: that is, your need ends with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; none but Allah can fill your deficiency.

Then He said: ﴿while Allah is the Free of need﴾ [Fatir 15]; that is, the opposite of need. Al-Ghani means the one who is independent of others, as Allah says in Surah at-Taghabun: ﴿So they disbelieved and turned away, and Allah was free of need﴾ [at-Taghabun 6]. Allah, the Mighty, possesses vast independence, and yet His independence is coupled with praise; hence He said: ﴿the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Fatir 15]. He is Free of need and is praised for His independence, because He bestows it upon others. But among the children of Adam, a person may be rich yet not praiseworthy. If he is rich and uses his wealth to dominate others and boast over people, and does not fulfil what is required of him, is he praiseworthy or not? He is not praiseworthy. But Allah, the Mighty, is Free of need and Praiseworthy.

The word (hamid) may be understood as an active participle (ism al-fa'il) or as a passive participle (ism al-maf'ul).

As an active participle: because He, glorified and exalted, is the One who praises; He praises from among His servants everyone who deserves praise, and therefore He lauds His messengers, prophets and righteous servants, and to praise them is to commend them.

And He is also praised for two things: for the perfection of His attributes, and for the perfection of His bounty. So He is praised for the perfection of His attributes and praised for the perfection of His blessings.

Here we say: the Praiseworthy is praised for the perfection of His independence and the perfection of His generosity through that independence, is this not so? Because not every rich person is praised for the wealth he possesses, but Allah, the Mighty, is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.

As for His saying: ﴿And Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Fatir 15], ﴿He﴾ (huwa) is the subject (mubtada'), what is it?
* Student: a pronoun of separation (damir fasl).
* The Shaykh: a pronoun of separation. The pronoun of separation has three benefits. What are they? Explain this to me.
* Student: Allah is the Free of need; that is, none other than Allah, glorified and exalted.
* The Shaykh: none other than Him, Allah alone and no other, as we say: Zayd is the excellent one, meaning no other. That is one. What is the second benefit?
* Student: It separates the predicate from the attribute.
* The Shaykh: The separation between the predicate and the attribute; that is, distinguishing between them. The third?
* Student: Emphasis.
* The Shaykh: Emphasis. If you say: Zayd is the one standing, it is more emphatic than your saying: Zayd is standing.

So the benefits are three: ﴿And Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Fatir 15].

Then He said: ﴿If He wills, He will remove you﴾ [Fatir 16]: a conditional sentence, in which the protasis is ﴿if He wills﴾ and the apodosis is ﴿He will remove you﴾.

﴿He will remove you﴾: that is, by removing you.

﴿And bring a new creation﴾ [Fatir 16]. ﴿Will bring﴾ (ya'ti) is strange in being kasra-marked, since it is an imperfect verb?
* Student: it is jussive (majzum) by the elision of the weak letter.
* The Shaykh: jussive by elision. Its original form is (ya'tī), but the yā' was dropped because it is conjoined to the jussive ﴿will remove you﴾.

His saying: ﴿and bring a new creation﴾, (badalikum) with a creation, that is, with a created thing: the evidence is His saying: ﴿and bring﴾, that is, a new created thing. This is a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle, that is, a created thing, like the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/18), and the wording is his, from the hadith of 'A'isha.]]. And like His saying: ﴿This is the creation of Allah; so show me what those other than Him have created﴾ [Luqman 11]: "creation" here means His creation, that is, what He created.

The word khalq may also be used as a verbal noun, as in His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, to Him belong creation and command. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-A'raf 54]. But here it is meant in the sense of a passive participle.

Allah says: ﴿and bring a new creation﴾ [Fatir 16], that is, a new created thing other than you. How can He remove us and bring a new creation? If we are destroyed, from where will the new creation come? Is it created before the removal, or after it?
* Student: after it.
* The Shaykh: Now suppose the creation has now been removed; from where will the next come? Allah is able to bring a new, independent creation. This is clear. Furthermore, He may remove those who exist and then bring their successors from among them, or the children who grow up may be considered a new creation relative to the adults who perished. This is like what was said about the Children of Israel when they refused to enter the holy land and said: ﴿In it are a people of tyrants﴾. Allah tested them, saying: ﴿It is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land﴾ [al-Ma'idah 26]. They wandered between Egypt and Syria, a month's journey, and remained there for forty years, unable to find the way, lost.

Some scholars, especially modern ones, said: this was so that that arrogant, humiliated generation would perish, and a new generation would arise in the desert, strong and wanting to enter the holy lands, because it grew up in the desert and wanted cities; it had strength and resolve qualifying it to enter that land, because the first generation, arrogant and obstinate, perished during this period. So said some scholars, especially modern ones. They said: the wisdom in Allah striking them with this wandering was that the elders would perish and the young would be renewed. Allah knows best.

Rather, Allah, the Mighty, is able to erase people, remove them, and bring a new creation: either a separate new creation, or from the offspring of these, or He may destroy those in this land, for example, and others come and occupy the land, is this not so?

There are now three possibilities: either a new, separate creation; or the descendants of the people who have gone; or other people who come from other lands and take the place of those who have gone, as He says: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, and they will not be like you﴾ [Muhammad 38].

His saying: ﴿That is not﴾ [Fatir 17]: this ﴿mā﴾ is the Hijazi negation, having fulfilled all the conditions of its operation, since its subject is (dhā) and its predicate is (‘azīz), but the additional bā' has entered upon its predicate in grammatical analysis.

﴿And that is not﴾, that is, your removal and the bringing of a new creation.

﴿And that is not for Allah a difficult matter﴾ [Fatir 17]. ﴿For Allah﴾ is a prepositional phrase governing and related to (‘azīz), placed before it.

His saying: ﴿bi-‘azīz﴾ (difficult). The author said: "severe", and the correct sense is 'azīz in the meaning of "unattainable", since ('azza) comes in the sense of "to be unattainable", as we have seen, and also in the sense of "to overcome", and in the sense of "power and measure"; its meaning here is closest to the sense of might and measure.

Here ﴿bi-‘azīz﴾ means "unattainable", and the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said "severe", because the severe is in itself unattainable through its strength and firmness. If it is not unattainable for Allah, then it is easy. Accordingly, we say that this is one of the negative attributes by which we describe Allah, the Mighty, while affirming the perfection of its opposite: ﴿And that is not for Allah a difficult matter﴾ [Fatir 17], because of His perfect ease. It is a matter easy for Him, glorified and exalted, to remove these and bring others. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, and they will not be like you﴾ [Muhammad 38].

Allah says: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [Fatir 18]. When He explained what the matter of these disbelievers would come to, and threatened those who departed from His obedience with His ability to remove them and bring a new creation, He mentioned the innocence of those who do not bear burdens from those who bear them; that is, the shirk of these polytheists does not affect those believing monotheists.

He said: ﴿And no bearer of burdens﴾. The author said: "A soul (nafs) that is ﴿bearing﴾ is sinful."

﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [Fatir 18]. ﴿Bearer (wazira)﴾: the author informed us, by estimating "soul" (nafs), that ﴿wazira﴾ is an attribute of an elided noun, its estimate being: soul.

His saying: ﴿wazira﴾, that is, sinful. Does this mean sinful in actuality, or that it is of those who possess sin and burden, namely the responsible, mature, rational person? That is, one who is fit to sin when he acts does not bear the sin of another, and the benefit of mentioning the "bearer" is that a child, for example, bears no sin, neither his own nor another's, unlike the adult who bears sin. Does he bear the sin of another?

He, the Mighty, says: ﴿And no bearer of burdens﴾ [Fatir 18]. The author said: "sinful, meaning does not carry."

The word ﴿taziru﴾ the author explained by saying "that is, does not carry". This is an explanation of the intended meaning, not the literal correspondence of the wording, since the literal meaning of ﴿taziru﴾ is "sins", for the burden (wizr) is sin. But we have often seen that Qur'anic exegesis may intend a literal explanation, and may intend an explanation of the meaning intended rather than the literal wording; that is, it does not carry the burden of another soul.

He also informed us, by saying "the burden of a soul" is an attribute of an elided noun, its estimate being "soul"; that is, Zayd does not bear the sin of 'Amr, and Hind does not bear the burden of Fatima, for example. Is this clear? Each bears his own burden. Allah, explaining this in a sentence that constitutes a rule, says: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ [al-Muddaththir 38], ﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned﴾ [at-Tur 21]. As for one who has earned nothing, he bears none of the sin of others. This is not contradicted by the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection"[[Related by Muslim (1017/69) from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah.]]. For his establishing it counts as a burden, since he is the one who opened the path and paved the ways; therefore he bears its burden and the burden of those who act upon it until the Day of Resurrection. So the verse here does not contradict the hadith.

He said: ﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he were a close relative﴾ [Fatir 18]. (﴿And if﴾ a soul ﴿heavily laden﴾ with burdens ﴿calls﴾ anyone ﴿to its load﴾ so that he may carry some of it, ﴿nothing of it will be carried﴾.)

"If it calls" means: if it asks. ﴿Heavily laden﴾ with what? With burdens. ﴿To its load﴾ so that some of it may be carried for it: ﴿nothing of it will be carried.﴾ The clause ﴿nothing of it will be carried﴾ is the apodosis; the protasis is ﴿if it calls﴾, which is jussive by the elision of the waw, the preceding damma being evidence of it. ﴿Will be carried﴾ is the apodosis, and ﴿nothing﴾ is the deputy subject. That is, just as one person does not carry another's burden, even if he is called upon and asked for help to carry or to lighten some of the burden of the bearer, it is not possible. In this world a person may be taken for another's offence. In this world also, if a man cries out to you for help because he is carrying something heavy, will you help him or not? You will help him. But in the Hereafter, if a heavily laden soul calls someone to bear some of its load, it will not be answered: ﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried﴾ [Fatir 18].

His saying: ﴿shay'un (nothing)﴾ is indefinite in a negative context, so it covers the little and the much.

His saying: ﴿muthqalatun (heavily laden)﴾ is also indefinite in a negative context, so it covers any heavily laden soul, whatever it may be: if it calls anyone among people to bear some of its burdens, nothing of it will be carried.

He then said: ﴿And even if he were a close relative﴾ [Fatir 18]. (﴿Even if he were﴾ the one called ﴿a close relative﴾, such as a father or son.)

The author's words "even if he were the one called" [lit. the called-upon]: could we not say "even if he were the caller"? It is possible, but they are interrelated: if the one called upon is close to the caller, then the caller is close to him. But which is more suitable in context: ﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he were a close relative﴾ [Fatir 18]?
* Students: the one called upon.
* The Shaykh: But ﴿if one heavily laden calls﴾; what is mentioned here is the caller. ﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he were a close relative﴾ [Fatir 18].

We say: the one called upon is closer, because if the intended meaning were the caller, it would be more fitting, Allah knows best, to say "even if she were a close relative", since He said ﴿if [a soul] calls﴾. It is known that the feminine pronoun, even metaphorically, is feminine, is it not?
* Student: feminine.
* The Shaykh: It is feminine. Ibn Malik said:
"It is required only with a verb whose subject is an attached pronoun or one that conveys a female referent."

So ﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if she were a close relative﴾ would also be correct if the caller were meant. But since He said ﴿even if he were a close relative﴾ in the masculine, it is understood that the doer is other than the caller.

His saying: ﴿qurba (close relative)﴾ means kinship, as in His saying: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of war booty, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger and for the near relatives (dhi al-qurba)﴾ [al-Anfal 41], that is, the kindred. And His saying: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for it any reward except affection for relatives (al-qurba)﴾ [ash-Shura 23]. So al-qurba here means kinship. If a father called upon his son on the Day of Resurrection to bear some of his burdens, would he answer? No, he would not answer. Rather: ﴿A man will flee from his brother, and from his mother and his father, and from his spouse and his children﴾ [Abasa 34-36]. Why? ﴿For every man that Day will be a matter that preoccupies him﴾ [Abasa 37].

﴿And even if he were a close relative﴾ [Fatir 18]. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The non-carrying in both halves is a ruling from Allah."

His saying: "the non-carrying in both halves": where are the two halves? His saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [Fatir 18], that is, will not carry.

And if one heavily burdened calls out for its load, nothing of it will be carried, even by a close relative (Fatir 18). Since this is from Allah, no one can carry anything for anyone else, even if they are willing. If someone said to another, "Your sins are upon me," could that be so? It is not valid, because the one who bears (the burden) is Allah. The ruling comes from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If someone sought help from another to carry his burden, and the other agreed to aid him in that, would it be valid? No. This is a ruling from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This act is in His saying (in the author's words: "The non-bearing in both cases is a ruling from Allah"), meaning that no one may go beyond it, that is, the ruling. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Follow our way, and we will bear your sins"﴾ (al-'Ankabut 12). Allah said: ﴿But they are not at all bearers of their sins. Indeed, they are liars﴾ (al-'Ankabut 12). That is, they say this, but they are not truthful in this undertaking: ﴿Indeed, they are liars.﴾

Then He said: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and additional burdens along with their burdens﴾ (al-'Ankabut 13). Not by their own commitment, but because they were the examples and the models, so they would bear their own burdens and the burdens of those whom they led astray.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ (Fatir 18). ﴿You can only warn﴾: this sentence contains restriction (hasr). Its means is ﴿innama﴾ (only). And what is restriction (hasr)?
* A student: Restricting one thing to another thing.
* The Shaykh: What is the meaning of restricting one thing to another thing?
* The student: ﴿Innama﴾ is a particle of restriction.
* The Shaykh: Yes. What is the meaning of restriction? 
* A student: Affirming the ruling for one thing.
* The Shaykh: Affirming the ruling for what is mentioned, and if you wish, say: for what is restricted to it, and negating it from anything else.

﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ (Fatir 18), as if it were said: "You warn none but those who fear their Lord."

﴿Tundhiru﴾ (you warn) comes from ﴿al-indhar﴾ (warning), which is informing accompanied by intimidation. This warning is informing accompanied by intimidation; or, if you wish, say: informing whose purpose is intimidation, since it is understood from the form and context of the speech, for example, that it is for intimidation. 

So the commander of an army who warns says, "Oh morning!" and people know that this is a warning to the army. Thus, warning means informing whose purpose is intimidation. So the Prophet, peace be upon him, is told by Allah: ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ (Fatir 18).

His saying ﴿who fear their Lord﴾: ﴿al-khashyah﴾ (fear/awe) is fear that arises from magnifying the one feared and knowing Him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ (Fatir 28).

Our saying that it is fear arising from magnifying the one feared is to include one who fears even if he is strong. That is, a strong person may be feared by others, so that is khashyah. If a weak person fears a strong one, that is khawf (fear). For this reason we say that khashyah is greater than khawf. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ (Fatir 28).

His saying ﴿who fear their Lord﴾ (Fatir 18) means: they fear Him with a fear arising from their magnification of Him together with their knowledge that He deserves to be magnified.

His saying ﴿who fear their Lord unseen﴾ (Fatir 18): ﴿al-ghayb﴾ (the unseen) is the opposite of what is witnessed and known. That is, (they fear Him while not having seen Him). This shows us that His saying ﴿bil-ghayb﴾ (unseen) is a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to the object: that is, they fear their Lord while He is absent from them and they have not seen Him. Pay attention! This is one of the two interpretations of the verse.

The second interpretation: they fear their Lord while they are absent from others, so the prepositional phrase is a circumstantial phrase relating to the subject. For among people there are those who display fear of Allah before others, but when they are away from people, they do not fear Allah.

Is such a person praised for his fear? No, because he is a hypocrite (muraa'). But the one who fears his Lord in the unseen is the one who is praised.

If you say: Can the verse be understood as having both meanings, so that those whom Allah praised fear Allah even though they have not seen Him, and fear Allah when they are away from people?

The answer: Yes. This is from the eloquence of the Qur'an, that it expresses something suitable for two meanings that do not contradict each other. These people fear Allah the Exalted although they have not seen Him, but they fear Him as if they saw Him, because they fear Him in the unseen and in the witnessed. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Ihsan is that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you."[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50), and Muslim (9/5), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]

His saying ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ (Fatir 18) does not contradict that he is a warner for all people: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ (Fatir 24), ﴿You are only a warner﴾ (Fatir 23), and similar verses indicating the generality of his warning. Why? Because the warning meant here is beneficial warning. That is, your warning only has an effect on those who fear their Lord unseen. As for one who does not fear Allah unseen, even if he is warned, he does not benefit from the warning. For this reason the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said, pointing to this: "Because they are the ones who benefit from the warning." ("Because they") means: those who fear their Lord unseen are the ones who benefit from the warning. Therefore the warning is restricted to them.

So the restriction here, restricting the warning to those who fear their Lord unseen, is meant as restricting its benefit. Who is it for? As for one who does not fear Allah, this does not benefit him. ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe. Even if every sign should come to them until they see the painful punishment﴾ (Yunus 96-97).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah﴾ (Fatir 17). What is the meaning of this, and what does ﴿that﴾ refer to?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Well done. That is, it is impossible (mumtani'). "Ṣaḥ" means it is easy, entirely easy.

In His saying ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah﴾ (Fatir 17), from which of the attributes is it?
It is from the attributes of the relative clause (silat al-mawsul), ﴿yakhshawna﴾ (they fear).

Here He said ﴿yakhshawna﴾ and ﴿wa-aqamu al-salah﴾ (and they establish prayer), so He connected the past tense to the present tense, because fear is continuous in all their deeds, including establishing prayer and other things.

His saying ﴿wa-aqamu al-salah﴾ (Fatir 18): the author said, "they maintained it" (adamuha). The reality is that establishing the prayer is more general than what he said, so his explanation is deficient, because establishing the prayer includes completing it, perfecting it, guarding it, and persevering in it.

Listen to the Exalted's saying: ﴿Successful indeed are the believers, who in their prayer are humbly submissive﴾ (al-Mu'minun 1-2). This is from establishing it. What does He say about it?
Then He said: ﴿And those who are continually attentive to their prayers﴾ (al-Mu'minun 9). This too is from establishing it: guarding it, striving for it, its obligatory parts, its complements, and its times.

In Surat al-Ma'arij He said: ﴿Those who are constant in their prayer﴾ (al-Ma'arij 23), and at its end He said: ﴿And those who guard their prayers﴾ (al-Ma'arij 34). So establishing the prayer includes everything that completes it, perfects it, and maintains it, so it is more general than what the author said.

His saying ﴿al-salah﴾ (the prayer) (Fatir 18) includes obligatory and voluntary prayers, because the definite article (al) indicates generality: that is, they established every prayer. The prayer is known; linguistically it means supplication (du'a').

In the Shari'ah it means worshipping Allah, the Exalted, with known statements and actions, opened with the takbir and concluded with the taslim.

He said: ﴿And whoever purifies himself - he purifies himself only for himself﴾ (Fatir 18). This sentence is conditional (shartiyyah): its protasis (fi'l al-shart) is ﴿tazakka﴾ (purifies himself), and its apodosis (jawab) is ﴿fa-innama yatazakka li-nafsihi﴾ (he purifies himself only for himself).

He said ﴿wa-man tazakka﴾ (and whoever purifies himself). The author said: "He purifies himself from shirk and other things."
﴿Tazakka﴾: that is, he purifies himself from shirk and other things, because zakah conveys the meaning of purity. The meaning of purification here is what is indicated by His saying: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself﴾ (al-A'la 14), and His saying: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies it﴾ (al-Shams 9); that is, whoever purifies his soul, namely cleanses it from shirk.

The author's saying "and other things" includes, for example, intending evil, sins, and intending bad things toward people, and other things a person must purify himself from. So it is general.

Does paying zakah enter into this? Yes, it enters, because paying zakah purifies from stinginess and (...). So it is included in His saying: ﴿And whoever purifies himself﴾ (Fatir 18).

His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿fa-innama yatazakka li-nafsihi﴾ (Fatir 18). The meaning of this is encouragement to purify oneself, because when you purify yourself, you benefit only yourself. Because (...) purifies himself, the harm is upon himself. So when you purify yourself, the one who benefits from your purification is you yourself. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, does not benefit from your obedience. As for others, they may benefit from your obedience, not because your good deeds are for them, but they may benefit from your obedience through being an example for them, and through the knowledge that results, or other things that fall within purification.

His saying ﴿fa-innama yatazakka li-nafsihi﴾ (Fatir 18): that is, he must strive to purify himself.

﴿And to Allah is the destination﴾ (Fatir 18). ﴿Al-masir⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ (the destination) means "the return" (al-marji'), as the author said. The prepositional phrase is attached to a deleted predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿al-masir﴾ is a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). This sentence conveys restriction, because the predicate was placed first although its place is to be delayed. That is: the destination belongs to Allah alone, that is, the return.

Is it in this world or in this world and the Hereafter? In this world and the Hereafter. To Allah is the destination in this world and in the Hereafter, so the return of all affairs is to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter.

Where do legislative rulings return? To whom? To Allah: ﴿And whatever you differ over, its judgment is with Allah﴾ (al-Shura 10).
Cosmic decrees return to Allah: ﴿But Allah does what He wills﴾ (al-Baqarah 253).
The retributive judgments that occur on the Day of Resurrection return to Allah. So the destination of everything is to the One who originated and created everything, and the One who originated and created affairs is Allah. So they return to Allah: from Him is the beginning and to Him is the end.

The author said, deducing from His saying ﴿And to Allah is the destination﴾ (Fatir 18): "Then He recompenses for deeds in the Hereafter." This indicates that the author restricted the destination here to the return on the Day of Resurrection.

The correct view is generality. On this basis, He, the Glorified and Exalted, recompenses and judges by decree and judges by law among His servants.

Now, the benefits (of the verse). Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor toward Allah, and Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ (Fatir 15).

* In this verse are many benefits, among them: all creation is in need of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, however much they attain wealth and strength, they are in need of Allah. This is from His saying ﴿O mankind﴾. This is a general expression from which nothing is excluded.
* Among them: showing the intensity of people's need for Allah. This is from His saying ﴿You are the poor﴾ with the definite article (al): ﴿al-fuqara'﴾ (the poor). Had He said "fuqara'" (poor) it would be less intense, but "al-fuqara'" means that in all our states we are in need of our Lord, the Glorified and Exalted.
* Among the benefits of the verse: showing Allah's independence from everyone; this is from His saying ﴿And Allah is the Free of need﴾ (Fatir 15).
* Among them: that Allah has absolute independence from every aspect. This is understood from His saying ﴿al-Ghaniyy﴾ (the Free of need), where the definite article (al) indicates generality and comprehensiveness.

If you say: how do you say that independence belongs to Allah alone, that He is the Free of need? That is, the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) indicates restriction, and perhaps we should take this benefit first.

* Among its benefits: that complete and absolute independence is specific to whom? To Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, by His saying ﴿He is the Free of need﴾ (Fatir 15).

If you say: how do you reconcile this with the affirmation of independence for other than Allah in the Book and the Sunnah? Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their restraint﴾ (al-Baqarah 273). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "It is taken from their wealthy and returned to their poor."[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1496), and Muslim (19/29), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas.] So it is established by the Book and the Sunnah that some humans are wealthy. How is that established?

The answer: The wealth of humans is limited, relative, deficient, and subject to cessation, just as it was originated. As for the independence of Allah, it is absolute, complete, eternal, and everlasting, (...) what is established in dominion, creation, and management, and similar matters.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: (...) the poor and the Free of need in it is a kind of perfection of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, by which the deficiency of humans becomes clear in comparison to the perfection of Allah. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾ (al-Rahman 26), then He said: ﴿But there remains the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor﴾ (al-Rahman 27), and ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ (al-Qasas 88). Describing the created being with deficiency, then affirming perfection for Allah, indicates the perfection of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that His perfection is very clear, because when you mention the defect of the other, the perfection of its opposite becomes clear to you.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the independence of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, is joined with praise. This is from His saying ﴿the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ (Fatir 15), unlike human independence, which may not be praiseworthy. How can it not be praiseworthy? Either...?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What else? (...) Either through stinginess, or because it comes without entitlement, like thieves and robbers, who may be wealthy but acquired it in an impermissible way. As for the independence of Allah, it is complete independence for which He is praised.

So He is praised for His independence and for His generosity in that in which He is independent.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirming two of Allah's names, al-Ghaniyy (the Free of need) and al-Hamid (the Praiseworthy). Is this correct? Al-Ghaniyy indicates an attribute: what is it?
* Students: Independence.
* The Shaykh: And al-Hamid indicates an attribute?
* Students: Praise.
* The Shaykh: Yes, praise; and together they indicate a third attribute, which is the perfection of independence. We mentioned in the rules (...) that a third attribute may arise from combining two names or two attributes, and we gave the example of al-'Aziz and al-Hakim there (...), because by their combination a more perfect attribute is produced.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation﴾ (Fatir 16).

* From this noble verse is derived: the complete power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as He explained that He is able to take us away and then bring a new creation.
* Among its benefits: affirmation of Allah's will: ﴿If He wills﴾ (Fatir 16).
* Among its benefits: a warning against opposing Him, the Exalted, because this threat is aimed at it, and a warning for us against opposing Him.
* Among its benefits also: that creation is originated, not eternal; this is from His saying ﴿If He wills, He can take you away﴾ (Fatir 16). This is the evidence. ﴿And bring a new creation﴾ (Fatir 16) also contains evidence, does it not?
As for the first: the indication is that what is capable of non-existence is capable of coming into existence or of being originated.
As for the second, which is His saying ﴿a new creation﴾ (Fatir 16): do we derive from it the establishment of the origination of Allah's acts with respect to the things created?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, because every created thing comes into being by creation, so if the created thing is new, the creating must also be new.
For example, Allah's creation of the fetus in its mother's womb is originated, is it not?
* Students: Originated.
* The Shaykh: Originated, because the created thing is originated. As for the category of Allah's act, it is eternal: that is, Allah, the Exalted, has never ceased being active. So there is a difference between describing Allah with action in absolute terms and describing Allah with action linked to an object. An action linked to an object is undoubtedly originated, while absolute action, that Allah has never ceased being active as He wills, is eternal.

Do we derive from this the permissibility of threatening a person with tangible things so that he will adhere to the command of Allah? Yes, because this is a threat from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so that we will adhere to His command.

So we say: tangible punishments, even if they lead to uprightness, are praiseworthy, because they are the act of Allah. For this reason Allah obligated us to apply the prescribed punishment to the adulterer and to cut off the hand of the thief, right? So that he may be deterred.

No one should say: "If you do that, you have led people to abandon the matter not for the sake of Allah." Because some people say: "How is this? How do you fall into (...)?" It means that a person does not commit adultery or theft except out of fear of the punishment. That means you are leading people to avoid the forbidden things not out of fear of Allah but out of fear of the punishment.

We say: this contains reform, and the means of reform is what is in the intention of the one who is trying to reform him.

Can we derive from it the permissibility of giving a prize to encourage the one who does a good deed, or not? That is, by way of reverse analogy (qiyas al-'aks, argument by reversal)?

* Students: No (...).
* The Shaykh: Do not agree with them: "They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise" [al-Qalam 9]. Do not compromise. Can it be derived from this verse the permissibility of giving rewards to the one who does a righteous deed by way of reverse analogy?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Brother! Yes, what is your opinion if there is an objection?
* A student: There is, but it is remote (...).
* The Shaykh: There is, but it is remote. ("There is" is a fronted predicate, and "remote" is a postponed subject!!)
* The student: (...) that Allah, glorified and exalted, only punishes them for committing sin; if they commit sin, He punishes them (...); if they perform obedience, Allah, glorified and exalted, rewards them for that.
* The Shaykh: He rewards them for that. Did you not come across the hadith: "Whoever loves that his provision be expanded and his life be extended, let him maintain his ties of kinship"?[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2067) and Muslim (2557/21), from Anas ibn Malik.]]
* The student: (...).
* Another student: (...) their ultimate return is to (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) That is, but there is encouragement in it.

In any case, what I meant was: can this verse be taken as evidence (...)? Reward for deeds is established in the Sunnah (the practice of the Prophet ﷺ) and also outside the Sunnah. The Messenger said: "Whoever kills an enemy, he has his spoils."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3051) and Muslim (1754/45), from Salamah ibn al-Akwa'.]] This is in jihad in the way of Allah, and his spoils are what he wears of clothing and the like, and this is a reward.

The scholars said: it is permissible to give a reward (ju'l) to whoever points them to a fortress or something similar, from matters that are of benefit to the mujahideen. It is permissible to give him a reward. And you have already learned that the Imam may inform the detachment (of the army), or not, when it returns and when it sets out. All of these are from the category of reward for doing good, and this is established.

But my intention is: do we derive it from the verse?

We say: we can derive it from the verse by way of reverse analogy.

If you say: "Establish for us reverse analogy, since we doubt the establishment of analogy in the first place"?

We say: we have the establishment of reverse analogy. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "And in the intercourse of one of you there is charity." That is, when a man comes to his wife, it is charity. The Companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, will one of us fulfil his desire and yet have a reward for it?" He said: "Tell me, if he had placed it in the unlawful, would he have incurred a sin?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Likewise, if he places it in the lawful, he has a reward."[[Narrated by Muslim (1006/53), from Abu Dharr.]] Do you understand?

* Also in the verse: evidence of the completeness of (Allah's) power, by His saying: "And that is not difficult for Allah" [Fatir 17].
* And in it: the correctness of the division by Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah) of Allah's attributes into affirmative (thubutiyyah) and negative (salbiyyah). I have mentioned to you that some people doubted the term "negative" and said: we should say (...).

Then He, exalted, said: "And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another" [Fatir 18], to the end.

* It is derived from the noble verse that a person does not bear the sins of others, by His saying: "And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another" [Fatir 18].
This benefit entails the establishment of the perfect justice of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, since He does not burden anyone with the burden of another.

* And among its benefits also: that imposing burdens is accepted only from one who is fit for it, by His saying: "bearer" (wazirah); because one who is not a bearer does not bear the sin of himself, let alone the sin of others. But the bearer bears the sin of himself and does not bear the sin of another.

* Among its benefits also: the prohibition of reliance on others. A person may act and say: "Allah will prepare for me someone who will supplicate for me, or ask forgiveness for me, or the like." We say: do not rely on this.

If someone says: what is the answer to His saying: "And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens" [al-'Ankabut 13]?

* A student: "And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens" [al-'Ankabut 13]; because they are the examples in that, in misguiding others, and by the following of others after them, they bear their burdens.

* The Shaykh: Because the burdens of others are in reality arising from their burdens, so it is as if they were the ones who did them. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection."[[Narrated by Muslim (1017/69), from Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah.]]

* From the benefits of the noble verse: we look at the reverse analogy. If the soul does not bear the sin of another, is it obligated to perform the duty of another, or does it stand in (...) for another?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: No. That is, just as a person does not bear the sin of another for committing sin, he does not bear the sin of another for abandoning an obligation. So if your father, or your son, or your maternal uncle, or your paternal uncle abandons an obligation, you do not bear its sin. The sin is upon that very man (...).

Because he says: "in" (inna), which is for emphasis, but "ma" (the restrictive particle) has been attached to it. His saying: "And to Allah" (...).

Read to us: that one other than oneself does not bear the burden of another even if he calls him to it; because of His saying: "And if one heavily laden calls [another] to [carry] its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he should be a close relative" [Fatir 18]. This is unlike the worldly life, where if someone calls you to help him with what he carries, or to carry it for him, you respond. But in the Hereafter, no. "And if one heavily laden calls [another] to [carry] its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he should be a close relative" [Fatir 18]. Therefore He said: "even if he should be a close relative" [Fatir 18].

* And among its benefits also: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is a warner; by His saying: "You are only a warner" [Fatir 18].

* And (this is a new benefit): only those who fear their Lord will benefit from his warning; by His saying: "You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen" to the end [Fatir 18].

* And among its benefits also: the fear that is praiseworthy is that which is in the unseen; by His saying: "Who fear their Lord unseen" [Fatir 18]. Because fear in public may be prompted by concern for the servants of Allah, but when it is in private, this is clear evidence that its possessor is sincere in his fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* And among its benefits also: the virtue of prayer, and that it (prayer) is a cause for benefiting from the warning of the Prophet ﷺ, like fear; by His saying: "And they establish prayer" [Fatir 18].

* And among its benefits also: that a man, or if you wish, say: that a person, when he purifies himself, the benefit of his purification is for himself, and Allah, glorified and exalted, gains nothing from it; by His saying: "And whoever purifies himself only purifies himself for [the benefit of] his own soul" [Fatir 18].

* A branch of this benefit: the commands of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are not for a benefit He gains by our obedience, but for our own mercy and benefit. Allah, exalted, said: "If you disbelieve, indeed Allah is free of need from you; and He does not approve for His servants disbelief. And if you are grateful, He approves it for you. And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another" [al-Zumar 7].

* And among them: the encouragement to purify the soul; by His saying: "And whoever purifies himself only purifies himself for [the benefit of] his own soul" [Fatir 18]. Every sensible person, when he knows that the benefit of an act returns to him, he will be concerned with it and perform it. So when you know that your purification of yourself is for your own benefit, you will be extremely eager for it.

Purification, as we have indicated, includes purifying the heart from all shirk, doubt, rancor, hatred, enmity and the like; and purifying speech from every objectionable utterance, meaning that a person says only what is good. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good or remain silent."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6475) and Muslim (47/74), from Abu Hurayrah.]]

Purifying actions also includes abstaining from indecencies, bad morals, and whatever else a person must purify himself from.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse also: the perfection of this Islamic religion, since it urges the purification of the self outwardly and inwardly: outwardly by words and deeds, and inwardly by the hearts.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that the return of all creatures is to Allah in His cosmic, legislative, and retributive rulings.
As for the cosmic rulings: it is evident that the return is to Allah, because no one can reverse Allah's cosmic decree, right?
As for the legislative: likewise, since the servants are created, nurtured, and worshipping Allah, Mighty and Majestic, it is required that they conform to His legislative rulings.
As for the retributive: the matter is clear, since none recompenses those who act for their deeds except Allah, glorified and exalted.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the prohibition of referring to other than Allah in matters that are specific to Allah; by His saying: "And to Allah is the destination" [Fatir 18]. So it is not permissible for us to refer to man-made systems of human invention, while we have the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ.

The Almighty said: (﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah﴾ at all times, ﴿while Allah is the Free of need﴾ from His creation, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾ in His dealings with them).

﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah﴾ [Fatir 15]. This address is general, to believer and disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked, the young and the old, male and female: all of mankind. Allah introduced this ruling with this form of address, which is a call (nida'), in order to alert the listener and to show the importance of the matter.

It may be said: everyone knows that he is in need of Allah, but have we acted according to the requirements of this knowledge? No. ﴿Nay, indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-'Alaq 6-7]. So Allah established this constant state, from which no human being is free, namely need of Allah, so that he would act in accordance with it, return to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and ask none but Allah.

﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need﴾ [Fatir 15]: this is a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya) which implies exclusivity (hasr), because both of its parts are definite. ﴿You are﴾ (antum) is a pronoun of definiteness, and ﴿the ones in need﴾ (al-fuqara') is marked with the definite article (al-), so it is definite.

﴿You are the ones in need﴾. And what of others than mankind: are they free of need of Allah or not? No, but since it is man who may see himself as independent of Allah, the need is restricted to him, as if He were saying: if no one is in need of Allah, then you are in need without doubt. If the rational human being who manages his own affairs is in need of Allah, then what of the beast? Is it not greater in need? Indeed it is greater in need of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, than man. But He addressed man with this because it is man who sees himself as having become independent of Allah and self-sufficient before Him.

Rather, some of the children of Adam have reversed the matter, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich﴾ [Ali 'Imran 181], and we seek refuge in Allah. So they reversed the matter, contrary to the reality to which the natural disposition (fitra) bears witness.

He said: ﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah﴾ [Fatir 15]. The word ﴿to﴾ (ila) here expresses the end point: that is, your need ends with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; none but Allah can fill your deficiency.

Then He said: ﴿while Allah is the Free of need﴾ [Fatir 15]; that is, the opposite of need. Al-Ghani means the one who is independent of others, as Allah says in Surah at-Taghabun: ﴿So they disbelieved and turned away, and Allah was free of need﴾ [at-Taghabun 6]. Allah, the Mighty, possesses vast independence, and yet His independence is coupled with praise; hence He said: ﴿the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Fatir 15]. He is Free of need and is praised for His independence, because He bestows it upon others. But among the children of Adam, a person may be rich yet not praiseworthy. If he is rich and uses his wealth to dominate others and boast over people, and does not fulfil what is required of him, is he praiseworthy or not? He is not praiseworthy. But Allah, the Mighty, is Free of need and Praiseworthy.

The word (hamid) may be understood as an active participle (ism al-fa'il) or as a passive participle (ism al-maf'ul).

As an active participle: because He, glorified and exalted, is the One who praises; He praises from among His servants everyone who deserves praise, and therefore He lauds His messengers, prophets and righteous servants, and to praise them is to commend them.

And He is also praised for two things: for the perfection of His attributes, and for the perfection of His bounty. So He is praised for the perfection of His attributes and praised for the perfection of His blessings.

Here we say: the Praiseworthy is praised for the perfection of His independence and the perfection of His generosity through that independence, is this not so? Because not every rich person is praised for the wealth he possesses, but Allah, the Mighty, is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.

As for His saying: ﴿And Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Fatir 15], ﴿He﴾ (huwa) is the subject (mubtada'), what is it?
* Student: a pronoun of separation (damir fasl).
* The Shaykh: a pronoun of separation. The pronoun of separation has three benefits. What are they? Explain this to me.
* Student: Allah is the Free of need; that is, none other than Allah, glorified and exalted.
* The Shaykh: none other than Him, Allah alone and no other, as we say: Zayd is the excellent one, meaning no other. That is one. What is the second benefit?
* Student: It separates the predicate from the attribute.
* The Shaykh: The separation between the predicate and the attribute; that is, distinguishing between them. The third?
* Student: Emphasis.
* The Shaykh: Emphasis. If you say: Zayd is the one standing, it is more emphatic than your saying: Zayd is standing.

So the benefits are three: ﴿And Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Fatir 15].

Then He said: ﴿If He wills, He will remove you﴾ [Fatir 16]: a conditional sentence, in which the protasis is ﴿if He wills﴾ and the apodosis is ﴿He will remove you﴾.

﴿He will remove you﴾: that is, by removing you.

﴿And bring a new creation﴾ [Fatir 16]. ﴿Will bring﴾ (ya'ti) is strange in being kasra-marked, since it is an imperfect verb?
* Student: it is jussive (majzum) by the elision of the weak letter.
* The Shaykh: jussive by elision. Its original form is (ya'tī), but the yā' was dropped because it is conjoined to the jussive ﴿will remove you﴾.

His saying: ﴿and bring a new creation﴾, (badalikum) with a creation, that is, with a created thing: the evidence is His saying: ﴿and bring﴾, that is, a new created thing. This is a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle, that is, a created thing, like the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/18), and the wording is his, from the hadith of 'A'isha.]]. And like His saying: ﴿This is the creation of Allah; so show me what those other than Him have created﴾ [Luqman 11]: "creation" here means His creation, that is, what He created.

The word khalq may also be used as a verbal noun, as in His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, to Him belong creation and command. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-A'raf 54]. But here it is meant in the sense of a passive participle.

Allah says: ﴿and bring a new creation﴾ [Fatir 16], that is, a new created thing other than you. How can He remove us and bring a new creation? If we are destroyed, from where will the new creation come? Is it created before the removal, or after it?
* Student: after it.
* The Shaykh: Now suppose the creation has now been removed; from where will the next come? Allah is able to bring a new, independent creation. This is clear. Furthermore, He may remove those who exist and then bring their successors from among them, or the children who grow up may be considered a new creation relative to the adults who perished. This is like what was said about the Children of Israel when they refused to enter the holy land and said: ﴿In it are a people of tyrants﴾. Allah tested them, saying: ﴿It is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land﴾ [al-Ma'idah 26]. They wandered between Egypt and Syria, a month's journey, and remained there for forty years, unable to find the way, lost.

Some scholars, especially modern ones, said: this was so that that arrogant, humiliated generation would perish, and a new generation would arise in the desert, strong and wanting to enter the holy lands, because it grew up in the desert and wanted cities; it had strength and resolve qualifying it to enter that land, because the first generation, arrogant and obstinate, perished during this period. So said some scholars, especially modern ones. They said: the wisdom in Allah striking them with this wandering was that the elders would perish and the young would be renewed. Allah knows best.

Rather, Allah, the Mighty, is able to erase people, remove them, and bring a new creation: either a separate new creation, or from the offspring of these, or He may destroy those in this land, for example, and others come and occupy the land, is this not so?

There are now three possibilities: either a new, separate creation; or the descendants of the people who have gone; or other people who come from other lands and take the place of those who have gone, as He says: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, and they will not be like you﴾ [Muhammad 38].

His saying: ﴿That is not﴾ [Fatir 17]: this ﴿mā﴾ is the Hijazi negation, having fulfilled all the conditions of its operation, since its subject is (dhā) and its predicate is (‘azīz), but the additional bā' has entered upon its predicate in grammatical analysis.

﴿And that is not﴾, that is, your removal and the bringing of a new creation.

﴿And that is not for Allah a difficult matter﴾ [Fatir 17]. ﴿For Allah﴾ is a prepositional phrase governing and related to (‘azīz), placed before it.

His saying: ﴿bi-‘azīz﴾ (difficult). The author said: "severe", and the correct sense is 'azīz in the meaning of "unattainable", since ('azza) comes in the sense of "to be unattainable", as we have seen, and also in the sense of "to overcome", and in the sense of "power and measure"; its meaning here is closest to the sense of might and measure.

Here ﴿bi-‘azīz﴾ means "unattainable", and the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said "severe", because the severe is in itself unattainable through its strength and firmness. If it is not unattainable for Allah, then it is easy. Accordingly, we say that this is one of the negative attributes by which we describe Allah, the Mighty, while affirming the perfection of its opposite: ﴿And that is not for Allah a difficult matter﴾ [Fatir 17], because of His perfect ease. It is a matter easy for Him, glorified and exalted, to remove these and bring others. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, and they will not be like you﴾ [Muhammad 38].

Allah says: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [Fatir 18]. When He explained what the matter of these disbelievers would come to, and threatened those who departed from His obedience with His ability to remove them and bring a new creation, He mentioned the innocence of those who do not bear burdens from those who bear them; that is, the shirk of these polytheists does not affect those believing monotheists.

He said: ﴿And no bearer of burdens﴾. The author said: "A soul (nafs) that is ﴿bearing﴾ is sinful."

﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [Fatir 18]. ﴿Bearer (wazira)﴾: the author informed us, by estimating "soul" (nafs), that ﴿wazira﴾ is an attribute of an elided noun, its estimate being: soul.

His saying: ﴿wazira﴾, that is, sinful. Does this mean sinful in actuality, or that it is of those who possess sin and burden, namely the responsible, mature, rational person? That is, one who is fit to sin when he acts does not bear the sin of another, and the benefit of mentioning the "bearer" is that a child, for example, bears no sin, neither his own nor another's, unlike the adult who bears sin. Does he bear the sin of another?

He, the Mighty, says: ﴿And no bearer of burdens﴾ [Fatir 18]. The author said: "sinful, meaning does not carry."

The word ﴿taziru﴾ the author explained by saying "that is, does not carry". This is an explanation of the intended meaning, not the literal correspondence of the wording, since the literal meaning of ﴿taziru﴾ is "sins", for the burden (wizr) is sin. But we have often seen that Qur'anic exegesis may intend a literal explanation, and may intend an explanation of the meaning intended rather than the literal wording; that is, it does not carry the burden of another soul.

He also informed us, by saying "the burden of a soul" is an attribute of an elided noun, its estimate being "soul"; that is, Zayd does not bear the sin of 'Amr, and Hind does not bear the burden of Fatima, for example. Is this clear? Each bears his own burden. Allah, explaining this in a sentence that constitutes a rule, says: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ [al-Muddaththir 38], ﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned﴾ [at-Tur 21]. As for one who has earned nothing, he bears none of the sin of others. This is not contradicted by the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection"[[Related by Muslim (1017/69) from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah.]]. For his establishing it counts as a burden, since he is the one who opened the path and paved the ways; therefore he bears its burden and the burden of those who act upon it until the Day of Resurrection. So the verse here does not contradict the hadith.

He said: ﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he were a close relative﴾ [Fatir 18]. (﴿And if﴾ a soul ﴿heavily laden﴾ with burdens ﴿calls﴾ anyone ﴿to its load﴾ so that he may carry some of it, ﴿nothing of it will be carried﴾.)

"If it calls" means: if it asks. ﴿Heavily laden﴾ with what? With burdens. ﴿To its load﴾ so that some of it may be carried for it: ﴿nothing of it will be carried.﴾ The clause ﴿nothing of it will be carried﴾ is the apodosis; the protasis is ﴿if it calls﴾, which is jussive by the elision of the waw, the preceding damma being evidence of it. ﴿Will be carried﴾ is the apodosis, and ﴿nothing﴾ is the deputy subject. That is, just as one person does not carry another's burden, even if he is called upon and asked for help to carry or to lighten some of the burden of the bearer, it is not possible. In this world a person may be taken for another's offence. In this world also, if a man cries out to you for help because he is carrying something heavy, will you help him or not? You will help him. But in the Hereafter, if a heavily laden soul calls someone to bear some of its load, it will not be answered: ﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried﴾ [Fatir 18].

His saying: ﴿shay'un (nothing)﴾ is indefinite in a negative context, so it covers the little and the much.

His saying: ﴿muthqalatun (heavily laden)﴾ is also indefinite in a negative context, so it covers any heavily laden soul, whatever it may be: if it calls anyone among people to bear some of its burdens, nothing of it will be carried.

He then said: ﴿And even if he were a close relative﴾ [Fatir 18]. (﴿Even if he were﴾ the one called ﴿a close relative﴾, such as a father or son.)

The author's words "even if he were the one called" [lit. the called-upon]: could we not say "even if he were the caller"? It is possible, but they are interrelated: if the one called upon is close to the caller, then the caller is close to him. But which is more suitable in context: ﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he were a close relative﴾ [Fatir 18]?
* Students: the one called upon.
* The Shaykh: But ﴿if one heavily laden calls﴾; what is mentioned here is the caller. ﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he were a close relative﴾ [Fatir 18].

We say: the one called upon is closer, because if the intended meaning were the caller, it would be more fitting, Allah knows best, to say "even if she were a close relative", since He said ﴿if [a soul] calls﴾. It is known that the feminine pronoun, even metaphorically, is feminine, is it not?
* Student: feminine.
* The Shaykh: It is feminine. Ibn Malik said:
"It is required only with a verb whose subject is an attached pronoun or one that conveys a female referent."

So ﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if she were a close relative﴾ would also be correct if the caller were meant. But since He said ﴿even if he were a close relative﴾ in the masculine, it is understood that the doer is other than the caller.

His saying: ﴿qurba (close relative)﴾ means kinship, as in His saying: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of war booty, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger and for the near relatives (dhi al-qurba)﴾ [al-Anfal 41], that is, the kindred. And His saying: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for it any reward except affection for relatives (al-qurba)﴾ [ash-Shura 23]. So al-qurba here means kinship. If a father called upon his son on the Day of Resurrection to bear some of his burdens, would he answer? No, he would not answer. Rather: ﴿A man will flee from his brother, and from his mother and his father, and from his spouse and his children﴾ [Abasa 34-36]. Why? ﴿For every man that Day will be a matter that preoccupies him﴾ [Abasa 37].

﴿And even if he were a close relative﴾ [Fatir 18]. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The non-carrying in both halves is a ruling from Allah."

His saying: "the non-carrying in both halves": where are the two halves? His saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [Fatir 18], that is, will not carry.

And if one heavily burdened calls out for its load, nothing of it will be carried, even by a close relative (Fatir 18). Since this is from Allah, no one can carry anything for anyone else, even if they are willing. If someone said to another, "Your sins are upon me," could that be so? It is not valid, because the one who bears (the burden) is Allah. The ruling comes from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If someone sought help from another to carry his burden, and the other agreed to aid him in that, would it be valid? No. This is a ruling from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This act is in His saying (in the author's words: "The non-bearing in both cases is a ruling from Allah"), meaning that no one may go beyond it, that is, the ruling. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Follow our way, and we will bear your sins"﴾ (al-'Ankabut 12). Allah said: ﴿But they are not at all bearers of their sins. Indeed, they are liars﴾ (al-'Ankabut 12). That is, they say this, but they are not truthful in this undertaking: ﴿Indeed, they are liars.﴾

Then He said: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and additional burdens along with their burdens﴾ (al-'Ankabut 13). Not by their own commitment, but because they were the examples and the models, so they would bear their own burdens and the burdens of those whom they led astray.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ (Fatir 18). ﴿You can only warn﴾: this sentence contains restriction (hasr). Its means is ﴿innama﴾ (only). And what is restriction (hasr)?
* A student: Restricting one thing to another thing.
* The Shaykh: What is the meaning of restricting one thing to another thing?
* The student: ﴿Innama﴾ is a particle of restriction.
* The Shaykh: Yes. What is the meaning of restriction? 
* A student: Affirming the ruling for one thing.
* The Shaykh: Affirming the ruling for what is mentioned, and if you wish, say: for what is restricted to it, and negating it from anything else.

﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ (Fatir 18), as if it were said: "You warn none but those who fear their Lord."

﴿Tundhiru﴾ (you warn) comes from ﴿al-indhar﴾ (warning), which is informing accompanied by intimidation. This warning is informing accompanied by intimidation; or, if you wish, say: informing whose purpose is intimidation, since it is understood from the form and context of the speech, for example, that it is for intimidation. 

So the commander of an army who warns says, "Oh morning!" and people know that this is a warning to the army. Thus, warning means informing whose purpose is intimidation. So the Prophet, peace be upon him, is told by Allah: ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ (Fatir 18).

His saying ﴿who fear their Lord﴾: ﴿al-khashyah﴾ (fear/awe) is fear that arises from magnifying the one feared and knowing Him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ (Fatir 28).

Our saying that it is fear arising from magnifying the one feared is to include one who fears even if he is strong. That is, a strong person may be feared by others, so that is khashyah. If a weak person fears a strong one, that is khawf (fear). For this reason we say that khashyah is greater than khawf. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ (Fatir 28).

His saying ﴿who fear their Lord﴾ (Fatir 18) means: they fear Him with a fear arising from their magnification of Him together with their knowledge that He deserves to be magnified.

His saying ﴿who fear their Lord unseen﴾ (Fatir 18): ﴿al-ghayb﴾ (the unseen) is the opposite of what is witnessed and known. That is, (they fear Him while not having seen Him). This shows us that His saying ﴿bil-ghayb﴾ (unseen) is a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to the object: that is, they fear their Lord while He is absent from them and they have not seen Him. Pay attention! This is one of the two interpretations of the verse.

The second interpretation: they fear their Lord while they are absent from others, so the prepositional phrase is a circumstantial phrase relating to the subject. For among people there are those who display fear of Allah before others, but when they are away from people, they do not fear Allah.

Is such a person praised for his fear? No, because he is a hypocrite (muraa'). But the one who fears his Lord in the unseen is the one who is praised.

If you say: Can the verse be understood as having both meanings, so that those whom Allah praised fear Allah even though they have not seen Him, and fear Allah when they are away from people?

The answer: Yes. This is from the eloquence of the Qur'an, that it expresses something suitable for two meanings that do not contradict each other. These people fear Allah the Exalted although they have not seen Him, but they fear Him as if they saw Him, because they fear Him in the unseen and in the witnessed. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Ihsan is that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you."[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50), and Muslim (9/5), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]

His saying ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ (Fatir 18) does not contradict that he is a warner for all people: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ (Fatir 24), ﴿You are only a warner﴾ (Fatir 23), and similar verses indicating the generality of his warning. Why? Because the warning meant here is beneficial warning. That is, your warning only has an effect on those who fear their Lord unseen. As for one who does not fear Allah unseen, even if he is warned, he does not benefit from the warning. For this reason the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said, pointing to this: "Because they are the ones who benefit from the warning." ("Because they") means: those who fear their Lord unseen are the ones who benefit from the warning. Therefore the warning is restricted to them.

So the restriction here, restricting the warning to those who fear their Lord unseen, is meant as restricting its benefit. Who is it for? As for one who does not fear Allah, this does not benefit him. ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe. Even if every sign should come to them until they see the painful punishment﴾ (Yunus 96-97).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah﴾ (Fatir 17). What is the meaning of this, and what does ﴿that﴾ refer to?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Well done. That is, it is impossible (mumtani'). "Ṣaḥ" means it is easy, entirely easy.

In His saying ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah﴾ (Fatir 17), from which of the attributes is it?
