The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said... I say: the living and the dead refer to sensory life and sensory death. Everyone knows the difference between the living and the dead, right? Even the disbelievers know the difference between the living and the dead. Do these four sensory meanings resemble the intellectual meanings, or are they different from them? They resemble them. So whatever resembles these sensory things among intellectual matters is like them.

He says: (The addition of "lā" in the three places is for emphasis.) This sentence indicates that we have an addition, and that the benefit of this addition is emphasis. Where is the addition? ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾ [Fatir 19]: there is nothing added here. ﴿Nor the darknesses and the light﴾ [Fatir 20] (...) ﴿Nor the shade and the scorching heat (21). And the living and the dead are not alike﴾ [Fatir 21–22]. How many are there?

Student: Five.

The Shaykh: Good. ﴿Nor the darknesses﴾ is one, ﴿nor the light (20). Nor the shade and the scorching heat﴾, ﴿nor the dead﴾: five. But the author made them three, because the opposed pairs in them are three. Look: (the darknesses and the light) is one unit, (the shade and the scorching heat) is one unit, and (the living and the dead) is one unit.

The main point is that the addition of "lā" in all these places, whether we say three or five, is for emphasis. For if it were said: "And the blind and the seeing are not alike, the darknesses and the light, the shade and the scorching heat, the living and the dead," the sentence would be correct. But the superfluous "lā" is used for emphasis.

There is also a second benefit in it: avoiding weariness and boredom. For if it were omitted, the coordinated items would become long, one with another, so the negating operator is repeated in order to be further from tedium.

If you say: Is there a parallel to this in the Book of Allah?

We say: Yes. There is a parallel in many places, among them what we recite in every prayer: ﴿not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah 7]. For if it were said: "not of those who have earned anger and those who are astray," it would be correct, but "lā" is added for emphasis.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah causes to hear whom He wills, but you cannot make hear those who are in the graves﴾ [Fatir 22].

﴿Indeed, Allah causes to hear whom He wills﴾. The author said: (His guidance, so the one being made to hear responds with faith). That is, Allah, the Exalted, calls to the Abode of Peace, as He said in another verse: ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace﴾ [Yunus 25]. Does everyone hear Allah's call to the Abode of Peace? As for sensory perception, everyone hears it. As for response, no: some people respond and some do not respond. That is why He said: ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus 25]. So Allah causes to hear whom He wills, that is, to follow these messengers (...).

﴿But you cannot make hear those who are in the graves﴾ [Fatir 22]. Regarding the grammar of ﴿mā﴾ here, what do we say it is?

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: No, it has a specific noun.

Student: Hijazi.

The Shaykh: Hijazi, and its noun is the pronoun ﴿anta﴾ (you), and the bāʾ in ﴿bi-musmi'in﴾ is superfluous for emphasis. ﴿Bi-musmi'in﴾ is its predicate, in the accusative, marked by a fatḥah that is presumed at its end, prevented from appearing by the motion of the superfluous preposition.

﴿Mā anta bi-musmi'in﴾. And His saying: ﴿man fi al-qubur﴾ (those who are in the graves): ﴿man﴾ here is the object of ﴿musmi'in﴾, because ﴿musmi'in﴾ is an active participle.

﴿Bi-musmi'in man fi al-qubur﴾. The author said: (That is, the disbelievers; He likened them to the dead, so they respond). That is, you cannot make them hear.

Student: (So they do not respond).

The Shaykh: No, I have (so they respond).

Another student: I have (so they respond).

The Shaykh: Yes, I have the correct version, the sound version that I have. What you have is wrong, because if it were (fa-yujibūna, so they respond) then the nūn would have to be dropped, since it is the answer to the negation in His saying: ﴿mā anta bi-musmi'in man fi al-qubur﴾ [Fatir 22]. As for the copy that the brother and his companions have, it is separated from what precedes it; that is, in their failure to make them hear, they do not respond.

In any case, the author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: ﴿You cannot make hear those who are in the graves﴾ [Fatir 22]. He said: (That is, the disbelievers). What appears to me is that what is meant is actual death. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, cannot make the dead actually hear, as Allah said: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Naml 80]. So if the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, went to a cemetery, the cemetery of the disbelievers, and said: "O people, fear Allah, worship Him," and similar things, would they hear this admonition and benefit from it? No, they do not hear it and benefit from it. But we say: we move from this to the point that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, cannot make the dead hear, meaning he cannot make the disbelievers hear, because their hearts are dead. Whoever has a dead heart, may Allah protect us, does not benefit from the admonitions he hears, so it is as if he does not hear.

Then He said: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Fatir 23]. The author explained ﴿in﴾ as ﴿mā﴾ (not), which indicates that ﴿in﴾ is negating. We mentioned earlier that among the signs of the negating ﴿in﴾ is that it is followed by an exception, that is, by ﴿illā﴾ (except). So: ﴿you are only a warner﴾.

He said: (A warner to them). The warner, as previously mentioned, is one who informs in a way that includes intimidation. Informing that includes intimidation is called warning (indhar).

As for His saying: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Fatir 23], is this restriction real or relative? It is relative, because the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is a warner and a bearer of good news, is he not? But the context here requires that only warning be mentioned, because it concerns confronting the disbelievers, and confronting the disbelievers requires warning more than good news.

As for His saying: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Fatir 23], how is it a contrast between it and the sentence before it? It is as if He says: You cannot cause guidance to reach the hearts of the disbelievers, but you can warn them, because that is your station: your station is warning. As for causing guidance to reach the hearts of these disbelievers who resemble the dead, that is not in your hands.

Allah, mighty and majestic, spoke the truth. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, could not guide even the closest of people to him and the most compassionate toward him, his uncle Abu Talib, did he? Yet Allah, mighty and majestic, willed to guide peoples from Persia and Rome, from those furthest from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in lineage and place, because the matter is in the hand of Allah, mighty and majestic. ﴿So remind; you are only a reminder. You are not over them a controller﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 21–22]. ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Fatir 23].

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good news and a warner﴾ [Fatir 24].

﴿We have sent you﴾: sending (irsal) here means the command to convey, or the fulfilling of a need. For example, you say: "I sent my servant to inform so-and-so of such-and-such," meaning I commanded him to convey it. "I sent my servant to buy such-and-such," I commanded him to buy the needed item, but the benefit is for the one sent to do it.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾ [Fatir 24], the bā' here may be for transitivity, meaning: We gave you truth and sent you with it.

It may also be a description of the message, meaning: We sent you with a message of truth. The meaning differs. On the second meaning, the sense of the verse is that the message of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is true. On the first meaning, its sense is that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, came with the truth. Although the two meanings are mutually implicating, they differ in terms of the object of the description. On the first, the object of the description is the message itself; on the second, the object of the description is what was sent, that is, the thing conveyed. Have you understood now or not?

﴿We have sent you with the truth﴾, that is, We gave you truth to convey to the people.

﴿We have sent you with the truth﴾, meaning our message to you is true, so the description refers to the message itself. That is, you are not a liar, but truthful. This is on the view that we make the description refer to the message. But if we make it refer to what was sent, the meaning is that what you brought is not falsehood, but is truthful in reports and just in rulings.

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good news﴾ [Fatir 24]. The author said: (With guidance) (﴿a bearer of good news﴾ to whoever responds to it, ﴿and a warner﴾ to whoever does not respond to it).

﴿A bearer of good news and a warner﴾: that is, you give good news and warn. You give good news of goodness to whoever responds, and warn of punishment to whoever does not respond and disobeys. This is because the Shari'ah includes commands and prohibitions. Whoever commits what is prohibited or abandons what is commanded, we confront with what? With warning. Whoever performs what is commanded and avoids what is prohibited, we confront with what? With glad tidings.

﴿A bearer of good news and a warner, and there is not a nation but a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24]. ﴿In﴾ here is (mā), meaning negating. ﴿Min ummatin﴾: ﴿min﴾ is a superfluous preposition, superfluous, or superfluous in a different way? It is permissible, on the reading that the first "zā'id" is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the hidden pronoun in the first "zā'id." The point is that it is superfluous in wording and superfluous in meaning.

﴿Ummatin﴾ is the subject, and the clause ﴿khalā fīhā nadhīr﴾ (a warner passed among them) is the predicate.

The Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 35, verses 19–24 (part 2 of 3):

What is an *ummah*? It is a group of people who follow one path: one method, one religion, or one nationality, or something similar. This is an *ummah*. Not every group is called an *ummah*. For example, we do not call you an *ummah* now except because you are on one path. But if a group gathers in one place and they are scattered, each one with his own method, we do not say, "These are an *ummah*," unless they are from one tribe or something similar.

﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ (Fatir 24), meaning a prophet who warned them. That is, God sent a warner to every nation. Why? So that the proof would be established against them, for if people had no warner, they would have a proof against their Lord, saying, "Our Lord, You did not send a messenger to us."

As God says: ﴿And had We destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so we could follow Your signs before we are humiliated and disgraced?"﴾ [Ta-Ha 134]. And He says: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good tidings and warners, so that mankind will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾ [An-Nisa' 165]. The discussion of what is in His saying, ﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24], of the difficulty and its answer, will come, God willing (...).

God says: ﴿And not equal are the blind and the seeing﴾ [Fatir 19].

* In this verse there are benefits. Among them is the eloquence of the Qur'an, for it moves its listener and reader from concrete examples to abstract examples. This is because no one doubts concrete examples, and no one can dispute them. For if you say, for example, "This is a lamp and this is light," no one contests it. So one moves from the perceptible to the intelligible meaning.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the virtue of sight, for the negation of equality between the blind and the seeing means the preference of whom? The preference of the seeing. For this reason they have greatly supplicated to God, the Mighty and Majestic: "O God, grant us enjoyment of our hearing, our sight, and our strength as long as You keep us alive."

We say the same about ﴿nor the darknesses and the light﴾ [Fatir 20]. It contains the same eloquence of the Qur'an as His saying, ﴿And not equal are the blind and the seeing﴾ [Fatir 19], and it contains the move from the concrete example to the abstract example.

* It also contains: the preference of light over darkness, because the negation of equality between them means the preference of light over darkness.

* Also: when we move from the concrete example to the abstract, that the path of guidance is one, while the paths of misguidance are scattered. This is from His saying, ﴿the darknesses [...] the light﴾ [Fatir 20].

We have mentioned a witness from the Qur'an for this, which is His saying: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [Al-An'am 153]. And He says: ﴿God is the Ally of those who believe; He brings them out from the darknesses into the light. And those who disbelieve, their allies are the taghut﴾ [Al-Baqarah 257]. In it, the taghut drags them into some kind of disbelief and sin. We ask God for well-being.

* Also: the shade and the heat are not equal. This is a concrete example from which one moves to the abstract example, namely that the shade of Paradise and the heat of Hell are not equal. Which is better? The shade of Paradise. O God, make us and you among its people.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: a warning against the deeds of the people of the Fire. For the negation of equality between the shade and the heat is a known matter, and a person being harmed by the heat is also a known matter. So in it is a warning against the deeds of the people of the Fire.

Can it be derived from this noble verse that there is no blame upon a person for seeking shade and seeking light?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Is that so? It is known, for since we have mentioned that this negation means the preference of light over darkness and the preference of shade over heat, there is no blame upon a person for seeking what is better. Indeed, it may sometimes be obligatory. For this reason, when the Prophet ﷺ saw a crowd and a man over whom shade had been cast, [he] for fasting in travel, he did not say, "Do not shade him," but he said: "It is not righteousness to fast while traveling" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1946), and Muslim (1115 / 92), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]].

And His saying: ﴿And not equal are the living and the dead﴾ [Fatir 22]: in it also is what has preceded in its counterparts. In it is the virtue of knowledge, and so it is. God, the Exalted, has said: ﴿Say, "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"﴾ [Az-Zumar 9].

Knowledge is jihad in the way of God. And if you wish, say, more accurately: knowledge is a weapon for jihad in the way of God, for knowledge may be carried by one who neither benefits from it nor benefits others. So it is a weapon, but when you benefit yourself and others, you become a mujahid through it. God says: ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it a great striving﴾ [Al-Furqan 52]. So knowledge is a weapon by which a person reaches jihad in the way of God.

* Among its benefits also, from the benefits of His saying, ﴿the living and the dead﴾ [Fatir 22]: that in it is an incitement to seek knowledge, and that it is the life of the *ummah* just as it is the life of the individual. It is not possible for a nation to live a life, I do not say a bestial life, a nation can live a bestial life without knowledge, but it is not possible for it to live a good life except by knowledge. All people seek a good life, but what makes it good? Knowledge, when it bears its fruit, which is faith and righteous deeds. God says: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [An-Nahl 97].

He says: ﴿Indeed, God causes to hear whom He wills, but you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir 22].

* Among its benefits: that God, the Mighty and Majestic, is the One in whose hand are the keys of affairs. Even you, O Muhammad, cannot make anyone hear. Rather, the One who makes hear is God.

In it: the affirmation of God's will, for His saying, ﴿whom He wills﴾.

* In it also: a refutation of the Qadariyya (1), who deny that the actions of servants fall under God's will, for His saying, ﴿Indeed, God causes to hear whom He wills﴾ [Fatir 22]. But this absolute will here, and everywhere it comes absolute, is restricted by what? By wisdom, for His saying: ﴿And you do not will except that God wills. Indeed, God is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan 30].

* Among its benefits: a person ought, indeed must, turn to God alone for bringing benefits and removing harms, for His saying: ﴿Indeed, God causes to hear whom He wills﴾ [Fatir 22]. So if the causing to hear is from God, do not ask anyone else. Ask only God. For this reason, we should always be people who call upon God, the Mighty and Majestic, while feeling that we are in need of God, and that God, Glorified and Exalted, is able to bring about for us what we hope for and what we call upon Him for. Do not rely on yourself and forget God. Turn to God always in supplication, in prostration, between the call to prayer and the iqamah, and in all times, places, and states of answering. For God, Glorified and Exalted, says: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [Al-Baqarah 186].

Then know also that supplication, along with your asking God for a need, is itself an act of worship by which you draw near to Him. So through this supplication you gain two fruits:

The first fruit: the reward for this act of worship.

The second fruit: the attainment of what is sought or the removal of what is disliked.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Messenger of God ﷺ cannot make those in the graves hear, for His saying: ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir 22]. So if the Messenger ﷺ went to the people of the graveyard and called them and said, "O people of the graves, believe in God and His Messenger! O people of the graves, do righteous deeds!" Would they hear? They would not hear.

If you say: What is the answer to what is established in the Sahih, that the Messenger ﷺ stood over the slain of the polytheists in the well of Badr and began calling them by their names and the names of their fathers: "O so-and-so son of so-and-so, did you find what your Lord promised to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised to be true." 'Umar said to him, "O Messenger of God, you are speaking to bodies that have decayed," or words to this effect. He said: "You are not more able to hear what I say than they are" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3976), and Muslim (2875 / 78), from the hadith of Abu Talhah al-Ansari.]]. That means they hear. So what is the answer?

* A student: The saying of Qatadah, may God have mercy on him: "Indeed God revived them so that they heard the words of the Prophet ﷺ as a punishment and humiliation for them, then He caused them to die again" [[Related by al-Bukhari (3976).]]. And 'Aisha says: "The people of the well do not hear the Messenger ﷺ, but the Messenger addresses them because of the punishment they find in the grave" [[Related by Ahmad in al-Musnad (26361).]].

* The Shaykh: As for what you mentioned from 'Aisha, there is no doubt that the words of the Messenger ﷺ refute it, for he said: "You are not more able to hear what I say than they are." As for what was mentioned from Qatadah, the meaning of his words is that it is specific to those people.

If you say: What is the answer to what is also established in the sound hadith, that "when the deceased is buried and his companions turn away from him, indeed he hears the sound of their sandals as they leave him" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1338), and Muslim (2870 / 70), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: This is at the time of burial. Also, hearing the sound of sandals does not necessarily mean hearing speech and invocation.

If you say: What is the answer to what Abu Dawud and others narrated, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr authenticated, and which Ibn al-Qayyim agreed with or did not oppose: that "no Muslim greets a grave of one he knew in the world except that God returns his soul to him and he returns the greeting" [[Related by al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab (8857) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in al-Istidhkar (1/185) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas; we have not found it in Abu Dawud.]]?

The answer is that it is said: this is in a particular state indicated by the hadith, and it does not necessarily follow that whoever hears the greeting upon him, which is an invocation for him, and returns the greeting to the one who greets him, hears everyone who speaks in his presence.

If you say: What is the answer to what the jurists said, that the deceased is harmed by the speech of the reprehensible person at his grave or by the reprehensible act at his grave?

The answer: the saying of any person other than the Messenger ﷺ is not a proof. It is cited in support, not as the basis.

Then, according to their opinion, may God have mercy on them, they interpret His saying, ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir 22] to mean: you cannot make hear those whom you call to faith and righteous deeds. For you do not make them hear in a way that they respond to it. But it is a hearing that needs (...).

This is the final answer to the one who says that the dead hear what is said near them and what they are addressed with. We say: ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir 22], meaning, hearing by which they benefit and respond. And God knows best.

Regarding these unseen matters, the obligation upon the believer is to believe only in what the text has brought, and to leave the rest to inquiry. Indeed, he must say, "Knowledge is with God," and so he does not affirm with certainty the negation, nor does he affirm with certainty the affirmation. Yes, he may affirm the negation with certainty and make what the hadith established an exception, for He said: ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir 22], and in another verse: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating﴾ [An-Naml 80].

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿You are not but a warner﴾ [Fatir 23].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Muhammad, the Messenger of God ﷺ, is only a conveyer and a warner. There is nothing in his hand to bring guidance to anyone, nor to remove harm from him, for He said: ﴿You are not but a warner﴾ [Fatir 23], meaning you are not a guide to people in the sense of granting success and right guidance. Rather, you are a warner, so you are a guide only in the sense of indicating.

He says: ﴿You are not but a warner﴾ [Fatir 23].

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24].

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾: In this is evidence that the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ is true, and that he is not a liar, for He said: ﴿We have sent you with the truth﴾.

* Among its benefits also: that the Messenger ﷺ is worthy of prophethood if we take ﴿with the truth﴾ as a circumstantial clause from the subject "We" (*na*), meaning: "Indeed, We have sent you while being truthful in that," so it contains evidence that the Messenger ﷺ is worthy of prophethood. This is known from other evidences, such as His saying: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am 124], but we want to derive it from this verse.

* Also: what the Prophet ﷺ brought is truth, not falsehood. When you look at his reports, you find them to be truthful, and when you look at his rulings, you find them to be just. This is the truth, for truth regarding a report is truthfulness, and truth regarding a ruling is justice.

* Among its benefits: the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ combined good tidings and warning, from His saying: ﴿as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [Fatir 24].

* Among its benefits also: that a person may combine two qualities that are opposite in meaning, though agreeing in purpose: a bringer of good tidings and a warner. For the bringer of good tidings is one who promises people good and opens for them the door of hope, while the warner is one who frightens them from (...). Between them there is a difference in meaning, yet they can meet in a single person. Shall we move from this benefit to the point that a person may combine qualities of faith and qualities of disbelief?

* A student: He warns and gives good tidings.

* The Shaykh: No, they are not necessarily linked. It is not necessarily so. If you see an army approaching the town, I warn them and do not give them good tidings. But if you see that the army has withdrawn, I give them good tidings.

In any case, what is known from the school of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah (2), which is the truth, is that a person may combine qualities of faith and qualities of disbelief, so he is a believer in one respect and a disbeliever in another. As the Prophet ﷺ said: "Two things among people are disbelief: slandering lineage and wailing over the dead" [[Related by Muslim (67 / 121), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. And the Prophet ﷺ also said: "Cursing a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (48), and Muslim (64 / 116), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.]]. Yet fighting him does not take him out of faith, as in His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, make reconciliation between them﴾ [Al-Hujurat 9], to His saying: ﴿The believers are but brothers, so make reconciliation between your brothers﴾ [Al-Hujurat 10].

* Also among its benefits: the whole matter belongs to God. No one shares in it, not even the greatest of people in rank. He does not share with God in what is specific to Him, for His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you﴾ [Fatir 24]. And it is known that the station of the sender is higher than the station of the one sent. And God knows best (...).

And He, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [Fatir 24].

The address in His saying ﴿Indeed, We have sent you﴾ is to the Prophet ﷺ.

Sending (*irsal*) is entrusting the one sent with something that he conveys to those to whom he is sent.

The sentence, as we observe, is emphasized with *inna*, and emphasis of a sentence indicates the importance of it, so that a person may believe in it with complete faith.

God says: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾ [Fatir 24]. The *ba'* here is either for transitivity, as you say, "I sent him with such-and-such," to clarify what he was sent with, or it is for accompaniment.

---

(1) Qadariyya: an early theological school that denied God's comprehensive decree over the actions of servants.

(2) Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah: the adherents of the Sunnah and the community, the mainstream of the Muslim community in creed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 35, verse 19–24 (part 3 of 3):

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (﴿بِالْحَقِّ﴾ with guidance (bil-huda)). It seems he took this explanation from the Almighty's words: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth﴾ [At-Tawbah 33]. However, the correct view regarding the verse is that what is meant by ﴿bil-haqq﴾ is the opposite of falsehood (batil), so it includes truthfulness in reports and justice in rulings; that is: with truthfulness in reports and justice in rulings. It is not guidance alone, but guidance, righteousness, reform and other things besides.

As for the Almighty's words ﴿with guidance and the religion of truth﴾ [At-Tawbah 33], it is indeed possible to say that what is meant by guidance there is beneficial knowledge, because He mentioned guidance and mentioned religion, thus mentioning knowledge and action.

As for here, we should not restrict ourselves to saying that "the truth" means guidance; rather we should make it more general than that, so that it includes the guidance which is knowledge, and includes the religion of truth which is right direction, righteousness and reform. The Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, his message encompassed all beneficial knowledge and the good of creation in their livelihood and their hereafter, and what he brought included truthfulness in reports and justice in rulings. The Almighty said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [Fatir 24].

﴿Bashiran (as a bringer of good tidings)﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) in the sense of mubashshir (one who gives good tidings), a state from the kaf in ﴿arsalnaka (We have sent you)﴾.

The author said: (﴿Bashiran﴾ to whoever responds to him, ﴿wa nadhiran (and a warner)﴾ to whoever does not respond to him).

Bushra (good tidings) is the announcement of what gladdens, and it may be used for announcing what grieves, as in the Almighty's words: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 21].

As for indhar (warning), it is intimidation; that is, informing of what frightens. The Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, his message was good tidings and warning, because it is either a command whose doer is given good tidings of what that command requires, or a prohibition whose performer is made to fear committing it. So the Sharia as a whole is good tidings and warning.

The author's statement, may Allah have mercy on him: (﴿Bashiran﴾ to whoever responds to him, ﴿wa nadhiran﴾ to whoever does not respond) — it may be said that it is better to keep the verse in its generality; that is, a bringer of good tidings to whoever responds to him and a warner to him at the same time, because whoever responds also needs warning. So good tidings and warning are inclusive of both whoever responds and whoever does not respond, even the one who does not respond is given good tidings if he responds: ﴿a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾.

Then He said: ﴿And there has been no nation but that a warner passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24]. ﴿In﴾ here means (ma), so it is negating, and we have mentioned a rule for it earlier; that is, we mentioned for the negating ﴿in﴾ a rule which does not encompass all its occurrences: that when ﴿illa (except)﴾ comes after it, it is negating, like: ﴿You are not but a warner﴾ [Fatir 23], ﴿This is not but manifest magic﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 110], ﴿This is not but a fabrication﴾ [Sad 7], ﴿This is not but the custom of the former peoples﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 137]. And among them also this verse: ﴿And there has been no nation but that a warner passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24].

And His words: ﴿min﴾ is extra, extra, extra in grammar and extra in meaning.

If you say: how can it be extra extra?

We say: because (zada) is used both intransitively and transitively. One says: "zada al-tin balla" (it added wetness to the mud), this is transitive. ﴿So it increased them in faith﴾ [At-Tawbah 124], this is also transitive. And you say: "zada al-mal" (the wealth increased), this is intransitive.

So the meaning of "extra extra" is: the first is extra from the deficient one, which is the intransitive; and the second extra is from the transitive.

And ﴿ummatin (nation)﴾ is a subject (mubtada') in the nominative, with a dammah presumed at its end, prevented from appearing by the locality being occupied by the vowel of the extra preposition.

﴿...illa khala fiha nadhir (but a warner passed among them)﴾ [Fatir 24]. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (﴿khala﴾ means passed away, ﴿fiha nadhir﴾ means: a prophet who warns it).

Here ummah means a group (ta'ifah), and it comes in the Qur'an in four ways:
It means a group, as here; it means a period of time, example: ﴿and he remembered after a period (ummah)﴾ [Yusuf 45]; it means religion and creed, ﴿And indeed this, your ummah, is one ummah﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 52]; and it means an imam (leader), in ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a ummah, devoutly obedient﴾ [An-Nahl 120].

No nation (ummah) ﴿but that a warner passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24], that is, a warner who warned it has passed and gone, and that is so that the proof may be established against the servants; because minds, however far they reach, cannot possibly know the rights that are due to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, nor can they know in detail what is due to Him of names and attributes. Although the intellect perceives that a human must worship his Creator, and perceives that the Creator must be described with attributes of perfection, this is in summary, not in detail. Therefore Allah sent the messengers so that the proof may be established against the servants: there has been no nation but that a warner passed among them.

It may be that prophets exist at one time in several places, and it may be that prophets exist at one time in one place. But that there should be a place where there was no prophet is impossible; all nations must have had messengers sent to them. A parallel to this is the Almighty's words: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, saying: Worship Allah and avoid the tyrant﴾ [An-Nahl 36] — "sent into every nation."

* Several benefits are derived from this noble verse:
* Among them: the affirmation of the Prophet's ﷺ messengerhood in an emphatic manner beyond doubt, from His words: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you﴾ [Fatir 24].
* And among them: the excellence of the Prophet ﷺ in being the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds, for messengerhood is a great station which none attains except one who is worthy of it, as Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am 124]. And the Almighty says: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some over others. Among them are those to whom Allah spoke﴾ [Al-Baqarah 253]. They — that is, the messengers — are preferred over others of creation, so in the verse there is excellence and distinction for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
* And among them: the explanation of what the religion of the Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, includes of truth, whose opposite is falsehood. If falsehood is in reports, it is lying; and if it is in rulings, it is oppression and injustice. Accordingly, the message of the Prophet ﷺ includes truth in reports and in rulings.
In it there is also an explanation of the excellence of this Islamic Sharia which the Prophet ﷺ brought.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that everything which is true, the Sharia has brought it, whether it explicitly stated it in its specific meaning or in its general meaning. Hence some jurists, or some scholars of usul, affirmed what is called al-masalih al-mursalah (unrestricted public interests) and made it an independent proof. The correct view is that it is not an independent proof, because these interests, if the Sharia testifies to them, they are from the Sharia, and there is no need to make them an independent proof; and if the Sharia does not testify to them, they are not interests, and whoever claims them to be interests is deluded.

So our affirming a fifth proof that we call al-masalih al-mursalah is an error. Why? For what I have just told you: that such an interest, if the Sharia testifies to it, is from the Sharia, indicated by the Book and the Sunnah; and if it does not testify to it, it is not an interest, so it is not considered.

Likewise, some claimed the introduction of a sixth proof, which is istishab al-hal (presumption of continuity), meaning that a matter remains as it was until its removal or cessation is clear. This also is not correct; that is, it is not valid to make it an independent proof. Why? Because the Sunnah has indicated it: a man was complained of to the Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, that he imagines he finds something during prayer, so he said: «He should not leave until he hears a sound or smells a smell» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (137) and Muslim (361 / 98), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Zayd].

So we build upon the continuation of the original state, and presumption of continuity; and then there is no need to make this an independent proof. Some scholars made these two proofs independent only because a person's mind suggests that this is something separate from the indication of the Book and the Sunnah, so he goes and makes it an independent proof. Otherwise, if he reflected, he would find that it exists in the Book and the Sunnah, and there is no need to establish it as an independent proof.

Some later scholars have been bold regarding the first proof, al-masalih al-mursalah, to the extent that they included in it what the Sharia testified to be invalid.

Among that: their saying that interest-based banking is permissible, on the basis of what they imagined to be unrestricted public interests.

They said: the economies of the world in the present age cannot be completed except by using this method. Words and methods which come other than what came in the Book and the Sunnah bring about corruption; so here they introduced something which the Sharia testified to be invalid. When the Sharia testifies to its invalidity, we testify that there is no interest in it, and that the imagined interest in it is followed by many corruptions.

Therefore we see that we should not...
So let it be an independent proof, otherwise it is not from the Sharia and has no interest in it; and the imagined interests in it, if they oppose the Sharia, must be followed by many corruptions.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: that the Prophet's ﷺ message comprises, with respect to reward, two matters: good tidings and warning; good tidings for whoever obeys, and warning for whoever opposes, whether that obedience is general or in some matters, and likewise we say regarding opposition.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that the end of people is either to a garden or to the fire, and there is no third abode, for the good tidings are of Paradise and the warning is of the Fire, and there is no third abode that people reach.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: encouragement to obey the Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, by His words: ﴿a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [Fatir 24], and a warning against opposing him, by His words: ﴿a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the kindness of Allah, exalted, to His servants by sending messengers to all creation: ﴿And there has been no nation but that a warner passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24]. Allah, glorified and exalted, explained this in His words: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 107]; that is, only so that Allah may show mercy to the worlds through you; and the Messenger himself is not the mercy, but he was sent for the mercy of creation, so that Allah may have mercy on creation through his message.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse also: the invalidity of using divine decree as an argument for disobedience to Allah; for His words: ﴿And there has been no nation but that a warner passed among them﴾. If the argument of divine decree for sins and transgressions were valid, it would not have been lifted by the sending of messengers, because divine decree is not lifted by sending messengers. The messengers were sent by Allah, exalted, as the establishment of proof against creation and also as mercy to them, both for this and for that.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the clarification that the Prophet ﷺ is not a novelty among the messengers such that his messengerhood should be denied, and it is said: "How did this man come with a message from Allah?" ﴿And there has been no nation but that a warner passed among them﴾. And this is supported by the Almighty's words: ﴿Say: I am not a novelty among the messengers﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 9].
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the deficiency of minds in knowing what is due to Allah, exalted; for if they were independent in that, they would not need the sending of messengers.
* And also among them: the invalidity of what the speculative theologians of the innovators have adopted, who built their creed upon what reason requires, and said: whatever reason requires affirming for Allah, we affirm it, whether or not it is mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah; and whatever reason negates, we must negate it, even if it is mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah; and whatever reason does not indicate either affirming or negating, we suspend judgment on it. Most of them said: we negate it, because affirming it requires an indication from reason; so if reason does not indicate its affirmation, it must be negated, for lack of evidence. What do you say about this benefit?

* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And affirming it? And what does not require either affirming or negating?
* The student: They suspend judgment, and most of them (...).
* The Shaykh: It is derived from His words: ﴿And there has been no nation but that a warner passed among them﴾. Its reasoning is that if minds were the reference, there would be no need to send messengers.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 35, verses 19–24 (part 1 of 3):**

Then Allah, mighty and majestic, said in the new lesson: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾ [Fatir 19]. That is, they are not equal in perceiving visible things. The meaning is not a negation of equality in every respect, because the blind may surpass the seeing in other matters. Rather, they are not equal in perceiving visible things, which is what the verse ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾ [Fatir 19] refers to, and this is clear.

If the blind man walks while there is a pit in front of him, or a stone, he falls into the pit and stumbles over the stone. The seeing man is the opposite. So this one and that one are not alike.

Which of them is more perfect? The seeing one. This is a sensory example (mathal hissi), and we must move from it to the abstract example (mathal ma'nawi).

As for the author's statement, "the believer and the disbeliever," it is open to question. It is as if he wants to say that the blind is the disbeliever and the seeing is the believer. But we say: No. The verse intends the negation of equality in clear sensory matters that no one denies, since the disbeliever, the heretic (zindiq), the obstinate one, and the arrogant one cannot claim that the blind and the seeing are equal. Yet he may claim that the believer and the disbeliever are equal.

He said: ﴿Nor the darknesses and the light﴾ [Fatir 20].

He said: (﴿The darknesses﴾ is disbelief, ﴿and the light﴾ is faith). This too is open to question. The apparent meaning is that Allah, glorified and exalted, intended sensory darknesses and sensory light, because the negation of equality between these two is something that cannot be denied, since it is perceived by the senses.

Darknesses are not equal to light. But there is no doubt that what is meant is the darkness of disbelief and the light of faith; that is, it is an allusion to this. That is why He used the plural for darknesses and the singular for light: the paths of disbelief are many, while the path of faith is one. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am 153], and He said: ﴿Allah is the Guardian of those who believe; He brings them out from the darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Baqarah 257].

Disbelief is darkness because it contains ignorance of Allah, mighty and majestic, and of what is due to Him.

Also in it: a person who disbelieves walks without guidance and proceeds in many deviant directions. His heart is scattered in every valley. Therefore you find disbelievers to be the most anxious of people and the furthest from steadfastness on a straight line. The believer, by contrast, is a believer on a straight line, knowing that he wants to reach whom? Allah. So you find him turning all his actions toward one path, which is reaching Allah, to the point that when he puts on his clothes he feels that by this he gains the pleasure of Allah. When he eats, drinks, sleeps, travels, stays silent, speaks, or refrains, he sees all of this as being in the way of Allah, on the road to Allah.

But the disbeliever is scattered. Therefore his method is darkness, because he is scattered and has no single goal that he pursues. His aims are many: deceived by the world, deceived by his leaders, deceived by people, caring only for their approval. We ask Allah for safety and well-being. He does not care whether Allah, mighty and majestic, is pleased. Therefore it is fitting that the way of the disbeliever be expressed in the plural, due to its dispersal and division. Is that right?

Third: He said: ﴿Nor the shade and the scorching heat﴾ [Fatir 21]. The author said: (the Garden and the Fire). That is, according to the author, what is meant by the shade is the Garden, and what is meant by the scorching heat is the Fire. But, as I said, the apparent meaning is that this is an example from a sensory matter that cannot be denied, and then one moves from it to an abstract matter.

Are the shade and the scorching heat equal? Which is better?

Students: The shade.

The Shaykh: Without doubt, the shade. The shade is well known: it is the shadow that the sun has withdrawn from. If you wish, say: the shade is the place where there are no rays of the sun. We say this because the Garden has no sun, and Allah said of it: ﴿And shade extended﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 30], even though there is no sun in it.

As for al-harur (scorching heat), it is on the pattern fa'ul, and it is hot wind. Some say it is hot wind by day, and al-samum is hot wind by night. Others say both have the same meaning: al-harur and al-samum are hot wind. This is well known and occurs in summer, and when the sun is present it becomes even more intense in heat.

Now we have the blind and the seeing, the darknesses and the light, the shade and the scorching heat. According to the author's view, we say: these three negations, or this negation in three places, are as follows. The first returns to the essence of the believer and the disbeliever; the second returns to the deeds and method of the believer and the disbeliever; the third returns to the abode and dwelling of the believer and the disbeliever. Is that right or not? So the first is a negation of essences, the second a negation in actions and method, and the third a negation regarding the final abode and refuge.

﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike (19). Nor the darknesses and the light (20). Nor the shade and the scorching heat﴾ [Fatir 19–21].

Fourth: ﴿And the living and the dead are not alike﴾ [Fatir 22] (the believers and the disbelievers). According to the author's view, there is repetition in the verse, because he explained the blind and the seeing as the believer and the disbeliever, and here he said: ﴿the living and the dead﴾ [Fatir 22] (the believers and the disbelievers).

If I wished to follow his approach, I would say: ﴿the living﴾ are the people of knowledge, and ﴿the dead﴾ are the people of ignorance, because of Allah's saying: ﴿Is one who was dead and We brought him to life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people, like one whose likeness is in the darknesses, from which he will never emerge?﴾ [al-An'am 122]. Also because Allah made revelation a spirit by which hearts and souls live. But I do not follow his approach. Rather, if I wished to follow his approach, I would say: the scholars and the ignorant.

﴿The living and the dead﴾ [Fatir 22]: the scholars and the ignorant. Is it clear? Because if I follow this approach, I have proof for it, which is His saying: ﴿Is one who was dead...﴾ and so on [al-An'am 122]. If I follow this approach, the verse is free from repetition. We all know that among the well-known rules of speech is that when the matter is between interpreting the statement as foundational (ta'sis) or as emphatic (tawkid), it must be interpreted as foundational, because that is the original principle. The original principle in speech is that it be independent, establishing new meaning, not merely emphasizing.

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: Ta'sis means the original is a foundation; that is, this is a new meaning different from the first meaning.

So if someone says, for example: this sentence is emphatic of the first, and another says: this sentence is independent in itself, then it is taken to be independent in itself.

Student: The first one said: the disbeliever and the believer. Then: the disbelievers and the believers. Does that not...?

The Shaykh: No, it is not apparent as plural and singular.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said... I say: the living and the dead refer to sensory life and sensory death. Everyone knows the difference between the living and the dead, right? Even the disbelievers know the difference between the living and the dead. Do these four sensory meanings resemble the intellectual meanings, or are they different from them? They resemble them. So whatever resembles these sensory things among intellectual matters is like them.

He says: (The addition of "lā" in the three places is for emphasis.) This sentence indicates that we have an addition, and that the benefit of this addition is emphasis. Where is the addition? ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾ [Fatir 19]: there is nothing added here. ﴿Nor the darknesses and the light﴾ [Fatir 20] (...) ﴿Nor the shade and the scorching heat (21). And the living and the dead are not alike﴾ [Fatir 21–22]. How many are there?

Student: Five.

The Shaykh: Good. ﴿Nor the darknesses﴾ is one, ﴿nor the light (20). Nor the shade and the scorching heat﴾, ﴿nor the dead﴾: five. But the author made them three, because the opposed pairs in them are three. Look: (the darknesses and the light) is one unit, (the shade and the scorching heat) is one unit, and (the living and the dead) is one unit.

The main point is that the addition of "lā" in all these places, whether we say three or five, is for emphasis. For if it were said: "And the blind and the seeing are not alike, the darknesses and the light, the shade and the scorching heat, the living and the dead," the sentence would be correct. But the superfluous "lā" is used for emphasis.

There is also a second benefit in it: avoiding weariness and boredom. For if it were omitted, the coordinated items would become long, one with another, so the negating operator is repeated in order to be further from tedium.

If you say: Is there a parallel to this in the Book of Allah?

We say: Yes. There is a parallel in many places, among them what we recite in every prayer: ﴿not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah 7]. For if it were said: "not of those who have earned anger and those who are astray," it would be correct, but "lā" is added for emphasis.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah causes to hear whom He wills, but you cannot make hear those who are in the graves﴾ [Fatir 22].

﴿Indeed, Allah causes to hear whom He wills﴾. The author said: (His guidance, so the one being made to hear responds with faith). That is, Allah, the Exalted, calls to the Abode of Peace, as He said in another verse: ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace﴾ [Yunus 25]. Does everyone hear Allah's call to the Abode of Peace? As for sensory perception, everyone hears it. As for response, no: some people respond and some do not respond. That is why He said: ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus 25]. So Allah causes to hear whom He wills, that is, to follow these messengers (...).

﴿But you cannot make hear those who are in the graves﴾ [Fatir 22]. Regarding the grammar of ﴿mā﴾ here, what do we say it is?

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: No, it has a specific noun.

Student: Hijazi.

The Shaykh: Hijazi, and its noun is the pronoun ﴿anta﴾ (you), and the bāʾ in ﴿bi-musmi'in﴾ is superfluous for emphasis. ﴿Bi-musmi'in﴾ is its predicate, in the accusative, marked by a fatḥah that is presumed at its end, prevented from appearing by the motion of the superfluous preposition.

﴿Mā anta bi-musmi'in﴾. And His saying: ﴿man fi al-qubur﴾ (those who are in the graves): ﴿man﴾ here is the object of ﴿musmi'in﴾, because ﴿musmi'in﴾ is an active participle.

﴿Bi-musmi'in man fi al-qubur﴾. The author said: (That is, the disbelievers; He likened them to the dead, so they respond). That is, you cannot make them hear.

Student: (So they do not respond).

The Shaykh: No, I have (so they respond).

Another student: I have (so they respond).

The Shaykh: Yes, I have the correct version, the sound version that I have. What you have is wrong, because if it were (fa-yujibūna, so they respond) then the nūn would have to be dropped, since it is the answer to the negation in His saying: ﴿mā anta bi-musmi'in man fi al-qubur﴾ [Fatir 22]. As for the copy that the brother and his companions have, it is separated from what precedes it; that is, in their failure to make them hear, they do not respond.

In any case, the author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: ﴿You cannot make hear those who are in the graves﴾ [Fatir 22]. He said: (That is, the disbelievers). What appears to me is that what is meant is actual death. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, cannot make the dead actually hear, as Allah said: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Naml 80]. So if the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, went to a cemetery, the cemetery of the disbelievers, and said: "O people, fear Allah, worship Him," and similar things, would they hear this admonition and benefit from it? No, they do not hear it and benefit from it. But we say: we move from this to the point that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, cannot make the dead hear, meaning he cannot make the disbelievers hear, because their hearts are dead. Whoever has a dead heart, may Allah protect us, does not benefit from the admonitions he hears, so it is as if he does not hear.

Then He said: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Fatir 23]. The author explained ﴿in﴾ as ﴿mā﴾ (not), which indicates that ﴿in﴾ is negating. We mentioned earlier that among the signs of the negating ﴿in﴾ is that it is followed by an exception, that is, by ﴿illā﴾ (except). So: ﴿you are only a warner﴾.

He said: (A warner to them). The warner, as previously mentioned, is one who informs in a way that includes intimidation. Informing that includes intimidation is called warning (indhar).

As for His saying: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Fatir 23], is this restriction real or relative? It is relative, because the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is a warner and a bearer of good news, is he not? But the context here requires that only warning be mentioned, because it concerns confronting the disbelievers, and confronting the disbelievers requires warning more than good news.

As for His saying: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Fatir 23], how is it a contrast between it and the sentence before it? It is as if He says: You cannot cause guidance to reach the hearts of the disbelievers, but you can warn them, because that is your station: your station is warning. As for causing guidance to reach the hearts of these disbelievers who resemble the dead, that is not in your hands.

Allah, mighty and majestic, spoke the truth. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, could not guide even the closest of people to him and the most compassionate toward him, his uncle Abu Talib, did he? Yet Allah, mighty and majestic, willed to guide peoples from Persia and Rome, from those furthest from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in lineage and place, because the matter is in the hand of Allah, mighty and majestic. ﴿So remind; you are only a reminder. You are not over them a controller﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 21–22]. ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Fatir 23].

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good news and a warner﴾ [Fatir 24].

﴿We have sent you﴾: sending (irsal) here means the command to convey, or the fulfilling of a need. For example, you say: "I sent my servant to inform so-and-so of such-and-such," meaning I commanded him to convey it. "I sent my servant to buy such-and-such," I commanded him to buy the needed item, but the benefit is for the one sent to do it.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾ [Fatir 24], the bā' here may be for transitivity, meaning: We gave you truth and sent you with it.

It may also be a description of the message, meaning: We sent you with a message of truth. The meaning differs. On the second meaning, the sense of the verse is that the message of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is true. On the first meaning, its sense is that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, came with the truth. Although the two meanings are mutually implicating, they differ in terms of the object of the description. On the first, the object of the description is the message itself; on the second, the object of the description is what was sent, that is, the thing conveyed. Have you understood now or not?

﴿We have sent you with the truth﴾, that is, We gave you truth to convey to the people.

﴿We have sent you with the truth﴾, meaning our message to you is true, so the description refers to the message itself. That is, you are not a liar, but truthful. This is on the view that we make the description refer to the message. But if we make it refer to what was sent, the meaning is that what you brought is not falsehood, but is truthful in reports and just in rulings.

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good news﴾ [Fatir 24]. The author said: (With guidance) (﴿a bearer of good news﴾ to whoever responds to it, ﴿and a warner﴾ to whoever does not respond to it).

﴿A bearer of good news and a warner﴾: that is, you give good news and warn. You give good news of goodness to whoever responds, and warn of punishment to whoever does not respond and disobeys. This is because the Shari'ah includes commands and prohibitions. Whoever commits what is prohibited or abandons what is commanded, we confront with what? With warning. Whoever performs what is commanded and avoids what is prohibited, we confront with what? With glad tidings.

﴿A bearer of good news and a warner, and there is not a nation but a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24]. ﴿In﴾ here is (mā), meaning negating. ﴿Min ummatin﴾: ﴿min﴾ is a superfluous preposition, superfluous, or superfluous in a different way? It is permissible, on the reading that the first "zā'id" is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the hidden pronoun in the first "zā'id." The point is that it is superfluous in wording and superfluous in meaning.

﴿Ummatin﴾ is the subject, and the clause ﴿khalā fīhā nadhīr﴾ (a warner passed among them) is the predicate.

The Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 35, verses 19–24 (part 2 of 3):

What is an *ummah*? It is a group of people who follow one path: one method, one religion, or one nationality, or something similar. This is an *ummah*. Not every group is called an *ummah*. For example, we do not call you an *ummah* now except because you are on one path. But if a group gathers in one place and they are scattered, each one with his own method, we do not say, "These are an *ummah*," unless they are from one tribe or something similar.

﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ (Fatir 24), meaning a prophet who warned them. That is, God sent a warner to every nation. Why? So that the proof would be established against them, for if people had no warner, they would have a proof against their Lord, saying, "Our Lord, You did not send a messenger to us."

As God says: ﴿And had We destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so we could follow Your signs before we are humiliated and disgraced?"﴾ [Ta-Ha 134]. And He says: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good tidings and warners, so that mankind will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾ [An-Nisa' 165]. The discussion of what is in His saying, ﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24], of the difficulty and its answer, will come, God willing (...).

God says: ﴿And not equal are the blind and the seeing﴾ [Fatir 19].

* In this verse there are benefits. Among them is the eloquence of the Qur'an, for it moves its listener and reader from concrete examples to abstract examples. This is because no one doubts concrete examples, and no one can dispute them. For if you say, for example, "This is a lamp and this is light," no one contests it. So one moves from the perceptible to the intelligible meaning.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the virtue of sight, for the negation of equality between the blind and the seeing means the preference of whom? The preference of the seeing. For this reason they have greatly supplicated to God, the Mighty and Majestic: "O God, grant us enjoyment of our hearing, our sight, and our strength as long as You keep us alive."

We say the same about ﴿nor the darknesses and the light﴾ [Fatir 20]. It contains the same eloquence of the Qur'an as His saying, ﴿And not equal are the blind and the seeing﴾ [Fatir 19], and it contains the move from the concrete example to the abstract example.

* It also contains: the preference of light over darkness, because the negation of equality between them means the preference of light over darkness.

* Also: when we move from the concrete example to the abstract, that the path of guidance is one, while the paths of misguidance are scattered. This is from His saying, ﴿the darknesses [...] the light﴾ [Fatir 20].

We have mentioned a witness from the Qur'an for this, which is His saying: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [Al-An'am 153]. And He says: ﴿God is the Ally of those who believe; He brings them out from the darknesses into the light. And those who disbelieve, their allies are the taghut﴾ [Al-Baqarah 257]. In it, the taghut drags them into some kind of disbelief and sin. We ask God for well-being.

* Also: the shade and the heat are not equal. This is a concrete example from which one moves to the abstract example, namely that the shade of Paradise and the heat of Hell are not equal. Which is better? The shade of Paradise. O God, make us and you among its people.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: a warning against the deeds of the people of the Fire. For the negation of equality between the shade and the heat is a known matter, and a person being harmed by the heat is also a known matter. So in it is a warning against the deeds of the people of the Fire.

Can it be derived from this noble verse that there is no blame upon a person for seeking shade and seeking light?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Is that so? It is known, for since we have mentioned that this negation means the preference of light over darkness and the preference of shade over heat, there is no blame upon a person for seeking what is better. Indeed, it may sometimes be obligatory. For this reason, when the Prophet ﷺ saw a crowd and a man over whom shade had been cast, [he] for fasting in travel, he did not say, "Do not shade him," but he said: "It is not righteousness to fast while traveling" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1946), and Muslim (1115 / 92), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]].

And His saying: ﴿And not equal are the living and the dead﴾ [Fatir 22]: in it also is what has preceded in its counterparts. In it is the virtue of knowledge, and so it is. God, the Exalted, has said: ﴿Say, "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"﴾ [Az-Zumar 9].

Knowledge is jihad in the way of God. And if you wish, say, more accurately: knowledge is a weapon for jihad in the way of God, for knowledge may be carried by one who neither benefits from it nor benefits others. So it is a weapon, but when you benefit yourself and others, you become a mujahid through it. God says: ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it a great striving﴾ [Al-Furqan 52]. So knowledge is a weapon by which a person reaches jihad in the way of God.

* Among its benefits also, from the benefits of His saying, ﴿the living and the dead﴾ [Fatir 22]: that in it is an incitement to seek knowledge, and that it is the life of the *ummah* just as it is the life of the individual. It is not possible for a nation to live a life, I do not say a bestial life, a nation can live a bestial life without knowledge, but it is not possible for it to live a good life except by knowledge. All people seek a good life, but what makes it good? Knowledge, when it bears its fruit, which is faith and righteous deeds. God says: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [An-Nahl 97].

He says: ﴿Indeed, God causes to hear whom He wills, but you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir 22].

* Among its benefits: that God, the Mighty and Majestic, is the One in whose hand are the keys of affairs. Even you, O Muhammad, cannot make anyone hear. Rather, the One who makes hear is God.

In it: the affirmation of God's will, for His saying, ﴿whom He wills﴾.

* In it also: a refutation of the Qadariyya (1), who deny that the actions of servants fall under God's will, for His saying, ﴿Indeed, God causes to hear whom He wills﴾ [Fatir 22]. But this absolute will here, and everywhere it comes absolute, is restricted by what? By wisdom, for His saying: ﴿And you do not will except that God wills. Indeed, God is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan 30].

* Among its benefits: a person ought, indeed must, turn to God alone for bringing benefits and removing harms, for His saying: ﴿Indeed, God causes to hear whom He wills﴾ [Fatir 22]. So if the causing to hear is from God, do not ask anyone else. Ask only God. For this reason, we should always be people who call upon God, the Mighty and Majestic, while feeling that we are in need of God, and that God, Glorified and Exalted, is able to bring about for us what we hope for and what we call upon Him for. Do not rely on yourself and forget God. Turn to God always in supplication, in prostration, between the call to prayer and the iqamah, and in all times, places, and states of answering. For God, Glorified and Exalted, says: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [Al-Baqarah 186].

Then know also that supplication, along with your asking God for a need, is itself an act of worship by which you draw near to Him. So through this supplication you gain two fruits:

The first fruit: the reward for this act of worship.

The second fruit: the attainment of what is sought or the removal of what is disliked.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Messenger of God ﷺ cannot make those in the graves hear, for His saying: ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir 22]. So if the Messenger ﷺ went to the people of the graveyard and called them and said, "O people of the graves, believe in God and His Messenger! O people of the graves, do righteous deeds!" Would they hear? They would not hear.

If you say: What is the answer to what is established in the Sahih, that the Messenger ﷺ stood over the slain of the polytheists in the well of Badr and began calling them by their names and the names of their fathers: "O so-and-so son of so-and-so, did you find what your Lord promised to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised to be true." 'Umar said to him, "O Messenger of God, you are speaking to bodies that have decayed," or words to this effect. He said: "You are not more able to hear what I say than they are" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3976), and Muslim (2875 / 78), from the hadith of Abu Talhah al-Ansari.]]. That means they hear. So what is the answer?

* A student: The saying of Qatadah, may God have mercy on him: "Indeed God revived them so that they heard the words of the Prophet ﷺ as a punishment and humiliation for them, then He caused them to die again" [[Related by al-Bukhari (3976).]]. And 'Aisha says: "The people of the well do not hear the Messenger ﷺ, but the Messenger addresses them because of the punishment they find in the grave" [[Related by Ahmad in al-Musnad (26361).]].

* The Shaykh: As for what you mentioned from 'Aisha, there is no doubt that the words of the Messenger ﷺ refute it, for he said: "You are not more able to hear what I say than they are." As for what was mentioned from Qatadah, the meaning of his words is that it is specific to those people.

If you say: What is the answer to what is also established in the sound hadith, that "when the deceased is buried and his companions turn away from him, indeed he hears the sound of their sandals as they leave him" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1338), and Muslim (2870 / 70), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: This is at the time of burial. Also, hearing the sound of sandals does not necessarily mean hearing speech and invocation.

If you say: What is the answer to what Abu Dawud and others narrated, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr authenticated, and which Ibn al-Qayyim agreed with or did not oppose: that "no Muslim greets a grave of one he knew in the world except that God returns his soul to him and he returns the greeting" [[Related by al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab (8857) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in al-Istidhkar (1/185) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas; we have not found it in Abu Dawud.]]?

The answer is that it is said: this is in a particular state indicated by the hadith, and it does not necessarily follow that whoever hears the greeting upon him, which is an invocation for him, and returns the greeting to the one who greets him, hears everyone who speaks in his presence.

If you say: What is the answer to what the jurists said, that the deceased is harmed by the speech of the reprehensible person at his grave or by the reprehensible act at his grave?

The answer: the saying of any person other than the Messenger ﷺ is not a proof. It is cited in support, not as the basis.

Then, according to their opinion, may God have mercy on them, they interpret His saying, ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir 22] to mean: you cannot make hear those whom you call to faith and righteous deeds. For you do not make them hear in a way that they respond to it. But it is a hearing that needs (...).

This is the final answer to the one who says that the dead hear what is said near them and what they are addressed with. We say: ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir 22], meaning, hearing by which they benefit and respond. And God knows best.

Regarding these unseen matters, the obligation upon the believer is to believe only in what the text has brought, and to leave the rest to inquiry. Indeed, he must say, "Knowledge is with God," and so he does not affirm with certainty the negation, nor does he affirm with certainty the affirmation. Yes, he may affirm the negation with certainty and make what the hadith established an exception, for He said: ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾ [Fatir 22], and in another verse: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating﴾ [An-Naml 80].

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿You are not but a warner﴾ [Fatir 23].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Muhammad, the Messenger of God ﷺ, is only a conveyer and a warner. There is nothing in his hand to bring guidance to anyone, nor to remove harm from him, for He said: ﴿You are not but a warner﴾ [Fatir 23], meaning you are not a guide to people in the sense of granting success and right guidance. Rather, you are a warner, so you are a guide only in the sense of indicating.

He says: ﴿You are not but a warner﴾ [Fatir 23].

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24].

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾: In this is evidence that the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ is true, and that he is not a liar, for He said: ﴿We have sent you with the truth﴾.

* Among its benefits also: that the Messenger ﷺ is worthy of prophethood if we take ﴿with the truth﴾ as a circumstantial clause from the subject "We" (*na*), meaning: "Indeed, We have sent you while being truthful in that," so it contains evidence that the Messenger ﷺ is worthy of prophethood. This is known from other evidences, such as His saying: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am 124], but we want to derive it from this verse.

* Also: what the Prophet ﷺ brought is truth, not falsehood. When you look at his reports, you find them to be truthful, and when you look at his rulings, you find them to be just. This is the truth, for truth regarding a report is truthfulness, and truth regarding a ruling is justice.

* Among its benefits: the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ combined good tidings and warning, from His saying: ﴿as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [Fatir 24].

* Among its benefits also: that a person may combine two qualities that are opposite in meaning, though agreeing in purpose: a bringer of good tidings and a warner. For the bringer of good tidings is one who promises people good and opens for them the door of hope, while the warner is one who frightens them from (...). Between them there is a difference in meaning, yet they can meet in a single person. Shall we move from this benefit to the point that a person may combine qualities of faith and qualities of disbelief?

* A student: He warns and gives good tidings.

* The Shaykh: No, they are not necessarily linked. It is not necessarily so. If you see an army approaching the town, I warn them and do not give them good tidings. But if you see that the army has withdrawn, I give them good tidings.

In any case, what is known from the school of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah (2), which is the truth, is that a person may combine qualities of faith and qualities of disbelief, so he is a believer in one respect and a disbeliever in another. As the Prophet ﷺ said: "Two things among people are disbelief: slandering lineage and wailing over the dead" [[Related by Muslim (67 / 121), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. And the Prophet ﷺ also said: "Cursing a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (48), and Muslim (64 / 116), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.]]. Yet fighting him does not take him out of faith, as in His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, make reconciliation between them﴾ [Al-Hujurat 9], to His saying: ﴿The believers are but brothers, so make reconciliation between your brothers﴾ [Al-Hujurat 10].

* Also among its benefits: the whole matter belongs to God. No one shares in it, not even the greatest of people in rank. He does not share with God in what is specific to Him, for His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you﴾ [Fatir 24]. And it is known that the station of the sender is higher than the station of the one sent. And God knows best (...).

And He, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [Fatir 24].

The address in His saying ﴿Indeed, We have sent you﴾ is to the Prophet ﷺ.

Sending (*irsal*) is entrusting the one sent with something that he conveys to those to whom he is sent.

The sentence, as we observe, is emphasized with *inna*, and emphasis of a sentence indicates the importance of it, so that a person may believe in it with complete faith.

God says: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾ [Fatir 24]. The *ba'* here is either for transitivity, as you say, "I sent him with such-and-such," to clarify what he was sent with, or it is for accompaniment.

---

(1) Qadariyya: an early theological school that denied God's comprehensive decree over the actions of servants.

(2) Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah: the adherents of the Sunnah and the community, the mainstream of the Muslim community in creed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 35, verse 19–24 (part 3 of 3):

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (﴿بِالْحَقِّ﴾ with guidance (bil-huda)). It seems he took this explanation from the Almighty's words: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth﴾ [At-Tawbah 33]. However, the correct view regarding the verse is that what is meant by ﴿bil-haqq﴾ is the opposite of falsehood (batil), so it includes truthfulness in reports and justice in rulings; that is: with truthfulness in reports and justice in rulings. It is not guidance alone, but guidance, righteousness, reform and other things besides.

As for the Almighty's words ﴿with guidance and the religion of truth﴾ [At-Tawbah 33], it is indeed possible to say that what is meant by guidance there is beneficial knowledge, because He mentioned guidance and mentioned religion, thus mentioning knowledge and action.

As for here, we should not restrict ourselves to saying that "the truth" means guidance; rather we should make it more general than that, so that it includes the guidance which is knowledge, and includes the religion of truth which is right direction, righteousness and reform. The Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, his message encompassed all beneficial knowledge and the good of creation in their livelihood and their hereafter, and what he brought included truthfulness in reports and justice in rulings. The Almighty said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [Fatir 24].

﴿Bashiran (as a bringer of good tidings)﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) in the sense of mubashshir (one who gives good tidings), a state from the kaf in ﴿arsalnaka (We have sent you)﴾.

The author said: (﴿Bashiran﴾ to whoever responds to him, ﴿wa nadhiran (and a warner)﴾ to whoever does not respond to him).

Bushra (good tidings) is the announcement of what gladdens, and it may be used for announcing what grieves, as in the Almighty's words: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 21].

As for indhar (warning), it is intimidation; that is, informing of what frightens. The Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, his message was good tidings and warning, because it is either a command whose doer is given good tidings of what that command requires, or a prohibition whose performer is made to fear committing it. So the Sharia as a whole is good tidings and warning.
