* The Shaykh: And affirming it? And what does not require either affirming or negating?
* The student: They suspend judgment, and most of them (...).
* The Shaykh: It is derived from His words: ﴿And there has been no nation but that a warner passed among them﴾. Its reasoning is that if minds were the reference, there would be no need to send messengers.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if they deny you﴾, meaning the people of Makkah. This explains the "wa" (and) in His words: ﴿And if they deny you, those before them had already denied﴾ [Fatir 25]. That is, it is no novelty that your people deny you, because those before them denied the messengers, as in His words: ﴿And messengers were denied before you, but they were patient over what they were denied and harmed﴾ [al-An'am 34]. That is, the matter is not limited to denial alone, but denial and harm by speech, harm by action, and beyond that, killing, for many of those to whom Allah sent messengers killed them.

He says: (﴿And if they deny you﴾ meaning the people of Makkah). Why do we restrict it to the people of Makkah? The correct view is that it is not specific to the people of Makkah, but includes them and others. The Messenger was denied by the people of Makkah, denied by the people of at-Ta'if, and by other polytheists. So the correct view is generality: ﴿And if they deny you, those before them had already denied﴾. ﴿Those who⦆ (alladhina): how do you parse it?

* Students: It is the subject (fa'il).

* The Shaykh: It is the subject. And where is the object? It is omitted; i.e., those before them denied their messengers. He says: ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs and with the scriptures and with the illuminating Book﴾ [Fatir 25], and still they disbelieved.

﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾: the (ba') here is for accompaniment, and it may also be for transitivity, meaning: they came bringing the clear proof that shows their truthfulness. The author's words "the miracles" is the expression of many later scholars, but the correct wording is "with signs," and "clear" (bayyinat) is an adjective of an omitted noun, its estimate being: "with clear signs," i.e., manifest.

The signs brought by the messengers are both sensory and non-sensory. Among the sensory signs is what Musa (peace be upon him) brought: the staff, the hand, and other things. Among the non-sensory signs is what he brought of the Torah. Likewise 'Isa and the other messengers: every messenger came only with a clear proof. It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "There is no prophet whom Allah sent except that he was given signs such that people believed on the basis of their likeness" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4981) and Muslim (152/239), from Abu Hurayrah].

This is so because it is neither wisdom, nor proof, nor mercy that a messenger should be sent to creation who permits the blood, wealth, and women of those who oppose him without a clear proof. Even if it were supposed that someone denied him while he had brought no proof, the denier would be excused, since the burden of proof is on the claimant. So it was part of Allah's wisdom, mercy, and establishment of His proof that He placed with the messengers signs that testify to the truth of what they brought.

The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, mentioned that the signs brought by the messengers, especially the sensory signs, are suited to what was prominent in their era, or to the most prominent matters of their time. They gave as an example that Musa (peace be upon him) brought the staff and the hand because magic had become prominent and widespread in his time. So he brought something beyond what the magicians could produce. The magicians only deceive and create illusions, while he brought reality. They threw their ropes and staffs, and it seemed to him, by their magic, that they were moving; it seemed so to him but it was not real. When he threw his staff, it became a real, actual thing that swallowed what they were faking.

They said: 'Isa (peace be upon him) came at a time when the art of medicine had advanced, so he brought something that physicians are powerless to do: he healed the blind from birth and the leper, raised the dead, and fashioned a figure from clay into which he breathed and it flew, becoming a real bird. This is beyond medicine. No physician, if a dead man stood before him, could say "Rise" and have him rise, ever. No physician could come to the graves, stand at a grave, and say "Come out," and have it come out; but 'Isa did so, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when you bring forth the dead by My permission﴾ [al-Ma'idah 110], bringing them out of their graves. No physician or anyone else can shape from clay the likeness of a bird and breathe into it so that it flies; never. No one can cure the blind and the leper of the illness that afflicted them as 'Isa (peace be upon him) cured them. Those with afflictions were brought to him; he wiped his hand over them and they were healed and it went away. That is, leprosy that had covered the skin, or most of it, would vanish when his hand passed over it, and wherever his hand touched, the skin returned to its natural state. No physician, however skilled in medicine, can reach this condition.

They said: Muhammad (ﷺ) came to a people who had reached the peak of eloquence, and he brought speech they could never match, and it is the speech of Allah. Allah challenged them in several verses to bring a surah like it, or ten surahs like it, or a discourse like it, and they could not. The point is that all that the messengers brought were clear signs.

He says: ﴿And with the scriptures﴾. He said: (like the scrolls of Ibrahim). (az-Zubur) is the plural of (zabur), which is what is written and inscribed, meaning the book. Had the author said "like the Psalms of Dawud," it would have been more fitting for the verse, because Allah did not mention the scrolls of Ibrahim as zubur, but He mentioned ﴿And We gave Dawud the Psalms﴾ [an-Nisa' 163].

(﴿And with the illuminating Book﴾ is the Torah and the Gospel.) The correct view regarding "the illuminating Book" is that it is not only the Torah and the Gospel, but every book Allah sent with a messenger, which illuminates the path for his community. It includes the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, the scrolls of Ibrahim, and others. No messenger whom Allah sent came without a book: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Book and the Balance﴾ [al-Hadid 25], and He the Exalted said: ﴿Mankind was one community, then Allah sent prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah 213]. So we cannot say that Nuh (peace be upon him) was sent without a book; he must have been sent with a book, but it does not follow from his being sent with it that this book is mentioned to us.

He says: ﴿And with the illuminating Book﴾. The author says: (so be patient as they were patient). This "wa" is a conjunction particle, and (az-Zubur) is conjoined to (al-bayyinat) by repeating the preposition.

* Student: The ba'.

* The Shaykh: As we said, it is either for accompaniment, meaning they came accompanied by these things, or for transitivity, as you say: "I brought him a dirham," "I brought him his food," "I brought him his drink," and similar. He says: (so be patient as they were patient). Did the Messenger (ﷺ) have patience? Yes, he was patient with a patience that only the steadfast of resolve (ulu al-'azm) could bear.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Then I seized those who disbelieved﴾ for their denial). The (ba') in the author's words is causal: ﴿I seized those who disbelieved﴾. Why did He seize them? For punishment. The people of Nuh He drowned; the people of Hud He destroyed with the wind; the people of Salih with the shout and the blast; the people of Lut He turned their cities upside down. Allah the Mighty and Majestic seized all deniers. Therefore He said: (﴿So how was My rejection﴾, i.e., My denunciation of them through punishment and destruction; i.e., it fell in its proper place). That is, the interrogative here is for affirmation: My denunciation of them through punishment was rightly placed. Hence if you were asked, "How was Allah's rejection of them?", the answer is: it was severe, and it fell in its proper place; it is entirely consistent with wisdom, and it was a severe punishment that left none of them behind.

* In this noble verse there are benefits. Among them: the denial of the Messenger (ﷺ) is no novelty among mankind, for nations denied before him: ﴿And if they deny you, those before them had already denied﴾.

* Among them: Allah's care for His Messenger (ﷺ) by mentioning what consoles him and eases the matter for him. Mentioning a similar calamity calls for comforting a person and making the matter easier for him. So if you come to a sick person and say, "By Allah, you are well today, and your illness is less than so-and-so's; so-and-so had an illness with such-and-such," he is consoled, is he not? He is consoled without doubt. Likewise if he suffers an accident and you say, "So-and-so suffered a greater accident," he is consoled. So in this there is Allah's care for His Messenger (ﷺ), in that He mentions to him what makes calamities easier and comforts him.

* Among the benefits of the verse: a warning to the deniers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because Allah mentioned the end of those before them, and their end was ruin and destruction. Allah pointed to this in His words: ﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and for the disbelievers are the like of it﴾ [Muhammad 10]. That is: do not think the destruction that befell the earlier deniers is specific to them; if you deny, what befell them will befall you.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Allah the Mighty and Majestic did not leave the messengers unguided, but gave them clear signs by which mankind is made to believe their likeness; as His words: ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾.

* Also among them: the perfection of Allah's wisdom, mercy, and the establishment of His proof. Why? It is drawn from His words: ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, because He gave these messengers clear proofs only for the complete establishment of proof, mercy, and wisdom.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that among the greatest clear proofs are the laws the messengers brought, contained in the books. The reason it is singled out, though it is among the clear proofs, is noteworthy: it is an explicit mention repeated with the governing particle, "with the clear proofs and with the scrolls," as if they were independent.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the heavenly books contain light, and whoever takes hold of them has taken hold of a light by which he walks in darknesses; as His words: ﴿With the scrolls and with the illuminating Book﴾.

* Among them: when a singular noun is intended to denote a genus, it becomes general; because His words "with the Book" are singular, yet were the books brought by the messengers one book? No, rather they are many books according to the messengers.

The reason it is singled out, though it is among the clear proofs, is noteworthy: it is an explicit mention repeated with the governing particle, "with the clear proofs and with the scrolls," as if they were independent.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the heavenly books contain light, and whoever takes hold of them has taken hold of a light by which he walks in darknesses; as His words: ﴿With the scrolls and with the illuminating Book﴾.

* Among them: when a singular noun is intended to denote a genus, it becomes general; because His words "with the Book" are singular, yet were the books brought by the messengers one book? No, rather they are many books according to the messengers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 35, verse 27:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ [Fatir: 27] to the end of the verse. Previously: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby﴾ to the end of the verse. The interrogative here (istifham) is for affirmation (taqrir), and this is the usual case when a negative particle occurs, or when a negative particle comes after the interrogative hamzah, that the question is for affirmation, such as: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1], ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81], ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ [al-Zumar: 36], and similar examples. When a negative particle comes after the interrogative hamzah, the usual meaning is that the interrogative is for affirmation.

His words ﴿Have you not seen﴾: the alif has been dropped because of the jussive (al-jazim), since the lam (of negation) puts the verb into the jussive, and a defective verb (al-fi'l al-mu'tall) is jussified by dropping its weak letter.

His words ﴿And of the mountains are tracts﴾ [Fatir: 27]: it is a subject and predicate, and the predicate is placed first, which is His words ﴿and of the mountains﴾.

His words ﴿diverse in their colours﴾ are an adjective of ﴿tracts﴾.

His words ﴿white and red﴾: it has been said that it is in inverted order, meaning "black and intensely black" (sud gharabib). It has also been said that it is in its original order, and that ﴿black﴾ comes in the position of emphasis for what precedes it, because gharib (the intensely black) is the very black.

His words ﴿Have you not seen﴾: the author said, "(Do you not know)", so the seeing here is knowledge-seeing ('ilmiyyah), and it is suspended from action by ﴿that﴾ and what follows it, because ﴿that﴾ and what follows it suspends verbs of the heart (af'al al-qulub) from acting. It is possible that the seeing here is sight-seeing (basariyyah), meaning: "Do you not look and see?" because what is mentioned is seen with the eye, and what is seen with the eye may be meant as seeing with the eye. But if we make it knowledge-seeing, that is more general, because this matter may not be seen with your eye, but you may hear of it in other lands besides your own.

His words ﴿that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾: by "sky" is meant height, and by "water" is meant rain. The sky does not mean the well-known celestial bodies, because water descends only from clouds, and clouds are high, yet they are between the sky and the earth.

His words ﴿and We bring forth thereby﴾: he said, "There is a shift away from the third person (iltifat 'an al-ghaybah)." If the speech were in one consistent pattern, it would say "and He brings forth thereby" with the third-person pronoun, but it has shifted from the third person to the first person ﴿We bring forth﴾. The shift has a benefit, indeed several benefits. One benefit shared in all its occurrences and places is alerting the addressee, because when speech is in one consistent pattern, a person continues with it and there is nothing to make him pay attention and notice. When the context changes from third person to first person, or to second person, or something similar, the person pays attention. That is, it serves as a sign of a change in style so that the addressee will be alert.

The second benefit here is His words ﴿We bring forth thereby﴾, for this "We" (na) indicates magnification, because bringing forth is greater than sending down with regard to the blessing upon us. If rain were sent down and did not bring forth plants, we would not benefit from the rain, as in the authentic hadith narrated by Muslim: "Drought is not that you are not given rain; drought is that you are given rain but the earth does not produce anything." [Muslim (2904/44) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] So since Allah's favour in bringing forth plants is greater, the shift to the first person is more fitting, due to the greatness of the favour in it. He said, ﴿and We bring forth thereby fruits diverse in their colours﴾. Here He said ﴿fruits﴾, and did not say "We bring forth thereby plants", although He said that in another verse: ﴿and We bring forth thereby the produce of every kind, and from it We bring forth green [plants], from which We bring forth grain piled up﴾ [al-An'am: 99]. But here He said ﴿fruits﴾, because the intended goal of what comes forth is the fruit, so Allah the Exalted made clear the intended end, which is the fruits.

He said: (﴿diverse in their colours﴾ such as green, red, yellow, and others), and this shows the power of Allah: these fruits are diverse in their colours. The word "colours" (alwan) may mean what the author mentioned, namely varied colours of redness, yellowness, greenness, and the like. It may also mean kinds (asnaf), because "colours" is used for kinds, as Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said regarding night prayer, in the Ramadan prayers: "Various colours (alwan) have been narrated concerning it," meaning types and kinds. When you look at what comes out of the earth, you find it has colours in its form and colours in its types and kinds, between sweet, bitter, middling, and sour, and other things well known. This last meaning, if we say that "colours" includes types, is more comprehensive than if we say that "colours" means differences in form.

A rule has already passed us: whenever the meaning is more comprehensive in the field of tafsir, it is preferable, because the more comprehensive includes the more specific and others, unlike the more specific. He said: ﴿diverse in their colours. And of the mountains are tracts﴾. This is a new sentence (jumlah isti'nafiyyah) in which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, also shows the perfection of His power with regard to the earth and its layers.

He said: (﴿And of the mountains are tracts﴾, the plural of (judda), a path in a mountain or elsewhere). "Of the mountains are tracts" means paths, that is, something resembling paths because it differs from the rest of the mountain, and it is also different in colour and in its nature. We now see some mountains, and especially when a mountain is opened, we see within it lines which may be black, or red, or brown, or white. The point is that we find in it lines that differ from the rest of the mountain. These are the tracts that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentions here. So mountains also differ in colour, and this difference in colour means a difference in nature and reality. A black pebble is not like a white or red pebble, or what resembles them and differs from them in colour. There must be a difference in the nature of this pebble, just as the difference in the colours of fruits shows their difference in taste and in nature.

He said: ﴿white and red tracts﴾. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned ﴿white and red﴾, whereas one would expect "white and black", because the usual opposite of white is black. But He said "red", because red is closer to white than black is. You will find in His words ﴿and intensely black﴾ that these tracts are white and red. The author said: (and yellow). We may also say: and blue, and other colours. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did not mention these two colours to limit them, but as an example.

He said: ﴿tracts﴾, (﴿diverse in their colours﴾ by intensity and weakness). Here the author explained "colours" as what? As nature, or as forms? As nature, because he said "by intensity and weakness" and did not say "such as red and white". In any case, as we said just before, "colours" is sometimes used for types. This difference in the colours of mountain stones is like the difference in the colours of fruits.

(﴿And intensely black﴾ is conjoined to ﴿tracts﴾, that is, rocks that are very black. It is commonly said "very black, intensely black (aswad gharibib)", and rarely said "gharibib black".) First: gharabib is the plural of gharibib, and gharibib means extremely black. The usual order would be "black and intensely black", but Allah the Exalted put the intense first and said "intensely black, black". Some have claimed that there is inversion and transposition in the speech. Others said: rather, it is in its proper order and has no inversion or transposition, but Allah, the Exalted, made clear the very intense black before the mention of black in general. Is this also observed? We find in the mountains tracts that are like a path or a line, purely black, and beside it a white, or red, or similar path. All of this is evidence of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And intensely black﴾. We see that this difference in the mountains is like the difference in fruits.

* Among the lessons of this verse: an indication that a person should reflect upon the creation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because of His words ﴿Have you not seen that Allah...﴾, for this is an affirmation, and affirmation is not complete unless the one being questioned looks at what he is made to affirm, until he acknowledges and confesses it.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: a demonstration of the power, wisdom, and mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through the sending down of water from the sky. There is great power in this water, which descends, and which at times becomes floods that destroy whatever buildings lie in their path and sweep away lands, although it descends from this thin cloud which an aircraft passes through, as we see, and which breaks apart when it passes over mountains and buildings and the like, and from it there descend these great waters. This is complete power and complete mercy. And the beneficial effects that this rain produces for the servants show complete wisdom, because this rain descends from above so that it covers high and low land. If it flowed like rivers, the lower land would be watered, even flooded, while the higher land would receive nothing. This is part of the complete wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He sends it down from above.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: an affirmation of causes, because of His words ﴿We bring forth thereby fruits﴾, for the "bi" here indicates causation. So there is in the verse an affirmation of causes, and that Allah, the Exalted, has connected things with their causes. It is well known that Allah is able to bring forth these fruits without water, but He has appointed a cause for everything.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: a demonstration of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in bringing forth these fruits of diverse colours, though they are in one land and watered by one water. This becomes clear to you when you look at flowers, how you find this wondrous difference among them although they are watered with one water.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the wisdom in the diversity of these fruits. If their nature were one, people would tire of them and would not attain full enjoyment. But when they differ, full enjoyment is attained and there is no boredom or weariness.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse also: a demonstration of the power, mercy, and wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in what we see of the diverse tracts in the mountains. This is evidence of power, in that He placed this between that. It is evidence of wisdom, because what is in the bellies of these mountains is generally minerals beneficial to people. It also shows mercy to creation, in depositing these things in the bellies of these mountains.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse also: a demonstration of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in that He makes some mountains pure black, and sometimes the whole mountain is black, and at times we see a black mountain beside a white mountain. All of this is part of the complete power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the lessons of this verse: what follows from reflecting upon these created things, namely taking lessons from them and deriving evidence from them for the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, which they contain.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And among mankind and the moving creatures and cattle are those of various colors. Thus, only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might, Forgiving.﴾ [Fatir 28]

The clause ﴿And among mankind and the moving creatures and cattle are those of various colors﴾ is a declarative sentence in which the predicate has been placed before the subject. ﴿Colors﴾ (ʾalwānuhu) is the agent (fāʿil) of ﴿of various﴾ (mukhtalifun), because mukhtalif is an active participle (ism fāʿil), and the active participle functions like its verb.

His saying ﴿Thus﴾ (kadhālika) is an adjective (ṣifah) of His saying ﴿of various﴾ (mukhtalif); meaning: varied in the manner of the variation of what has been mentioned.

His saying ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ is also a sentence composed of a verb, a subject and a direct object, and it contains restriction (ḥaṣr), whose means is ﴿only﴾ (innamā). The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might, Forgiving﴾ serves as a justification for what precedes it, as will come, God willing.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And among mankind and the moving creatures and cattle﴾. "Mankind" (al-nās) are human beings. They said: its original form is (unās), but the hamzah was dropped for lightness because of frequent use, just as it was dropped from (sharr) and (khayr), whose originals are (asharr) and (akhayr). It was also dropped from (Allah) according to the view of many linguists, its original being (al-ilāh). The intended meaning of "mankind" is the children of Adam, and they were so named because some of them are at ease (yanʾas) with others.

He said: ﴿The moving creatures﴾ (al-dawābb) is the plural of (dābbah), and it is used with several meanings. It is used for everything that crawls upon the earth, as in His saying: ﴿And Allah created every moving creature from water﴾ [al-Nur 45], and as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And there is no creature moving on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾ [Hud 6], which includes everything that crawls on the earth, whether human, animal, insects and other things. The word dābbah is also used for what moves on its belly, such as snakes, and for quadrupeds such as the donkey. So what is meant by it in this verse?

We say: what is meant by it is everything other than mankind and cattle, so it includes everything that crawls on the earth except mankind and cattle. If you say: why not make it inclusive, and make this a case of general coordinated with specific in relation to ﴿mankind﴾, and of specific coordinated with general in relation to ﴿cattle﴾?

That is, if someone says: what is meant by the moving creatures is everything that crawls on the earth, but they were conjoined to mankind as a case of general conjoined with specific, and cattle were conjoined to them as a case of specific conjoined with general.

We say: this is possible, but the division (of categories) rules it out, so what is meant by the moving creatures is everything other than mankind and cattle, and what is meant by cattle is what people benefit from, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He has made for you of the ships and cattle that which you ride﴾ [al-Zukhruf 12], and He the Exalted said: ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, from what Our hands have made, cattle, and they are their owners? And We have subjected them to them, so some of them they ride and some of them they eat. And for them therein are benefits and drinks; so will they not be grateful?﴾ [Ya-Sin 71–73]. So what is meant by cattle here is what people benefit from, such as camels, cows, sheep, lawful birds and other things.

﴿Of various colors, thus﴾. Does ﴿of various colors﴾ mean color, form, or also kind? It includes all of these. Thus people's colors vary: this one is white, this one is black, this one is red, and this one is between them, and the variation of color is evident. Their kinds also vary: this one is male, this one is female; this one is a scholar, this one is ignorant; this one is foolish, this one is forbearing. Apply this reasoning to the rest.

Likewise the moving creatures vary in color by form, and vary in their categories and types. Among them is what harms, among them is what is harmful, among them is what is beneficial, and among them is what is neither harmful nor beneficial nor injurious. So they are of four categories: among them is the beneficial, among them is the harmful, among them is the injurious but not seriously harmful, and among them is what is neither injurious nor harmful. Examples of the beneficial: cattle; examples of the harmful: snakes, scorpions, predatory beasts and the like; examples of the injurious: cockroaches, beetles, dung beetles and the like; mosquitoes may be harmful. Examples of what is neither injurious nor harmful: ants and other of the many creatures we see; birds, for example, that we see flying in the air, which are not lawful to eat but do not cause harm.

His saying ﴿thus﴾: the author said: (like the variation of fruits and mountains), so the variation among the creations of Allah the Exalted includes animals, what animals benefit from such as fruits and other things, and the layers of the earth such as mountains.

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾. When He mentioned these categories, and in them is what indicates the perfection of Allah the Mighty and Majestic in the attributes contained in these mentioned categories, He made clear that the one who knows this is the one who fears Allah. So He said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾, meaning: none fears Allah except the people of knowledge. Khashyah (fear) is the highest fear, or if you wish, say: it is fear founded on knowledge. Some said: it is fear founded on the greatness of what is feared, and it is not impossible that khashyah is fear in all three types; that is, it is the highest type of fear, or fear founded on knowledge, or fear founded on the greatness of what is feared. As for fear devoid of khashyah, it may arise from ignorance, when a person fears something because he is ignorant of it; otherwise he is not worthy of being feared (like the disbelievers of Mecca). The author was right in his saying: (unlike the ignorant). As for the example of the disbelievers of Mecca, it is not restrictive but illustrative; every disbeliever is in reality ignorant, and this is ignorance of knowledge or ignorance of conduct? It is mostly ignorance of conduct, for otherwise the disbeliever may have knowledge but, may Allah protect us, persists in his rebellion and does not believe.

(...) Blessed and Exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby fruits of differing colors?﴾ The interrogative here (...) is for affirming causes; it necessitates that we say the act is obligatory, because a cause necessitates the existence of the effect, and this requires that we make obligatory upon Allah the Mighty and Majestic the existence of the effect upon the existence of the cause. The theologians (mutakallimun) denied wisdom, such as the Jabriyyah for example; they denied the wisdom of Allah, saying: if we affirm wisdom and causation, it follows that we make obligatory upon Allah the Exalted that He act, as their opponents the Mu'tazilah said. The Mu'tazilah say that what is most beneficial is obligatory, and some say that goodness is obligatory upon Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because this is what wisdom requires. Those Jahmiyyah, on the contrary, say: Allah the Mighty and Majestic creates a thing without cause and without wisdom, because if you affirm wisdom and cause it follows that you make obligatory the effect, or the act which is the effect of this cause, and this requires that we make obligatory upon Allah the Mighty and Majestic the doing of a thing. So what is the answer?

We say: affirming wisdom or cause does not necessitate that we make anything obligatory upon Allah; rather, what wisdom requires of Him is that He act, and that the effect exist when the cause exists. We have not made it obligatory, but what Allah made obligatory upon Himself by the requirement of His name (the Wise) and His attribute of wisdom. Allah's making obligatory upon Himself is not impossible, just as His forbidding Himself is not impossible. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'am 54], and He the Exalted said in the sacred hadith: "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice to Myself"[[Narrated by Muslim (2577/55) from the hadith of Abu Dhar.]]. So Allah may forbid Himself, and make obligatory upon Himself whatever He wills; but as for us, no. So if it is said, for example: this is a benefit, therefore it must be, we say: yes, we commit to this; but did we make it obligatory upon Allah? No; rather Allah is the One who made it obligatory upon Himself. This does not contradict His perfection, but is part of the requirement of His perfection. However, the danger in this matter is that we suppose the benefit lies in such-and-such, while in reality the benefit lies in its absence; this is what is to be feared. Then we believe that this is obligatory upon Allah while He has not made it obligatory, believing it is obligatory upon Allah on the basis of our understanding that it is a benefit and good, and then we make it obligatory upon Allah. This is the danger. But when the benefit is truly established, there is no objection to saying that Allah the Exalted made it obligatory upon Himself that there be benefit, because this is what the name Allah the Wise requires; and in this case no transgression or injustice has come from us, but we have spoken according to the wisdom of Allah the Exalted. Here He said: ﴿So We brought forth thereby fruits﴾ (...) and Exalted.

Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might, Forgiving﴾. ﴿Exalted in Might﴾ means: possessor of might. The scholars said: might is of three types: might of rank, might of subjugation, and might of inaccessibility. As for might of rank, it means that Allah the Exalted is possessor of a mighty rank, and rank means station, honor, nobility and the like. Might of subjugation: that Allah the Exalted is dominant and not overcome. From it is His saying the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Give it to me, and he overcame me in speech"﴾ [Sad 23], meaning: he overpowered me.

Might of inaccessibility: that Allah the Exalted is protected against any deficiency in His essence or His attributes. From it is the saying: "a land that is 'azaz", meaning hard and firm, which nothing crosses because of its firmness, and nothing affects it because of its strength and hardness. So might has three meanings: might of rank, might of subjugation, and might of inaccessibility.

﴿Forgiving﴾ means possessor of forgiveness, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ra'd 6]. Forgiveness (maghfirah) is the covering of sin and overlooking it, and its derivation supports this, for it is derived from al-mighfar, which is what covers the head and by which arrows are warded off; in the mighfar there is covering and protection. On this basis we say: al-Ghafur is the possessor of forgiveness, which is the covering of sin and overlooking it. This meaning is supported, beyond the evidence of derivation, by what is established in the sound hadith: that Allah the Mighty and Majestic meets His believing servant in private, makes him acknowledge his sins until he confesses them, then says: "I covered them for you in this world, and today I forgive them for you"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768/52) from the hadith of Ibn Umar.]]. That is, I overlook them; and in this world Allah covered them over the servant. The mention of might and forgiveness here after the mention of fear indicates that Allah the Exalted is worthy of being feared, because He is Mighty; and that if any of the fear due to Him falls short, it is met with what? With forgiveness. He is Mighty, and therefore worthy of being feared; and He is Forgiving if anything of the fear due to Him the Exalted falls short.

As for the benefits of the verse, we say, and by Allah we speak:

* It is derived from the noble verse: the demonstration of the power of Allah the Exalted through the variation of the colors of mankind, the moving creatures and cattle, that is, their kinds and forms; because the variation of these colors, though they are one thing or one type, is evidence of power. For example, two persons among the children of Adam cannot be alike in everything at all; if their creation were assumed to be alike, they would differ in character, and equality in character is impossible, since people differ in it enormously, more than the difference in outward form, though outward difference is more apparent because it is seen. But the difference in character is greater, because people cannot agree or be equal in it at all, since any word that comes from one of them and not from the other introduces a difference.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of the fear of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, since only the people of knowledge are characterized by it.

* Also among its benefits: the virtue of knowledge, since it is a cause of the fear of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and khashyah is a quality with praiseworthy effects; for when a person fears his Lord he avoids His disobedience and performs His commands out of fear of Him the Exalted. For this reason, when Allah the Mighty and Majestic mentioned the reward of ﴿those who believed and did righteous deeds, they are the best of creation (7). Their reward with their Lord is gardens of perpetual residence beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾ [al-Bayyinah 7–8], He said: ﴿That is for whoever fears his Lord﴾, which is evidence that fear necessitates faith and righteous action.

* Also among its benefits: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, al-'Aziz and al-Ghafur, and the affirmation of the attributes they contain, which are might and forgiveness, and the affirmation of the ruling and effect they contain. Is that correct? As for al-Ghafur, yes: it has an effect and a ruling, as Allah said at the end of Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾, ﴿and Allah is over all things competent﴾ [al-Baqarah 284].

(Al-'Aziz): does it have a ruling? What is it? We said that among its meanings is dominance; and if ('azza) means (ghalaba), it becomes transitive, so it has a ruling, that is, an effect. Thus the affirmation of what the two names contain of attribute and ruling, which we sometimes express as effect. It has passed us earlier that the names of Allah the Mighty and Majestic are either intransitive or transitive; the intransitive names establish the name and the attribute, and the transitive names establish the name, the attribute and the effect.

* Student: the author's statement "in His kingdom."

* The Shaykh: ("Indeed, Allah is Mighty" in His kingdom, "Forgiving" of the sins of His believing servants.) We have not explained the author's words.

As for his statement ("Indeed, Allah is Mighty" in His kingdom): this is based on the view that might means dominance, as many commentators explain it, so they say: al-'Aziz means al-Ghalib (the Dominant). But the explanation we mentioned, we do not restrict it to His kingdom. You say: He is Mighty, and we do not confine it to the kingdom, because Allah the Exalted is Mighty in His kingdom, Mighty in all His attributes, and Mighty in His legislation; the might is general as long as we say it is the might of inaccessibility, of rank and of subjugation.

As for ("Forgiving" of the sins of His believing servants), restricting it in this way is also open to question; if the author had said: Forgiving to whoever repents to Him, or who asks His forgiveness, it would have been more comprehensive, because Allah the Exalted forgives even non-believers if they repent to Allah: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, they will be forgiven what has already passed﴾ [al-Anfal 38]; ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar 53]. Generalization is therefore preferable to restriction.

Then He, exalted is He, said: (﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah, establish the prayer, and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾ [Fatir 29] — zakat and other than it) ﴿hope for a commerce that will never perish﴾ — destroyed.

The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of this verse is clear, with no difficulty, except that His saying ﴿Indeed, those who recite﴾ (إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يَتْلُونَ) requires a predicate. What is the predicate? The predicate is the clause ﴿hope for a commerce that will never perish﴾ (يَرْجُونَ تِجَارَةً لَنْ تَبُورَ). This is the correct view among the grammarians (al-mu'rabun); the meaning is: these people who did that hope for a commerce that will never perish. So the clause يَرْجُونَ is the predicate of إِنَّ.

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah﴾. The author said: (they recite). The correct view is that tilawah (recitation/following) is more general than qira'ah (reading). Tilawah has two kinds: verbal tilawah, which is qira'ah, and practical tilawah, which is following the Qur'an by affirming its reports and complying with its commands. This is why one says talahu, meaning "he followed him," i.e., came after him. So tilawah is more general than qira'ah, and it has two kinds: verbal tilawah, where a person reads the Qur'an, and practical tilawah, where he follows it by complying with its commands and affirming its reports. Practical tilawah requires understanding the meaning, does it not? Yes, because one cannot act except on what one understands. On this basis, the action of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, was a perfect application of this verse, because they would not go beyond ten verses until they had learned them and what they contained of knowledge and action. They said: "So we learned the Qur'an, knowledge and action together" [[Narrated by al-Tahawi in Mushkil al-Athar (1452) and al-Firyabi in Fada'il al-Qur'an (169), from the narration of Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami.]].

Allah says: ﴿Indeed, those who recite﴾ (إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يَتْلُونَ). The verb يَتْلُونَ is present tense, which indicates continuity, unlike if He had said "those who recited" in the past tense, which would not convey the meaning that the present tense يَتْلُونَ conveys.

As for His saying ﴿the Book of Allah﴾ (كِتَابَ اللَّهِ): does it mean the Qur'an, or is it more general than that? The answer: it is more general than that. ﴿The Book of Allah﴾ refers to the books that Allah revealed to the messengers, so it includes all books. This ruling covers the believers of this Ummah and the believers of earlier nations. Therefore the meaning of "the Book" here, ﴿the Book of Allah﴾, is every book that Allah revealed to His messengers.

﴿They recite the Book of Allah and establish the prayer﴾ (يَتْلُونَ كِتَابَ اللَّهِ وَأَقَامُوا الصَّلَاةَ): this is coordinated (ma'tufah) with يَتْلُونَ. The author said: (they maintained it). The correct view differs from what the author said. Its meaning is that we choose a word that matches the wording more closely: "they established the prayer" means they performed it upright (mustaqimah). So performing the prayer includes doing it complete with its conditions, pillars, obligations and recommended acts. Does it also include maintaining it regularly? Yes, it includes maintaining it too, because maintenance (idamah) is part of establishing (iqamah). On this basis we say "they established the prayer," meaning they performed it upright, in the manner required of them. If a person maintains the prayer but neglects its pillars or obligations, would one say that he established the prayer? No. The man who came and prayed without being at ease in his prayer had been praying this prayer since he embraced Islam, and the Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: "Pray, for you have not prayed" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (757) and Muslim (397/45), from Abu Hurayrah.]]. Although he maintained the prayer and prayed, he had not prayed, since he did not perform it upright in the required manner. So the correct view is that iqamah here means that he performs it in the manner required of him. The prayer is known to everyone and needs no definition, since it is a worship with known statements and actions, opened with the takbir and concluded with the taslim.

He said: ﴿and spend from what We have provided them﴾ (وَأَنْفَقُوا مِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ). Anfaqu means they expended and gave out. ﴿From what We have provided them﴾ means from what We have given them, since rizq means giving.

As for His saying ﴿from what We have provided them﴾ (مِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ): is min (مِن) here to specify the kind, or to indicate a part? It is better to take it as specifying the kind, so that it includes those who spend all their wealth in the manner that Allah and His Messenger are pleased with, since they too fall under this description.

As for His saying ﴿secretly and openly﴾ (سِرًّا وَعَلَانِيَةً): sirran is a verbal noun (masdar), but it is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: discreetly and openly. Secrecy means concealing the spending so that no one knows of it except the one who receives it. Openness means making it known to people, either fully and comprehensively, or in a relative sense, where those around them know of it. They are praised for all of this. It will come, if Allah wills, in the mention of the benefits that this varies according to the circumstance.

He said: (zakat and other than it). Other than zakat includes obligatory spending on relatives and voluntary charities (sadaqat al-tatawwu'), so the spending here is comprehensive.

He said: ﴿they hope for a commerce that will never perish﴾ (يَرْجُونَ تِجَارَةً لَنْ تَبُورَ). Yarjuna means they aspire to and seek this commerce from Him.

﴿A commerce that will never perish﴾ (تِجَارَةً لَنْ تَبُورَ), meaning it will never be destroyed, as the author said. What is this commerce? Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned it in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, shall I guide you to a commerce that will save you from a painful punishment? You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the way of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you, if you only knew. He will forgive you your sins﴾ [al-Saff 10-12]. Here there is a exchange and a reward: the exchange is faith in Allah and striving in His way; the reward is ﴿He will forgive you your sins and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings﴾ [al-Saff 12]. This commerce is undoubtedly the most profitable of commerce and the most lasting of commerce. It is the most profitable, because its return is ten-fold, and a good deed is rewarded with ten times its like up to seven hundred times and many more multiples. It is also undoubtedly the most lasting, because it is in Gardens of Eden, that is, gardens of permanent dwelling in which there is no departure. And Allah knows best.

﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah and establish the prayer﴾, and so on. What is meant by the recitation of (...)?

* From this verse several benefits are derived. Among them: the virtue of reciting the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic, from His saying ﴿they hope for a commerce that will never perish﴾.

* Among them: hope should be placed in its proper place, such that a person has done a deed for which he hopes for reward. As for hope without deeds, it is mere wishful thinking that does not benefit the servant. In the hadith: "The intelligent one is he who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death, and the incapable one is he who follows his desires and wishes upon Allah [vain] wishes" [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2459) and Ibn Majah (4260), from Shaddad ibn Aws.]]. So there is no hope except with deeds. In the authentic hadith also: "None of you should die except while thinking well of Allah" [[Narrated by Muslim (2877/82), from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]], and in the authentic hadith: "I am as My servant thinks of Me" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7405) and Muslim (2675/2), from Abu Hurayrah.]]. All these texts and others like them apply only to one who does the deeds by which he can hope for that and think well of Him. If someone sins and becomes arrogant toward the worship of Allah, and says, "I think well of Allah," this is a delusion, since such a good opinion must rest on something. If he says, "I hope for the mercy of Allah," we say: this is a delusion unless you act. This is why He, exalted is He, said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and struggled in the way of Allah — those hope for the mercy of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 218]. These are the ones who hope, and it is similar here.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: reward in the Hereafter does not cease, from His saying ﴿that will never perish﴾. Indeed, we may say that this is even more general, so that a person is rewarded in this world with continuous reward that extends into the Hereafter, since a person may see the reward of good deeds in this world, and their reward in this world continues into the reward of the Hereafter, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Thus does Allah reward the righteous, those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying, "Peace be upon you; enter Paradise"﴾ [al-Nahl 31-32].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of establishing the prayer, from His saying ﴿and establish the prayer﴾. It includes, as we said in the explanation, both the obligatory prayer (fard) and the voluntary prayer (nafl). What applies to the obligatory prayer applies to the voluntary prayer, and what applies to the voluntary prayer applies to the obligatory prayer, unless there is evidence distinguishing between them. I think we have compiled the differences between the obligatory and voluntary prayers, and they reached twenty-eight differences. Some of them are clear and indicated by the Sunnah, and some are less clear. The main principle is that establishing the obligatory prayer is establishing the voluntary, and establishing the voluntary is establishing the obligatory. This is the principle: whatever is established in one of them is established in the other, unless there is evidence.

* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of spending, since He followed the prayer with it: ﴿and establish the prayer and spend﴾. It indicates that this spending includes zakat and other than zakat, because Allah, exalted is He, always mentions the prayer and zakat together.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the one who spends does not confer a favor upon Allah, mighty and majestic, since he spends only from what Allah has provided him. So however much your soul may lead you to self-admiration and pride in your spending, remember His saying: ﴿from what We have provided them﴾. Whatever you spend, you have no favor in it upon Allah, mighty and majestic. Rather, Allah has the favor upon you in it, both in its existence and in its expenditure. In its existence: because had Allah not provided you, you would not have obtained it. In its expenditure: because many people withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty: ﴿And let not those who withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty think it is better for them. Rather, it is worse for them﴾ [Al 'Imran 180]. So among Allah's blessings upon you is that He bestows upon you the ability to spend after He has bestowed upon you provision and giving.

* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: as for spending, we do not say that secrecy is better in it, nor that openness is better in it. Rather, it depends on the circumstance. Sometimes secret spending is better, and sometimes open spending is better, according to what the situation requires. This differs from sadaqah (voluntary charity), where the principle is secrecy. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿If you disclose your charities, they are good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 271], because sadaqah carries a kind of burden of obligation upon the recipient. He may be humiliated before people if the charity is made known to him, so concealing it is better. In the authentic hadith about those whom Allah shades in His shade: "A man who gave charity and concealed it" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1423) and Muslim (1031/91), from Abu Hurayrah.]].

As for general matters and public announcements, such as if we wished to spend on a general charitable project in which no burden is placed on a specific person, here openness may be better. Likewise, if a person came to us and said, "I hope you will collect for me from people," here openness may be better, so that others may follow your example. This man who asked us to collect for him does not mind whether people know that he is being given charity or not.

The main point is that we say: secrecy and openness in spending are both good, but the better form of sadaqah is secrecy, because of what making it public does to the recipient's heart. As for general matters, or charity to a specific person whom he asked us to collect for, for example, here openness may be better.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an admonition about sincerity (ikhlas), from His saying ﴿they hope for a commerce﴾. They do not desire a commerce that will perish and be destroyed; that is, they do not desire it for showing off (sum'ah). Reputation and standing among people is indeed a gain for a person and may be considered a commerce, but it is a perishing commerce that vanishes when the person vanishes or when what he became known for vanishes, because whoever is praised for something is blamed for its loss. But the one who hopes for Allah's reward, and makes his intention and purpose good, is the one who has gained a commerce that will never perish. So there is an admonition here about sincerity, and that a person should be sincere to Allah, mighty and majestic, in his obligatory or limited deeds, and in his deeds that extend to others: the limited ones like prayer, and the extended ones like charity.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿That He may pay them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty﴾ [Fatir 30]. He said: ﴿That He may pay them﴾, meaning He gives them their rewards in full and complete. The pronoun is the subject, referring back to Allah, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah﴾.

His saying: ﴿That He may pay them﴾. This lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah). It has also been said that it is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil). If it is the lam of consequence, it is connected to ﴿they hope for a commerce that will never perish﴾. Their outcome is that Allah pays them their rewards. If it is the lam of causation, it is connected to ﴿recite﴾, ﴿established﴾, and ﴿spent﴾, meaning: they recite so that He may pay them their rewards; they establish prayer so that He may pay them their rewards; they spend from what We have provided them so that He may pay them their rewards. That is, they intend what Allah has ordained as rewards for these deeds. This verb takes two objects, the first here being the pronoun (the hā'), and the second being ﴿ujūr﴾ (rewards). It belongs to the class of the sisters of kasā (akhawāt kasā, verbs that take two objects not forming a subject-predicate relation).

* A student: "From the sisters of kasā."

* The Shaykh: "Yes, from the sisters of kasā and a'ṭā (to clothe and to give), because it governs what cannot be a subject and predicate. Every verb that governs two objects, where one cannot be the predicate of the other, falls under this category (bāb kasā)."

(﴿That He may pay them their rewards﴾, meaning the reward for their mentioned deeds.) This payment is well known to all of us: a good deed is rewarded tenfold up to seven hundredfold, up to many multiples. For example, prayer is a good deed rewarded tenfold up to seven hundredfold and beyond. With congregation, how many good deeds is it? Twenty-seven good deeds, each rewarded tenfold.

He said: ﴿and increase them from His bounty﴾, coordinated with (﴿that He may pay them﴾): meaning He increases them in gift and reward from His bounty. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains, and Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah 261].

His saying: ﴿and increase them from His bounty﴾ includes bounty in this world and in the Hereafter. As for this world, when a person does a righteous deed sincerely for Allah, Allah makes the deed beloved to him, so that he increases in deeds. This is something observed. Likewise, when he gives and spends, Allah increases him from His bounty. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Whatever you spend, He will replace it﴾, meaning He brings its replacement. So the increase includes an increase in rewards, an increase in deeds, and an increase in the wealth spent: the increase in deeds, because I have said that whenever a person does a righteous deed, Allah makes the deed beloved to him and increases him in it; the increase in wealth, ﴿Whatever you spend, He will replace it, and He is the best of providers﴾ [Saba 39]; ﴿And what you give in usury to increase the wealth of people will not increase with Allah; but what you give in zakah, seeking the countenance of Allah, those are the ones who receive multiplied reward﴾ [al-Rum 39]. ﴿And increase them from His bounty﴾, meaning from His gift, which He bestows upon them.

(﴿Indeed, He is Forgiving﴾ of their sins, ﴿Appreciative﴾ of their obedience.) This is the reason for what preceded: the payment of rewards and the increase from His bounty. That is, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because He is Forgiving and Merciful, pays them their rewards and increases them from His bounty. This indicates Allah's forgiveness of the doer and His appreciation of him.

(al-Ghafūr) is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālaghah), or an attributive adjective (ṣifah mushabbahah), derived from (al-ghafr), which is covering together with protection, because the root's origin is al-mighfar (helmet), by which covering and protection are achieved. So what does it mean that Allah is Ghafūr? It means Allah covers sins and overlooks punishment. I do not know how much we sin between ourselves and our Lord, yet Allah, Mighty and Majestic, covers them. On the Day of Resurrection, He pardons their punishment; and by this forgiveness is realized.

As for al-Shakūr, we say about its form what we said about Ghafūr: it is either an intensive form or an attributive adjective. He, Exalted is He, is Shakūr, meaning He appreciates whoever does a righteous deed. Among His appreciation is that He multiplies the reward: a good deed tenfold up to seven hundredfold and beyond. Consider the perfection of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His attribute: He is the One who bestows upon you the deed, then appreciates you for it. ﴿Is the reward for good except good?﴾ [al-Rahman 60]. Glory be to Allah the Mighty! Our Lord bestows goodness upon us, then says: "What is the reward of your goodness but that We do good to you?" He is the One who graced you first and then second. This shows you the vastness of Allah's generosity, all praise be to Allah, and that He, Mighty and Majestic, is vast in generosity.

* In this verse there are several benefits. First: that a person seeking reward is a great aim, because the lam, as we pointed out earlier, is not the lam of consequence but the lam of causation. This is if we say it is for causation, and it is suitable for causation. That a person acts for the sake of reward is not considered a deficiency, contrary to the Sufis who say: "Do not worship Allah for Allah's reward, but worship Allah for Allah Himself." We say to them: this is an error. Allah described the noblest of this Ummah and its best as those who seek bounty from Allah and His pleasure. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are harsh against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾ [al-Fath 29].

Nevertheless, we do not say: you do not worship Allah for Allah; worship Allah for Allah and for Allah's reward, for you will not reach Allah except after reaching Allah's reward. The meeting with Allah, which is complete pleasure, occurs when? In Paradise. For this reason Allah said: ﴿Whoever is distanced from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has triumphed﴾ [Al 'Imran 185]. This is the complete triumph.

And His saying: ﴿Those who patiently seek the countenance of their Lord and establish prayer﴾ [al-Ra'd 22]. When do they see the Face of Allah? When they enter Paradise: the complete seeing of Allah's Face occurs after entering Paradise. The conclusion: this verse and similar ones indicate the weakness of the path taken by those Sufis who say: "Do not worship Allah for Allah's reward, but worship Allah for Allah." We say: how many verses show that worship is for Allah's bounty and reward.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the guarantee of reward, meaning that reward is guaranteed for the worker who deals with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, on the basis that the lam is of consequence; that is, this deed will certainly be paid in full: ﴿That He may pay them their rewards﴾.

There is also another aspect of the guarantee of reward: that Allah called it a reward (ajr), and a reward must be paid to whoever did the work. Indeed, a sound hadith qudsi says: Allah, Exalted is He, said: "Three, I will be their adversary on the Day of Resurrection: a man who gave in My name and then betrayed; a man who sold a free person and consumed his price; and a man who hired a worker, took full work from him, but did not give him his wage." [[Recorded by al-Bukhari (2227) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] If Allah is the adversary of these, because they did not give the wage, this indicates that the reward Allah guaranteed to His servants will certainly be realized, but the work must be valid.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the reward of good deeds is more than what is obligatory, based on His saying: ﴿and increase them from His bounty﴾. The increase in bounty has been explained in the tafsir.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the two noble names al-Ghafūr (the Forgiving) and al-Shakūr (the Appreciative), and the attributes they contain: forgiveness and appreciation; and also the effect they contain, which is the ruling. From Ghafūr it is taken that He forgives, and from Shakūr it is taken that He appreciates whoever deserves appreciation.

* Also in this noble verse: evidence for the establishment of voluntary acts (al-af'āl al-ikhtiyariyyah, acts that occur by Allah's will) for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, based on His saying: ﴿That He may pay﴾, ﴿and increase﴾. This is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community), who affirm for Allah, Exalted is He, voluntary acts, that is, acts that occur by His will, for He, Exalted is He, does what He wills. This is in contrast to those who claim that Allah, Exalted is He, is never described by anything that is newly occurring.

The Qur'an verse is given here as Fatir 31–32 requires, and the commentary follows.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 35, verse 31–36 (part 1 of 4):

He says: ﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth, confirming what is before it﴾ [Fatir 31]. The sentence here, ﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth﴾, comes in the restrictive nominal form (al-jumla al-ismiyya al-mahsura), and there are two ways of restricting it. The first: definiting its two pillars, the subject (mubtada') and the predicate (khabar). So "alladhi" (that which) is the subject and "al-haqq" (the truth) is the predicate.

The scholars of rhetoric (ahl al-balagha) have said that defining both pillars of the nominal sentence conveys restriction. The second way of restriction is the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), which is his saying ﴿huwa al-haqq﴾ (it is the truth). The separating pronoun has the function of restriction, a second function of emphasis, and a third function of separating the predicate from the attribute.

He says: ﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth﴾. ﴿We have revealed to you﴾: revelation (al-wahy) is Allah, the Exalted, informing His prophets and messengers of one of His laws. This is revelation in the legal sense (shar'an). As for its linguistic sense, they said that revelation is informing quickly and secretly; that is, a gesture, a whisper and the like are called revelation. But in the legal sense...

Some of it is not revelation. Sometimes the Prophet ﷺ was asked about something and did not answer, and then revelation came down and he answered with a prophetic statement. An example is the story of Ya'la ibn Umayyah, who had entered into 'umra while wearing perfume (khaluq), and asked the Prophet ﷺ about that, but he did not answer him until revelation came [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1536) and Muslim (1180/6), from the hadith of Ya'la ibn Umayyah]. Sometimes he is asked about something and then revelation comes down concerning it as the speech of Allah, the Qur'an, and he conveys it to them ﷺ.

He says: ﴿alladhi awhayna ilayka﴾ [Fatir 31]. What is meant here is definitely the Qur'an, as evidenced by his saying ﴿min al-Kitab﴾ (of the Book). This is because "min" (of) is explanatory (bayaniyya), clarifying the vagueness in the relative pronoun "alladhi" (that which). The relative pronoun (ism mawsul) contains vagueness, so when "min" comes after it, it is explanatory.

﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book﴾ [Fatir 31]: (the Qur'an). "Kitab" (Book) here means "maktub" (written), because this pattern (fi'al) often comes in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul). Examples are "ghiras" (planted), "bina'" (built), "firash" (spread out), meaning "maghrus" (planted), "mabni" (built) and "mafrush" (spread). So "kitab" means "maktub" (written). Written where? Written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), written in the scrolls that are in the hands of the angels: ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder. So whoever wills may remember it. [It is recorded] in honoured scrolls, exalted and purified, in the hands of scribes, noble and dutiful﴾ [Abasa 11–16]. It is written in the mushafs that are in our hands. Thus it is written in three forms: the Preserved Tablet, the scrolls in the hands of the angels, and the mushafs in our hands.

He says: ﴿huwa al-haqq﴾ [Fatir 31]. ("Huwa") is a separating pronoun, and "al-haqq" is the predicate of "alladhi". So that which Allah revealed to His Messenger ﷺ is the truth. Allah emphasised this with how many emphases? With two emphases: the separating pronoun, and the definiting of both pillars of the sentence, ﴿alladhi awhayna ilayka min al-Kitab huwa al-haqq﴾ [Fatir 31].

His saying ﴿al-haqq﴾ means the thing that is established as true in reports and just in rulings. So all the rulings of the Qur'an are just and all its reports are true; there is no falsehood in them in any way, and no injustice in its rulings in any way. This is because when you contemplate its rulings you find that it gives every person his right; therefore it is just in its rulings. When you contemplate its reports you find them all true, and this is truthfulness in reports. Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice. None can alter His words, and He is the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ [al-An'am 115].

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided for them secretly and publicly, hope for a commerce that will never perish﴾ [Fatir 29]. Have we taken up the discussion of it?

﴿confirming what is before it﴾ [Fatir 31]. His saying ﴿confirming what is before it﴾: the author said: (what came before it of the scriptures), meaning confirming what came before it of the scriptures, because the scriptures that preceded it are "before it" (bayna yadayhi). Do you not see that a man who is in front of you has gone ahead, and you say "the man is before me" (bayni)? Sometimes "ma bayna al-yadayn" is said of the future too, because it is also in front of you, as in His saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾ [al-Baqarah 255], meaning their future and their past.

His saying ﴿confirming what is before it﴾: the manner in which it confirms the earlier scriptures is in two ways.

The first way: it affirmed them, that is, it established that they are true. The Qur'an confirms the authenticity of the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and other scriptures, and shows that they are true.

Likewise, the second way: ﴿confirming what is before it﴾ because the earlier scriptures foretold it, so its descent is a confirmation of them. So it confirms what is before it in two ways. The first: that it confirms what preceded it, that is, it said that they are true and established scriptures, and it made belief in them obligatory. The second: that it confirms what they foretold, that is, it descended in conformity with what they foretold, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the former peoples﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 196]. The Qur'an. "Zubur al-awwalin" means their scriptures, meaning that it exists in their scriptures and that it would be sent down, just as Muhammad ﷺ was likewise covenanted upon every prophet that they would believe in him. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And [mention] when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I give you of Scripture and wisdom and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him." He said, "Do you affirm and accept My commitment on this?" They said, "We affirm it"﴾ [Ali 'Imran 81]. The point is that its confirmation of what is before it is in two ways.

He says: ﴿confirming what is before it. Indeed Allah is, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾ [Fatir 31] (knowing of the hidden and the apparent). The connection of this sentence to what precedes it is that it conveys warning, admonition and encouragement. It is both encouragement and warning, because when He informed that this Qur'an is the truth, people divided regarding this truth into two groups: a group that believed in it and a group that rejected it. Is that not so?

To all of these we say: Allah, the Exalted, is Acquainted with you and Seeing. Those who believed in it, their belief and their action in accordance with what it brought will not be lost, because Allah is Acquainted with it and Seeing of it, and He will reward them for it. Those who denied it, their condition will also not be hidden from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and He will punish them according to what their denial, rejection and arrogance require. So the sentence, in relation to those who believe in this Qur'an, is good news, and in relation to those who deny it, is warning and admonition.

His saying ﴿Acquainted and Seeing﴾: ("khabir") is an active participle in the intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha). If you wish, say that it is a resembling attribute (sifah mushabbahah). The second is better when it relates to knowledge. The best thing to say about this is that it is from the category of the resembling attribute. Why? Because the resembling attribute indicates permanence, whereas the intensive form may indicate occurrence, and the occurrence of acquaintance in relation to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is impossible, is it not? The occurrence of acquaintance is impossible, because He has always been and will always be Acquainted.

So we return and say: it is necessary to make "khabir" a resembling attribute, because if we made it an intensive form from "khabara" it would give the false impression of renewed acquaintance and knowledge, and this is impossible with respect to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

His saying ﴿Seeing﴾: the word "basir" may be meant to indicate knowledge, and it may be meant to indicate perception by sight, and both meanings do not contradict one another. It has passed with us in the principles of tafsir that if a verse may bear two meanings that do not contradict each other, it is interpreted by both, because that is broader in its meaning and more eloquent. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is Seeing of His servants in terms of looking and sight, and in terms of knowledge. In regard to the apparent objects of perception, there is both sight and knowledge; in regard to things heard, there is knowledge: ﴿Indeed Allah is, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen of Our servants﴾ [Fatir 32]. ﴿We caused to inherit the Book those who﴾: first, the word "awratha" (caused to inherit) here governs two objects. Were their original forms a subject and predicate or not? They were not originally a subject and predicate, and on this basis it belongs to the pattern of "kasa" (clothed) and "a'ta" (gave). Where is the first object and where is the second? In ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen of Our servants﴾, "alladhina" (those who) is the first, and "al-Kitab" (the Book) is the second. Because who is the inheritor? Is the Book the inheritor of those, or are those the ones who inherited the Book? Those are the ones who inherited the Book. That is, We caused those whom We have chosen of Our servants to inherit the Book. And what is the meaning of "awrathnahum iyyahu" (We caused them to inherit it)? It means: We made them its inheritors. So those whom Allah chose, Allah caused them to inherit the Book, that is, He made them inheritors of it.

As for the word "al-Kitab": the author said (the Qur'an), but we should make it more general, because if we said that "the Book" is the Qur'an, and we said that it was inherited from those who came before us, then the Qur'an would have been sent down to those who came before us, and that is not the case. So what is meant by "al-Kitab" here is the genus, not the Qur'an specifically. That is, all the good that is in the earlier scriptures is present in the Qur'an. So we have inherited from those before us everything of good that they were given. The foundations that are obligatory upon every Muslim in every place and time are present in the Qur'an, but the laws that differ according to nations, and according to time and place, these differ from those who came before us. Something may be obligatory upon us that was not obligatory upon them, and something may be forbidden to us that was not forbidden to them: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'ida 48]. As for the foundations, we have inherited them from those before us. So the foundations, which are the mother of the religion, we have inherited from those who came before us.

He says: ﴿those whom We have chosen of Our servants﴾ [Fatir 32]. ﴿Those whom We have chosen﴾ means We chose. It is derived from "al-safwa" (the choice part), and its original form is "istafaynā" (istaftaynā), but for a morphological reason the "t" was changed to "ṭ", so it became ﴿We have chosen﴾, meaning We chose them.

His saying ﴿of Our servants﴾: does the term mean general servanthood or specific servanthood?

Student: Specific.

Shaykh: That is, those whom We chose from among the believers, or whom We chose from all the servants? It appears that it is general servanthood, meaning those whom Allah, the Exalted, chose from among His servants who submit to Him in the universal sense (kawnan). By them is meant this nation, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿You are the best nation produced for mankind﴾ [Ali 'Imran 110]. So those whom Allah chose from among His servants are this nation, by the verse we have cited, which is in Al 'Imran, and by another proof from this very verse itself, because this nation is the last of the nations. Therefore it is not possible that what they have of the Book be inherited by others. They are inheritors, not those from whom inheritance is taken. If they are inheritors and not those from whom inheritance is taken, then they are the ones who were chosen.

His saying ﴿So among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ [Fatir 32] (by falling short in acting upon it), that is, by the Book, ﴿and among them is one who is moderate﴾ (who acts upon it most of the time), ﴿and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ (who adds to the action teaching and guiding to action) ﴿by permission of Allah﴾ [Fatir 32].

Allah, the Exalted, divided this nation that He caused to inherit the Book into three divisions, and He began with the least and then the less: the least in rank and then the less. He said: ﴿So among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir 32]. The one who wrongs himself is the one who has neglected some obligatory duties or committed some prohibited acts. He abandons congregational prayer although it is obligatory upon him, leaves out part of the zakat without paying it, delays the hajj although it is obligatory upon him immediately. This is the one we say wrongs himself. Committing prohibitions: drinking alcohol, fornication, theft, looking with forbidden gaze. This is the one we say wrongs himself.

The original meaning of "zalim" (wrongdoer) is "naqis" (deficient), because injustice (zulm) is deficiency. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Each of the two gardens gave its produce and did not fall short therein at all﴾ [al-Kahf 33], meaning it did not diminish. Everyone who does evil has fallen short in what is obligatory upon him. Therefore every evil deed is considered a deficiency in what is obligatory on you, because what is obligatory upon you toward yourself is to look after it with its due care. You are responsible, and the first thing you will be questioned about is yourself. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed your self has a right over you, and your family has a right over you" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1975) and Muslim (1159/182), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As]. He began with the self. Just as it is obligatory upon you to look after the interests of your child, your wealth and your family, it is obligatory upon you to look after the interest of your own self. Indeed it is the first obligation among the rights of creatures after the right of Allah and His Messenger.

So whoever commits a prohibition has wronged himself, why? Because he has deprived it of its right of trust, since you are entrusted with it and must look after it with its due care. Whoever abandons an obligation has wronged himself, because what is obligatory upon him is to do the obligation in order to fulfil the trust concerning himself. This is the one who wrongs himself. And among them is the moderate one. The moderate one is the one in whom no injustice to himself has occurred and who has not advanced in good. That is, he upholds the obligations and avoids the prohibitions, but he does not increase in voluntary acts, and he is not eager to complete the obligations in the most perfect manner, and he does not avoid the disliked acts.
