Visiting graves is travel on foot: a man goes to the cemetery, stands and looks at these graves and takes a lesson: these people were stronger than him and had more wealth than him, yet they came to what they came to, so that he knows he will come to what they came to, whether the time be long or short.

Therefore, travelling on the earth is by the heart and by the foot. Which is more beneficial for a person, travel by the heart or travel by the foot? Travel by the heart is more comprehensive and easier, because a person can circle the whole world in a single hour, and more easily. Travel by the foot has a stronger effect, because one witnesses it, and "the one who sees is not like the one who hears." For this reason, "the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, when we entered upon the dwellings of those who were punished, ordered that we should not enter except weeping, lest what afflicted them afflict us" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2980/38) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.]], so that we take a lesson and correct our course.

﴿Have they not travelled through the earth﴾: the particle ﴿fi﴾ (in) here, the scholars said, means (upon), and it cannot be for enclosure. Why? Because enclosure requires that the traveller be inside the container, and it is known that one who travels on the earth does not travel inside the earth. Does he dig a tunnel to travel in it? No, he travels on its surface. They said: ﴿fi﴾ means (upon), and a parallel to it is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And I will crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha 71], meaning: upon the trunks of palm trees.

His saying ﴿fi al-ardh (in the earth)﴾ may mean the genus, and may mean a specific known earth (the definite article here, al-). It could be the generic (jinsiyyah) or the specific ('ahdiyyah). On the first, the intended meaning is travel across the genus of earth, both that which was struck by wrath and that which was not. On the second, the intended meaning is the earth that was struck by wrath, so the definite article here is for a mental (dhihni) or mentioned (dhikri) reference? It is a mental reference, because a mentioned reference requires that something mentioned be present to which the article refers; if nothing has been mentioned, it is a mental reference.

As for his saying: ﴿so that they see how was the end of those before them﴾ [Fatir 44]: the fa' here, it is said, is conjunctive, and it is said it is causal. If it is conjunctive, it is in a jussive position, meaning the verb after it is jussive; if it is causal, the verb after it is in the subjunctive. On the causal reading, the sense is: "Have they not travelled through the earth, so that by their travelling they might see." On the conjunctive reading, the sense is: "Have they not travelled through the earth and not seen how was the end of those before them."

Is the seeing here seeing of the heart or seeing of the eye?
* A student: Both.
* The Shaykh: If we say the travelling is travelling on foot, then the seeing is seeing with the eye; if we say the travelling is travelling of the heart, then the seeing is seeing of the heart. So it includes both, according to how we interpret the travelling mentioned earlier.

﴿so that they see how was the end of those before them﴾: this interrogative sentence has suspended (ta'liq) the verb "see" from acting; that is, "so that they see what their end was", meaning what outcome they had: were they given ease and honour, or were they punished and destroyed? Look! When the intelligent person looks, he will take a lesson, and measure the present by the absent.

﴿how was the end﴾: the end (ʿaqibah) of a thing is its outcome. ﴿those before them﴾: what was the end of those before them? Destruction. Their end was destruction. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning, and at night. Will you not then reason?﴾ [As-Saffat 137-138]. Look at their traces: what were they? Ruin. If the ruin and its cause was denial and arrogance, then the cause that led to destruction before will lead to it again afterwards, since there is no difference.

Allah said: ﴿and they were greater than them in strength﴾ [Fatir 44]. (They were): to whom does the pronoun refer? To the earlier ones.

﴿greater than them in strength﴾: that is, stronger than them in might. Yet their strength did not benefit them nor protect them; they were destroyed. Consider the people of 'Ad who said: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15]. What did Allah say? ﴿Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15]. The 'Ad were among the strongest nations in bodies, firmness and resolve, to the point that they challenged, saying: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ Allah said: ﴿Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?﴾ and He destroyed them by the most gentle of things: He destroyed them by wind. Pharaoh said: ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 51], boasting of the flowing of the rivers, which were waters beneath him, and he was destroyed by drowning, by the very water he had boasted of. So the intelligent person, when he sees the state of these nations and their strength, and that this did not benefit them nor protect them from the punishment of Allah, must take a lesson.

He said: ﴿and they were greater than them in strength﴾. The waw here in His saying ﴿and they were﴾ may be conjunctive, and may be for the circumstantial state (hal). The sense: "while they had indeed been greater than them in strength, Allah destroyed them for their denial of their messengers." ﴿And Allah was not one to be frustrated by anything in the heavens or on the earth﴾ [Fatir 44].

Here, if a person reflects on the verse, he says: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, did not mention the end of these deniers in the verse: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth so that they see how was the end of those before them, though they were greater than them in strength?﴾. Why did He not mention it? Relying on this traveller who travels and sees; that is, its meaning is: judge for yourself about these people, and there is no need for me to remind you that Allah destroyed them, because you will judge this from what you see of their traces.

(﴿And Allah was not one to be frustrated by anything﴾ he said: he would precede it and escape it.) ﴿in the heavens or on the earth. Indeed He is ever Knowing, Competent﴾. He said: ﴿And Allah was not one to be frustrated﴾. The lam here the grammarians call the lam of denial (lam al-juhud), which is the negation, because it occurs after it, that is, after a negation. Its rule, the rule of the lam of denial, is that it occurs after a negated state (kawn manfi).

If we want to bring it closer to the beginner, we say: it occurs after (ma kana) or (lam yakun): ﴿Allah would not forgive them﴾ [An-Nisa' 137]. We say the lam is the lam of denial. ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [Al-Anfal 33]; we say the lam is the lam of denial. When the lam occurs after (ma kana) or (lam yakun), attached to a present-tense verb, it puts the verb in the subjunctive, either by itself, as is the view of the Kufans, or by an implied (an) after the lam, according to the disagreement. We only call it the lam of denial, but the rule I stated first, that it occurs after a negated state, is more general than our saying that it follows (ma kana) or (lam yakun). Why is it more general? Because it can come after (ka'in): you say, "I am not about to punish you," for example, or "not about to stand," and so on. So when we say "after a negated state" it is more general; but when addressing a beginner in grammar, he may find the phrase "negated state" hard to grasp, so we tell him: when it occurs after (ma kana) or (lam yakun), it is the lam of denial, and it puts the present verb in the subjunctive, either by itself, as the Kufans hold, or by an implied (an) after the lam.

﴿And Allah was not one to be frustrated by anything﴾: ﴿min﴾ is a superfluous preposition (harf jarr za'id), superfluous in grammar and superfluous in meaning; that is, it adds to the meaning. What is the added meaning? Emphasis of the negation: this negation is emphasised.

As for His saying ﴿to be frustrated by anything﴾: if we say ﴿min﴾ is a superfluous preposition, then we parse ﴿shay'in﴾ (thing) as the subject, in the nominative, marked by a presumed (muqaddarah) damma on what? 
* A student: The ya'.
* The Shaykh: ﴿shay'in﴾ is the subject in the nominative with a presumed damma?
* The student: On the hamzah, on the alif.
* The Shaykh: On the hamzah, on the alif?!
* The student: (...) on the hamzah.
* The Shaykh: On the hamzah?! We do not know of anyone who said "presumed on the hamzah." Who knows the i'rab?
* A student: Presumed on the ya'.
* The Shaykh: Wrong.
* The student: On its last letter.
* The Shaykh: On its last letter.
* The student: Its appearance was prevented by the position being occupied by the vowel of the superfluous preposition.
* The Shaykh: Yes, correct.

﴿from anything in the heavens﴾ [Fatir 44]. The author said: (would precede it and escape it). This is an interpretation, and there is nothing wrong with some of its implications, as the Exalted said: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outrun Us? Evil is what they judge﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 4]. But frustration (al-'ajz) in reality is the lack of ability to do a thing, and this is better than the author's interpretation. You say: Allah the Exalted would not prevent what He wills from happening; there is no frustration in His power, rather He is capable of everything: creating what does not exist, annihilating what exists, changing a state, or other things. Allah the Exalted is not frustrated by anything in the heavens or on the earth, because when He wills a thing His command is to say "Be" and it is, without any effort; one word makes the thing according to His will, may He be blessed and exalted. So nothing frustrates Him in the heavens or on the earth, and if nothing frustrates Him in the heavens or on the earth, then He will not be unable to destroy those who denied the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

He says: (﴿Indeed He is ever Knowing﴾, that is, of all things, ﴿Competent﴾ over them). The sentence's position relative to what precedes it is that it gives the reason for what He said: ﴿And Allah was not one to be frustrated﴾ [Fatir 44]. He gives the reason for this negated ruling by His saying: ﴿Indeed He is ever Knowing, Competent﴾ [Fatir 44]. Knowledge (al-'ilm) is the perception of a thing as it is, and capability (al-qudrah) is the ability to act without incapacity; this is capability, and strength (al-quwwah) is the ability to act without weakness. It is more specific than capability in one respect, and more general in another, as we will mention.

What is the reason that He, the Mighty and Majestic, cannot be frustrated by anything, through His knowledge and His power? Because one who is incapable of a thing is so either because he does not know the causes by which to change it, or because he lacks the power. If you consider the incapacity of any incapable person, you will find that the cause of his incapacity is either that he does not know, or that he does not have the power. If someone were told: "We want you to repair this broken watch," he would say, "Alright, give it to me," and yet he knows nothing at all. Does he have the ability to fix it or not?
* Students: No, he cannot.
* The Shaykh: How can he not? He has tools for the craft, and he has physical strength; can he repair it or not?
* Students: He cannot.
* The Shaykh: Why?
* Students: Because he has no knowledge.
* The Shaykh: Because he has no knowledge, he cannot repair it; he may make it worse.

There is another man who has knowledge, who has studied the science of repairing watches, for example, but he has no physical capacity, being paralysed. Can he repair it? No, he cannot, because of lack of power. So the negation of incapacity from Allah the Mighty and Majestic is because of His perfect knowledge and His perfect power. From this we know that there is no pure negation in the attributes of Allah; rather every negation in the attributes of Allah includes the affirmation of a perfection. A pure negation cannot exist. For this reason, when He negated incapacity, He explained the cause: ﴿Indeed He is ever Knowing, Competent﴾. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Allah, blessed and exalted is He, said: ﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that if a warner came to them, they would surely be better guided than any [other] nation. But when a warner came to them, it increased them not except in aversion﴾ [Fatir 42]. (...)

﴿so that they see how was the end of those before them﴾ [Fatir 44]: what is meant by travelling here? (...).

Travelling on the earth: by the heart and by the foot. The point of the proof is that Allah rebuked those who did not travel on the earth so that they would see how was the end of those before them.

* Among its benefits: we should look at the end of the earlier ones with the gaze of taking a lesson from their outcome when they denied their messengers, and not with admiration for their strength, their craftsmanship, their architecture and similar things. If we apply this to the reality of people today who go to the dwellings of Thamud, we find that they go there not to take a lesson from what Allah did to them as punishment for denying the messengers, but to look at how strong they were, their craftsmanship, their ornaments and similar things. This is forbidden: a person may not go to the dwellings of these deniers for this purpose, because of the saying of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping; if you are not weeping, then do not enter upon them" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2980/38) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.]].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: there are lessons in history by which the intelligent person takes heed, because of His saying: ﴿so that they see how was the end of those before them﴾ [Fatir 44].

* Among the benefits of the verse: the use of a qiyas al-awla (a fortiori argument), because of His saying: ﴿and they were greater than them in strength﴾. If Allah destroyed them although they were stronger than these, then destroying these is all the more fitting.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: no matter how great human strength is, it does not protect them from Allah in anything, because of His saying: ﴿so that they see how was the end of those before them, though they were greater than them in strength﴾ [Fatir 44]. For this reason, when 'Ad said: "Who is mightier than us in strength?" it was said to them: ﴿Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15].

• Among the benefits of this noble verse: traveling through the earth, whether by heart or by foot, is a lesson not only for those to whom the messengers were sent but also for the messengers themselves. The destruction of those who denied the messengers is a victory for whom? For the messengers. It is well known that when God destroys your enemy, it is undoubtedly a victory for you.

• Among the benefits of this noble verse: the negation of incapacity (ʿajz) from God, the Mighty and Majestic, based on His saying: ﴿Nor was God such that anything in the heavens or on the earth could cause Him to fail.﴾ This is because it negates incapacity from Him on account of the perfection of His knowledge and power.

• Among the benefits of this noble verse: some of God's attributes are negative (salbiyyah, i.e., attributes of negation), meaning they are denied of God. The governing principle is that every attribute of deficiency is negated of God, the Mighty and Majestic. This is a general rule, just as every attribute of perfection is affirmed of Him. However, the details require evidence, because this rule is general, based on His saying: ﴿And to God belongs the highest description﴾ [an-Nahl 60] and ﴿And to God belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-Aʿraf 180]. But the determination that a specific attribute is affirmed of God or negated of Him requires evidence.

• Among the benefits of this noble verse: God, glorified and exalted, does not negate anything of Himself except to affirm the perfection of its opposite. Because He said: ﴿Nor was God such that anything could cause Him to fail,﴾ He then said: ﴿Indeed, He is ever Knowing and Competent.﴾ From this it is derived that every attribute negated of God is not intended as mere negation, since mere negation has no benefit. Pure negation is pure nonexistence, and nonexistence is nothing, let alone a perfection. Also, negation may be caused by incapacity, as in the words of the poet:

"A tribe that does not betray a pledge of protection,
and does not wrong people even by the weight of a mustard seed."

Is this praise or blame? It is blame, because due to their incapacity they are unable to wrong people, and they do not betray pledges. Negation may also be caused by the absence of capacity (qabiliyyah) for the attribute, not because of perfection, but because the thing is not capable of that attribute. For example, if you say, "The wall of our house does not wrong," and someone praises his house by saying that its wall does not wrong anyone, is this correct?

• Students: The absence of capacity.

• Shaykh: Yes, it is correct that it does not wrong anyone, but not because it is just, having complete justice. Rather, it is because it cannot accept the word "wrong," so negating it of the wall is like affirming it. Even if you say, "The wall wrongs," no one would believe you.

So God's negated attributes, which scholars call negative attributes, include the perfection of their opposites. That is, because of the perfection of His knowledge and power, nothing in the heavens or on the earth can cause Him to fail.

• Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that there is more than one heaven, as shown by the plural form ﴿the heavens﴾, which are seven according to the text of the Qur'an and the Sunnah (the Prophetic tradition): ﴿Have you not considered how God created seven heavens in layers?﴾ [Nuh 15]. The Sunnah also clearly indicates that there are seven heavens, as in the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "O God, Lord of the seven heavens and what they shade."[1]

• Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of two of God's names, al-ʿAlim (the All-Knowing) and al-Qadir (the All-Powerful), and what they include of an attribute or a ruling. The attribute is knowledge and power, and the ruling is that He knows and has power over everything: ﴿Indeed, He is ever Knowing and Competent.﴾ Then God, exalted, said..

• Student: (...).

• Shaykh: And what?

• Student: Traveling through the earth (...).

• Shaykh: Traveling through the earth for recreation, you mean?

• Student: No, for reflection (...).

• Shaykh: Traveling through the earth for reflection is permissible. If its benefit outweighs its harm, it is praiseworthy. If its harm outweighs its benefit, it is not advisable. For example, if someone goes to contemplate the signs of God in lofty mountains, rivers, seas, and similar things, this is good and praiseworthy. But if it requires expenses greater than what a person benefits from, then it is forbidden, because that is a waste of wealth. However, if the expense is small, or if this man is wealthy and it does not harm him but benefits him in terms of faith, then there is no harm in it.

[1] Narrated by Ibn Khuzaymah in his Sahih (2565) and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih (2709), from the hadith of Suhayb ibn Sinan.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for what they have earned, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single creature moving on it. But He defers them until an appointed term. And when their term comes, indeed Allah is ever, of His servants, Seeing.﴾ [Fatir 45] (Law) here is conditional. (Law) comes as a conditional, as it does here, and it comes to express wishing, like His saying: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam 9]. You say, for example: "If only (law) I had the wealth of so-and-so," meaning: I wish I had the wealth of so-and-so. So it comes as a conditional, it comes to express wishing, and it also comes as a verbal particle (masdariyyah) meaning (an, that).

We have said: it is conditional. When it is conditional, its response is either affirmative or negative. If it is affirmative, the more common usage is to include the lam (of emphasis) in it; if it is negative, the more common usage is to omit the lam. An example of the affirmative is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Had We willed, We would have made it crumbled debris﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 65]. Where is the response? ﴿We would have made it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 65]; the lam is in it. And Allah, exalted is He, said in the same surah: ﴿Had We willed, We would have made it salt water﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 70]; the response is ﴿We made it﴾, and the lam has been omitted from it. As for when its response is negated with (ma), the more common usage is that (ma) is not joined with the lam. So you say, for example: "If there had come to me [someone] whom I did not humiliate." And here Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for what they have earned, He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾ [Fatir 45]. The lam may be joined with (ma), but that is rare, like the saying of the poet:

"And if we were given the choice, we would not have parted..." ........................
The more common form is "ma iftaraqna" (we would not have parted).

Allah, exalted is He, says: (﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task﴾ [Fatir 45] for sins) ﴿for what they have earned, He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾. His saying: ﴿yu'akhidhu﴾ means He punishes; and taking to task for a sin means punishing for it.

His saying: ﴿an-nas﴾ (mankind) is general, including the disbelievers and including the disobedient among the believers. So, if Allah were to take all of mankind to task for what they have earned, He would not leave upon it a single creature.

His saying: ﴿bima kasabu﴾ — (ma) may be a masdariyyah, meaning: "for their earning," and it may be a relative pronoun (mawsulah). If it is a relative pronoun, the returning pronoun must be assumed, and its assumed form is: "for what they earned."

His saying: ﴿bima kasabu﴾ means: for what they have acquired of sins. Allah, exalted is He, called sins "earning" (kasb) because the doer receives their recompense, so it is as if he earned this recompense — though it is an earning that is a loss, not a profitable earning? A losing earning. For this reason, when it is combined with righteous deeds, a different word is used; Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah does not burden...﴾ [al-Baqarah 286] (...)

His saying: (﴿upon it [the earth]﴾ [Fatir 45] means: the earth). How did the author say "(i.e., the earth)" and refer the pronoun to something not mentioned? Some of them said: it refers to something mentioned, namely His saying: ﴿Nor is there anything in the heavens or on the earth that could ever cause Him to fail. Indeed He is ever Knowing and Competent﴾ [Fatir 44]; and the whole discourse is in one context, the context of the disobedient, their end and their punishment, so the speech is of one order, and the earth is therefore mentioned. Others said: it is not mentioned, but it is known from the context, because the creatures are only upon the surface of the earth, so it is known from the context; and what is known from the context does not need an explicit referent. Do you not see His saying: ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad 32]? What is ﴿it was hidden﴾? The sun, although it has not been previously mentioned, but it is known, because it is what hides behind the veil. He says: (﴿upon it, a single creature﴾ — a breathing soul that crawls upon it). ﴿min﴾ is a preposition; is it an extra (ziyadah) or not?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: Because it came after a negation: ﴿not leave upon it a single creature﴾, meaning: he would not leave upon it a creature; but ﴿min﴾ was added to it to emphasize generality.

The author said: (a breathing soul that crawls upon it). The nasmah is every being that breathes, because it is derived from al-nasam, which is breathing, and everything that has a spirit breathes. The meaning is that everything on the earth would perish. As for the disobedient humans, their destruction is clear; as for others, it is by the evil consequence of them: by the evil consequence of the disobedient, these creatures die, either by Allah, mighty and majestic, withholding rain and plants so that these creatures die because they find no sustenance, or they die by plagues that sweep them away because of people's deeds.

Then he said: (﴿But He defers them until an appointed term﴾ — that is, the Day of Resurrection). ﴿But He defers them﴾ means: mankind, and the agent is Allah.

﴿until an appointed term﴾ means: a period. ﴿appointed﴾ means specified. And what is it? The Day of Resurrection, as Allah, blessed and exalted, said in Surah Hud: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed (103). And We do not defer it except for a known term﴾ [Hud 103–104] (...) specified. ﴿an appointed term﴾, specified with whom? With Allah, glorified and exalted; and no one knows this term except Allah, for knowledge of the Hour belongs to none but Allah, glorified and exalted. The most knowledgeable of humans and the most knowledgeable of angels were unable to know it: when Gabriel asked the Prophet ﷺ about the Hour, he said: "The one asked about it is no more knowledgeable than the one asking." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50), and Muslim (9/5), from the hadith of Abdullah, from Abu Hurayrah.] An appointed term must come; everything specified is near, but the undefined term is that which a person awaits until it occurs, whereas the specified term must certainly be reached.

﴿So when their term comes﴾ means: the period has ended and the Day of Resurrection has arrived, whether it is the Greater Resurrection or the Lesser Resurrection. The Greater Resurrection is general for all people, and the Lesser is the death of each person. ﴿indeed Allah is ever, of His servants, Seeing﴾, so He will recompense them for their deeds, rewarding the believers and punishing the disbelievers.

The clause ﴿indeed Allah﴾ is the response of the condition ﴿So when their term comes﴾.

If someone says: what is the connection of the response to the condition, ﴿So when their term comes, indeed Allah is ever, of His servants, Seeing﴾? That is, you might expect: "So when their term comes, Allah punishes them."

It is said: His saying ﴿indeed Allah is ever, of His servants, Seeing﴾ is more eloquent than "when their term comes, Allah punishes them," because some of these people may be pardoned by Allah and not punished; but He mentioned that He is Seeing of their deeds and recompenses them for them, and if He wishes not to punish them, He does so for those who deserve pardon.

* This noble verse contains benefits, among them: the vastness of the forbearance of Allah, glorified and exalted; its aspect is that if He were to take them to task for what they earned, He would not leave a single creature upon it, but He is forbearing, mighty and majestic, and gives respite so that people may repent.

* Among its benefits: the perfection of Allah's power, exalted is He, in that He is able to destroy the world in an instant: ﴿He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾.

* Among them: clarifying the evil consequences of sins, and that they may encompass the sinner and others, indeed the accountable and the unaccountable. Otherwise, these creatures, which are far more numerous than humans and jinn, what is their sin, since they are not accountable? But this is from the evil consequence of sins, that it includes even those who are not accountable.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the refutation of the Jabriyyah, by His saying ﴿for what they have earned﴾, for He affirmed for the servant an earning. The Jabriyyah say that man is compelled to act; he cannot acquire, he is forced to do good or evil.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirming the wisdom of Allah, mighty and majestic, in recompensing workers for their deeds, by His saying ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for what they have earned, He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾ [Fatir 45], but in His forbearance He defers them until an appointed term.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that whatever destructive or diminishing punishment befalls mankind, it is only by what? By what their hands have earned..
